index.html: Welcome to this space that feels a bit out of time, a bit out of the world.​    It's "a bit out of time" because walking for years through mountains, forests, and borders as part of a spiritual practice like pilgrimage connects us more to the present, transforming it into a gift, though it might seem anachronistic in our modern era.    It's "a bit out of the world" because the solitude, silence, and practices of pilgrimage encourage a withdrawal from worldly affairs, yet paradoxically, they anchor us even more deeply in it.I hope you've arrived here after our paths have crossed, but even if not, you are welcome. This blog was created (by my friends, for me) to share my journey with anyone interested in it.Of course, as is often the case, the most important, the most beautiful, the most thrilling aspects of this journey are beyond words—they can't truly be expressed or transmitted. But I hold onto the hope that you might find in my writings a glimpse of what drives a man to leave everything behind and walk the world for years, with a Name on his lips.My name is Emmanuel, and I am a pilgrim.I wish you to be well.I wish you to be happy.
blog/a-pilgrims-trials-and-kindness-alon:
Kindness along the Way


		23/4/2024
	
     ​That morning, I woke up as we all like, after having had a great night's sleep. By that, I mean that the night had passed without me noticing anything. It's interesting, I find, that what defines a good night is that we have seen nothing of it, that we were totally absent from it. So unconscious that we have no idea what happened. And the less we know, the better the night was! I find this very similar to the paradox of the spiritual, which defines that we can access it to the extent that we are not there to do or wish it.     In short, I slept really well. And I knew it because when I woke up, I felt great. Everything seemed to be heading towards a good day. I stretched, watching the sun rise. It was good. I don't know about you, but here we went from the intense cold of winter to the heat of summer without any transition. Within three days, the snow had melted, and it was 25 degrees Celsius. I folded my tent and repacked my backpack like every morning I walk, while enjoying the song of the birds already back. And I set off.     In the first village that I passed, a small, very small church was there. I was heading there to enter, but as often, it was closed. As I sat on the few steps of its entrance, through the window of the house next door, someone was waving at me. A sign that I translated by deduction from the situation as: don't move, we'll bring you the keys. And in fact, a gentleman was already approaching me. After the usual introductions, Petrus introduced me to this church, almost a chapel in size, then left me the keys and told me to come and have breakfast when I had finished and closed the door.     An hour later, I was welcomed by the whole family present: the grandfather, the grandmother, the son who is also the village priest, officiating in the other much larger church which he immediately offered me to also visit after eating. There were also the two small children. My host called a friend who told me he was speaking French. Five minutes later, we were all around a bottle of Palinka, a glass in hand, chatting in French/English/Romanian, while the meal was cooked. Marius, who came down from his pastures especially for this, actually has very good French, a little rusty from lack of practice but good enough to have a good discussion. I then visited the farm, stopped by to see cows, goats, dogs, cats... and as the morning began to end, Petrus and his father had to be gone for half an hour, so I stayed waiting, taking advantage of the opportunity to recharge the batteries and use the Wi-Fi.     I was planning my route a bit to go to the next big city where I planned to receive a package from France. As my bank card was soon to expire, I had to receive a new one, and I took advantage of this necessity to receive other materials. It's a bit complicated to organize all this when you're traveling. But I had already crossed the town in question a few months ago before heading into the north-northeast of Romania, and so I contacted a guesthouse that I knew there to ask them to receive the package for me so that I only had to pass by to collect it... Everything is in the timing...     The idea being to spend as little time as possible in the city because the city is expensive for the pilgrim's budget, and also because after so much time alone in the mountains or forests, the city, with its agitation, its smells, its noises, becomes for me a place of passage more than of stay... But having to pass there, I intended to optimize the opportunity by taking advantage of the shops to buy clothing items which deteriorate so quickly, and to find a dry cleaner where I could have my down sleeping bag washed. Natural goose down requires special dry washing and many hours of drying to achieve satisfactory results. Impossible to do it in the washing machine at home...    And then Petrus came back, and we went to the main church. He had to stop at the village grocery store to get the keys, which was a good thing because I needed to restock the food box in my bag. While he went about his business with the shopkeeper, I did my shopping. When it was time to pay, the shopkeeper refused my money and told me that she was offering me the whole thing: a piece of bread, a few tomatoes, bananas, a tin box of flageolets, one of vegetable pâté, a piece of cheese, and a bar of chocolate.     The church opposite is tall and narrow. We went up to its bell tower to see the bells, of course, but also the view. Then Petrus left me the keys and told me to join him at home when I was done. I usually take my time in churches, as in places that make you want to sit quietly and close your eyes (without sleeping).     I finally went back to get my bag, say goodbye, and thank everyone who had so kindly welcomed me. I was, of course, invited to stay the night or longer if I wanted. Marius, who had also returned, invited me to come and see his flock. But it was still early in the afternoon, and I felt good about continuing on my way. So I took the stick (Spine) and the bag (Expiation) and got back on my way.   The small village was spread out in length. Towards its end, particular smells came to my nostrils, and I suspected their origins. Someone was distilling nearby, I was sure. I looked around as I walked for clues—smoke, for example, or a stream of fresh water. But I didn’t have to look for long because, just on the side of my path, I passed in front of a small hut where some people were busy while others chatted around a table with many glasses, looking at the hearth full of flames under an alembic.     As I passed, Valentin, the boiler, was going out to get wood from the customer’s trailer, which was filled with two large barrels and all kinds of pieces of wood: old boards, pieces of furniture, and a few logs. I was very happy to be invited inside, because the atmosphere was good, but also because I was really curious about the process.     The small room was divided into two areas. On one side, the alembic was embedded in masonry with the hearth below. A notched wheel, a steering wheel, and a connecting rod turned the scraper paddles inside the copper tank to prevent the heated contents from burning. Nearby was a large water tank where the arm of the alembic was immersed to cool the alcoholic vapors.     And then there was the friendly corner, just at the entrance: a table, a sofa, some chairs, lots of drinks, dry sausage, not-so-dry sausages, bacon, cold cuts, bread, a few bottles, and a wire hanging from the ceiling with a light bulb at the end above it all.     I stood there asking all the questions I had. I had a lot of them, and Valentin patiently answered everything whenever his occupation as a distiller allowed. He also managed to balance this with chatting with the many people who stopped by. It was a real hub of village life. When the door was open and the street glowed red from the fire, people clearly knew it was a good time to stop in for a drink, a bite to eat, and a chat.    The cars stopped and started again. There were bursts of laughter and loud voices. Valentin, though the host, never lost his concentration. Even while participating in the discussions, welcoming everyone, and offering glasses of little plum, little cherry, little mirabelle plum, or little house cognac—you see the scene—he never stopped monitoring his still. If everything looked like a good time, he was still very much at work. Adding a piece of wood from time to time, he told me the temperature must be gentle and constant. The slowness allows the aromas to develop, it seems. Judging by what I tasted, for sure, the guy was bringing out the aromas.     I stayed to watch the first distillation come out. In this case, it was from 250 liters of grapes from the customer’s garden.     When finished, in addition to seeing the process of emptying the tank and filling the distillate for the second distillation (to rise to 54 degrees of alcohol), I wanted to see the alembic emptied, to see the copper, and to observe the paddles that scrape its bottom while rotating. In short, I was curious. It was then that Valentin's wife, who lives across the street, offered me a shower. A hot shower! The pilgrim never refuses a shower, because a hot shower is not only refreshing but also unpredictable—you never know when the next one will be. And then, coming out all clean, she offered to wash my clothes as well, using the neighbor's washing machine. Valentin suggested that I stay the night so I could see and taste the finished product while allowing my laundry to dry.     So, I spent the evening at their place—a beautiful Tzigane family, full of colors. Tzigane, yes, a word I was warned against because it is considered discriminatory. Tzigane means gypsy in the Gypsy language, but as I've learned multiple times, it’s a term used with pride within their own community. "We are Gypsies; we call ourselves Gypsies. The term Rroms, with two Rs, is a government policy term that we never use among ourselves," Valentin explained to me. I must admit, the relational dynamics between "gypsies" and sedentary people, between Roms and Rroms, escape me. The more I discover, the less I understand.     On several occasions, I heard the term Gadjo Dilo used for me, pronounced with kindness and laughter. I understood the reference to the French film about a young Frenchman (Romain Duris, I think) traveling through Romania in search of Gypsy musicians. I vaguely remember the film, but one scene where the character cleans his host’s house while they are away stayed in my memory and made me laugh, as it did Valentin when I recounted it.     Finally, the last drop of the distillation finished falling. We filled cans with the finished product. The customer was happy and left, even though he could have slept in his car for a few hours before driving—but, well.    I spent a wonderful evening at Valentin's table. His house was as welcoming as his distillery, with many people coming and going. Neighbors, family—up to 18 of us gathered at one point before I finally retired to bed. In the morning, the silence contrasted sharply with the previous night. I hurried to drink the coffee that had just been offered because I wanted to go to church. It was Sunday morning, and Petrus was officiating. I had sent him a message the night before, explaining that I hadn’t managed to leave the village and, despite telling him I planned to continue, I had ended up staying at someone else’s house just 400 meters away. I never know how things will turn out, but so far, they always go well.     I stayed in the church for four hours, meditating gently while the service was conducted. Long ago, I abandoned the idea of trying to follow what was happening—the language isn’t mine, and the liturgical traditions are different from those in which I grew up. Instead, I used the fervent atmosphere to deepen my meditation.     At the church exit, after greeting and chatting with Petrus, someone offered me a large loaf of bread—special Lenten bread for the pre-Easter fasting period. Then a gentleman approached, saying he had noticed me during the morning, absorbed in stillness. He invited me to his house for lunch, and it was hard to refuse. I agreed, but only after attending a blessing ceremony for a newly furnished room in a house opposite the church, where I had been invited.     I had attended similar ceremonies in other traditions but never among Orthodox Christians, so I was curious. The ceremony was brief, and I stayed longer because the daughter of the homeowner spoke French. She was happy to practice a little and asked about my journey. We chatted around the buffet set up for the guests. She was a college professor who also worked in an international call center, hence her proficiency in the language.     Afterward, I went to the shepherd’s house for lunch. It was a simple, rudimentary home. He invited me to stay as long as I wanted—now or when I returned. He was a kind, rustic man who prepared me some farm eggs. We talked about religion, and my pilgrimage resonated deeply with him. He lived with extreme simplicity, and his perspective touched me. He was insistent that I stay, go see his goats (more than a hundred, many of them kids of the year), but I took my leave, eager to walk a bit.    I returned to Valentin's to collect my backpack and resume my journey. But when I arrived, it was a party—loud music, smoking barbecue—the youngest's birthday. Valentin told me I couldn’t leave yet and urged me to stay a little longer. It was only after many toasts and conversations that I managed to leave. By then, the afternoon was already gone, and I laughed as I walked out, realizing it had taken me a day and a half to cover 800 meters! This somewhat answers the frequent question about how many kilometers I travel each day. And still, I could have stayed two weeks if I had wanted to, given how warmly I was invited.     But I am a pilgrim. It’s the path I travel that defines me. I didn’t cover much ground that day. A few hundred meters before the next village, I found a pleasant spot to pitch my tent and quickly fell asleep. The next morning, not feeling well and with a bad headache, I stayed there all day. I left again the following day.     Coming down from my bivouac site, I came across Paul, who was returning from dropping his children off at school. Paul is one of Valentin's neighbors, and we had spent a lot of time talking since he was one of the few at the time who spoke English. He was busy removing the old plaster from his house, right next to Valentin's. During his breaks, he would join us in front of the still.     Surprised to see me again, I explained to him that I hadn’t walked the day before. After some discussion, we went our separate ways. I crossed the village, then the next one, where I saw Valentin leaning against his car, parked on the side of the road. "You were sick! Come to my house! Rest, recover, and then go again!" Valentin, genuinely concerned, took some time to let me leave. I had to explain that it was just a momentary discomfort and that I felt much better after a full day of rest. I truly appreciated his kindness, which went beyond a simple welcome. I don’t know if I can explain it—it feels like there’s something magical in these encounters.    In another village, as I walked on the sidewalk, I found myself next to a little lady carrying a small bag of groceries. We walked at a similar pace, giving each of us time to discreetly observe the other. She must have been around 65 years old and still seemed vigorous. She wore a veil on her head. Then she spoke to me, seemingly curious about what I was doing there. I think she said something about my bag because she used the word "greu" (pronounced gréo), which means heavy—a word I know well. It’s the impression you get when you see my backpack. I often joke that when people ask how much it weighs, I respond that it weighs "too much, and then some."    Walking slowly, I took out my phone to play a short pre-recorded introductory message that explains the essentials in a few moments. She stopped, seemingly shocked. "How long have you been walking?" she asked, using the translator I handed her. "Three and a half years, soon," I replied. The information struck her forcefully, and I saw a wave of emotion cross her face. "But how far will you go?" she asked. I smiled, not quite knowing how to answer, and pointed to my chest with my index finger. "I’m going there," I said. She looked at me and burst into tears.     Thin. I hadn’t expected that. She put her face in her hands and cried. I hesitated, then gently placed my hand on her shoulder, consoling her with soft strokes. We stood there for a few moments. There was something beautiful in the situation—something magical. Her emotion didn’t seem negative; I even sensed a kind of peace. Finally, she smiled, wished me well, and gave me the customary blessing: "May God accompany you." I continued straight, while she turned right. A few hundred meters later, I turned around to look back at her. At the same moment, she turned as well, and from a distance, we waved. It was one of those surreal encounters I experience relatively often.     In the next village, as I arrived at an intersection, a taxi was parked on the shoulder, blocking my pedestrian path. The driver spoke to me, asking where I was going. After a few moments, he invited me to his house for coffee and a break. I got into his taxi, and he assured me he would drop me back at the exact spot so I could say my journey was entirely on foot.     Hari, as he introduced himself, has been a taxi driver since returning to Romania after spending a few years in England working in security to save money. He preferred to return home after saving enough to start his own business—a life path I encounter often here. We talked for two hours over coffee prepared by his wife. He explained that a woman living a few houses down had told him about a stranger in the village. That’s why he came to meet me. It was the lady I had met earlier. He also invited me to stay the night, but I declined. With a few hours of daylight left, I wanted to keep walking. True to his word, Hari dropped me off at the precise spot where we had met, and I continued on my way.     I crossed the village and walked along the road. It was a major road I needed to follow for a little while longer before turning onto less trafficked side roads. Walking there was somewhat unpleasant, but I made good progress. The flat monotony of the path lent itself to inner contemplation. My body was occupied with its routine, leaving my mind free to wander.   Time passes quickly like this, and so does the distance. It's when the body gets tired that I naturally look around for a suitable place to sit down and take a breather. Sitting on a stone at the edge of a small village, a gentleman, alerted by his dog’s incessant barking, came out from his small farm to meet me. After introductions, he asked if I needed anything and offered me milk from his farm. I couldn’t refuse. Fresh, organic milk. He filled a 2.5-liter bottle with milk, rich in flavor and freshly drawn from the tank in his small milking parlor.     This is how surreal the journey becomes—the welcome I receive from the people I meet. It has been like this for more than three years now, and I can continue like this. Every day I walk, and every day I meet people, have these kinds of encounters. I will continue like this.    The next day, at the entrance to a village, I was stopped by a man surrounded by a crowd of children. He was working on the fence of his small plot of land and, as usual, asked what I was doing there. I gave my standard response: pilgrim/French/not understand. Suddenly, I heard a woman’s voice say in French, "Ah, you're French, but what are you doing here? Have you eaten? Come inside the house, sit down." She gave me a plate of soup with a thick, two- or three-centimeter slice of bread that she baked herself in a wood-fired stove. Then the man cooked some potatoes, and we all ate together. This is how I met the family of Arabella, Christian, and their six children. I spent the night at their place.    Two days later, while resting on a bench at the crossroads of a road and a street in a small village, a car stopped next to me. The driver rolled down his window and asked what I was doing there. He spoke both English and French, while his wife next to him spoke fluent German. Within a minute, Eugène, the driver, and his wife Héléna invited me to their home for lunch and a shower. Eugène was the priest of his village, and Héléna was a religious icon painter who had previously been a professional opera singer.    The connection was instant. Eugène invited me to stay in his vacation home, a disused sheepfold in the hills 4 km from his house. He had set it up as a small retirement retreat. It was perfect for me because I could organize the delivery of my package from France to the nearby city and wait until it arrived, aligning my visit with Eugène’s schedule.     I stayed there for three nights. The small wood stove in the room kept me warm. The space was simple: a bed, a table, a chair, a small shelf, and, at the foot of the bed, a piece of furniture with a television. Eugène came to see me every day, sometimes with Héléna, bringing food, sharing a glass of homemade wine, and chatting.    I left with a superb memory of this couple, so evidently in love. Eugène, with his Santa Claus appearance, radiated kindness and honesty. Héléna, older but vibrant and brilliant, exuded the sensitivity and refinement of a true artist. As I left, I thought I could have stayed much longer. Eugène had even invited me to return and live in the sheepfold if I wanted.     At the edge of the village where we had met, in the church where Eugène was officiating that morning and Héléna was singing (I couldn’t miss that), I stopped at the last house. Sitting on a bench against a fence, I pulled out my topographical map to plan my path. I wanted to avoid the main road and noticed a small river flowing in my direction. A dike beside it looked walkable, though its meanders would lengthen my route. Still, it was a better option than dealing with road traffic.   As I sat there, a woman of about 70 emerged from her house. The dogs had, of course, announced my presence. She asked what I was doing there, so I played my pre-recorded introduction. She began to cry. "Oh no," I thought, "there’s nothing sad here." She stood before me, tears streaming down her small face, her gray hair tucked under a loosely tied scarf.    I didn’t know what to do, but a wave of affection for this little lady moved me to act. I gently hugged her and smiled. Then, speaking softly in French, I said a few words—not because she would understand them, but because in that moment, it wasn’t the meaning of the words that mattered, but their tone and timing.     So, the neighbor across the street comes out to ask what's going on. A very recognizable woman in her attire—the tight scarf on her head and the skirt, but above all, the colors. I spend a moment there explaining, discussing, and consoling before embarking on the dike which, according to the map, takes me to the city.     The arrival at Targu Mureș takes place under pouring rain that hasn’t stopped for two days. I go directly to the guesthouse waiting for me. I plan to spend two days there; the package has already arrived, but the letter containing the bank card is late. That gives me time to go wash my sleeping bag.    For this, I head to a dry cleaner in a large shopping mall. Cleaning a natural goose-down sleeping bag requires industrial dry cleaning. Many small dry cleaners are not equipped for this. After dropping it off, I visit the local tourist office to ask for some information, including a dentist's contact. Since I’m in town for a few days, I figure a quick dental check-up wouldn’t hurt. But, as you know, appointments aren’t easy to get quickly. It’s not the Tourist Office’s job to arrange this, but the staff member is helpful and offers to assist. He makes the calls—it’s easier in Romanian—and after a few minutes, the third dentist he contacts gives me an appointment for the next morning at 10 a.m. Miraculous, right?   I go as planned, and to describe the atmosphere that continues to surround me, the dentist refuses to let me pay. I leave with numerous free samples as well.    The next day, I retrieve my sleeping bag. I take the bus and arrive at the dry cleaner’s counter. The lady hands me my bag in a large transparent plastic cover—you know the kind. I’m immediately about to open it, but she stops me. She doesn’t speak English but seems to suggest I don’t need to open it now. Strange... I tell her I have a compression bag for the sleeping bag so it can fit neatly in my backpack with all the straps tightened. Much more practical for the bus. Yet something in her attitude raises my suspicion, so I decide to examine the sleeping bag right away to ensure everything is in order.     Good thing I do! The bag is as dirty as when I brought it in. What’s more, it now has a bad smell—worse than before! So this, I realize, is the reason for her behavior. She didn’t wash the bag—or perhaps she tried, then gave up after seeing how much work it would take. Whatever the case, my sleeping bag is now in worse condition than when I dropped it off.     She insists the smell is normal for goose feathers. But I know my sleeping bag well, having spent over 2,000 nights in it and had it professionally cleaned several times before. I show her the dark marks that prompted me to bring it in for cleaning in the first place. They are still there. She explains they didn’t come out in the wash, even though she “washed it twice to be sure!” I know I’m being scammed. She took the money (cleaning a sleeping bag is generally expensive) and is pretending everything is fine.     Seeing there’s nothing more I can do or say, I resign myself and leave. I won’t be able to take it to another dry cleaner before my departure since I’ll have to leave the city soon. My budget doesn’t allow me to extend my stay in the guesthouse.     Two days later, I left the city and pitched my tent near the river. I got ready to go to bed and climbed into my sleeping bag. I had dried it as best as possible above a radiator in the room I occupied. The smell was still there but slightly diminished. When I brought my feet inside, I felt something unfamiliar. A seam... There was a seam that my feet were rubbing against. Normally, there was none—or rather, the seams were designed to be discreet, both to sight and touch. But here, a new seam was present, on top or in place of the original one. After examining it, I noticed that a roughly made seam, clearly done with a sewing machine, ran along the length of the sleeping bag, cutting through all the compartments containing the precious goose down.     I now understood that the scam wasn’t just the non-cleaning of the bag but the substitution and replacement of the original materials. You have to understand—a high-quality goose-down sleeping bag like this is very, very expensive. To sleep well, even at temperatures as low as -28°C this past winter, or -43°C in the Himalayan mountains, you need a bag you can trust. It can literally save your life.     I had bought mine used from someone who had returned from an expedition to Everest. These days, many people, not necessarily mountaineers, make that climb as part of commercial expeditions. For example, company executives may do it as part of team-building exercises or self-challenging endeavors. Most of them will never undertake such an experience again, and after descending, they resell or give away their equipment. I was fortunate to acquire a sleeping bag like that and used it extensively for over 17 years. The bag had served me well and lost some of its quality over time. I could no longer rely on it for temperatures below -30°C, but for temperatures as low as -25°C or -28°C, with proper clothing, it worked fine.    That night, in addition to the affront and the bad smell, I was cold. It wasn’t even below zero, but I had to wear warm clothes just to sleep. The feeling of having lost a reliable companion of many adventures—the sense that the bag had been desecrated—was painful at first. After some time, I consoled myself by imagining that some child might sleep under a super goose-down quilt next winter. It was just one less attachment for me to let go of.     I share this story because, until now, I’ve only shared the good moments, the meetings, and the behaviors that could belong to the realm of fairy tales. It wouldn’t be honest to represent my story without also sharing the less positive experiences. This is the second time since my departure that I’ve had a bad experience. (The first, which I kept to myself, involved a grocer in a small village refusing to give me the correct change for a bill, claiming it was half its actual value.)    This little misadventure isn’t pleasant, but honestly, compared to the three years I’ve tried to describe (which I can only partially convey despite my lengthy writing efforts), you’ll agree with me that this anecdote is insignificant, right? Or even compared to just the fortnight I told you about before... Or even just today, as I sit in my tent near the river, walking along its bank toward the Lipova Monastery.     Resuming my writing, which dates back a little now, I reflect on the bread that was offered to me at the church yesterday, along with a bottle of liturgical red wine. Another loaf, also offered yesterday by a French-speaking baker in a village I passed through, came with a tour of his bakery, where I recharged my batteries over coffee and homemade tomato juice. A huge piece of goat cheese and hard-boiled eggs came from a shepherd’s wife I met the day before yesterday in the meadow near her village. Her husband had called her to say I was approaching. She gave me coffee, a hot bean soup, sautéed potatoes, and breaded soy patties while the eggs hardened.     Oh, and the rest of the provisions I bought were thanks to the money a kind gentleman had given me. And yes, as I left the village yesterday, a man on a bike handed me a bag containing a jar of zacusca (so delicious!) and a pot of homemade plum jam.      And you know what? I don't know about you, but here it feels like spring—or even summer. So yes, I will have to find a replacement in preparation for next winter, but for now, I don’t really need more than the little I have left. And I have time ahead of me. So everything is fine.     Voilà for the news.     I hope everything is going well for you.     I wish you all the best.     See you soon.     Pretty P.S.:     Two days after this misfortune, Gabriel—whom you know because I described my meeting with him and his shed in the mountains where I had stayed to rest—informed me that the Bucharest mountaineering club had collected money to buy a new sleeping bag so that I can continue to walk. Moving, right?
about.html: My name is Emmanuel. I am originally from France. Since September 26, 2020, I have been on a traditional walking pilgrimage. This means that I follow a set of rules derived from the itinerant monasticism of the Middle Ages, and among others from various traditions where this concept exists. I carry a backpack with a tent and a sleeping bag, some equipment, and travel on foot to all the Marian sites that are indicated to me along the way.     To date, I have walked more than 8,385 km, crossing France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia from east to west, then Lithuania and Poland again, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, and Romania, where I am currently.     I visit monasteries, basilicas, and sanctuaries dedicated to Mary. My approach is spiritual and has a religious aspect, but I would need to explain it in more detail. I will do so on my blog. The journey is mostly internal; the quest lies in the path that teaches me, transforms me, shapes me. The journey through hills and valleys is its support. The destination serves as motivation.     From a personal standpoint, the experience is magnificent and powerful. I immerse myself in it as deeply as possible, with the uninterrupted duration of the practice helping in this. I have discovered that freedom and happiness are not found but learned.​I work on it with all my heart.     I share as best I can with the people I meet along the way, ever since I left. This is the best I have to offer. And because I perceive a thirst, a craving in those I meet, I feel it is my duty as a pilgrim to give back what I receive by taking the time to answer questions and describe my path.     For the inner journey, most of it is ineffable. When it can be spoken, it's often inaudible... so I keep it to myself, as each spiritual experience must be, to incubate internally. Each person may eventually perceive something through my writings. That would be wonderful.     I wish you well-being and happiness.
blog/aglona/index.html:
Aglona


		17/8/2021
	
      Hello to everyone,      It’s time to move on.     The festival here in Aglona has ended.   It was huge, and even though far fewer people came this year, the entire event was still impressive. Security was tight, with police, the army, secret services, TV, radio, journalists, and everything else you'd expect from a festival important enough to draw the country’s president and many VIPs.     One of the most special parts was the choir singing every day for a week beforehand. Even if you’re not a fan of religious music, hearing those voices live, right in front of you, is deeply moving.    The last two days were crowded and busy, especially Sunday from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., but just two hours after it ended, the entire place was empty. All the cars and buses were gone, military tents dismantled, civil security tents packed away, cameras, sound systems, and lights all removed, food trucks vanished. Everything became quiet again.    I spent the next day organizing myself—saying goodbye to the priests who so kindly welcomed me, buying food for my journey, washing my clothes, and enjoying a hot shower in the monastery to be fresh and ready to leave in the morning.     Aglona, in Latvia, is a beautiful place. There’s a Basilica dedicated to Maria, set in the middle of a lovely park with a lake and a spring. The water from the spring is so good—really fresh, not cold, but refreshing and soft, with a great taste. I drink far more than I need every time I go to fill my bottle. It’s that nice. Of course, I’m not the only one. One of the priests, smiling, told me there are more people coming to fill their bottles at the spring than there are visiting the Maria icon! But since the spring is sacred and said to be miraculous, it’s all good.     The journey here was, as always, wonderful. I met kind people (including a truly sweet dog who welcomed me in such a heartwarming way. She barked, yapped, and moaned the way dogs do when they’re happy to see someone. It felt like I was her master returning after a long absence. She moved me deeply with her softness and gentleness, and we walked together for two hours before she returned home. Such a beautiful encounter).    I was also invited to stay for two days in a small town just after crossing the border. It was amazing to have warm, homemade meals prepared by my host, who said she wanted me to feel at home—and I did. She was such a lovely person, a former doctor in epidemiology for 16 years before working at customs. You can imagine how fascinating our conversations were!     This has been a truly wonderful time.     But you might get bored if I describe again how wonderful it is to walk through unknown places and feel so welcomed. So I think I’ll skip that part...    Instead, I’ll tell you about my plans for what’s next: I plan to wait until this evening to decide where I’ll go next.    Let me explain, because I get this question a lot. I always focus on my destination, and only my destination, until I finish my visit to that place I set out to reach. I stay dedicated to it, fully immersed in the experience. Then (and here’s a playful word twist—“end/and”), once the visit is over, I decide what’s next.    This approach gives me the freedom to wait until the last moment. Maybe someone will suggest a beautiful place nearby that I hadn’t considered. In that case, I can make it my next destination. If no one suggests anything, I have a few ideas in mind and choose one based on logic and my current location.    This creates a very satisfying sense of liberty. It feels like everything is open and possible, that I don’t even have to think about it until the last moment, and then it can be anything. It feels good. Simple. And once the choice is made, it becomes my goal. I don’t care how long it will take, or what the exact path will be. I just go. I put one foot in front of the other and repeat, repeat, repeat. Whatever I’m meant to see, I’ll see. Whoever I’m meant to meet, I’ll meet. Whatever challenges arise, I’ll face them. And here’s something I can assure you: I’m confident that everything will turn out fine.    Confidence is a delicious warmth, and my experiences over these past 11 months have given me that—a warm and fulfilling confidence that everything is and will be good.    Isn’t it beautiful to live this way, especially in these times? I wish I could share the feeling with you more fully, but words seem so weak compared to what I feel.    I wish you happiness and well-being.    Happiness is a duty—our first duty!    Sincerely,    Emmanuel    Post scriptum:    You know what? Last week, I found around 700 grams of chanterelles (Cantharellus cibarius or girolles in French). They were so tasty! We ate them together—four people who had invited me to share their meal by the lakeside. It was perfect because I had no way to cook them, and they had everything needed. They seemed to love mushrooms as much as I do, and they knew that the first chanterelles of the year are especially delicious.     But that’s not even the best news. Okay, let’s agree that’s great news. But the better news is this: just before I arrived in Aglona, I found a Boletus edulis. A small one, shaped like a champagne cork. I left it there because it was all alone, hoping it will grow into a big family. But do you see my point? It’s mid-August, and there are already Boletus edulis popping up—not even in the woods, but right in the middle of the path! If that’s not a sign of good things in life, I don’t know what is.    Post scriptum 2:   I’m now headed toward Šiluvos atlaidai in Lithuania, west-southwest from where I am. On the way—about 50 km from my destination—I plan to visit the Hill of Crosses, which has caught my interest.   I left Aglona after lunch today, walking until a heavy rain came down, forcing me to stop. I pitched my tent and tried to “dry” whatever I had on me. I’ll start again tomorrow!
blog/accident/index.html:
Accident


		28/8/2023
	
     The story I’m about to tell you made me cry—really cry—hot and heavy tears for over an hour. Yet, I’m pretty sure you’ll laugh...    Life in the tent is punctuated by rituals. Unpacking and repacking your backpack every day, without forgetting anything and ensuring that everything is properly placed, requires it. Every item comes out of the bag, goes into the tent, and then back into the bag again.     I sleep on the right side. Nothing to do with the “right side of the bed” couples talk about—it’s simply that the zipper of the tent entrance, which is a mosquito net, makes it more convenient to be on this side rather than 30 cm further.     My half-full backpack, stuffed with winter clothes, is to my left, level with my thigh. It fits well in that spot, as long as it’s positioned slightly at an angle and, importantly, with the straps facing me. This way, the rounded part of the bag aligns with the tent floor without pressing against the tent wall. The goal is to avoid contact between the tent fabric and the double roof. If the two fabrics touch and it rains, capillary action will cause water to seep through. We don’t want that.    This bag position also allows easy access to the two belt pockets on the backpack and the anti-bear spray, which is fixed midway up in a pocket I designed myself on the shoulder strap. It’s pointless to keep a spray at the bottom of the bag. If needed, you can ask a bear to wait a minute—but I assure you, it’s completely useless.     Near my left arm are two waterproof (well, nearly waterproof) boxes I use to store food. These prevent any leaks from finding their way onto my sleeping bag. I’m sure you get the idea.     At the level of my head, in the corner, are my water bottles and canteens. Finally, at my feet, I store items that I won’t need in the evening: the compression sack for the sleeping bag, my hat...     In the tent’s awning, my shoes are placed at the top right. The left side has an elastic band used to roll up and secure the door when it’s open. However, when it rains, the seam of this elastic slowly lets water in. It drips—not much, but enough that if a shoe is left there overnight, it might be filled with water by morning. We definitely don’t want that.   To the left of the awning is where I place rubbish—paper, plastic, and similar items—until morning, when I collect it all to throw into the first trash bin I find.    Then there’s a large bottle with a wide neck that I’ve had for a while now. It’s placed on the opposite side of the shoes. I could explain what it’s for, but it’s not essential to the story, and some of you might not be ready for that. Let’s just say that when sleeping in a tent, such a bottle is incredibly handy for men in their fifties who don’t want to waste the hard-earned warmth in their sleeping bags by getting up multiple times during the night...     Why am I telling you all this?     Well, imagine that tonight, as I was turning to adjust my pillow (my jacket and pants rolled up in a very specific way, offering real comfort all night long), I got on all fours on my self-inflating mattress. This mattress, about 3 or 4 cm thick, inflates on its own when unrolled and only requires a few breaths to make it comfortable before closing the valve. It allows you to sleep on damp and cold ground—even on snow or ice, as often happens to me in winter.     And then disaster struck.   From that moment, everything happened quickly—a rapid succession of actions, reactions, questions, decisions, and regrets, all compressed into a few dozen seconds, probably less than a minute.     As I got into position, on all fours, ready to reshape my pillow, I heard a loud Pchiiiittttt and felt a breath of air against my thigh. My first thought was that I had just punctured my mattress with my knee pressing on a sharp stone or thorn. I assumed it was likely a cutting stone because the Pschiiit was powerful, and I felt the air escaping against my skin, indicating a large opening.   Of course, I instinctively shifted and turned around to see what was happening—my first mistake, albeit an understandable one. Anyone would have done the same.    It’s worth noting that this happened in a tent with a roof height of maybe one meter and a ground width of 1.20 meters. As I turned and prepared to inspect the situation, my vision blurred—a kind of cloud was there, as if mist had entered the tent.     And then everything escalated.     I inhaled, and the mist scratched my throat and lungs. Something was very wrong. That’s when I realized what had happened: I had accidentally triggered the bear spray.    Normally, the spray has a safety pin to prevent this from happening. But today, I had walked under many low-hanging branches, and it’s entirely possible that one of them dislodged the pin without me noticing.     I don’t check my gear in the evening anymore. I know it would be more logical to do so—I used to at the beginning of my pilgrimage—but for some time now, after a long day of walking, I’m too exhausted to do anything but lie down and rest. I only check my equipment in the morning. That’s when I inspect for holes in my clothes, loose straps, places that need reinforcing, and, of course, the bear spray—specifically, whether its safety pin is in place. I devote about two evenings a week to equipment maintenance. It’s not as though “we” build solid things these days...     So there I was, turning around, my face in the cloud, breathing in. I told myself, "It itches, but it’s fine... It’s not that strong. I’ll finish this breath, hold it, and go out." I even thought, This spray isn’t very effective. It’s not strong enough to repel a bear determined to steal my cheese.   That was a mistake—an important one. Looking back, I now believe that if you ever find yourself in the same situation, it doesn’t matter whether you’re inhaling or exhaling—just block your breath immediately, wherever it is... for about 40 minutes, at least. If you pass out, even better—it will spare you what’s coming next.    And remember to close your eyes. I almost forgot that part. Closed eyes are better, even if, like me, you think it’s too late. Just close them.     With my breath held, lungs full, and in a high position, I turned around as quickly as I could and felt for the zipper tab. Thankfully, I knew where it was because of practice and the way I position myself in the tent—it’s always in the same spot. That was fortunate, because by this time, my eyes were blurred with tears beginning to form. But my eyes weren’t the main issue—it was my throat.     My throat itched severely, burning like hell (if you’ll allow the comparison). It was awful. Then I started coughing, which didn’t help me open the mosquito net, let alone hold my breath. Every cough required me to inhale, which was both inevitable and excruciating.     I managed to reach the main opening in the double roof. It has two zippers that leave the upper central part of the fabric open for ventilation when desired, which I’d left open that night. I plunged my head out into the “fresh” air. I say “fresh” because, with the burning sensation in my throat, it didn’t feel refreshing at all.     Now on my knees in the awning, I found the two zippers and pulled them down simultaneously to close the opening.     The coughing became violent. It felt like I was about to cough my lungs out. I wished my throat would simply cease to exist. My face, hands, and thigh burned like I’d received four overlapping sunburns all at once.    I was terrified of vomiting. I had to concentrate hard to prevent it—not just because of the cleanup that would follow, but also because the combination of coughing, extreme difficulty in breathing, and vomiting could be dangerous, even suffocating.    I manage to extract myself from the tent, crawling on all fours. I move about ten meters away and collapse there, feeling like I might die—or almost. Suffocation... Violent coughing, my eyes streaming, my nose running, my mouth burning, and saliva dripping onto the ground. I can only breathe in short, jerky gasps, focusing intensely on calming myself enough to get some oxygen. Oxygen is important, after all...    And then the burning starts. It was already burning, but now it intensifies. It rises and rises, building even more. Touching the affected areas is a serious mistake—don’t do it. Don’t touch. Must not touch. I’m pretty sure it’s swelling too. I have to wait... 10 minutes... 20 minutes... 30 minutes...     Finally, it starts to subside. And that’s when I have the worst good idea of the year.    I’m camped next to a water source. It’s great to have running water when you’re sleeping in a tent. Spring water means freshness. Really fresh, even cold. With the burning sensation, you can imagine the allure, the temptation. It’s like a jug of lemonade with ice cubes clinking in front of someone lost in the Sahara! Or like a Coulommiers cheese on a table in front of a homesick Norman expat! Or a basket of chanterelles in front of... well, you get the point.     I stand up and walk past the tent to grab the tea towel/handkerchief/cleaning rag drying on top of it. I’m already imagining the bliss of a cloth soaked in clear, fresh water, gently placed on my burning skin. I even wonder if it will make a sizzling sound, like water hitting a hot pan, when I put it over my face.    Bitter mistake. The cold relief never comes. At first, it seems fine—good, even. But no. It’s a mirage. Placebo effect. The burning sensation returns, worse than before. But not immediately! No, it gives you just enough time to wet all the affected areas you thought would be soothed. And then, it hits. Too late, though—you’ve already committed. And now you’re crying again...     Anyway, I’ve just endured two truly painful hours, and now I’m waiting for the right moment to go back into the tent and try to sleep. Meanwhile, I’m wondering what I’ll do if I don’t find the spray’s safety pin. The chances of finding it are slim, but I have hope because one of the spots where the branches rubbed against my gear is just above the spring near where I set up camp. Maybe, with a little luck...     Et voilà.    This, along with the time my tent flooded a few months ago, will definitely remain one of the most ridiculous experiences I’ve had on this pilgrimage. Definitely. But this one is already funny, in hindsight. So everything is fine... no real harm done.      See you soon.      I wish you all well and happy...     P.S. 1: Do not try to reproduce this experience at home. I want to clarify that this was done by an experienced moron—I mean, an experienced and over-trained pilgrim. A professional.      P.S. 2: I may send a review to the tent manufacturer:      VENTILATION: Tested bear spray indoors and nearly died. 0/10.     By the way, if there’s a lawyer among you, I wonder if there’s a way to sue. At no point in the instructions does it say the spray shouldn’t be used alone in the evening in your tent!     P.S. 3: I’m kidding, of course. No need to send me legal advice! I mention this more for those who are worried about the NSA and Chinese spies.     P.S. 4: Ah yes! On another note, I need to digress: the secret code/password thing seems to have confused a lot of you, and I’m sorry for that. It was just a way for me to measure how much of my messages were being read. By asking the reader to reply with a password in their next message, I could be fairly certain they had read the text to the end.     So don’t worry if you didn’t know what to put—your confusion was as much proof of reading as the best of codes. (Some of my favorites were: “GTOULU” (French phonetic for "IReadAll"), “Draculement,” and “AZERTY734”...) The NSA has nothing to do with it. No need for tinfoil hats; the Chinese hear perfectly fine anyway.   P.S. 5: Speaking of paranoia—I think I heard the bears laughing at me in the distance. They probably smelled what had happened (they can detect an animal carcass 35 km away and go straight to it) and likely heard me coughing my lungs out. I imagine that in the local dens, the story will now be told by mother bears to their cubs to help them fall asleep for hibernation.     I can even picture two bears meeting, one standing on its hind legs with one paw on a tree and the other clutching its stomach, recounting the tale of the pilgrim gassed in his tent to another bear lying on the ground, hitting the dirt with its paw in laughter.     That thought makes me smile... but I think I was already asleep by then.     P.S. 6: I’ve totally broken my postscript record!
blog/arrival-in-lithuania/index.html:
Arrival in Lithuania


		10/6/2021
	
     ​So, how to say this... I’m a bit shy to share my arrival in Lithuania. I’m afraid you might think I’m exaggerating or embellishing things, or maybe that I ate the wrong mushroom, or even that I’m having some kind of psychological breakdown—I don’t know. But honestly, even I have difficulty believing I’m not dreaming all of this.      It’s been a week now since I arrived in Lithuania, and I have to say, the place I came through is stunning. The northern part of Poland was already breathtaking, with its national parks, wetlands, and all. But once I crossed the border, I’ve been in a kind of ecstasy.     The landscape is overwhelmingly beautiful: vast forests, crystal-clear lakes, and charming little rivers. Seriously, wait until you see the pictures—you’ll understand!     As the weather is clearly turning to summer, the walking can get sweaty. The sun shines brightly from 3:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m., and it’s around 28°C. So yes, it feels hot while walking. But can you imagine? So far, I’ve been able to wash, swim, or splash myself every single day in places so idyllic you’d think they were taken from a summer vacation brochure or a postcard—no, better than postcards! The water is crystal clear and wonderfully refreshing, cool enough to take all the heat out of your body but not so cold as to leave you shivering.     The ground here is mainly sandy, whether on the roads or forest trails. Taking a swim, washing, or rinsing clothes (without soap, of course, to protect the environment—but with fine, soft sand that scrubs gently) has been such a pure pleasure that it fills me with joy. At least, it does for me. These stunning spots are everywhere, as lakes range from several kilometers wide to just a few hundred meters, and I come across one every 5 km at most.     You see?     Now, to complete the picture, imagine the air filled with the scent of pine resin, mixed with the intoxicating fragrances of the season. Every day, I pass dozens of blooming lilacs, carpets of lily of the valley with a scent so strong it’s almost overwhelming, and countless flowering trees, bushes, and meadows. Every open field between forests is covered in flowers!     You might think I’m being overly enthusiastic. But I grew up in the countryside; I know what flowered meadows are. And yet, I’m amazed by what I’m seeing here. Just wait until you see the pictures—really, the whole picture! No wonder the place where I entered Lithuania is a national park and a popular tourist destination for Russians, Belarusians, and Ukrainians.     And the wildlife! The mosquitoes are so in love with French cuisine—utterly enthusiastic about French gastronomy!     And the birds! My God, the birds! There are still swallows here, you know. And robins. And cuckoos. And... well, I’ll stop now. You get the idea.     Now, about the people!    You might think that no country can have it all—the beauty, the landscapes—and also have kind, welcoming people. That would be too much, wouldn’t it? Unfair! Unrealistic! But you’d be completely wrong. Totally wrong.     At first, even I didn’t believe it. After a few encounters, I thought, “This is too much—it can’t be real.” I half expected a hidden camera to pop out or something. But let me give you some examples...     The first village I crossed was a small one, just a few kilometers past the border. I was walking along the road/path out of the forest, taking in the charm of a new country, with a touristy air about me, my nose in the air, admiring the scenery. Most of the houses are made of wood. Many don’t even have fences, and if they do, they’re often beautifully crafted from wood.  The roads are mostly dirt, which means sand—brown sand, yellow sand, black sand... Comfortable for walking, let’s say, but dusty. Only a few are paved, and honestly, that’s nice because cars drive slower (though dustier, too—I just step aside and position myself with the wind to avoid being coated in it).     At a crossroads, a couple about my parents' age called out to me with enthusiastic gestures and started walking through their garden toward me. At that point, I honestly thought I was about to be told I was on a private path or trespassing. But when they reached me, I realized—almost strangely—that they just wanted to say hello, ask who I was, and what I was doing.     I had barely finished saying "Emmanuel" when the woman immediately invited me to come to the veranda for a coffee! Seriously? The whole thing felt surreal—pleasant, but a bit beyond reality in how fast and simply it all happened, completely out of the blue.   I ended up staying with them for maybe two hours, first over coffee, which turned into breakfast, and eventually lunch. But wait—the best part? For the first hour, we couldn’t even communicate properly! They didn’t speak any English or French, and my phone was painfully slow downloading the Lithuanian language set for Google Translate. So you can imagine how tenuous our conversations were. But still, they showed me warm hospitality and genuine kindness. The woman even called her son to help translate a bit. And once the language pack was downloaded, everything became much easier, of course.     When it was time to leave and they were going back to their day, I took the opportunity to sit at their table and repair my shoe. The zipper on the right one had broken an hour earlier, and it took me nearly an hour to sew it securely while my phone charged nearby.     See? A cool arrival and a perfect first contact with the place. I left feeling happy, well-fed, caffeinated—and with a fully charged phone!     Before continuing, please check out the pictures of their place. I mean, come on—what a gorgeous spot! A wooden house flanked by two buildings: one a cute barn and the other a series of stables, chicken coops, and workshops you’d expect to find on a farm. In front of it all was a tiny, picturesque house, and behind, down their backyard, lay a lake. The view was just breathtaking. God... It was a beautiful arrival.     And then I went on my way again, with freshly repaired shoes and a big smile on my face. I walked around the lake for maybe two hours, though I was a little too far to actually see it—remember, the forest?     Suddenly, I heard someone running behind me and calling out. It was a man who had seen me on the road from his house and had run out after me just to chat! We tried to communicate as best as we could, at least enough to establish the basics: that I was a Frenchman who had arrived here on foot, and for him to tell me that it was great! We shook hands, and then he left. I stayed there for a moment, wondering what had just happened.     That day, I kept walking until I arrived at a place that felt like one of those spots where you just drop your backpack, sit down, and stay—quiet and happy. Maybe not for life, but definitely for the rest of the day and for the night!     See the picture! A lovely flat clearing with lush grass, a shore of very fine, smooth sand, a small pontoon, and the lake. It was a free outdoor shower, free laundry, and pure relaxation—all in one spot.     Some people were there too, doing the same as I: enjoying the place. They had come by bike, on foot, or by car from nearby villages or even farther away. A quick splash in the water, a short swim, a bit of friendly chatting—and then, before I knew it, evening came, and they were all gone.     When I arrived, I asked if it was a public spot, free to access, free of charge, and whether it was okay to camp and swim. Of course, they said! "Feel free," they said. "You are welcome." It felt so nice to feel welcome. Really, it felt so nice.     I set up my tent, swam for maybe an hour, washed all my clothes for another hour, hung my clean laundry on a string someone else had stretched between two trees, and then went into my tent and fell asleep like a baby in his loving mother’s arms.     What is wonderful about those places where you sleep is that they are still there in the morning when you wake up!     And the early mornings in those places are spectacular. The loud concert of birds, the soft and warm sunlight filtering through the trees and reflecting on the water, the gentle lapping of the water—it all rocks you and invites you to linger a bit longer in your half-awake dream.     I got up a little later than usual, feeling fully rested and completely relaxed, thinking that place and the last few days had been just perfect. I wished for more, craved more. And I wasn’t disappointed. In fact, it was so perfect that I even began to doubt my experience. I started to think it was just too perfect, that the beautiful encounter I’m about to describe was too good to be real. I mean it—so good, so nice, so human, so rare.    I walked about 3 km to reach the next village and went straight to its center, looking for a church and a shop. I arrived at the church just before ten o’clock and went inside, only to discover it was packed and crowded. Mass was about to start in 20 minutes, so I decided to stay.     It was my first Lithuanian celebration, and I have to say, the priest was really special to me. He smiled a lot, joked with people, and moved from one person to another, seeming genuinely happy to say hello and exchange a few words with each and every one. His way of being was something I found truly rare.     After the mass—though you can imagine how much of it I was actually able to follow—I waited a bit for the crowd to thin out because I needed some space to put my backpack back on. As I was getting ready, a beautiful young lady came straight to me with a preoccupied smile, as though she were deep in thought, making calculations.     She asked if I was a pilgrim and if I knew where I would sleep that night, but before I could say more than "yes," she gently pushed me aside to let someone pass and told me to join her outside. Kornelija—that’s her name—was with her older sister and her mother. She was elegantly dressed in a beautiful summer dress, which she had chosen especially for church that day to please her mother.     I immediately thought of an old French song that goes: "Salade de fruits, jolie, jolie, tu plais a mere, tu plais a mon pere..." But that reference might not mean much to you if you’re not French...    She struck me as a dynamic, beautiful, slender, tall young woman of 28, who could easily be mistaken for 20 when she smiled or for 35 when she thought seriously. She had particularly beautiful, delicate, and slender hands. Her blue eyes sparkled with intelligence, playfulness, and a gentle, soft rebellion. Even though I sensed she could be stern or severe, her warm openness and enthusiasm made it nearly impossible to say anything but "yes" to whatever she asked.     We planned to meet 12 kilometers away, which she estimated would take me about four hours, at her grandmother’s old farm where I could stay, rest, and meet her family, including her brothers. And with that, she said, "See you later," and she was gone...     I went shopping and started my way, which, as she said, would be on the same path leading to her place. I thought of that meeting as another beautiful one.     About half an hour later, as I was leaving the village, a car stopped beside me. She popped out, hugged me, and asked if I wanted them to take my luggage in their car. I politely declined, explaining that I preferred to carry it myself—it’s part of my journey, my karma. She introduced me to her mother, who was driving, got back in the car, and left, waving enthusiastically as they drove off.     I stayed two nights in a beautiful place. The entire family is just incredibly lovely. They are all beautiful—not just physically, but their souls seem to shine a little through them. They have a brilliance about them. And I’m not just talking about Kornelija studying pure mathematics, or her youngest brother studying political science, or the fact that they are all fully fluent in English, Norwegian, and Russian. No, I’m talking about their shiny, smiling eyes that radiate kindness and intelligence.     You know me well enough to understand that I have very little experience with close family dynamics, so I might be easily surprised and impressed—and yes, I absolutely was! But it felt completely legitimate:     They talk to each other! It’s like they genuinely care about what the other says! They hold hands and close their eyes to pray before meals. They smile at each other and hug to say hello or goodbye. They ask their mother for blessings, which she gives by tracing a small cross on their foreheads with her thumb. They care for each other—it’s obvious.     This isn’t my world. I come from somewhere else entirely. But it’s a wonderful world, and they invited me into it so completely, so trustingly, so gently. It felt surreal. It couldn’t be real. And yet it was—for two magical days.     I met everyone I could. We ate flowers and raw food, bathed in the river, and talked for hours. Then we cooked over a wood fire before enjoying a sauna until midnight. A traditional sauna—jumping into the river behind the garden to cool off when it got too hot and sweaty. We covered our bodies in a half-clay, half-vase paste. Only after I’d happily plastered my entire face with it did they tell me how hard it would be to wash off!     And you know what? When it was time for me to leave—remember, I have a rule of staying no more than three days in one place—they half-seriously, half-jokingly invited me to bend my rule and move to the next village to their father’s old house and stay there instead.    When I was finally ready to go, Ignas, the youngest brother, decided to come with me. He packed his camping gear, as well as Kornelija’s, who had left in the morning to meet another brother in the next town. Ignas assured me we absolutely had to meet him before I left. That brother was walking toward us, planning to join us at our campsite for the night.     We met him in the late afternoon and set up camp together. Later that night, Kornelija joined us on her bike after finishing whatever had kept her in town for so long.     We spent the evening and part of the night sitting around a fire, sharing stories and laughter after a lovely dinner.     In the morning, we bathed together in a nearby lake, went to see a farmer to get some "real cheese" for the French guy (me), and said our goodbyes.     Ignas stayed with me the whole day again so we could walk together to the next town and talk along the way.     Now, if I tell you that the town we’re in is one of the most beautiful and peaceful towns I’ve ever seen, would you believe me? It’s surrounded by forest, with forests even in the town center, along with lakes and a river... It’s beautiful and green. You can swim in the lake if you want—it's allowed, and the municipality keeps it clean for that purpose.     We spent the night in his grandmother’s flat since she wasn’t there. And we stayed the next day as well, except for the morning when I got up early to run some errands: getting money, having coffee, taking a little tour of this beautiful town, and shopping for new shorts or trousers because my constant walking had worn them out really fast.    Later, we met again in town, had more coffee, visited a special second-hand shop, and then went to the library to make a kind of paper to show people along my way, introducing myself in Lithuanian. Afterward, we met his cousin and went to a restaurant together, then took a long walk through the town park, talking the entire way. Finally, we returned to the flat, where I am now in bed, ready to sleep and writing this message.     Ignas went out for the evening. I wanted to go to bed early to start my journey early tomorrow. He had some plans to figure out for his next move and the coming weeks. So we said our goodbyes in case I leave tomorrow morning without seeing him again.     Before I leave, I need to switch off the flat’s utilities: turn off the main water tap, take out the trash, close the windows, lock the door, and put the key in the mailbox. Then I’ll go.     I’m alone in the flat of people I only met this past Sunday. And you know what? I already miss them...     Am I just that lucky? Or blessed? Or maybe both? But seriously, think about it: how many people do you know who would give their home for the night to a total stranger who doesn’t even speak their language?     I feel like I’m living in a dream. A beautiful dream. The only way it could get better would be if the mosquitoes became vegetarian!     And honestly, I’m starting to believe it could happen. Why not?

Crossing the Balkans


		11/1/2025
	
     A lot of time has passed since the last update. I had many opportunities to write, but I didn't really feel like I had anything particular to say. So, I didn't.     I could have shared that over the past few months of autumn, I traveled across Serbia, passing through Belgrade and the mountains, receiving a warm welcome everywhere I went. I could have mentioned that this year wasn’t very good for mushroom hunting in the area I visited, as the summer was too hot and dry, and the autumn wasn’t rainy enough to sufficiently moisten the soil for the mycelium to grow. But I didn’t...     I could have used the fourth anniversary of my departure on September 26, 2020, as an occasion to send an update...     Or the milestone of 9,000 km that I reached upon entering Bosnia-Herzegovina, although we all know how imprecise this calculation can be.     I could have mentioned the Christmas celebrations, celebrated at least three times depending on the church, of course...    But no, I wasn't really in the mood, I guess... and I felt it was better not to share than to force myself to write you irrelevant or uninteresting news. Though it doesn't mean that the one I am writing now will be relevant and interesting, but at least it comes from a genuine desire to share, strong enough to make me break my comfortable silence.     I am now in Bosnia and Herzegovina, between the capital of Sarajevo and the town of Mostar, where I am headed. I found a nice route on my maps to get there. A path through the mountains, avoiding the major roads in the valley. I even found a water source along the way, so I could easily get water without having to carry too much. It was perfect—a solid plan! So I set off on that route. It was nice because it took me through all the places where the Olympic Games had been held before. It was strange to cross through them.     The area was beautiful, albeit a bit tough, something like a 1500 m positive elevation change from the capital... You have to know that the mountains are directly around Sarajevo. The Olympic village is maybe 25 km from the center... I had just left this lovely capital when the first snowstorm hit... beautiful.... I had to stop and find a place to pitch my tent because the snowfall was intense. I'm not sure, but I think I wasn't even technically out of the Sarajevo municipality when I pitched my tent on a tiny hill, in the woods, under a heavily cloudy sky and during a thick snow episode... I stayed the next day because it was still heavily snowing, and because why not? 😂.     The next morning, the entire area was covered with a good 50 cm of snow, with all the tree branches around bent under the weight... It was beautiful, magical as only snow can be... It was my Christmas present!     Packing the tent became a bit harder than usual as I first had to clear all the snow around, and also remove the ice from the edge of the tent roof... And then roll the frozen fabric into the bubble I had fixed under my backpack. But I managed it; this wasn’t my first rodeo. I continued on my way uphill... As I was walking on the main road, I wasn't in too much snow. There was about 5 to 10 cm depending on when the last snowplow had passed... It was still snowing, but only lightly. Nothing compared to the past two days... So cars and trucks were going slow. I felt comfortable... My plan through the mountains was good. The entire way was through roads... No paths... So I would be clear to go, as the snow plowing seemed very efficient in the area... And that is the keyword: in the area... Efficient indeed...     So I walked up and up and decided to find a place to pitch the tent again as night falls fast around 4 PM. Knowing that when there's so much snow, you have to dig the place you choose for the tent to fit, but also to have enough room to walk around, you need to count about 1 hour to build your camp... 1 hour of intense work because once the backpack is off your back and on the ground, you don't want to get cold, you don't want to start working in the night, and there is a lot of work to do. First, it's about 3 or 4 m³ of snow to shovel out... without a shovel... I use one of my food containers to do so. That was about when the second snowstorm hit me... which I found totally okay because I was about to finish and ready to get inside. And I did...     The next day, it snowed again and I stayed. The spot I had found was next to the main road. It wasn't really pleasant because of the traffic, but I didn’t have much choice. About 20 meters to the side, there was a flat area, free of trees and just big enough for my tent, but not much more. I think my tent was visible from the road, but only slightly, through some branches covered with snow and only from one specific spot on the road. Motorists would have to be looking sharply in that exact direction and not focusing on their way, and this for about 2 seconds before their view was obstructed by bushes, trees, and snow. But still, at least one person saw me, probably when I was setting up the tent. How do I know? Because at one point, while I was comfortably settled in, a policeman knocked on my tent door. He might have called me from the road, but I had my audio earplugs in as I was listening to a book to drown out the traffic noise. The guy was tense, annoyed... probably because he had to walk the 35-meter path in 60 cm of snow, slalom around trees, following my footsteps to my camp. When I opened the tent and looked out at him, he wasn't really smiling. He was a bit loud, like someone issuing authority orders, and asked me to come to his car. I greeted him with a nice smile (I assume it was nice...), but I added: "Sir, I am in my underwear in my sleeping bag, can't you check my passport here?" He refused. "Get dressed and come down to the road"...     So I did. I took it easy, but really, it’s not that simple when you're in a tent in the cold, dressing again in clothes that are still wet from your day, and getting out. I mean, it’s a pain. You lose the calories you had been conserving in the sleeping bag. You have to gear up again... It's not like just jumping into clothes in a dressing room and going. But I took it easy and went down to the road to meet the guy, managing to keep an authentic smile. I put myself in his shoes, thinking, “What the heck is that?!”    He, with an authoritarian and borderline angry tone, demanded, "Your passport!"    After examining it, he asked, "You are French?"     "Yes, sir," I replied.     "What are you doing here?"    "I am resting, I was tired... I needed to sleep... But when you arrived, I was also listening to an audiobook, so I didn't hear you..."     He cut me off, "Why?"     "Why am I tired?" I asked.     "No, why are you here?" he clarified, slightly annoyed.    "Because it's a reasonably flat and discreet enough place to put the tent. I don't disturb anyone here, it's public, so it's good enough for me... I couldn't find a better spot on the way."     He then cooled down a bit, "It is dangerous, sir..."     "Dangerous? No, it's a safe place... Why? What danger?"     "Sir, it is minus 15°C..."      I smiled, "Exactly! It's not even really cold yet..."     There was a moment of silence.     He looked at me, half amused and half in disbelief. "There are bears and wolves in this area..."     It's possible, but I doubt it... Not many, I'm sure. The bear and wolf threat is often exaggerated to scare tourists. The place isn't really interesting for a bear, even less for a pack of wolves. And even so, I've had my share of bear visits in Romania, Slovakia, and Hungary... I'm not really worried anymore.     "I'll do my best not to disturb them, sir..." But then I smiled and added, "I have bear spray with me."     He handed me back my passport.     "How did you find me? Did you see me from the road? Because I'm pretty well hidden, especially now that the tent is covered by snow..."     "Someone phoned the police station..."    "Really? Phoned for what? I'm doing nothing wrong, I'm respectful of the place and collect all my rubbish... Why would someone complain?"     "Are you used to this?"  I smiled, pretending not to acknowledge that it's kind of uncommon, perhaps even unconventional: "To sleep?"     "To sleep in these conditions?"     "You mean comfortably set up in my tent? Yes, I am. A lot..."     Finally acknowledging that I was not totally naive, incompetent, or unaware, he said, "Ok... You can stay... Have a good night, sir."     "Thank you, sir. And please tell your team that if another one calls to say there is a guy here, just answer: 'Yeah, there is a guy there...'" I continued, mimicking a jaded voice, and pretended to make a distressed call in a panicked voice: "'Yes, but he is in a tent!'" Then, miming the phone to my ear, I responded in the same nonchalant jaded voice: "'Yeah, he's in a tent!' 'But sir, it is highly unusual!' 'Yes, it is. Anything else?'"     At that moment, he laughed... I made him laugh, and it made me very happy... A small success, sometimes delicious!    I walked back to my tent, he returned to his patrol... I am still smiling at that exchange today while writing it...   I slept very well. The morning was sunny, blindingly so, because of the pure white snow everywhere. But it was really comfortable... I packed everything and continued on my way. That day, I planned to cross through a ski resort, perhaps have lunch there in a restaurant to charge my batteries while enjoying a hot meal, and then proceed on the upper mountain road to cross the mountain range. That was the plan... and it went well up until the lunch, the battery recharge, and the hot meal. After that, things got tricky because I learned there was about 2 meters of snow up there. Walking was out of the question, of course, but maybe the roads were okay.     So I went looking for information about the snow conditions on the roads in the upper part and I especially wanted to be sure that all the roads on my itinerary were cleared of snow. But it was really difficult to find anyone who knew. Most people I asked were guessing, answering generally, or not at all. I went to the police, the ski resort staff... I tried anyone I could think of to extract solid information. But I ended up with nothing reliable enough for me to attempt the mountain pass. And it was getting late. So I decided to abandon my plans and head back downhill, on the main road. Not really pleasant, but I had no other choice. Night was falling at 4 PM, and I had to find a hotel for the night. Also, because I would use a lot of internet data to make new plans and chart a new itinerary... and it was not a cheap place, I can tell you that... But again, I didn't have many options.     So, I spent the night in a glorious hotel just for an eye and half a leg (they gave me a generous discount). Refreshed, I set out in the morning, easily heading downhill, pondering a new itinerary that would make me backtrack just a bit before turning west to take a road that would showcase the 1984 Olympic Games installations.     It was a lovely day. The sun shone brightly throughout. The path gently sloped downwards. It was a comfortable walk...
