The Olympic Games installations were a bit disappointing as most of them had simply been left to decay. But I guess it costs a lot to maintain those, and there probably aren't enough people using them... Even the large hotels built to host all the athletes and staff are now crumbling into ruins...   I was truly impressed by the ski jumps. On TV, we're used to seeing those long ski jumps plunging downhill into the void. Watching athletes, half jumping and half flying with their skis slightly opened, bodies straight as ash tree planks, arms at their sides trying to gain aerodynamic lift... it's not that impressive on the screen.    But once you see the installation they're flying from, it's a different story. Just the thought of them jumping, the visualization of them flying—it's genuinely awe-inspiring. It gives you chills... Gone is the thought, "Yeah, I could do that." No. A big no. I wouldn't jump that even if I were paid for it, not even to reclaim the eye and half a leg I'd spent previously.    In the afternoon, around 3 PM, I stumbled upon a small restaurant on the side of the road. There was just a trench in the snow to access it; the snow in the place was about 1.8 meters deep. I paid for a hot meal, charged my batteries for the little I had used during the day, and continued on my way after leaving a few coins and a note from my wallet. The kind owner insisted on giving me two beers to take with me, which he slipped into the pocket of my backpack.    It was getting late, so I walked quickly, my eyes carefully scanning both sides of the road for a potential place to pitch my tent. Roads on mountain slopes aren’t the best for finding camp sites, but I eventually managed one after 3.5 km.    While walking down the main road, I noticed a small road branching off uphill. I followed it and about 100 meters later, in the area between the two roads, I found a flat, tree-free spot big enough to accommodate my tent. It was eight meters from this small road, and the main road was about 40 meters down, mainly below me—so the spot was really quiet and out of view. That was ideal because I wanted to stay two nights there. The second night would be New Year's Eve, and I didn’t want to be in the town 12km down during that time. I don’t enjoy the noisy, hysterical behaviors of New Year's celebrations, especially the crackers and domestic fireworks. The idea of staying comfortably and quietly in my tent was a far better prospect.    I ventured off the small road toward the campsite I had chosen. There was a 1.4-meter-high embankment completely filled with snow, followed by a relatively flat area with about a meter of snow up to the campsite. As I descended the embankment, I slipped and ended up half-sitting in the snow and leaning against the embankment. The snow was fresh and very powdery, and it quickly filled the space where I had just been. The 35 meters to the site were tough to navigate, but I made it. I set my bag down in the snow and sat on it to rest a bit after the strenuous crossing. After choosing the exact spot, I began the laborious task of digging out the snow to clear the ground, moving about 4 cubic meters in total.   This exercise kept me warm as the sun had set for the day, and the snow on my clothes constantly melted, leaving me quite wet. But I successfully cleared the area, ensuring there was enough space to maintain access all around the tent. You know the drill...    Thus, I secured a beautiful and comfortable place to stay for two nights. As expected, I could hear the distant thunderous noise from the town downhill the next night without being disturbed by it.    On my way down after packing up, I stopped at a charming guest house, hoping they had a restaurant—and therefore, hot coffee. It was about 2.5 km from the campsite. It was another very sunny morning, and a couple was outside drinking tea. I joined them at a nearby table and greeted them. Assuming the man was in charge, I asked him for coffee, but it turned out he wasn't the host. They were on holiday with a group of friends from a club, spending a few days celebrating and walking the passable trails. My coffee arrived, and so did the man, Adnan, who sat at the next table. We started chatting about my adventures. After a few questions, he offered me breakfast, and I eagerly accepted. We talked more as I ate.     Then, we moved inside the guest house to use the WiFi and to show him my route on the map. It was so bright outside that it was difficult to see anything on the screen.    Inside, the guest house was cozy and decorated like a museum with old alpinist gear. That's when I realized they were a club of alpinists. And guess what their last destination was? Nepal! Specifically, the Solukhumbu Valley—an area I'm very familiar with, where I've spent a lot of time, made many friends, and created fond memories. So, we had plenty to discuss. Sometimes, the world feels incredibly small...    I spent about an hour and a half at the guest house, chatting and meeting people who were equally interested in my adventure and my spiritual journey.     When it came time to leave, I approached the owner to settle my bill for the coffee and food. As my hand reached for my wallet in my back pocket, Adnan intervened, insisting on covering the cost. His generosity was deeply appreciated, yet little did I know, this gesture would soon be a source of regret. I accepted his kindness graciously.    With my backpack, hat, and gloves, I bid farewell to everyone and resumed my journey. I still had about 8 km to descend into town, and another 2 km to reach a spot I had identified on the map as suitable for setting up camp for the night. My plan was to grab a hot lunch and a few groceries in town before heading straight to the campsite. But things were about to deviate from my plan.   The descent was relatively easy. Going downhill is always easier when the slope is gentle. However, steep descents can be more challenging and hazardous than ascending. Fortunately, the elevation change here was mild, and I reached the town around 1:30 PM. With nightfall not until 4 PM, I felt I had ample time. At the restaurant, the limited vegetarian options led me to choose a vegetable pizza. I sat at a table next to a power outlet, stood up to ask if I could use it to charge my battery, and also inquired if they accepted Visa or only cash. "Cash only," he replied, as was typical in many shops in the country.     Having recently left the capital with enough cash for my mountain crossing—where I expected no ATMs—I reflexively reached for my wallet to confirm I had enough. But my hand met nothing. My wallet wasn't there.    Time seemed to freeze in that instant. Silence enveloped both inside and outside. I was paralyzed by a sudden stillness.    Then, my mind raced wildly, bombarded by a flurry of thoughts—regrets, assumptions, plans, realizations—all at once. Tumultuous.     A bit bordélique, as we would say in France:   Empty back pocket! No wallet. I had no memory of moving the wallet from that pocket to another. How was this possible? Irrelevant! I checked the pocket thoroughly, only to discover a hole at the bottom...     What exactly did I lose? What was inside and how much? No, not now. First, cancel the pizza.     It must have fallen out along my path, likely right after I tore the pocket. But I had no memory of tearing it, nor of any incident that could have caused such damage without my noticing.   I needed to retrace my steps... First, find a place to leave my backpack so I could quickly backtrack...     Cancel the pizza because, as of now, I had no money and no way of getting any for several days...     The embankment, the embankment next to the campsite where I sank into it both ways... My wallet might be there.     Would I have realized if it fell out when I undressed in the tent? Not sure...   When had I last used my wallet? This morning at the guest house, no—they offered me breakfast... But did I reach for my wallet? No, I hadn’t completed the motion.     Cancel the pizza now, Emmanuel! It would only complicate things to order food without the means to pay.      I couldn’t believe it. I had really lost my wallet.      The pocket, the treacherous pocket of my brand-new pants! Traitorous pants!      I needed to go to the police. If I explained everything, they should be able to help me.      But first, stop the pizza order!      Actions, Emmanuel, actions!      I rushed to the counter, called the waiter over, and asked him to cancel the pizza order because I had just realized I lost my wallet. I asked if I could leave my backpack here while I went to the police station. "No problem," he told me, giving me directions to the station just 300 meters away, on the right. And off I went.     I walked quickly, doing two things simultaneously: first, trying to recall all the places I had stopped and sat—a rock, a safety barrier, on my backpack—any spot where I might have cracked my pocket without realizing it. Second, I strategized about the steps I needed to take—blocking my Visa card, phoning France to arrange a money transfer, and reporting the loss of my ID and driver’s license.     I arrived at the police station, which was exactly as you might expect on New Year's Day—minimally staffed with four policemen. They couldn’t help me find a place to sleep that night, nor could I leave my bag there while I searched for my wallet, and they wouldn’t dispatch a patrol to take me uphill to look for it. However, they mentioned that a patrol had been informed there was a missing wallet somewhere in the mountains. That made me laugh—it was so absurd it was almost funny, though I’m pretty sure the officer was serious.     Of course, these answers didn’t come easily. I had to explain everything from the beginning to an officer who seemed to listen attentively until he abruptly summarized, “So you are French!” and then asked for my passport.     Eventually, they found someone who spoke better English, and we managed to communicate more effectively. The best they could do was give me access to the WiFi at the station. That was helpful; I called Adnan, the man I had met at the guest house that morning, and explained my situation. He was busy but sent a friend to pick me up at the station. After retrieving my backpack from the restaurant, we headed back to the guest house.     Leaving my backpack at the guest house, I took my headlamp and torch, and set out on foot to retrace my steps from the morning and the previous day's evening walk from the restaurant—where I had last used my wallet. I ended up covering about 10 km, including the campsite, but found nothing resembling my wallet.     When I returned to the restaurant, slightly out of breath, the owner invited me to rest by the wood stove. It was already night, and the temperature outside was dropping. He then offered me a glass of hot tea and asked if I’d like him to prepare dinner for me, the same as last time. Accepting his kind offer seemed like a good idea—I could definitely use some hot food. So, I enjoyed a warm meal before heading downhill.      At the campsite, 3.5 km down, I quickly realized that I couldn't do much without a shovel. The day had been sunny, and the snow had melted slightly, only to harden as evening approached. This was nothing like the fluffy, powdery snow of the morning. So, I returned to the guest house to retrieve my backpack, with a plan to find a place to sleep and start again in the morning.      Upon my arrival at the guest house, Adnan and his group were in full celebration mode for the New Year—music, dancing, eating... exactly what you'd expect from a group of friends enjoying their time together. The room was filled with the sounds of folklore music and the sight of folklore dancing, a lively scene that warmed the heart. The energetic group dance went on and on, with everyone sweating and smiling.      Adnan found me a room next to the entrance where I could wait and have a drink. When he returned, he offered me to stay the night. It was too dark and cold to venture out again, and I could sleep on the sofa in the room. The guest house was full, but this was the best he could offer. I accepted right away, quickly concluding that it was much better to stay here than to search for a spot to pitch my tent in the middle of the night.      I occasionally joined the party, but mostly I wasn't in the mood and didn't want to intrude. So, I mostly kept to myself, even though many guests, breathless and sweaty from dancing, would sit with me for a while to chat about mountains, pilgrimage, and various topics. The room I was in served as a common multi-purpose area, strewn with everyone's coats and bags, and fridges full of drinks. The kitchen was just opposite. Whenever the owner-cook found a moment for himself, he would lie down on the sofa opposite mine and close his eyes. He didn't speak English, so our exchanges were silent but comforting.     It was a pleasant evening. At one point, Adnan approached me and revealed that they had organized a collection of money for me without my knowledge. He handed me the collected funds to help me in the coming days. I was taken aback and overwhelmed by such a kind gesture. It was not only unexpected but profoundly helpful.     Now that I was a little rested and no longer in immediate distress, I began making plans. I would walk down to the town early the next morning, retracing my steps carefully all the way. If I didn’t find the wallet, I planned to rent a hotel room, leave my stuff there, and then try to find a shovel. The next day, I would return to the campsite to move all the snow necessary. I wasn’t ready to consider the wallet lost until I had done that. If it was still missing after that, I would accept defeat. Meanwhile, my French support team (Franz) informed me that nowadays, you can temporarily block a bank card without canceling it. You can make a temporary opposition for a few days and then call to have the card reactivated—great news! I was safe to continue my search.     I spent a good night sleeping on the sofa. In the morning, I was probably the first awake. I repacked my backpack—I had opened it the previous evening to take a hot shower. Just when I finished, the guest house owner came to me with a platter of coffee and breakfast. That was very welcome. I warmly thanked him and set off.      Unfortunately, my walk back was fruitless. No sign of the lost wallet. But I harbored a big hope of finding it at the campsite. I had half slipped, half fallen on a small slope there, and it seemed possible, even logical, that this was where I might have torn open my back pocket. Since it was in at least one meter of fresh, powdery snow, the wallet could easily have fallen there without my noticing and might be buried under the snow.     Undeterred and as planned, once I reached town, I headed straight for a hotel, the cheapest possible. After searching unsuccessfully for a shovel elsewhere, I returned to the hotel, hoping they might have one. Fortunately, they did have a shovel and allowed me to take it up to the mountains the next day. Filled with renewed hope, I prepared for another attempt to retrieve my lost wallet.     It was too late to venture out, so I decided to take advantage of the comfortable room to perform some maintenance on my tent. I also harbored a faint, tiny hope that perhaps the wallet had fallen out in the tent while I was dressing or undressing and that I might have overlooked it when packing. It was highly improbable, but hope tends to cling to such possibilities. After unpacking and thoroughly searching the tent—and not finding the wallet—I spent almost four hours stitching and reinforcing parts that needed attention.    I went to bed satisfied and woke up early, fresh and ready to face the day. It was a cloudy morning. After breakfast, I picked up the shovel and started my trek back to the campsite, 12 km uphill. I tried hitchhiking, but it wasn’t easy for cars to stop for a big guy carrying a shovel. So, I walked while trying to hitch a ride, turning around whenever I heard a car. About 3 km into my journey, it started to snow. Normally, I would have my backpack with me, which not only keeps my back warm but also carries an umbrella protected in a PVC pipe. Regrettably, I hadn’t thought to bring the umbrella, so I was at the mercy of the elements.      I had walked nearly all the way up, close to the guest house, when a car finally stopped. A fellow Muslim brother. He drove me the remaining 2 km to the campsite and, as he was early for a prayer meeting in a small mosque in the forest, he offered to help me dig.     For an hour, we dug together, taking turns with the shovel. His kindness was invaluable. After he left, I continued alone for three more hours, shoveling snow and breaking it down with small jabs of the shovel to ensure the wallet wasn’t hidden in a big chunk. The snow was formidable; 20 cm had fallen since the start of my search. Now, my woolen hat (I had brought only my woolen hat for the cold, not my walking hat), my jacket, trousers, shoes, and socks were getting really wet. In such conditions, things deteriorate quickly. Snow sticks to the wet fabric, melts, and wets it further, causing more snow to stick and soak through until you're completely wet and chilled.      Despite the worsening weather, the intense physical effort kept me from feeling cold. I felt the chill of the wet clothes, but I wasn't cold—yet.     I had cleared all the area where I thought my wallet could be. I don't know exactly how many cubic meters of snow I shoveled, but I wouldn’t be surprised if it was around eight. Finding nothing, I had to finally accept that I had truly lost my wallet. Without further delay, I grabbed the shovel and headed downhill.    The snow on the road was thick, with visibility limited to about 10 meters. No cars were passing, so I took out my bike flashing lights to signal my presence should any vehicle approach. The first to appear wasn’t a car but a snowplow, followed by a long line of cars taking advantage of the freshly cleared path. They were all heading uphill, while I was going down. After walking about 1 km, cars began to descend. The snow was already 12 to 15 cm deep, and the cars moved slowly. I stopped to help some tourists from the Netherlands fit chains to their van, then continued walking. About 1 km later, a car stopped and gave me a ride down. I was thoroughly wet and starting to feel cold, something that rarely happens to me.      Upon reaching the town center, I still had another kilometer and a half to walk to my hotel. By then, I could truly feel the cold biting. Once at the hotel, all I wanted was a steaming hot shower, but to my dismay, there was no hot water left. Exhausted, I went straight to bed, trembling and shivering, trying to warm up, which I eventually did. Unfortunately, by the next morning, I had developed a significant fever—it had been a long time since I last had one like this. Now, three days later, the fever is subsiding, and I'll be on my way tomorrow.      So there you have it, my New Year's adventures. All is well now. I lost some money, spent more than usual, and expended a lot of time and energy, only to end up right back where I was 12 days ago had I not taken the mountain path. But that's life, and I still have a big smile on my face.     I walked fine yesterday, and I'm back in my tent now, eager to finish this news update. It's snowing lightly... I'll try to send this today, or tomorrow at the latest.     I wish you a beautiful New Year. But most of all, I wish you happiness and well-being, no matter what.     See you soon,     Emmanuel.     P.S.: The promised blog will soon be available. There were some delays, but my Polish support team tells me we're nearly there... I'll keep you updated on that too.
blog/feast-with-gabriel/index.html:
Feast with Gabriel


		8/8/2023
	
     I would like to drive the point home, because some nails deserve to be nailed, and the subject of the last message is one of them. I hope this expression makes sense in English, as it does in French.    So, coming back to my last message: I wrote it as I was leaving a pretty little village to head toward the mountains (or rather hills—no offense, but I spent several years in the high Himalayan altitudes, so...) of the Carpathians. To be precise, sub-Carpathian Transylvania! Yeah, I know, it sounds professional. It was a history/geography teacher friend of mine who tipped me off to the full designation.    In short, coming back (and by coming back so much, I’m sure I’ll finally get there) to these nails that deserve to be driven in: after spending three days in these hills—yes, yes, these magnificent mountains, which are truly beautiful—I descended on the other side to a small village. I had the same hope as always: to find a grocery store, preferably one that accepts credit cards, to recharge my batteries, and to wash myself. The pilgrim classics.    Upon entering the village, a welcoming concrete wall seemed to have been built just for my backpack and me to rest against. It’s 36 degrees Celsius in the shade... and I’m not in the shade. So, I’m soaked in sweat and happy to breathe while sitting, almost comfortably, with my bag supporting my back.     A car stops. The gentleman, speaking through the open window, says something to me. After a few gestures on my part to explain “French/Pilgrim/Not understanding,” he points to a spot further up one of the streets at the intersection where we are. In English that’s as good as my Hungarian, he says: “Vateur. Oundrund méteur.” Which translates as: “If you want, there’s a source of drinking water a hundred meters higher up this street.”    Yes, I know, it’s just a few words, but I include the non-verbal gestures and the tone in my translation—it adds something.    This is great news, I think to myself as the man drives away, because all my water bottles are empty, and I’m thirsty. It’s funny how the moment you realize you’re out of water, thirst immediately kicks in, as if by magic. The mind is strange, isn’t it? In short, thirst is real.     The information is tempting, even though it’s uphill and not on my route. Spring water is often very fresh—if not outright cold—and frequently very tasty, which fits my situation perfectly. It’s the kind of water you drink even when you’re not thirsty, until your stomach feels tight because you’ve overdone it. Yes, I assure you... I speak from experience. Anyway, subjectively, I estimate I’ll drink at least three liters.     So, I get up and walk.    The place does not disappoint. It’s a small spring, like many I’ve come across: two rectangular, interconnected basins, with a pipe coming out of the rock, pouring clear liquid. And the water is really good... and really fresh.    And I drink. Not three liters, but at least one, then half of another shortly after. I splash water on my head and wet my hat (which prolongs the cooling effect while it dries—about five minutes).    As I lounge, wash my hands, re-wet my face, re-re-wet my head, and soak my arms, a gentleman comes to do much the same as me.     We greet each other, and the conversation begins. After a few moments, comes the comment to which I am now accustomed—common to my situation—delivered with a handshake: Respect! Yes, many people use this word after I play them the brief message recorded in my translator, which succinctly summarizes my situation over the past three years, listing, among other things, the countries I’ve crossed. Respect.   So, Tibor and I talk, and I go into a little more detail... The landscapes, the silence, the encounters, the freedom, the joy of living, the happiness, the kindness received, the welcomes... All of it, you see.   Then, two women pass by on foot. They greet Tibor and exchange a few words, without stopping completely. That is, until he seems to speak of me, because I recognize the words “French” and “kilometers”. I translate this in my mind, with some detailed extrapolation, as: “This is a French pilgrim who has walked 7,500 km to get here. Do you know where he could sleep tonight?”    The women stop for a moment, then leave. Tibor tells me via the translator that I should follow them because they might ask their boss about getting me a room for the night. They work in a sort of hotel or motel, he explains—they are in the kitchen.    I finish filling my water bottles, say goodbye to Tibor, take my backpack, and leave at a rapid pace (fortunately, it’s downhill) to catch up with the women and follow them to the establishment. It’s just opposite where I had been sitting previously... Small world. Though, admittedly, the village is small too—but that’s not the point.   They invite me inside, and while they try to reach the boss, they offer me a meal: a good vegetable soup, some sautéed potatoes, and pan-fried cheese. In the end, they can’t get me a room at the hotel because everything is booked—apparently, there’s a wedding.    But they tell me a friend of theirs is inviting me to her house. I finish eating, and she comes to pick me up to take me there.    She’s a petite lady, around 75 years old (72, in fact). Very kind, she walks with me up the street where the spring is located but further along, to her house. She shows me a sofa bed in the living room, which she immediately begins to prepare while I still have my backpack on my back.     Once I un-shoulder my backpack and take off my shoes, she shows me the bathroom. A shower! My God! Have I already said how good a shower feels? Because, my God, a shower feels amazing...     So, here I am, lying down now. It’s 7:45 p.m., and I’ll sleep soon. My batteries are recharging. Earlier, I went shopping at the store, knowing it would be closed tomorrow, Sunday. Margret—that’s her name—cooked the hard-boiled eggs I bought for the road, just to add some variety. We shared a little aperitif under the pergola in her garden, a ‘little pear.’    She invited me to dinner, but as I had a late and rather heavy lunch (cheese in the pan...), I preferred to lie down. And write to you, to tell you... A little tap on the nail’s head, because I think it deserves it.    And since you have to strike the nail while it’s hot (I’m sure this is a saying—maybe not as common as the one about iron, but still), I might as well continue.     This morning, on my way down to the church, I filled all my bottles and canteen at the spring I visited the day before. I filled up completely because my plan was to set up my tent in the forest 4 km past the village and rest there for two days and three nights. You know the drill.    But one of the first lessons of the road is learning to easily let go of your plans to be guided by others—plans that often turn out to be much better... Certainly in my case...     Margret tells me to wait for her after mass so we can say goodbye. And, as planned, at the end of the mass, just outside the church, I see her as well as the gentleman from the day before, Tibor.    He is a teacher here and would like to introduce me to a friend who speaks French: Gabriel. Contrary to his habit, Tibor sat especially next to Gabriel during the service this morning to inform him of my presence and the opportunity to practice a language that is otherwise hard to use in the area.     Gabriel does indeed speak very good French, occasionally using English for words that escape him due to lack of practice. Thanks to him, my "goodbyes" to Margret and Mr. Teacher are smooth and direct.     When it’s time for me to get back on my way, Gabriel asks if I’m in a hurry or if I have time for a coffee at his place, just five minutes away on foot. After "checking my schedule", I assure him that I have all the time necessary to meet and answer any questions. This is one of the rules I’ve set for myself: to remain available to share what I receive. It also helps me avoid drying out, which is always a risk for a hermit.     So, I spend the morning chatting in French with him and his wife. Then, because he has errands to run, he invites me to accompany him. Together, we feed the farm animals a few kilometers from the village, visit a miraculous spring whose water has been renowned since the Middle Ages, and stop at a recently rebuilt chapel next to the ruins of the one built by King "Machin" after the spring water below cured his army of the infection that was decimating his ranks. We also visit a small wildlife reserve hidden deep in the countryside, where a pond fed by another spring—delicious and fresh water again—houses many rainbow trout that Gabriel regularly feeds.     Along the way, he shows me numerous signs of plantigrade activity. Apparently, there are a few bears in the immediate vicinity, five if I understood correctly. (I know this is a long parenthesis, but I’ll close it now.)     During all this, Gabriel invites me to stay and rest at a small chalet on the farm where we fed the sheep, pigs, chickens, and dogs. In addition to having the renowned spring nearby, the place is special, he says. Certainly bucolic, but more than that. It seems conducive to healing.    And I have to admit, without fully understanding why, it’s one of those places where you feel good—immediately and simply. Gabriel suggests I stay more than two days. In fact, he says, I could stay as long as I want to enjoy the place.     He also offers that, if I want, I could see the family doctor, a general practitioner with extensive experience, who could prescribe more thorough examinations than those done at the hospital last time. I could wait for the results and decide on the next steps accordingly.    He will regularly drive by to feed the animals, so if I need anything, I could benefit from a trip by car to the village to resupply. But, as he showed me while taking me around the place, here in the courtyard set up for hosting family or friends (equipped with a wood-burning oven, a wood-burning grill, and a wood-burning stove, all built from bricks—perfect for enjoying good times at the table with good company), there is a fully stocked fridge where I can help myself.    As far as vegetables are concerned, the organic vegetable garden is just behind the chalet. Everything I see here is available to me, if I wish. And to reach the spring for bathing, he showed me his quad parked in the barn, explaining how to start and use it.     He wished me a good evening and a good night when he left. Through the window of the SUV he was driving, he told me that the herdsman, whose herd’s bells are ringing all around the area, would come this evening to bring me fresh milk. He suggested I invite him to have a Palinka (a “little plum!”) or whatever he prefers and to insist if he hesitates out of politeness or fear of disturbing me. Since it’s outside of his schedule, it’s acceptable—and it would help him feel welcome to have a little drink.     And that’s precisely the feeling Gabriel creates: feeling good. I am welcomed, well-received. His concern is exactly that: for me to feel good. And it happens easily.    He offers me his trust without hesitation and with abundance, sharing the treasures of his life, the enjoyment of this place and its resources, his warm hospitality... and I just met him for the first time this morning.     I’m finishing this message, comfortably seated in the armchair of a small chalet in a stunning corner of nature in the middle of the Carpathian Mountains. One of those dangerously comfortable armchairs that’s hard to leave without a very, very good reason.     On the table, I have peppers and capsicums, apples and plums from his garden, tomatoes from his dad’s garden, cucumbers from the same source, bread from his bakery, and croissants. Two fresh honeycombs from his beekeeper friend. Cheese in the fridge, along with some pastries, French butter, olives in brine, Greek-style dried olives, hard-boiled quail eggs in addition to those I already had, porcini mushrooms, and homemade canned chanterelles.     And there’s the fresh sheep’s cheese that Margret gave me before I left her house—for the road, she said, for the road.     I just uncorked a bottle of red wine that Gabriel took out for me, likely because he suspected I wouldn’t have helped myself. And because he knows I enjoy a small glass of red wine with cheese. I let the bottle breathe after removing the cork, waiting for the herdsman, who should arrive soon.     Isn’t this a nail that deserved to be driven in a little further?     Wow...     I’ll now take some pictures so you can see—so you can believe.     I wish you the best.     See you soon...     Evening P.S.: Maybe I’ll wait until morning to take the photos, due to the light. It’s already a bit late... And then, there’s the armchair. Come to think of it, I feel like I haven’t fully explored its comfort yet, if I can put it that way.    Re-P.S.: Regarding the use of secret codes, I received many completely acceptable proposals. Even though the purpose of the request lay elsewhere, I’d like to share some of them with you. But first, let’s talk statistics. Thanks to the codes, I determined that out of 281 messages sent (yes, you now understand the strategy, given that Signal or WhatsApp only allow sending five at a time for anti-spam reasons)... let’s get back to it.     97% of my messages were opened, and 68% received a response, either with a small emoji or a message. Only 42% included a code in the reply. This doesn’t mean the remaining 58% weren’t read, as some people told me they didn’t understand the secret code thing. Still, it gives an idea.     On the other hand, almost all of the 42% of confirmed readers insisted I continue writing—even long messages—emphasizing how much they were appreciated, which I appreciate just as much. I’m writing this because I want to share a “top ten” list of less secret codes.    Re-re P.S., but now from the morning: I just remembered an important detail. There’s a small Italian coffee maker next to the gas stove. Gabriel took out the can of coffee that goes with it, and it’s full. So, after a glass of real milk—milk that smells and tastes of cows and the flowers they eat—I’ll have an espresso to go with my croissant.   If I add that this is one of those places where you sleep exceptionally well... you’ll probably understand. You’ve likely come across such places yourself. As someone who changes locations regularly, I assure you there are some places that are clearly better than others for sleep, and it’s not due to external conditions, decor, or anything obvious. It’s a kind of intrinsic atmosphere.    This place is one of them. You sleep deeply here. Even disturbances during the night, like a majestic storm or the dogs, didn’t compromise the restorative effect of a good night’s sleep. Just that—sleeping well—is so good. And a hot coffee with a croissant afterward... how to describe it? It’s like drinking a good coffee in the morning after having slept well.     One last P.S. for the road:     There are four dogs here, each with their own personality.     There’s a huge grandmother, about the size of half a bear, but she’s very gentle—except with the youngest. He’s utterly sassy and annoying, like a two-year-old dog. He runs around, licks, nibbles, plays, or wants to play, and steals the dishcloth every time I leave it too close to the boundary he’s not supposed to cross under the courtyard. She regularly growls and snaps her jaws at him, trying to calm him or keep his boundless energy at bay, so she can resume the nap she started a year ago... in vain.     The insolent little one rolls onto his back, pretends to be submissive, and lets out fake barks that no one believes. He wags his tail in all directions while squirming on the ground, sending completely contradictory signals that no one pays attention to anymore.  Then there’s the very small one with curly hair, who seeks cuddles even more than the scatterbrain. She runs sideways, muzzle to the ground, twisting her back as if she’s already stretching toward a hand even before reaching the potential caresser. Her light-colored eyes give her a slightly “quirky” look, but it suits her well.   Lastly, there’s the big dad, who’s massive too, but he’s a soft caramel. He stays discreet in his corner, but when approached, he’s clearly happy.     There’s no blood relation among them, but they share a very good bond.     A band of good companions—joyful and friendly.
blog/fulda/index.html:
Fulda


		6/12/2020
	
     A beautiful day. I first discovered the beautiful city of Fulda, which is historically very attractive.    Then, a very nice family with whom I’ve been chatting all afternoon until now—it all started with an invitation to lunch when I asked for water to refill my bottles. I had noticed a scallop shell hanging from a nail on the facade of their house, and I thought to myself that they must be people who had made the famous pilgrimage to Saint Jacques de Compostela... or at least sympathizers of the pilgrim that I am.     And then I was offered a hot shower, a wash for my clothes, a charge for my phone’s battery, and a very friendly fight with the dog Bruno (because he’s brown).   I’m sleeping in the camper van parked in the yard tonight. It’s very practical, the bed is comfortable, and I’m indoors. This saves me from setting up and taking down my tent, which I would have otherwise placed in the garden.     We just had a traditional hot spiced wine—red wine, lots of spices, a little sugar, and that’s it. It’s a drink for this season, and yes, it keeps you warm.      Everything is okay... I’ll sleep well, even if I didn’t make much progress today. I walked maybe 10 or 12 km, but it was a beautiful day... Gray skies, but beautiful nonetheless...
blog/decision/index.html:
Decision


		18/11/2023
	
     ​Again, it’s been a while since I shared my journey with you. I had nothing new or special to say. No change in the pilgrim’s experience of the path.   But ultimately, I’m not required to be original or new all the time, especially when there is nothing new to share. So, I might as well pick up the nail where I left it last time—if you remember the metaphor.     So, here it is.    I came down from the forest through a small grassy meadow to reach a small road downhill. I had just spent three nights in this lovely forest, in a quiet and protected area. When I first arrived there, I was in a bit of a hurry. It was my birthday.    I had stopped at a restaurant to enjoy a hot meal and a power outlet. When I left, I quickly felt the urgent need to find a bathroom—in real hurry. It happens. For the restaurant’s defense, I don’t think the food quality was to blame, but rather the possible presence of non-vegetarian elements in the preparation. Something like pork fat for cooking, perhaps. For many people who are unfamiliar with vegetarianism, inattentive, or simply mischievous, cooking vegetables with lard still counts as a vegetarian dish...   For someone like me, who has abstained from meat products for more than 32 years, my digestive system reacts immediately—and violently.     Of course, this isn’t ideal on a busy road where each side is occupied by buildings and fenced-off properties. The few kilometers that followed were epic: tiring, distressing, and punctuated by numerous “open toilet breaks.”     Happy birthday, Emmanuel!     So I didn’t really choose where to stop. As soon as I saw a perpendicular path leading to a forest, I followed it until I found a welcoming place. I came down from that spot well-rested after three nights there. As I arrived at this small road, intending to follow it to a larger one, a gentleman in his garden spotted me and called out from afar.     He was far enough away that he had no idea who I was or what I was doing there, just that I had the look of a backpacker. Far enough, too, that I couldn’t really hear him, but I could see he was calling out. So I changed my direction and walked toward him. When I got within earshot, I said my usual line: "French/pilgrim/not understand." He replied, “Ah, okay! Coffee?”    The proposition was clear and tempting. A hot coffee early in the morning is always welcome, especially with the chill of the season. So, getting one just as I was starting my day was unexpected but very pleasant.     We sipped it together, joined by his wife on the terrace of their house, where he was finishing work on an outbuilding. It was a very nice encounter—simple and full of kindness. After an hour with them, I got back on the road. The main road wasn’t pleasant to walk along, as important roads often aren’t. The number of vehicles, and especially their speeds, made walking uncomfortable, stressful, and dangerous.   But I had no alternative, so I carefully monitored the traffic coming toward me. I wore headphones to block out the noise—whether with music, an audiobook, or even just silence.     At the intersection where I needed to take the left branch, a pedestrian crossed the road to meet me and asked what I was doing there. I showed him the short text recorded in my translator, summarizing the main ideas in one paragraph. After several handshakes and a few "very goud, very goud," I continued my walk toward the small grocery store located right at the intersection.     With my backpack emptied of all food, and having not eaten the day before or that morning, I thought a stop for provisions would be welcome. I placed my bag on one of the benches on the small terrace near the entrance—village grocery stores often have a café/bar attached with a terrace—and went inside.     Two cans of vegetable pâté, a block of cheese, five nicely red tomatoes, two bananas, and a loaf of sliced bread later, I stepped outside to grab the coins I had forgotten in the jacket on my bag, intending to add them to the 50 lei note I had already given. I wanted to simplify payment by offering a rounded amount. When I returned to the counter, the lady indicated that I owed nothing. “It’s for me,” she said. “Drum bun. Have a nice journey.”     Isn’t that surprising? Isn’t it pleasant? Isn’t it touching?     Apparently, the gentleman I had met earlier had entered after me, and while I was choosing my cans of pâté, he briefly introduced me to the lady. That’s how she ended up giving me back my money and saying, “It’s for me.”     After carefully putting the entire donation into the appropriate boxes in my bag, I resumed my journey, only to discover a roadside restaurant just a little further along the way. A sort of container-turned-chip shop/French fry/kebab stand. The idea of a hot and different meal tempted me. After all, I could save what I had bought for later. Hot food isn’t an everyday luxury. So I stopped.     Leaning on the counter, the gentleman ahead of me saw me, and we exchanged greetings. After my customary "French/pilgrim/not understanding" introduction, he began speaking in surprisingly good French—leftovers from high school, he said. It was not only practical but also pleasant to have a conversation and a translator for my order, just to ensure the hamburger I was ordering was truly vegetarian!     When his order was ready, he shook my hand and went on his way. A very nice meeting with a local teacher—Romanian, of course. While waiting for my burger, wallet in hand and ready to pay, I noticed the lady preparing it was on her phone, while another finished assembling a bag of fries and another burger.     I assumed it was a phone order—until she handed me her phone. On the screen was a message she had just written and translated for me: “The two burgers and fries are for you. It’s free. We wish you well. Have a nice journey.” I don’t want to sound melodramatic, but I nearly cried.   It’s not just the gesture itself—it’s the repetition, the frequency. The consistency. It touches something deep inside. You see? So the nail sinks in...    It was still only midday, and I had about ten kilometers left before reaching my destination: the Basilica of Cacica. I’m here now. Well, not precisely in the basilica as I write these words, but I’m right next door—maybe 200 meters away. I’m staying in a family home. It was one of the priests from the basilica who approached me as I was leaving. Night had already fallen; it was almost 5 p.m.     “Do you know where to sleep?” he asked me.     “No, not yet,” I replied.     “Come with me,” he said.     He led me to a neighbor’s house, and the neighbor then took me to another house, just behind his, on the other side of the garden.    He showed me the kitchen as he plugged in the refrigerator. Then he led me upstairs to the bathroom, saying there would soon be hot water (he knew the exact words a pilgrim would appreciate—or perhaps my smell made it clear how necessary it was!). And then he showed me the bedroom. “You stay as long as you want,” he said.     I’ve been experiencing this for three years. Three years!    Maybe you don’t realize—I don’t know. You can only read what I can write, and many things cannot be put into words. But imagine living this...     So.     Today, I decided something important.    Three years was the length of time I initially hoped to experience when I decided to go beyond southern Poland and the Czestochowa Monastery. It seemed enough—not to learn everything I wanted, but to establish something permanent.     Certainly, the impression is profound. Certainly, the imprint is there, the trace is marked. But I feel its fragility. I intuitively sense that there is much more. The nails can go further, deeper, to ensure they don’t come out.     I’m probably not a good student. I’m a very slow learner.     But I want to continue. It’s not that I don’t want to stop—I want to continue.     The nuance is very important.     So.    I’m heading back tomorrow morning. This may seem obvious to you, but it wasn’t. In recent months, I’ve experienced certain conditions that made me doubt—doubt the relevance of continuing this path, at least in this way. And the desire to continue is not a sufficient condition for a serious practitioner. Alone, it can lead to confusion, which is the opposite of what I’m seeking.    So I stopped to reflect on the path—the one I’ve traveled and the one ahead. But neither is as eloquent as the silence and well-being I feel this morning, walking under the snow that has been falling heavily since yesterday.     It’s beautiful. It’s good. I feel good. I feel free. I am happy.     I think I’ll wait until I truly can’t continue before stopping.   Put yourself in my place—wouldn’t you look further for what the nail fixes? What work it participates in and contributes to? Would you have better things to do?     I wish you the best.     See you soon.
blog/ask-bilbo/index.html:
Ask Bilbo!


		23/8/2021
	
     ​I know, it hasn’t been that long since I gave you my latest news. But I have to share what seems so important to me in my journey. I know I am redundant, and yet each time again, I am touched and moved by this kindness that welcomes me.     I must begin by telling you that the last days since I left Aglona have been wonderful. I have been alone and in silence since resuming my walk. The intermittent rain refreshes pleasantly this end of summer. However, it is not too important to hinder my progress. When the rain is really too strong, I stop, put up the tent and take refuge there, but it’s not that often. A few days ago though, I got a downpour that was Hollywood chewing gum level event, if you remember the nineties advertisement. It was so huge, so tropical shower level that it becomes fun in itself. You no longer have to worry about getting wet, it’s so impossible not to that it’s no longer a problem.    So it’s true that the atmosphere is really humid, but the good in that is that it attracts mushrooms which end up throwing themselves at my feet begging me to pick them up (yes like this). That’s awesome! I eat raw Boletus Edulis, because they are so fresh that there is no need to cook them. Which is good because I have nothing to cook anymore from a long time now. Yesterday I found the flesh of a big champagne cork shape one really sweet. It surprised me. Crunchy and sweet. Happiness...    And then I also collect Chanterelles. I keep them in a bag and try to dry them a bit as much and as often as possible. I always end up being invited by someone to cook them...     And then I arrived in this village where a grocery store was at the entrance. It was good because I needed to fill my backpack with food again. I did my shopping there, paid for everything, and the lady in charge of the grocery store asked me where I was coming from and what I was doing. She then offered to charge my phone if I needed, and we chatted.     It’s crazy how what I do—walking like this, a long pilgrimage, a long-lasting spiritual discipline—can inspire or make sense to the people I meet. It is even disturbing. My approach, however very particular, very surprising, very unusual, very incongruous even, turns out to be full of meaning also for those I meet... Full of meaning and nourishing too. Strange, isn’t it? There is even a kind of envy that I feel, a craving. As if I were realizing in this journey what many would like to, what many are starving for... I guess that’s why having the rule to take the time to share with whoever is interested is important.     After a while, she kindly offered me a coffee, which I gratefully accepted, because coffee is good! Especially when it’s offered like this. Of course, the coffee was served with many biscuits, chocolate, and white cheese bars sweetened and coated with chocolate or caramel (it’s pasty, somewhere between hard cream and fresh cheese, and sweet. I like it...).   We chatted using Google Translate until a client, an English teacher at the village college, arrived. So we chatted in English. Nice exchange.     Of the few new customers who passed by during my break at the grocery store, a dozen I would say, I had a friendly exchange with ten. More than half spoke with me or with the grocer, who told them about what we had already discussed. Four of them offered me their phone numbers in case I needed anything or help on my way.     Before going to sleep near the village lake, the grocer gave me a bag of tomatoes and cucumbers (the Baltic countries seem to have an impressive addiction to cucumbers... Small cucumbers, like big pickles... Over the past month, there hasn’t been a single day I’ve spent without cucumbers...).     I spent four hours in her shop, chatting with her while she worked or with her customers. It was really relaxed, and I managed to recharge my phone and power banks. Great! I gave her the bag of Boletus edulis mushrooms and chanterelles that I had picked that morning. It felt completely natural to give them to her. Then we said goodbye.     The evening was good! A swim in the lake, washing myself and my clothes. A beautiful night without rain (which is nice because the sound of rain on the tent canvas can be really loud!). And this morning, I resumed my journey.     In the afternoon, I arrived at a small country road—unpaved, with no tarmac—where I noticed someone walking about 100 meters ahead of me. It was a lady. Elderly. Old, but still walking briskly (87 years old! Respect!). It took me nearly a kilometer to catch up and walk alongside her. I could immediately tell she was a character—a nice one.    When she heard someone approaching behind her (I had deliberately rubbed my foot on the ground to make a little noise, so as not to startle her), she turned around with a warm smile, not a trace of fear or surprise. That alone says a lot.     We introduced ourselves and decided to walk together to her house, half a kilometer away. We had not gone 50 meters before I inherited one of the bags of tomatoes from her garden, which she carried in each hand.    Arriving in front of her house, I was invited in for a coffee. I gladly accepted! A good cup of coffee never hurts! (French proverb—or if not, it should become one soon...).    Watch the little movie I made—sorry, it’s in French; I didn’t think about it at the time. But aside from showing the beautiful place where she and her husband live, you can see her smile, her enthusiasm, her kindness. Notice the touching gesture of the small tablecloth she placed on the table for me, to hold the cup of coffee, along with a few slices of cheese on a plate, homemade donuts, and the white cheese treats I mentioned before.     Then I met her husband, as kind as she was.    I was invited to stay the night.    I was invited to use the sauna and shower.   I was invited to visit the property—a superb estate that belonged to her grandparents. It included a house, a barn, a garage, a henhouse, a sauna, and toilets behind the barn. There was a magnificent vegetable garden with enormous raspberries and blackcurrants. By the way, the homemade blackcurrant jam I ate with evening porridge was delicious.    Even the grass was soft and comfortable to walk on barefoot—something I was invited to do almost immediately.    She told me that tomorrow morning, before I leave, we will eat the mushrooms she collected, with potatoes. How does she know it’s my favorite dish at the moment—fresh mushrooms and potatoes, seriously! Ask Bilbo!!!    And then, go look at the pictures—come on, watch that splendid breakfast! ??    Finally, her husband showed me his workshop and his neatly arranged wood; she showed me her sober and simple interior. He showed me the sauna; she showed me the henhouse...    I’m falling asleep as I write these words... The evening meal, the sauna, the comfortably firm sofa bed, the faint smell of wood fire coming from the burner...    Once again, these people touch me and move me with the warmth of their welcome, the smiles in their kind eyes, and the care they show me, even though I’m a total stranger, completely unknown to them.
blog/gietrzwald/index.html:
Gietrzwald and Olsztyn


		2/1/2022
	
     I am walking, walking, walking, and somehow, now we are in winter. Of course, I had a few hints and clues—everything is white. Everything is frozen. Literally, outside or inside (which, to be honest, are very blurry concepts anyway). My food has turned into ice-cream: fruit ice-cream, tomato ice-cream, cheese ice-cream, hummus ice-cream—you get the idea. I can’t even cut a piece of butter; it’s too hard. So I eat frozen bread with frozen camembert (when I can find some)...     Ah yes, I’m back to sleeping with my bottle of water inside the sleeping bag. It’s the only way to have something drinkable by morning. Not much room in there, but that’s okay—she’s not a bad bed companion, except when the cork leaks. (And it’s absolutely necessary to avoid rolling onto it during the night... Otherwise, it’s fine.)    But you know what? It’s beautiful. Really beautiful. It’s so cold that the snow stays perfectly white, even after cars drive over it. Sounds are muffled, and the contrasts are sharper, making it much easier to spot wildlife. I see animals from far away or very close when they’re trying to hide. They stay completely still, totally immobile but highly alert, thinking they’re invisible, just waiting for me to pass. But on the white snow, I can see them clearly. I enjoy that a lot.     Oh, and my backpack feels lighter because I’m wearing almost all my clothes. I know it’s just a trick—after all, I’m still carrying the same weight—but I guess it’s a psychological thing. My backpack doesn’t feel so heavy!    Temperatures have dropped to minus 16°C at night, and now it’s even that cold during the day. I guess we’ll soon hit minus 20°C at night.     I’ll send photos this time, as I’ve managed to take and keep some. Unfortunately, the ones from my last message seem to be lost—or maybe they’re just hiding too well in my phone...     Today is the New Year, I’ve been told. That explains all the fireworks last night that woke me up in my tent in the small woods where I was camping. Well, to be honest, I knew it was coming—first, because it happens roughly every year at the same time! And secondly, someone reminded me of it a few days ago.    I chose to spend the night in the woods because I didn’t feel like being in the town that was the next stop on my journey. I wasn’t inclined toward big noises, excitement, or anything else that comes with New Year’s celebrations in town. I guess I’ve become more interested in quietness and silence. That’s the effect of spending all day in peace and sleeping in forests!    It’s strange, though. Even when I’m invited to stay indoors nowadays (which happens often), I find myself missing the cold. My hosts, out of kindness and worry—or maybe trying to compensate for the nights I’ve spent outside at minus 15°C—always propose to turn up the heating in the room I’m sleeping in, to make it cozy and warm. But I can’t. These days, I sleep best in the cold. Just being inside is enough—no heating required!    Now that you have a sense of the atmosphere of these days, I have to tell you about my journey. Since the last time I wrote, I’ve crossed the border and arrived in Poland. Thanks to the help of a Polish friend—whom I’ve officially declared my topographic planner-in-chief—I’ve joined one of the Jacobs Ways. (For my Indian or Nepalese friends who might not know, Jacobs Ways are part of a network of pilgrimage routes across Europe that lead to Santiago de Compostela in Spain.)    Following these routes is great for many reasons. First, they are usually very well signposted, making navigation easier. Second, they are designed to avoid big roads as much as possible. And third, they are planned by locals to guide you through beautiful places—old villages, historical sites, or cultural gems you might otherwise miss if you don’t know the area or can’t speak the language. (Speaking of which, did I mention that Polish is a nightmare to pronounce? I think I’ve sprained my tongue!)    And here’s the best part: the Camino I’m currently following passes through three places I really wanted to visit.    Święta Lipka, a very famous Baroque-style basilica dedicated to Mary, is located in a rather small village. It has a huge organ, and I tried to record it with my phone. Unfortunately, the phone isn’t the best tool for live recordings, and I’m afraid the result doesn’t do justice to the incredible concert I was lucky enough to stumble upon the day I arrived. Still, you can listen and let me know what you think.    Then there was Gietrzwałd. I have to say, it’s an incredibly beautiful place. I enjoyed my time there immensely.     Initially, I had planned to arrive in Gietrzwałd on Christmas Eve, but that morning, as I woke up in the forest just outside the town, I felt so comfortable, so at peace with the place where I had spent the night, that the idea of entering the town during the hustle and excitement of Christmas Eve made me a little anxious. So, I decided to stay in the woods for another day and night and only arrived in Gietrzwałd on the 25th. It was a wonderful decision. Honestly, if you ever take a walk and don’t know where to go, head there—it’s such a special place to be!     Now, I’m on my way to Licheń, about 350 km ahead. Licheń isn’t on the Jacobs Way, but I just have to leave the path at one point, and it’s only 40 km south.     One of the best parts of this journey has been crossing through beautiful old villages and towns. On the way, I’ve also encountered castles.   One castle I passed was open for visits, and it even had a restaurant inside—double jackpot! When I arrived at the restaurant, I met some very kind people visiting Poland with their Canadian friends. It was a lovely encounter, but by now, I guess you know that all the encounters I’ve had have been wonderful—always, everywhere. It’s crazy how true that is.    They invited me to share their table for lunch and were very curious about my walk. After lunch, we explored the castle together. At first, I was thrilled—walking inside a castle is like living a childhood dream, and I loved it. But then, I was disturbed by what I saw on display. I had expected swords, crossbows, armor, and chain mail—things that stir the imagination of an adventurer. Instead, 90% of the exhibition consisted of torture instruments and machines from the Middle Ages, used by the Inquisition and other authorities of the time.    It was overwhelming, even sickening, to see such an extensive collection. The sheer variety, complexity, and elaborateness of these devices left me feeling deeply unsettled. The contrast between the cruelty on display and the peaceful, meaningful journey I’ve been on for the past 15 months created a dissonance I found hard to bear.    Thankfully, shortly after that, I was warmly welcomed by a community of religious sisters. Their kindness and hospitality quickly helped erase the heavy feeling, restoring my sense of peace.    And then, sometime later, I arrived in the town with the castle where Copernicus lived for many years! That was a much nicer visit!   Yes, I am a pilgrim, not a tourist. I don’t go out of my way to visit many places, but when something is directly on my path, of course, I let the child in me enjoy it. What could be better than a drawbridge, a dungeon, a crenellated guardrail, a trebuchet, a mangonel, a ballista, or a catapult?    Voila. This whole journey feels like a dream I am living. Truly, it seems like my feet barely touch the ground these days. Maybe that’s why my backpack feels so heavy! Did I tell you I gave it a name? "Expiation"—I find it very fitting while making a Christian pilgrimage.    Even when something bad happens, I am so lucky that it often turns into something good. Let me give you another example because I’m not sure it’s easy to imagine how much, how often, and in what ways things just seem to work out.    One day, I was invited by a religious sister I met as I was leaving the church next to her congregation house. She welcomed me to stay the night, which meant I had a bed, but most importantly—a bathtub. A hot bath. I hadn’t taken a full hot bath in over three years! (I see you raising an eyebrow: yes, three years without a bath, but I take showers... sometimes.) But a bath! You know what I mean—being fully submerged in steaming hot water, getting clean, sure, but more than that, truly relaxing... until, of course, the phone rings or someone knocks on the door, because that’s a universal truth of bathtubs!    At the time, I was expecting a parcel from my friends in France for my birthday. I asked the sister to call my next destination to see if they could receive the parcel and hold it for me until I arrived. Unfortunately, it wasn’t possible. I wasn’t too worried because, these days, solutions always seem to appear.    And, sure enough, the next morning, Sister Alina (yes, I think it’s fine to share her name) came to me with a solution. Someone who overheard her story about the failed parcel plan, without knowing me at all, without ever having met me, offered to have the parcel sent to his home. Not only that, but he and his wife promised to bring it to me by car, wherever I might be!    I explained to him that I didn’t know exactly where I would be when the parcel arrived and that I was afraid I might be far away by then. But he simply said, “No problem, I’ll drive to you.” And that’s exactly what happened! Ten days later, he received the parcel, contacted me for my location, and after finishing his workday, he and his wife drove two hours to meet me. They handed over the package, chatted with me for a while, and then drove back home. Just like that.    And here’s the kicker: that very night, after I received the parcel—which included replacement parts for my tent—the temperature dropped so much that the aluminum structure of my tent froze and snapped. Like... well, like frozen aluminum. (A very apt analogy, wouldn’t you agree?) But because I had just received the new parts, I was able to repair the tent immediately.    This morning, another aluminum pole snapped... But it’s just that I walked exactly where I shouldn’t have. There are mornings like this. But hey, you know what? I arrived in a village just after that and got invited to stay for the night, even though it was still morning. So after spending a few hours talking, washing myself, and doing my laundry, I managed to repair my tent, so tomorrow will be fine! Great, no?    I used the extra time to write you this message. I could have done it while staying at the pilgrim center in Gietrzwald, but I wasn’t in the mood. I started writing it, but then thought I’d finish it in the tent... But guess what? It’s too cold to keep your arms out of the sleeping bag, and if you only keep your hands out, you get frostbite on your fingers in minutes. So I guess I had to meet these people. And this meeting could easily not have happened because, when I arrived in the village, I realized I had forgotten my hat on a bench about 1.5 km back. This has never happened before—first time. So I walked back to fetch it, then walked all the way back to the village where I met these people and got invited.    Now, another story—and the last.    I got sick in mid-December. I was invited by such kind people, really nice. A beautiful family. Then I was invited to stay a little longer to rest. And I was happy because it was such a nice place with such nice people. So I proposed to cook an apple tarte, Normandy style. I’m very easygoing when it comes to making tarts... Let’s call it cultural exchange!     So I was in the middle of preparing this tart, and I tried a piece of apple to get an idea of how much sugar I should use. And guess what? I had the worst, no-taste apple possible. You know those industrial tomatoes, the ones genetically modified by companies that want to save the world from hunger? One very famous one starts with "MON" and ends with "ENTO." I got exactly the same sensation tasting this apple as when eating their tomatoes. No smell, no taste... You only know it’s a tomato (or apple) because it looks like one before you bite into it. After that, it’s just your brain trying to fill in the blanks for those who know what a tomato or apple is supposed to smell and taste like. (I guess those who’ve never had a real one might get shocked when they finally taste one from a traditional seed-grown garden.) But I’m digressing—excuse me.    I was really disappointed with the apples! It’s basically very hard to make a good apple tarte if the apples aren’t tasty or sugary at all. I guess my disappointment was really obvious because Ania and Krzysztof (yes, I use names, but that’s between us!) asked me what was wrong. Then they tried the apples themselves and were very satisfied...     So either they had no taste in apples, or I had lost mine...     Do you see where this is going? No?     They explained to me, while handing me a bottle of essential oil to test if I could smell anything, that one of the effects of a certain virus going around these days (you’ve probably heard of it) is the total loss of taste and smell.     Imagine the situation: I was with people who had welcomed me very kindly and generously into their home, and I realized there that I was sick with the virus. Honestly, I felt really, really uncomfortable at the time. There’s so much being said about this virus that eventually, I felt guilty—not because of the disease itself, as my doctor had already warned me that I wasn’t part of the population at risk of developing a severe form, but because I was afraid of the fear this virus arouses in people. And, of course, I was afraid of transmitting it to others.     You can perhaps appreciate the delicacy of the situation. Guilt is the easiest emotion to arouse in humans. But I didn’t even have time to dwell on that because my hosts immediately asked me to stay with them until I got better. They tried to put me at ease straight away, reassuring me that I could and should stay with them.     They insisted I shouldn’t be afraid, and that’s when I told them, “I’m not afraid of the disease; I’m afraid of the fear of the disease.” They understood me completely and reassured me by saying, first, that she had already been sick and it hadn’t been a big deal for her. Second, he was in great health, and even when she was sick, he hadn’t caught the virus. Then she mentioned that her parents, who were coming to visit that weekend, were vaccinated.     So, all was okay. She promised to prepare me herbal teas and potions and assured me I had nothing to worry about. I could stay with them without any problem, doubt, or guilt. And I did. And it worked out. After five days of full rest—two of which I spent mostly sleeping—I got slightly better every day. By the fifth day, I was totally fine, and my taste and smell had returned. That part had been the worst because they cooked such nice food, and I couldn’t enjoy it. I mean, I couldn’t even tell the difference, except by texture, between raw garlic, peanuts, or a piece of chocolate! How horrible is that?     Once I got better, I proposed a new cultural exchange in the form of a chocolate pear tart and a spinach pie with Roquefort. They’re easy, fast, and good. I’ve made them dozens of times since leaving France, though I’ve succeeded in only a few of those attempts. Thankfully, this was one of the successful ones.     I stayed with them for about a dozen days, and honestly, I’m so grateful I fell sick while in their care. I had already been considering stocking up on food and water, heading into the woods, putting up my tent in a remote, hidden spot, and staying there for a week. But instead, I ended up with these wonderful people.    On top of being friendly and welcoming, their reaction was so cool, full of normality and reason, which seems rare these days. I was deeply touched. I felt at home, and they appreciated that I felt that way.     So basically, I got sick, but it turned out to be a nice experience! Cool, no?    And it brought me to Gietrzwałd for Christmas, which, in a way, is perfect timing for the pilgrim I am. (You know, Ania and Krzysztof insisted that I spend Christmas with them and their whole family. I know they would have really liked that, and they even offered to come pick me up from where I was. But, well, you know me and birthdays... I declined. Still, I feel so lucky. Truly.)     Voila. I think it’s time for me to stop writing. It’s getting really late, and I still have about an hour to go to send this along with pictures to everyone. So, yes, that’s it for today. I have no idea how long this message is. Hopefully, not too much. I’ll add lots of pictures to balance it out!     Anyway...     I wish you all a beautiful year.     I wish you well and happy.     See you.
blog/germany-2/index.html:
East Germany


		23/12/2020
	
​     Good evening from the former East Germany.     It's hard to say how much I enjoy the country, to be honest, because most of the time I’m alone in nature, and it feels very similar to home. When I pass through a village or town, perhaps due to the virus, the weather, and the end-of-year period, it often feels like a ghost town everywhere. I appreciate the architecture, but I can’t really get a sense of the area’s atmosphere—it’s the people who create that, and here, they are absent.    I do notice a strong difference between West and East Germany in terms of the wealth of housing, cars, and infrastructure. The west is impeccable, while the east is much less so.     So, let’s just say I like what I see most of the time, as well as my walking experience...     I have a few more weeks in East Germany, and then it will be Poland.     Yesterday, as a sort of duty to humanity, I made a detour to the former Nazi concentration camp of Buchenwald, which was later transformed by the Soviets into a special internment camp (causing more deaths than under the Nazi regime). Suffice it to say, the place has a "tense" atmosphere, and it feels incredibly heavy. It was closed due to Corona, so guided tours and access to the exhibition buildings weren’t possible. However, the entire camp itself was open, and a few explanatory panels outside provided the essentials. That was enough—I can imagine the rest.     Today, I came across ostriches. It was strange to see them at a bend in the path, in a meadow...     I also came across a dead penguin!     The last photo shows its corpse lying on the ground! 🤭😂    The large buildings visible just above, which look like towering communist administration or propaganda headquarters, are, in fact, a biscuit factory!     I have a fascination with twisted trees. An abnormal tree can be very beautiful... like these faces!    I also met a gentleman after Leipzig who has a collection (apparently in the world’s top 20!) of metal bottle caps, classified by country, type, and era! Like all enthusiasts, it was great to listen to him talk about his passion—especially how it all started. His three-year-old son had found a very colorful bottle cap while walking with his parents (which, from what I’ve observed, Germans do a lot. A LOT! Really... It’s such a healthy habit). Anyway, the child refused to let go of the bottle cap for several days, so the dad started bringing him a new one every day, placing it on his bedside table. And this is how, 28 years later, he ended up with a collection of over 100,000 metal bottle caps...     He also has several tens of thousands of duplicates and triplicates, all intended for exchanges...
blog/five-years-walking-across-europe-15:
Five years walking across Europe — 15 countries,                                                     10,000 km, 5 winters. And now, a pause...


		28/8/2025
	
       Dear you all,    For the past 4 years and 11 months, I have had the privilege of walking across Europe on a pilgrimage, visiting about 150 Marian places in 15 countries.    I did it in one continuous journey, crossing France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, then Lithuania again, Poland again, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Croatia — covering about 10,000 km. Ten thousand kilometers with my backpack, my hat, my stick, all on foot, in the tradition of pilgrimage.     I can’t explain how beautiful and powerful that experience was. How magnificent it was to learn freedom, happiness, to cross mountains, forests, rivers, and beautiful lands. To sleep beside lakes, under the shadow of trees, on a soft mattress of moss, on sandy beaches. To meet so many kind people, receiving the warm gift of their hospitality, the incredible gift of their trust, their beautiful curiosity about me, about my way, about my approach to spirituality, to life — or simply to pilgrimage itself.     I don’t feel as if I spent 5 years on the road. It passed in a flash, the seasons rolling like the weeks of a single month. Yes, 5 months — no more. That’s how it felt. But not for my body, not for my flesh.     So yes, I must tell you: I decided to come back to France. I just arrived yesterday, and I am going to stay for a while before resuming my pilgrimage. I need to recover my health, which slowed me down so much over the past 2 years. And I also need to earn and save enough money for the next part.    Because I am not done yet. Far from it. Pilgrimage is a practice. A spiritual practice. An inner quest. You know how long it can be if you truly aim to go deep, to learn truth, and to meet your Self.    My plan — or more honestly, my wish — is to continue as soon as I am ready. I am less than halfway. There are still many destinations to reach, and my intended path was this:Croatia, Slovenia, Austria, southern Germany, Switzerland, southern France, Italy, then by ferry to Albania, Kosovo, North Macedonia, Greece, Turkey, Lebanon, Israel, Jordan, Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, Morocco, then by ferry to Portugal, through Spain, back to France, Belgium, the Netherlands, western Germany, and finally southern Poland — where I was initially going, where it all began. A long way still ahead.    That is the plan, or maybe just the hope. It would have been fantastic to complete it all in one stretch. But I will wait, and prepare. Hopefully the world will have time to calm down a little, for peace to come, for the way to clear.     If this seems sudden or rushed to you, it is not. My silence these past months may already have been a sign that I was going through hard times. And a few weeks ago, arriving in Dubrovnik, Croatia, I decided I should stop there, because I was going so slowly, with such difficulty, that it no longer made much sense to continue.    But crossing the town, visiting its churches and resting in each one, taking something like 11 hours to cross what I could normally walk in just one, gave me new energy — and I changed my mind. I see now, five weeks later, that I actually made the decision to stop there. It took me all this time to accept it, to integrate it.    So when the moment came to take the decision again, it was easy. Painless. Obvious. I was ready. I was sure, determined. I have no regrets. I gave everything I could. I went fully into this experience, this practice. I am at peace with myself in letting it take its course.    I am happy. I am grateful. I feel lucky. Blessed. And contrary to what I feared, I find myself calm and serene in the middle of this restless activity — such a contrast with the 5 years of silence and solitude I just lived. Yet it does not affect me, does not disturb me. I stand in the middle of this agitation, I recognize it, and I am well. It gives me a slightly surreal feeling, a kind of detachment.     Now I will prepare for the rest, and let you know when the time comes.     We can stay in touch — I would love that.     Thank you so much for everything.     I wish you well.     I wish you happiness.     Emmanuel     I am attaching many pictures from the past months, for you to see my way.

How magnificent it was to learn freedom, happiness, to cross mountains, forests, rivers, and beautiful lands.
