To meet so many kind people, receiving the warm gift of their hospitality, the incredible gift of their trust, their beautiful curiosity about me, about my way, about my approach to spirituality, to life — or simply to pilgrimage itself.     I don’t feel as if I spent 5 years on the road. It passed in a flash, the seasons rolling like the weeks of a single month. Yes, 5 months — no more. That’s how it felt. But not for my body, not for my flesh.     So yes, I must tell you: I decided to come back to France. I just arrived yesterday, and I am going to stay for a while before resuming my pilgrimage. I need to recover my health, which slowed me down so much over the past 2 years. And I also need to earn and save enough money for the next part.    Because I am not done yet. Far from it. Pilgrimage is a practice. A spiritual practice. An inner quest. You know how long it can be if you truly aim to go deep, to learn truth, and to meet your Self.    My plan — or more honestly, my wish — is to continue as soon as I am ready. I am less than halfway. There are still many destinations to reach, and my intended path was this:Croatia, Slovenia, Austria, southern Germany, Switzerland, southern France, Italy, then by ferry to Albania, Kosovo, North Macedonia, Greece, Turkey, Lebanon, Israel, Jordan, Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, Morocco, then by ferry to Portugal, through Spain, back to France, Belgium, the Netherlands, western Germany, and finally southern Poland — where I was initially going, where it all began. A long way still ahead.    That is the plan, or maybe just the hope. It would have been fantastic to complete it all in one stretch. But I will wait, and prepare. Hopefully the world will have time to calm down a little, for peace to come, for the way to clear.     If this seems sudden or rushed to you, it is not. My silence these past months may already have been a sign that I was going through hard times. And a few weeks ago, arriving in Dubrovnik, Croatia, I decided I should stop there, because I was going so slowly, with such difficulty, that it no longer made much sense to continue.    But crossing the town, visiting its churches and resting in each one, taking something like 11 hours to cross what I could normally walk in just one, gave me new energy — and I changed my mind. I see now, five weeks later, that I actually made the decision to stop there. It took me all this time to accept it, to integrate it.    So when the moment came to take the decision again, it was easy. Painless. Obvious. I was ready. I was sure, determined. I have no regrets. I gave everything I could. I went fully into this experience, this practice. I am at peace with myself in letting it take its course.    I am happy. I am grateful. I feel lucky. Blessed. And contrary to what I feared, I find myself calm and serene in the middle of this restless activity — such a contrast with the 5 years of silence and solitude I just lived. Yet it does not affect me, does not disturb me. I stand in the middle of this agitation, I recognize it, and I am well. It gives me a slightly surreal feeling, a kind of detachment.     Now I will prepare for the rest, and let you know when the time comes.     We can stay in touch — I would love that.     Thank you so much for everything.     I wish you well.     I wish you happiness.     Emmanuel     I am attaching many pictures from the past months, for you to see my way.

I felt the chill of the wet clothes, but I wasn't cold—yet.     I had cleared all the area where I thought my wallet could be. I don't know exactly how many cubic meters of snow I shoveled, but I wouldn’t be surprised if it was around eight. Finding nothing, I had to finally accept that I had truly lost my wallet. Without further delay, I grabbed the shovel and headed downhill.    The snow on the road was thick, with visibility limited to about 10 meters. No cars were passing, so I took out my bike flashing lights to signal my presence should any vehicle approach. The first to appear wasn’t a car but a snowplow, followed by a long line of cars taking advantage of the freshly cleared path. They were all heading uphill, while I was going down. After walking about 1 km, cars began to descend. The snow was already 12 to 15 cm deep, and the cars moved slowly. I stopped to help some tourists from the Netherlands fit chains to their van, then continued walking. About 1 km later, a car stopped and gave me a ride down. I was thoroughly wet and starting to feel cold, something that rarely happens to me.      Upon reaching the town center, I still had another kilometer and a half to walk to my hotel. By then, I could truly feel the cold biting. Once at the hotel, all I wanted was a steaming hot shower, but to my dismay, there was no hot water left. Exhausted, I went straight to bed, trembling and shivering, trying to warm up, which I eventually did. Unfortunately, by the next morning, I had developed a significant fever—it had been a long time since I last had one like this. Now, three days later, the fever is subsiding, and I'll be on my way tomorrow.      So there you have it, my New Year's adventures. All is well now. I lost some money, spent more than usual, and expended a lot of time and energy, only to end up right back where I was 12 days ago had I not taken the mountain path. But that's life, and I still have a big smile on my face.     I walked fine yesterday, and I'm back in my tent now, eager to finish this news update. It's snowing lightly... I'll try to send this today, or tomorrow at the latest.     I wish you a beautiful New Year. But most of all, I wish you happiness and well-being, no matter what.     See you soon,     Emmanuel.     P.S.: The promised blog will soon be available. There were some delays, but my Polish support team tells me we're nearly there... I'll keep you updated on that too.

It was kind of her, though.   Then I rejoined the gentleman selling watermelons on the side of the road to answer a few questions he had. While eating a fruit he had just opened to share with me, I explained a little about my journey and my path. It was a pleasant moment. Plus, there was the free watermelon—a generous but "poisoned" gift, weighing at least 6 kilos. I expected my bag to be excessively heavy. It weighed 47 kilos! That’s definitely too much. I’ll have to make some decisions to reduce this. I plan to do that soon, once I reach the town where I can send items back to France that I no longer need.    Before I left to resume my journey, he handed me a small bundle of notes he had prepared by quietly emptying his cash counter. Each floor had a few simple but well-appointed rooms and dormitories.    After settling in, I rushed to the sports store on the other side of town to buy or order the items I frequently need to replace. There was no access to the driver from whom I expected to buy a ticket—not even a hygiaphone. The driver gestured at me through the window, pointing backward with his thumb. Following the direction indicated, I saw boxes attached to the poles. Payment was only possible via contactless credit card or by scanning a QR code and using a payment app on a phone—none of which suited me.     It was the mother of the two little girls who helped. He’s pleasant and friendly, and assures me there’s no issue with staying in the spot I’ve chosen for the night—and possibly the next. I find it remarkably aesthetic. He heads down into the garden and returns with three large, beautiful tomatoes, weighing over a kilo and a half in total. They’re enormous, sun-split, and incredibly juicy, with the rich taste and aroma of proper tomatoes.     Before we leave, he steps inside, speaking aloud the whole time, and comes back with a large bottle of very fresh sparkling water—cold even—a can of red beans, and a packet of biscuits. I politely refuse the can of tuna and pâté, explaining my vegetarianism...     Leaving this place where I stayed for two nights, I passed through a small village nearby to refill my water bottles. Spotting a restaurant, the idea of a cooked meal tempted me, so I stopped at the café next door to wait for the restaurant to open in an hour. The café owner, also the bartender, offered me a drink and a smile. He suggested putting my water bottles in his refrigerator while I waited, a kind gesture but unnecessary since the bottles would heat up quickly once I left. I chatted with him and the regular patrons playing cards at a nearby table. Then I picked up my bag, said my goodbyes, and set off, knowing I’d pass by again as the river and the nearby bridge were the only crossings in the area.    I chose to walk along the bank without the asphalt cycle path, which is hard underfoot and radiates the sun’s heat. Satellite views showed that side had more vegetation, offering shade for my route today and tomorrow.    At the restaurant, I had a meal while chatting with the young owner and her mother, who cooked the food. She invited me to recharge my devices at the outlets behind the checkout and suggested I shop at the nearby grocery store while leaving my things safely there. She seemed taken aback by my pilgrimage story and thanked me for coming to her restaurant and sharing it.    As I left and passed the café again, an outdoor table called me over. The story of the French pilgrim had spread, and I was easily recognizable. I happily stopped to answer questions while enjoying a drink they offered. The café exuded a warm, village atmosphere. I don’t mind spending time like that. The only thing I can offer in exchange for the kindness I receive is sharing my experiences, and I do so gladly. By the time I left, the sun had lowered, making the heat less oppressive.    I stopped a kilometer past the village, with about 20 kilometers ahead before reaching the next village where I could get water. The map showed a leisure camp halfway along the route. I figured I could ask for water there. At 5–6 liters a day, my dependence on water is clear.    The camp turned out to be a leisure center with an entry fee, offering a massive swimming pool, children’s play areas, a terrace, deck chairs, a restaurant, and two bars—one inside the pool. It was clearly a popular spot for families from nearby areas.     I arrived through an unguarded back entrance, the overgrown grass suggesting it wasn’t a usual path. Heading toward the building, I sought a manager to explain my entry and ask for tap water. Once inside, I thought I might pay the fee, eat, and use the pool. I don’t particularly enjoy crowded, noisy pools filled with chlorine, but a pool likely meant a nearby shower, which interested me.     One of the owners greeted me and handed me a bottle of chilled mineral water from the fridge. He said I couldn’t use the pool shower but would instead have access to a private one in a room he’d open for me. He explained that the room wasn’t yet cleaned but would be soon. He called over a young employee, around 25 and fluent in English, to tell me I was welcome to a shower, food, and even a night in the room if needed. Additionally, his wife could do my laundry if I wanted. I was stunned but accepted the invitation, as everything felt genuine.     After a shower and meal, I lay in the room near an outlet, charging my phone and writing these notes. A couple of hours later, the young man knocked on the door. When I opened it, he handed me a bag of food that his brother had gone to buy for me in the village, along with some money. I began to refuse, but he insisted, saying it was a local tradition.    “My father passed away some time ago,” he explained, “I’m doing this in his name.” I asked for his father’s name—it was Sergio.     Sergio made good boys, I think...    He then asked if I’d agree to take a photo with one of the employees who wanted a souvenir of the Frenchman who came on foot from France. Then, of course, he wanted one as well, followed by the bosses. We took the first few pictures straight away, while the group photos with the bosses and all the staff were planned for the next morning at my departure, with everyone gathered, my equipment, and the sun just right.    Another beautiful day ended with a good night’s rest. In the morning, I woke up early—four years of living by the solar rhythm does that. I wandered over to the swimming pool, which was calm and serene. One of the brothers who owns the camp was already there, tending to the water. A swimming pool in full sun with hundreds of daily bathers requires a lot of maintenance, he explained, before showing me the water pumping station in the basement and the filtration and cleaning systems. Even more so when I discovered that they didn’t use any chemicals for water treatment—just salt and filtration. Impressive. Afterward, I went for a swim, and when he returned with coffee, I joined him for a break. Morning bliss: a dip in cool water followed by a coffee break.    When I finally left the camp, it was already late. I knew because it was 32°C, and I was struggling. Stocked up on drinking water and food, my bag was heavy again, as always. After walking just 800 meters, I was drenched in sweat and my heart was racing. I stopped for half an hour to cool down, dry off, and let my body recover. I drank water, rested, and set off again. Another kilometer passed, and I had to stop once more—it must have been 34°C by then. They’d warned me at the camp that the temperature would rise to 38°C today. I knew I’d have to stop by midday, likely around 11 a.m., and wait for the sun to dip and the temperature to drop before continuing.    I decided to push forward for another stretch. After just 400 meters, I spotted a place that seemed perfect for waiting out the hottest hours.    I was walking along the top of a riverside embankment. A few meters below, there was a flat area, maybe a few meters wide, followed by another slope down to the riverbank. There, a small, cleared beach appeared, likely the work of local fishermen. Fishing is a common pastime in Romania. The area was lush with vegetation, shaded by enormous willow trees. I was certain the sun wouldn’t reach the spot until it was setting, long after I would have left.     I hadn’t planned to stop yet—I still had enough energy for another stretch or two before resting. But something about the place called to me. Its idyllic setting, with easy access to the water and none of the mud or dense plants that often make getting in and out difficult, was irresistible. Though I knew I might find a similar spot later, this one felt right. So, I went down.    The place was magnificent. I set my bag against a tree stump by the small beach and leaned back, stretching my legs toward the water. The wildlife I’d disturbed upon arrival—moorhens diving, herons and ducks taking flight, frogs disappearing into the depths—had all scattered. I let the sweat finish dripping off as I relaxed.    The river was calm, about fifteen meters wide, flowing slowly but powerfully due to its depth—three to four meters at the center. The water was turbid but not dirty or unappealing. Perhaps my perception was influenced by the heat and the sweat stinging my eyes, making the idea of a swim all the more tempting.   I stayed put, letting the water flow and time pass. Ten minutes went by without a single movement. The local wildlife began to resume its activity, likely forgetting I was there.   Then, suddenly, off to the side among the water plants about two meters from the bank, something started thrashing wildly. Powerful, noisy strikes—perhaps paw knocks, though they didn’t make sense to me. There were about ten blows, strong and loud, but they didn’t seem to indicate movement or predation. It was as if the creature, still unseen, was trying to push the vegetation around it with great force. It was baffling.     I watched, motionless, trying to identify it. My first guess was a frog, but it would have to be enormous to create such commotion. Perhaps a bullfrog—they can weigh up to a kilo—but the behavior didn’t align. A turtle, maybe? No, turtles are slow and deliberate. Could it be a coypu? It certainly wasn’t a moorhen—the tightly packed rushes would act as bars, and a moorhen is too small to make such a racket. Whatever it was, its powerful display didn’t match anything I’d encountered before. Strange.    I remain still, immobile, concentrating. I can't see the animal, but I am overwhelmed by an unsettling feeling that something is deeply wrong.     It begins again, violently, with bursts of energy, and I feel worse. An inexplicable worry grows within me, as if a foreign emotion has invaded my mind. I try to observe myself, analyze what is happening both outside and within. The rushes move with each blow, water splashes, then calm returns—but inside me, the turmoil persists. The calm feels deceptive. It's as though... as though what I'm feeling doesn't belong to me.     I sense despair.   The thought is irrational, even absurd. How could I be feeling something that isn't mine? It seems delusional, yet the sensation is so vivid that I can't push it away. I try reasoning with myself, but introspection can mislead.    Before I realize it, I am already moving, gripped by urgency. My shoes come off quickly; I force myself to remove my socks, though I feel an almost compulsive need to step into the water immediately. First one foot, sinking 10 cm into water, 10 into mud. Then the other, deeper now—20 cm of water, 30 of silt. With a third step, I reach the area where I saw the movement. I still can't identify the creature, but I see a dark mass. It must be it.     I hesitate only briefly before stepping further. The mud is treacherous, and I could easily sink, but I try to distribute my weight by stepping on the rush stems and vegetation, hoping they act like snowshoes on the surface. My arms stretch toward the submerged mass.     It works. I sink, but slowly. My presence triggers another violent commotion, and suddenly, I understand. It’s a trapped wader. The bird is lying in the water, its body submerged, one wing resting on the vegetation, and its head barely emerging among the thick stems. Its legs are hopelessly tangled in fishing line, wrapped tightly around plants and limbs—a careless trap left by fishermen who didn’t bother to clean up.     The bird is exhausted, almost lifeless, held up only by the vegetation. It barely has the energy to keep its head above water. When I carefully grasp it, speaking softly to reassure it, the bird doesn’t even struggle. Its frailty is heartbreaking.     I must act quickly. The water now reaches my thighs, and there's no firm ground beneath me. I shift my weight to one foot and pull out my pocketknife. The tangle of wire, plants, and legs is so dense that I cut through everything preventing me from returning to the bank with the bird. I make rough, decisive cuts, freeing it just enough to retreat.    Pulling my leg out of the mud is arduous, the sticky silt clinging to me stubbornly. When I finally succeed, I shake off the muck in the water, noting its lack of odor—perhaps a sign of the river's health.     Back on the bank, I sit cross-legged, leaning against my backpack with the bird cradled in my lap. Its legs stretch out before me, and I begin untangling the mess. The tightest loops dig into its flesh, too snug to fit my blade underneath. I start with the easier knots, gradually loosening the rest. It takes ten painstaking minutes. Throughout, the bird barely moves.    I speak gently, tenderly, trying to soothe its instincts and fears. Whether it’s my tone, its exhaustion, or resignation, the bird remains calm, only watching me with quiet intensity.     When the last thread is cut and I confirm it has no injuries, I place the bird on the ground in front of me. Weak but free, it pinches my fingers with its beak. I can’t tell if it’s a gesture of gratitude or the feeble defense of a creature still wary of me. I choose to believe it’s the former.     Releasing it, I watch as it slowly rises, unsteadily finding its footing. After a moment, it runs toward the bushes and disappears into the greenery.     I stay seated, motionless. Time passes. Everything is quiet. I realize after these serene moments that I experience a pleasant feeling of intense satisfaction, of deep contentment. And yet I remain calm and still. Everything has been so calm. Like in a dream, as if detached. Executed without agitation, without even emotions I believe, and the result was a succession of moments of accuracy, of sure and precise movements. What remains is this deep feeling of calm and contentment. I feel like I’m on drugs.     When I get up to go rinse, and then bathe while I'm at it, I hear it fly away. It emerges from the thicket, climbs the small slope leading to the dike, and takes off. It seems to be doing well. Today, I tell myself, I saved a life. It makes me smile. I feel good.     I bathe. That feels good too.    I leave once dried, carrying this feeling of having done something—not necessarily important, though from the bird's perspective it certainly was—but something right. And that’s what gives me a real, deep, and strangely persistent contentment. I then walk with a light step despite a heavy backpack. The sun has gone down, and so has the temperature.     I am now approaching the border with Serbia. I know this all the more because I am stopped by a border police patrol as soon as I leave the path running along the river. They check my passport, ask where I'm going, and inquire about my route to ensure I plan to pass through an official border post. Then they let me go, mentioning the village grocery store I’m about to pass. Over the next two days, it will take me to reach the border, I encounter 12 patrols in total.     Each patrol checks me, sometimes barely an hour apart. The closer I get, the more I sense their tension. They seem worried I might cross illegally. This strikes me as illogical since they’ve already checked my passport, confirmed I’m French, and thus know I don’t need any special authorization, papers, or visas to leave Romania or enter Serbia. I’ve "shown white paws" (proven innocence) at every check.     Now, however, these checks take up to an hour because the patrols are perplexed by my case and call for a superior to ensure no mistakes are made. Each time, I recount a bit of my story, answer trick questions designed to uncover any possible deception, and then respond to their personal curiosity while we wait for their superior. They scrutinize my passport meticulously, examining each seam, feeling the thickness of the pages, and watching my reactions as much as they inspect the document itself. If the passport were fake, I would surely betray tension or anxiety, their demeanor seems to suggest.    After inspecting the passport, they go to the vehicle’s onboard computer, typing away. They return, acting as though something is amiss, then scan the passport cover to access the biometric chip. But they lack a network connection to verify it, which makes me smile. I remain patient. They ask again where I’m going.     "Uh, where I’m going tonight, or in general?" I respond, seeing their puzzled faces. "Tonight, I’m going here," I say, pointing to a spot on my phone map. "But I’m heading to this customs post," I add, marking the pin from my planned itinerary, "and, in general, to Serbia. And more broadly, I’m going to Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the sanctuary of Medjugorje."     I try to be precise, knowing every word seems scrutinized as if they’re determined to uncover some hidden motive. After all the fuss, they hand back my passport and tell me I can proceed, but warn me not to approach the border.     I smile at them, repeating once again that my planned itinerary is clear and shows exactly where I’ll pass and how close I’ll get to the border. "Yes, okay," they reply, "but don’t go near the border, okay?"     An exchange of deaf, almost.     And then come the last kilometers. I leave the bushes where I spent the night. Barely 300 meters later, I hear a 4x4 SUV quickly approaching behind me. I don’t even turn around. I know it’s a border police patrol, and I know they lack internal communication, as the previous six patrols have already informed me. So, this seventh patrol has no idea about my presence yet and rushes toward me on the small dirt road as if they’re about to catch me with no chance of escape.    The same scenario unfolds: passport control, questions, answers, doubts, a call to the chief. After 15 minutes, the chief arrives, inquires with his subordinates, then with me, then back to the others. After lengthy discussions, he authorizes me to continue (so generous!)—but only if I take a detour back to the main road. Ahead lies a village on my chosen route, where I plan to eat at a restaurant, shop, and refill my bottles. We can see the village, about 2 km away, at the end of the road. The main road, however, is 600 meters to my left, requiring me to retrace my steps a few hundred meters to join a dirt road leading to it.     I have no desire to comply. The detour adds nearly 3 km to the remaining 8 I have, forcing me onto a busy road with no shade or safe resting spots. Walking straight to the village makes far more sense, even without the shade. This is an agricultural region: flat fields stretching to the horizon, with sparse vegetation barely reaching the size of bushes.     I ask if there’s a specific reason for this demand. He replies with a rhetorical question: "Do you know where you are?" Of course, I know—I’ve just spent 15 minutes showing my route on my topographic app. With condescension, he tells me I’m near the border, in a restricted area where I’m not allowed to walk. This sounds nonsensical, though I’m not entirely sure. I ask the size of the restricted area. He claims it extends 30 km from the border, which is utterly implausible. If true, it would mean I can’t walk anywhere off main roads leading to border posts—even those on smaller roads, like the cycle path I used since Timisoara!    The chief seems intent on forcing me to take a route that suits him better than my planned itinerary. I demonstrate on the map that my route is much more logical for a pedestrian, avoiding the long zigzags of the main road, which adds 3 km and runs through villages. I also explain that the main road is far more dangerous—long straight stretches where vehicles speed recklessly.     Now he gets angry. He refuses to let me continue. He orders me into the patrol vehicle, offering to drop me at the border post—not to help, but to rid himself of the "problem." I refuse, not to antagonize but to preserve the integrity of my pilgrimage, done entirely on foot, as traditional pilgrims would. It would frustrate me deeply to admit that, among 8,912 km, I had to take a police car for a dozen kilometers to appease an anxious, authoritarian customs officer.     The chief then claims the dirt road I’m following is prohibited to the public, even pedestrians, as it’s reserved for agricultural vehicles. At this point, he loses all credibility. His uniform is tainted by his dishonest, authoritarian attitude, prioritizing personal convenience over proper conduct. I firmly refuse his orders, pointing out that the only "problem" is my presence on camera, triggering alarms for patrols unaware that I’ve already been checked seven times. This is their problem, not mine—it’s simply their job to manage it.     As the situation escalates, I call the customs officers I met upon entering Romania. By chance, they’re hiking with their families on the Via Transylvanica. They confirm my rights: the restricted area is only 20 meters from the border, and tractor paths are entirely permissible for pedestrians. They even express frustration that I’ve been harassed over something so straightforward.     I hand my phone to the chief. His expression falls as he realizes he’s speaking to a colleague—someone fluent in Romanian and familiar with the law. Caught abusing his authority and lying, he loses face—not just personally but for his uniform. This saddens me, not for him, but for the respect his position should command.    Stanley Milgram’s experiments on authority should be studied more, I think. It might reduce such unnecessary abuses of power and the resulting erosion of respect for authority, regardless of the uniform. Romania hasn’t yet reached France’s level, where authority often lacks respect, but encounters like this suggest it might someday.     After hanging up, the situation resolves quickly. I’m "authorized" to proceed and leave without delay, having already wasted an hour in this absurd exchange. The chief drives off, but the patrol car trails me, alternating between crawling at my speed and stopping 100 meters ahead, waiting for me to catch up, then speeding past again. By the time I reach the village, I’m covered in dust, clinging to my sweat-soaked clothes. It seems that, having embarrassed himself, the chief sought to dirty me in return.     I would be checked five more times, but each interaction would be professional. Still, better internal communication could have spared a lot of unnecessary trips and tension for the patrols.     Later that evening, I’d meet two teams in vans equipped with telescopic thermal cameras. These officers were friendly and, after chatting by the roadside, gave me a tour of their setup. Half the van housed detection equipment; the other half contained an office space with two gamer-like seats, joysticks, keyboards, and four screens. They spent nights in this cramped space, spotting shrews from 3 km away in total darkness.     They were really nice guys. After the visit, they asked me many questions to which I answered with pleasure. Their interest and questioning were genuine, sincere, and personal. Before leaving, they advised me to ask the watchman of the nearby silo for permission to pitch my tent on the property. They explained that while I could continue to the spot I had planned, a bit further along the dirt road leading to the border, I might be woken up multiple times during the night by patrols. Sleeping under the watchman’s surveillance would likely ensure a full night of rest. When I asked if they could send a radio message to notify all patrols of my presence, they explained that due to shift changes, the safest option was to ask the watchman. They were confident he would agree.     So, I went to see the watchman at the gate and asked if I could stay on the cooperative grounds. "No worries, put yourself wherever you want on this side," he said, gesturing to an area near the path I’d take in the morning.     I pitched my tent there, a simple setup without the rainfly due to the heat but still enclosed to protect against mosquitoes. I took a "bottle shower" after sunset to rinse off sweat and dust. Over time, I’ve learned to manage a full shower with just 1.5 liters of water, adding another liter if I wash my hair. Carrying water on my back has made me very economical with it. Despite the floodlights illuminating the area around the massive silo and the adjacent park of agricultural vehicles, I had a radiant night.     In the morning, the watchman kindly offered me fresh mineral water from an office fountain. After a handshake and a wish for good luck, I resumed my journey.    Customs control stopped me barely 100 meters later. I was 5 km in a straight line from the border post I intended to cross and 8.5 km by the main road. Given the past two days, I thought this would be a quick check—just a confirmation that I was the "French guy" they’d already heard about. Perhaps a brief exchange, a reminder not to cross illegally, and a "have a nice day."     But no, the same procedure unfolded: a full hour-long check, calls to superiors, and eventually, a personal escort. I couldn’t help but wonder how this compared to approaching the Iron Curtain during its time.     This time, the escort vehicle followed me at a distance of 200–300 meters. The front passenger used binoculars, which made me smile internally, as I had planned to cross a small stretch of wasteland the car couldn’t navigate. They would need to find another path, losing sight of me for a few minutes.     Unfortunately, nature called, and the sparse, flat terrain offered little privacy. I had hoped the tall grass of the wasteland would suffice, sparing the binoculars operator any traumatic sights. However, they anticipated my route and were already waiting on the other side. I’ll spare the details of my necessary stop, but let’s say my training in India has diminished any lingering embarrassment.     The second patrol escorted me to within 1 km of the border post, where we parted ways after several friendly exchanges. One officer seemed genuinely interested in the spiritual aspect of my pilgrimage, while both maintained a professional yet relaxed attitude. They seemed to share my sense of the absurdity of the situation.   During my final break before reaching the post, a surveillance drone appeared overhead. Hovering about 50 meters up, it fixed its camera on me, scanning the surroundings. Leaning against my bag, I raised a hand in greeting to help it locate me. After a few minutes, the drone moved, scanned the area again, then left.     Shortly afterward, another patrol arrived. The officer, one of the morning’s chiefs, asked if I was okay. I said I was resting from the sun and the heavy load. "Was that your drone?" I asked. "Of course," she replied, then asked, "You’ll pass the border at the post, right?" I didn’t answer verbally, but my expression must have spoken volumes. She wished me a good trip and left.     Finally, I reached the border and crossed without issue. A Romanian officer even came out of the post to offer me a bottle of cold water and wish me safe travels.     Whenever locals ask if I’m well-received in their region, I always say I’ve encountered kindness, generosity, and warm welcomes everywhere. Crossing into Serbia, I felt confident this would continue.     I wasn’t disappointed. In the first village, I approached a man cycling to ask about getting a local SIM card. He accompanied me to exchange currency and then helped me buy a SIM card, ensuring it suited my needs.     At a café where I stopped to activate the SIM and recharge, the owner offered me a coffee on the house, saying it was her way of welcoming me as a first-time visitor.    Later, at a restaurant, the staff refused payment for my meal, saying it was their treat. The owner even helped me refill my water bottles at a hand pump outside, making the task easier by pumping while I filled.     All of this happened within three hours of entering Serbia. It was a warm welcome to new territory.     As I write these words, I’m by a river where I bathed with delight every two hours during the day. My tent is pitched 3 meters from the water, shaded and hidden by large trees. I’m seated comfortably on a chair left by regulars, likely fishermen or swimmers. My back rests against one chair, my feet on another—a classic "working position."    A fisherman arrives and sets up nearby. We greet each other, exchange pleasantries, then fall into a companionable silence. I continue writing while he fishes. After a couple of hours, less successful for him than for me, a couple visits him with cold drinks. They offer me an iced coffee, insisting despite my polite refusal. We chat briefly as I give up my chair to the lady, gallantry obliges.     When they leave, they hand me a bottle of ice water.    The fisherman lingers a bit longer, hoping for a catch, then eventually packs up. Shaking my hand, he asks if I’ll be there tomorrow. "No, I’ll be back on the road in the morning," I reply. A fish splashes loudly in the water, as if mocking him.     "So goodbye," he says, "and good trip."     "Goodbye, thank you."     He leaves, and I retreat to my tent. Darkness has almost fully fallen. Another great day.

Meeting with a Doe


		20/7/2024
	
     Hello everyone,     Three months without news—I’m overdoing it a bit.     Here’s the update:     Since last time, many good things have happened, and no bad things. That’s a decent balance.    Still, I feel like complaining. Firstly, because it’s a basic human need, and secondly, because I’m French. As the cliché goes, the French love to complain, followed by a good protest.     My chosen subject of complaint: the temperature. For the past two and a half months, it’s been consistently 35⁰C, with spikes to 38⁰C and even 43⁰C on three occasions.   It’s unbearable. Walking in this sun and heat is no longer just challenging; it’s becoming dangerous. I’ve had to adjust my walking schedule to avoid the midday extremes.     I now wake up 30 minutes to an hour before sunrise to pack my things. When daylight breaks, I fold the tent and start walking early, continuing until around 11 a.m. or noon—longer if I haven’t found a suitable resting spot. Romania is an hour ahead of Central Europe, so the timing feels slightly off.  I stop in the shade of forests, caves, or villages—often meeting new people in cafés or restaurants. These breaks allow me to recharge my batteries—both electrical and social. Sometimes, I’m invited to stay, which I often accept, drawn by the promise of a shower and good company.     I set out again around 4:30 or 5 p.m., walking until I find a welcoming place to stop or until the sun sets, usually around 8 p.m.    I don’t always pitch the tent. In this summer weather, sleeping under the stars is comfortable, with the Milky Way serving as my sleeping bag. It also saves time tidying up in the morning.    Sleeping outdoors has taught me to tolerate the local fauna. Insects often crawl over me as I sleep, but I’ve learned not to react. An earwig running across my skin or a beetle tangled in my hair no longer bothers me as much. I used to think they got caught intentionally, but after observing, I realized their shell design is to blame. If I don’t carefully untangle them, they risk losing legs or antennae—or worse, pulling out my hair.    Some beetles pinch, likely to express their discomfort, creating mine. When that happens, I wake up, fully aware of the incident—unlike many other encounters that don’t disturb my sleep. It’s like how we notice a sore knee only when we bump it, even though we probably hit it just as often when it doesn’t hurt. A beetle in your hair is a similar, unforgettable experience.    Larger creatures, from shrews and hedgehogs to grass snakes, foxes, and weasels, tend to keep their distance. Without the tent obscuring their view or smell, they quickly recognize me as human—the ultimate nightmare—and flee without hesitation.     If they are sane, everyone flees. So when that doesn’t happen, it’s a notable and often touching event.     For example, one morning during this pilgrimage, I was lying on my mattress (it’s still necessary to isolate yourself from the dampness of the ground to sleep better), my head resting on my hand, against my bag, and leaning against a tree at the edge of a wood. Like a hunting dog curled up and asleep, I faced a small grassy clearing. I was awakened by a presence.    It didn’t feel alarming. I stayed calm, listening. I believe the brain, even while asleep, can hear and analyze sounds in the immediate environment, alerting us if necessary. I’ve experienced this four times now during nocturnal visits from bears. But this time, there was no urgency, no danger.    I opened my eyes. About fifteen meters away, an enormous doe was grazing nonchalantly. I say enormous because it was not a deer but an adult doe—and an adult doe is large. She grazed noisily on the grass. Well, noisy for someone like me, now awake and trying to be still. In the calm morning silence of nature, after a good night’s sleep, I lay motionless, amazed by the spectacle. Usually, such encounters are fleeting, as frightened animals quickly flee.    I savored the moment, staying as still as possible while observing her. Then, about ten meters away, I noticed a small fawn, likely old enough to have lost its spots. I wanted to lift my head slightly to see it better but didn’t dare move.     Eventually, I had to adjust—or perhaps my breathing changed—because the doe suddenly raised her angular head. Her whole body tensed, motionless, on alert.     That’s when we locked eyes. We stared at each other, directly into each other’s gaze—a moment suspended in time. It felt so real that it was almost unreal. Probably just a fraction of a second, but it felt eternal. Both of us were frozen in attentive silence.    And then, as nothing happened, she seemed to decide that I wasn’t a threat and resumed grazing.    That’s what moved me the most. The moment of eye contact was intense, but her choice to start grazing again, despite knowing the worst of predators—the most destructive of creatures—was nearby, truly touched me. It felt as though she had decided to trust me.     I felt accepted, as if I had become part of her world. You can’t imagine how proud this made me. It’s a moment etched in my memory, one that strengthens me when I recall it. Hindus have a term for such experiences: “Darshan.”    We stayed like that for a few minutes. She tore at the tender grass, taking a step between each bite, while I remained still, listening to my heart pound as if I were receiving a kiss for the first time.     These are the kinds of moments that can happen when you sleep under the stars.   I’m nearing the Serbian-Romanian border. My journey continues toward the sanctuary of Medjugorje in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which means crossing Serbia.     I hope the summer won’t be as hot as the spring, though I’m not optimistic.     I hope everything is going well for you and wish you health and happiness.     See you soon.     P.S.:     I have a good excuse for being late with updates. I’ve overexposed myself to phone screens while working on putting a blog online. I’ll share the address once it’s ready.    Writing and sending these updates, attaching photos, and sending them to all my contacts has become tedious. Platforms like Signal or WhatsApp only allow sending to five contacts at a time. Between each batch, I have to reselect text and photos, then sift through my contact list to choose the next five while remembering who hasn’t received it yet.     With several hundred contacts—and the list growing—the process isn’t getting any easier.    The blog should simplify things while improving practicality. It might even reach others who haven’t met me but could appreciate the content.     What content? Nearly all the updates I’ve sent since starting this pilgrimage in September 2020, plus a selection of the best photos, and complete answers to frequently asked questions.     Voila. A good excuse, right?

After introductions, he asked if I needed anything and offered me milk from his farm. I couldn’t refuse. Fresh, organic milk. He filled a 2.5-liter bottle with milk, rich in flavor and freshly drawn from the tank in his small milking parlor.     This is how surreal the journey becomes—the welcome I receive from the people I meet. It has been like this for more than three years now, and I can continue like this. Every day I walk, and every day I meet people, have these kinds of encounters. I will continue like this.    The next day, at the entrance to a village, I was stopped by a man surrounded by a crowd of children. He was working on the fence of his small plot of land and, as usual, asked what I was doing there. I gave my standard response: pilgrim/French/not understand. Suddenly, I heard a woman’s voice say in French, "Ah, you're French, but what are you doing here? Have you eaten? Come inside the house, sit down." She gave me a plate of soup with a thick, two- or three-centimeter slice of bread that she baked herself in a wood-fired stove. Then the man cooked some potatoes, and we all ate together. This is how I met the family of Arabella, Christian, and their six children. I spent the night at their place.    Two days later, while resting on a bench at the crossroads of a road and a street in a small village, a car stopped next to me. The driver rolled down his window and asked what I was doing there. He spoke both English and French, while his wife next to him spoke fluent German. Within a minute, Eugène, the driver, and his wife Héléna invited me to their home for lunch and a shower. Eugène was the priest of his village, and Héléna was a religious icon painter who had previously been a professional opera singer.    The connection was instant. Eugène invited me to stay in his vacation home, a disused sheepfold in the hills 4 km from his house. He had set it up as a small retirement retreat. It was perfect for me because I could organize the delivery of my package from France to the nearby city and wait until it arrived, aligning my visit with Eugène’s schedule.     I stayed there for three nights. The small wood stove in the room kept me warm. The space was simple: a bed, a table, a chair, a small shelf, and, at the foot of the bed, a piece of furniture with a television. Eugène came to see me every day, sometimes with Héléna, bringing food, sharing a glass of homemade wine, and chatting.    I left with a superb memory of this couple, so evidently in love. Eugène, with his Santa Claus appearance, radiated kindness and honesty. Héléna, older but vibrant and brilliant, exuded the sensitivity and refinement of a true artist. As I left, I thought I could have stayed much longer. Eugène had even invited me to return and live in the sheepfold if I wanted.     At the edge of the village where we had met, in the church where Eugène was officiating that morning and Héléna was singing (I couldn’t miss that), I stopped at the last house. Sitting on a bench against a fence, I pulled out my topographical map to plan my path. I wanted to avoid the main road and noticed a small river flowing in my direction. A dike beside it looked walkable, though its meanders would lengthen my route. Still, it was a better option than dealing with road traffic.   As I sat there, a woman of about 70 emerged from her house. The dogs had, of course, announced my presence. She asked what I was doing there, so I played my pre-recorded introduction. She began to cry. "Oh no," I thought, "there’s nothing sad here." She stood before me, tears streaming down her small face, her gray hair tucked under a loosely tied scarf.    I didn’t know what to do, but a wave of affection for this little lady moved me to act. I gently hugged her and smiled. Then, speaking softly in French, I said a few words—not because she would understand them, but because in that moment, it wasn’t the meaning of the words that mattered, but their tone and timing.     So, the neighbor across the street comes out to ask what's going on. A very recognizable woman in her attire—the tight scarf on her head and the skirt, but above all, the colors. I spend a moment there explaining, discussing, and consoling before embarking on the dike which, according to the map, takes me to the city.     The arrival at Targu Mureș takes place under pouring rain that hasn’t stopped for two days. I go directly to the guesthouse waiting for me. I plan to spend two days there; the package has already arrived, but the letter containing the bank card is late. That gives me time to go wash my sleeping bag.    For this, I head to a dry cleaner in a large shopping mall. Cleaning a natural goose-down sleeping bag requires industrial dry cleaning. Many small dry cleaners are not equipped for this. After dropping it off, I visit the local tourist office to ask for some information, including a dentist's contact. Since I’m in town for a few days, I figure a quick dental check-up wouldn’t hurt. But, as you know, appointments aren’t easy to get quickly. It’s not the Tourist Office’s job to arrange this, but the staff member is helpful and offers to assist. He makes the calls—it’s easier in Romanian—and after a few minutes, the third dentist he contacts gives me an appointment for the next morning at 10 a.m. Miraculous, right?   I go as planned, and to describe the atmosphere that continues to surround me, the dentist refuses to let me pay. I leave with numerous free samples as well.    The next day, I retrieve my sleeping bag. I take the bus and arrive at the dry cleaner’s counter. The lady hands me my bag in a large transparent plastic cover—you know the kind. I’m immediately about to open it, but she stops me. She doesn’t speak English but seems to suggest I don’t need to open it now. Strange... I tell her I have a compression bag for the sleeping bag so it can fit neatly in my backpack with all the straps tightened. Much more practical for the bus. Yet something in her attitude raises my suspicion, so I decide to examine the sleeping bag right away to ensure everything is in order.     Good thing I do! The bag is as dirty as when I brought it in. What’s more, it now has a bad smell—worse than before! So this, I realize, is the reason for her behavior. She didn’t wash the bag—or perhaps she tried, then gave up after seeing how much work it would take. Whatever the case, my sleeping bag is now in worse condition than when I dropped it off.     She insists the smell is normal for goose feathers. But I know my sleeping bag well, having spent over 2,000 nights in it and had it professionally cleaned several times before. I show her the dark marks that prompted me to bring it in for cleaning in the first place. They are still there. She explains they didn’t come out in the wash, even though she “washed it twice to be sure!” I know I’m being scammed. She took the money (cleaning a sleeping bag is generally expensive) and is pretending everything is fine.     Seeing there’s nothing more I can do or say, I resign myself and leave. I won’t be able to take it to another dry cleaner before my departure since I’ll have to leave the city soon. My budget doesn’t allow me to extend my stay in the guesthouse.     Two days later, I left the city and pitched my tent near the river. I got ready to go to bed and climbed into my sleeping bag. I had dried it as best as possible above a radiator in the room I occupied. The smell was still there but slightly diminished. When I brought my feet inside, I felt something unfamiliar. A seam... There was a seam that my feet were rubbing against. Normally, there was none—or rather, the seams were designed to be discreet, both to sight and touch. But here, a new seam was present, on top or in place of the original one. After examining it, I noticed that a roughly made seam, clearly done with a sewing machine, ran along the length of the sleeping bag, cutting through all the compartments containing the precious goose down.     I now understood that the scam wasn’t just the non-cleaning of the bag but the substitution and replacement of the original materials. You have to understand—a high-quality goose-down sleeping bag like this is very, very expensive. To sleep well, even at temperatures as low as -28°C this past winter, or -43°C in the Himalayan mountains, you need a bag you can trust. It can literally save your life.     I had bought mine used from someone who had returned from an expedition to Everest. These days, many people, not necessarily mountaineers, make that climb as part of commercial expeditions. For example, company executives may do it as part of team-building exercises or self-challenging endeavors. Most of them will never undertake such an experience again, and after descending, they resell or give away their equipment. I was fortunate to acquire a sleeping bag like that and used it extensively for over 17 years. The bag had served me well and lost some of its quality over time. I could no longer rely on it for temperatures below -30°C, but for temperatures as low as -25°C or -28°C, with proper clothing, it worked fine.    That night, in addition to the affront and the bad smell, I was cold. It wasn’t even below zero, but I had to wear warm clothes just to sleep. The feeling of having lost a reliable companion of many adventures—the sense that the bag had been desecrated—was painful at first. After some time, I consoled myself by imagining that some child might sleep under a super goose-down quilt next winter. It was just one less attachment for me to let go of.     I share this story because, until now, I’ve only shared the good moments, the meetings, and the behaviors that could belong to the realm of fairy tales. It wouldn’t be honest to represent my story without also sharing the less positive experiences. This is the second time since my departure that I’ve had a bad experience. (The first, which I kept to myself, involved a grocer in a small village refusing to give me the correct change for a bill, claiming it was half its actual value.)    This little misadventure isn’t pleasant, but honestly, compared to the three years I’ve tried to describe (which I can only partially convey despite my lengthy writing efforts), you’ll agree with me that this anecdote is insignificant, right? Or even compared to just the fortnight I told you about before... Or even just today, as I sit in my tent near the river, walking along its bank toward the Lipova Monastery.     Resuming my writing, which dates back a little now, I reflect on the bread that was offered to me at the church yesterday, along with a bottle of liturgical red wine. Another loaf, also offered yesterday by a French-speaking baker in a village I passed through, came with a tour of his bakery, where I recharged my batteries over coffee and homemade tomato juice. A huge piece of goat cheese and hard-boiled eggs came from a shepherd’s wife I met the day before yesterday in the meadow near her village. Her husband had called her to say I was approaching. She gave me coffee, a hot bean soup, sautéed potatoes, and breaded soy patties while the eggs hardened.     Oh, and the rest of the provisions I bought were thanks to the money a kind gentleman had given me. And yes, as I left the village yesterday, a man on a bike handed me a bag containing a jar of zacusca (so delicious!) and a pot of homemade plum jam.      And you know what? I don't know about you, but here it feels like spring—or even summer. So yes, I will have to find a replacement in preparation for next winter, but for now, I don’t really need more than the little I have left. And I have time ahead of me. So everything is fine.     Voilà for the news.     I hope everything is going well for you.     I wish you all the best.     See you soon.     Pretty P.S.:     Two days after this misfortune, Gabriel—whom you know because I described my meeting with him and his shed in the mountains where I had stayed to rest—informed me that the Bucharest mountaineering club had collected money to buy a new sleeping bag so that I can continue to walk. Moving, right?

I'll see about the rest later, but I really think that going over the pass is too difficult, to the point of being dangerously difficult.     It's hard to go back. But inevitability helps with choice.     I'm going back down. It's normally less hard because it goes downhill, and I walk in a track not yet completely closed by the snow carried by the wind. The further down I go, the more I know I made the right choice. My legs are shaking with the effort. I finally arrive at the cabin. It's 11 a.m. I remain there haggard, sitting on the bench. There are fir trees around; I have some nylon twine which could be sufficient for making both in terms of strength and length. And then I have parachute-type cord which could be used to attach them to my shoes... But we sink in much less. 30cm at most in powder...     But that doesn't solve the avalanche problem, nor the food problem...    No, I will have to retrace my steps for 24 km, then take a national road for the distance of 204 km to arrive at the same place where I would have been in 60 km if I had been able to pass these 6.5 km of snow-covered mountain...    Good. Without regrets, I think I did my best. And then you have to look on the bright side: I didn't die stupidly in the mountain! That’s it already, right?     And then it’s magnificent all around.     SO...

     ​Again, it’s been a while since I shared my journey with you. I had nothing new or special to say. No change in the pilgrim’s experience of the path.   But ultimately, I’m not required to be original or new all the time, especially when there is nothing new to share. So, I might as well pick up the nail where I left it last time—if you remember the metaphor.     So, here it is.    I came down from the forest through a small grassy meadow to reach a small road downhill. I had just spent three nights in this lovely forest, in a quiet and protected area. When I first arrived there, I was in a bit of a hurry. It was my birthday.    I had stopped at a restaurant to enjoy a hot meal and a power outlet. When I left, I quickly felt the urgent need to find a bathroom—in real hurry. It happens. For the restaurant’s defense, I don’t think the food quality was to blame, but rather the possible presence of non-vegetarian elements in the preparation. Something like pork fat for cooking, perhaps. For many people who are unfamiliar with vegetarianism, inattentive, or simply mischievous, cooking vegetables with lard still counts as a vegetarian dish...   For someone like me, who has abstained from meat products for more than 32 years, my digestive system reacts immediately—and violently.     Of course, this isn’t ideal on a busy road where each side is occupied by buildings and fenced-off properties. The few kilometers that followed were epic: tiring, distressing, and punctuated by numerous “open toilet breaks.”     Happy birthday, Emmanuel!     So I didn’t really choose where to stop. As soon as I saw a perpendicular path leading to a forest, I followed it until I found a welcoming place. I came down from that spot well-rested after three nights there. As I arrived at this small road, intending to follow it to a larger one, a gentleman in his garden spotted me and called out from afar.     He was far enough away that he had no idea who I was or what I was doing there, just that I had the look of a backpacker. Far enough, too, that I couldn’t really hear him, but I could see he was calling out. So I changed my direction and walked toward him. When I got within earshot, I said my usual line: "French/pilgrim/not understand." He replied, “Ah, okay! Coffee?”    The proposition was clear and tempting. A hot coffee early in the morning is always welcome, especially with the chill of the season. So, getting one just as I was starting my day was unexpected but very pleasant.     We sipped it together, joined by his wife on the terrace of their house, where he was finishing work on an outbuilding. It was a very nice encounter—simple and full of kindness. After an hour with them, I got back on the road. The main road wasn’t pleasant to walk along, as important roads often aren’t. The number of vehicles, and especially their speeds, made walking uncomfortable, stressful, and dangerous.   But I had no alternative, so I carefully monitored the traffic coming toward me. I wore headphones to block out the noise—whether with music, an audiobook, or even just silence.     At the intersection where I needed to take the left branch, a pedestrian crossed the road to meet me and asked what I was doing there. I showed him the short text recorded in my translator, summarizing the main ideas in one paragraph. After several handshakes and a few "very goud, very goud," I continued my walk toward the small grocery store located right at the intersection.     With my backpack emptied of all food, and having not eaten the day before or that morning, I thought a stop for provisions would be welcome. I placed my bag on one of the benches on the small terrace near the entrance—village grocery stores often have a café/bar attached with a terrace—and went inside.     Two cans of vegetable pâté, a block of cheese, five nicely red tomatoes, two bananas, and a loaf of sliced bread later, I stepped outside to grab the coins I had forgotten in the jacket on my bag, intending to add them to the 50 lei note I had already given. I wanted to simplify payment by offering a rounded amount. When I returned to the counter, the lady indicated that I owed nothing. “It’s for me,” she said. “Drum bun. Have a nice journey.”     Isn’t that surprising? Isn’t it pleasant? Isn’t it touching?     Apparently, the gentleman I had met earlier had entered after me, and while I was choosing my cans of pâté, he briefly introduced me to the lady. That’s how she ended up giving me back my money and saying, “It’s for me.”     After carefully putting the entire donation into the appropriate boxes in my bag, I resumed my journey, only to discover a roadside restaurant just a little further along the way. A sort of container-turned-chip shop/French fry/kebab stand. The idea of a hot and different meal tempted me. After all, I could save what I had bought for later. Hot food isn’t an everyday luxury. So I stopped.     Leaning on the counter, the gentleman ahead of me saw me, and we exchanged greetings. After my customary "French/pilgrim/not understanding" introduction, he began speaking in surprisingly good French—leftovers from high school, he said. It was not only practical but also pleasant to have a conversation and a translator for my order, just to ensure the hamburger I was ordering was truly vegetarian!     When his order was ready, he shook my hand and went on his way. A very nice meeting with a local teacher—Romanian, of course. While waiting for my burger, wallet in hand and ready to pay, I noticed the lady preparing it was on her phone, while another finished assembling a bag of fries and another burger.     I assumed it was a phone order—until she handed me her phone. On the screen was a message she had just written and translated for me: “The two burgers and fries are for you. It’s free. We wish you well. Have a nice journey.” I don’t want to sound melodramatic, but I nearly cried.   It’s not just the gesture itself—it’s the repetition, the frequency. The consistency. It touches something deep inside. You see? So the nail sinks in...    It was still only midday, and I had about ten kilometers left before reaching my destination: the Basilica of Cacica. I’m here now. Well, not precisely in the basilica as I write these words, but I’m right next door—maybe 200 meters away. I’m staying in a family home. It was one of the priests from the basilica who approached me as I was leaving. Night had already fallen; it was almost 5 p.m.     “Do you know where to sleep?” he asked me.     “No, not yet,” I replied.     “Come with me,” he said.     He led me to a neighbor’s house, and the neighbor then took me to another house, just behind his, on the other side of the garden.    He showed me the kitchen as he plugged in the refrigerator. Then he led me upstairs to the bathroom, saying there would soon be hot water (he knew the exact words a pilgrim would appreciate—or perhaps my smell made it clear how necessary it was!). And then he showed me the bedroom. “You stay as long as you want,” he said.     I’ve been experiencing this for three years. Three years!    Maybe you don’t realize—I don’t know. You can only read what I can write, and many things cannot be put into words. But imagine living this...     So.     Today, I decided something important.    Three years was the length of time I initially hoped to experience when I decided to go beyond southern Poland and the Czestochowa Monastery. It seemed enough—not to learn everything I wanted, but to establish something permanent.     Certainly, the impression is profound. Certainly, the imprint is there, the trace is marked. But I feel its fragility. I intuitively sense that there is much more. The nails can go further, deeper, to ensure they don’t come out.     I’m probably not a good student. I’m a very slow learner.     But I want to continue. It’s not that I don’t want to stop—I want to continue.     The nuance is very important.     So.    I’m heading back tomorrow morning. This may seem obvious to you, but it wasn’t. In recent months, I’ve experienced certain conditions that made me doubt—doubt the relevance of continuing this path, at least in this way. The water was enough to last until the next evening and the walk the day after to the next well or spring, whether natural or human-made.     As for food, it was tight. I decided to save the madeleine for the next evening and the banana for the departure the day after because walking on a completely empty stomach slows me down more than I already am from fatigue. So, I chose to stay and enjoy the luxury of a garden swimming pool, even if it meant fasting for a while. Fasting now and then is good...    When I finally left, my plan was to pass through the next village, 7 km away, to look for a grocery store (though none was indicated on my map) to buy food. Then, I’d walk another 2 km to find a place in the forest to pitch my tent and spend two days resting. You know the cycle I already described in my last message. I also needed to figure out how to recharge my power banks. I had no charge left in two of the three, and only 40% in the last one.    Normally, I expect to be invited to charge my batteries at the grocery stores or bars in the villages I pass through. After buying food and sipping coffee or a drink, I typically spend an hour or so charging everything.     But here’s the problem: I had no more money with me. The local currency is Lei, and I had only 15 Lei left. I had Euros and my bank card, but the small village grocery store didn’t accept either. You can see the complexity here—no way to buy food and no real excuse to ask to stay an hour to recharge my phone. This was a situation that could potentially become problematic, forcing me to walk 45 km to the next ATM.     But it’s been three years that everything has gone wonderfully well, and I am starting to get used to it—a certain confidence is becoming anchored.   When I speak of habit, I should clarify that it does not alter the quality of perception and wonder. At least, I hope not to get used to it in that way. Simply, the occurrence of these positive outcomes is such that I no longer listen to anxieties, doubts, or uncertainties. Despite what could easily become unpleasant or even difficult, I’ve reached an irrational yet very real serenity: it’s going to be fine.     So, here I am in this village. And there’s a grocery store! I find it easily. The lady running it does not accept cards or Euros, as expected and anticipated.     But she tells me to wait, grabs her phone, and calls her boss. He arrives 15 minutes later, agrees to exchange some Euros for me, and allows me to recharge my batteries in the shop.     I wait outside, sitting on the benches set up for the local regulars. Thirty minutes pass. An hour. The first battery gets recharged, but the other two, which typically take five hours, are not done yet. I tell myself that I can continue charging them partially until my phone, which is also charging, reaches 100%. Then I’ll leave. So I begin writing this message...     My bag is full of food and water. I’m ready...    And then the boss comes back with a friend and a bottle, offering me a beer and a polanta (a little plum! Or in this case, a pear). We talk.    He also has a guesthouse in the village, and after hearing my plan to pitch my tent in the next forest, he suggests I set it up in the garden of his guesthouse instead. I can shower and do laundry if I want—and of course, I will! I can also finish recharging my batteries there.     I met a couple of very nice hosts there, about to leave as they were taking the road early in the morning. I was invited by the owner of the place to share supper—a good hot vegetable soup. It was a nice change from bread, cheese, and tomatoes.    We spent the evening together discussing various things. They offered me a packet of dried fruit, a kilo of apricots, a bar of chocolate, a dozen hard-boiled eggs, and two cereal bars.    I said goodbye to them in the early morning and took the opportunity to remove my laundry from the line where it was trying to dry, because despite the lingering night, the sky was heavy with clouds. And, in fact, a few moments before I went back to sleep in the shelter of my tent, the rain began to fall.    Now, I’m seated at the patio table. Everyone has gone, and I’m alone. I’ll close the gate when I leave, as agreed. I’m finishing this message while charging my phone. In a moment, I’ll be back on the road, freshly washed, my clothes clean, my batteries and phone fully charged, my bags full of food and fruit, my water bottles full of water, and my pocket full of Lei (well, full enough 😜).    I don’t know why, but again I feel the need to explain these small, almost intangible things. Actually, it’s not so much about explaining as it is about sharing. But to share, I feel compelled to explain everything in detail: everything is fine... It went well. Kindness is a succulent spice.     It’s been like this for three years. In addition to being really pleasant to live with, it’s fortifying.     Voilà. That was a little hello from Transylvania.    P.S.: Sad news—my felt hat has given up the ghost. After almost three years of (almost) good service, after several repairs, seams, and other DIY rescue operations, it has finally reached a point of no return, with the material disintegrating. I gave it the last care and attention it deserved before letting it go. Even though the hat wasn’t much to look at just three months after I started my journey, its loss feels a little painful.     But hey! Good news: three hours after the lid of the trash can definitively sealed the fate of the first one, a gentleman offered me a new hat. He warned me that the gift was really fragile—not to say of poor quality—but, as he pointed out very pertinently, it would hold up until I could find a real one: a sturdy one, a solid one, a "real" hat.     So voilà, I walk protected temporarily, with the hope that finding a robust hat is not a utopia—that the very concept of a solid hat is not a myth.    Re-P.S.: Yes, I walk with garlic in my backpack. But no, that has nothing to do with the fact that I’m in Transylvania. It’s because I encounter far more mushrooms than vampires. With all the precipitation here, combined with the heat, mushrooms grow nicely and profusely. And it must be said, a little garlic suits them particularly well when I simmer them over a wood fire.    As for the vampires, the tale of the Count of Dracula and all that—I believe it’s a myth. A bit like solid hats, I guess...    And P.S. again, but the last one, I swear: I wanted to measure whether, and how much, my long messages are actually read. So, I thought that to check, you could write a secret code at the beginning of your reply message next time you write to me. This would allow me to gauge the relevance of persisting in writing and sending such long texts to people who might not have time to read them all. 😃    Now, as for the secret code—I have no real idea. That is to say, the idea of a secret code seemed very good to me when I thought of it, but I didn’t get any further than that. Well then, I’ll let you choose what seems most appropriate. Just make sure to specify that it’s indeed the code... ​😜😜😜
blog/hippie-family/index.html:
Hippie Family


		25/5/2021
	
​     Good morning!     I’m doing really well, still immersed in this beautiful experience. I’m living a rare and precious freedom, experiencing kindness, goodness, and benevolence in almost all the exchanges I have with others, which is deeply satisfying. I revel in the noisy silence of nature and the quiet stillness of solitude. I’m living a childhood dream of escape, reliving Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn.     The only possible downside is that, according to the universal law of impermanence, this will have to end at some point…      In the meantime, I’m enjoying it to the fullest!     Today I’m staying indoors, which is nice.     I’m with a “hippie family” in northern Poland. They’re incredibly welcoming—pure peace and love. The father is no longer here. There are four children, aged 21 to 2. The mother is a tour guide in the national park! As a result, she knows the flora and fauna exceptionally well.     She makes decoctions from dandelion petals, ointments from some roots I can’t name (a local plant along with Whichstings in Ball, Whichstinks in Flower, Whichstains of the Spring, and Noideawhat in Branches), healing balms, laxative jams, regenerative juices... She walks barefoot, doesn’t drink alcohol (we’re in Poland! Some told me there were locals who don’t, but most people insisted that was a modern myth. And yet, here they are—crazy, isn’t it?).     And she doesn’t smoke either. Hippies without drugs!     (Note: not all mushrooms are recognizable ???).     She also runs workshops on plant knowledge, glass painting, talisman and jewelry making…     Her house is an incredible mess—something between a provincial antique store, a grandfather's attic, and what you’d imagine a healer’s cabin deep in the woods might look like. There are plucked dreamcatchers and necklaces, small whitened vertebrae, horned or toothed skulls, rusty tools, and a big old nail... Antlers from deer, roe deer, and elk. Lanterns—lots of kerosene lanterns. Pots, bottles, and flasks—some not entirely empty, plump or thin, tinted and translucent, but rarely transparent due to deposits inside or outside. Carpets and cushions. Tables completely covered with no space for seats. A fish trap. Homemade candles scented with relaxing plant oils sit next to hypoallergenic, superfatted handmade soaps.     Jars of more or less dusty preserved things: a demijohn with raspberries discolored by alcohol, jars filled with who-knows-what floating in more or less liquid substances, mushrooms, shelled nuts, bouquets of dried nettles, and countless flowers—of what exactly, I couldn’t say.    The numerous shelves overflow as much as the tables and every other horizontal surface. The walls and beams are covered with all sorts of hanging items—likely suspended from nails she must have scavenged from the garden. There’s even a dangling teddy bear... or something resembling one.     When she first saw me—dragged along by an inebriated individual, Andreï, who insisted at the village grocery store that I absolutely had to come and see this place—she hugged me. I barely had time to feel self-conscious about not having used a bottle of water to wash myself beforehand. Without even asking who I was, she welcomed me in, immediately showing me where to leave my backpack and where I could sleep in one of the free dormitories. No concern for a key—it seems the place doesn’t have one.    "It's a blue house leaning against the hill. We don't knock; those who live here threw away the key long ago!" she said. (I couldn’t help but think of Maxime Le Forestier’s song San Francisco from 1974—exactly this vibe. But I guess you’d have to be an old French person to remember that big hit from the '70s.)     She pointed out a small high table, with a tray fixed to the wall next to a socket from which a kettle protruded, offering tea or coffee. She told me not to worry and that I could stay as long as I wanted, just like the all-smiling gentleman next to me, now chatting with Andreï. He had apparently arrived months ago during a bike ride and never left.     She then asked if I wanted to come with her to visit the neighbors. She was already super late (though this seemed rather normal based on her casual demeanor and what I later observed). I completely understood—my own sense of time is so blurred from walking for months that days and months feel surreal. She reassured me she’d make breakfast when we returned (yes, Andreï, it’s still morning!).     Note: At least he was only drinking beer—it could have been vodka!    There was no time to feel unsure of myself, no opportunity to feel embarrassed. Just pure, unfiltered welcome, as though I’d already been part of this place for three years. And so, I smiled.     In short, a few hundred years ago, she would have been burned in the village square by the Inquisition, or even stoned by some virtuous person in power—no doubt about it!     But now, between journalists showing up with booms and cameras at the fair where she was selling her creations and products while simultaneously teaching people how to make lucky dolls from scraps of fabric (you just sit on the pile and get started...), and the television crew set to arrive the next day for a reportage and interview, she has become well-known and appreciated—not just as a curiosity.     I saw people bringing her game animals taken during herd management, killed by hunters for the forest department. Others brought her coffee because they had just returned from Africa and thought of her. It’s truly heartwarming to see. Her daughter even told me, “She’s famous.”     At the festival/street market where we were, the stand next to hers was thrilled to be placed beside her. The vendor told me her presence would bring him more visibility and customers.     What were the chances of meeting her, of encountering this world, this reality? Seriously?     Anyway…    Phone charging. A burning hot shower (because wood-fired heating is not thermoregulated). Clean clothes (finally—my socks were starting to sting my eyes without me even bending down!). Black coffee. A hot meal—not just bread, butter, cheese, tomato, or banana this time. (She’s a great cook, I must admit.)     And conversations.     Silence.     More conversations.     Another way of living. Another way of seeing. Other ways, in general...     It’s nice.     Voilà!     Wishing you lots of good things,     Peace and love.     P.S. You can check her out online—just type Biebrzańska Wiedźma into Google.
blog/goldap-and-andrzej/index.html:
Goldap and Andrzej


		22/11/2021
	
    The fact that I am receiving more and more messages asking me for news tells me that I may have once again stretched the time limit for updating my progress. And now, as I reread myself, I realize that this message is going to be really long. Maybe to compensate for the delay. Well, if it’s too much, don’t hesitate to complain.     And something else: regarding the photos, I am experiencing an as-yet unsolved problem. They are missing, or at least a large part of the period I am writing about now. I do not know why or if I will be able to find them in the depths of my phone’s memory, or if they are definitely gone. So I apologize to those of you who enjoy the photos—especially those who don’t care much for the reading and just like to look at the pictures!     The last time I wrote to you, I stopped at the Hill of Crosses, of which I have fond memories, though they already feel a little distant. There has been a lot of water under the bridge since then—and lots of things floating with it.    There was Šiluva, the fourth destination on my journey. A place I’ll let you discover on the internet if you wish, as it is described there far better and in more detail than I could manage. I stayed there for four days, hosted by the pilgrims’ center. The team in charge of the center and welcoming pilgrims was very dynamic and enthusiastic. Once again, I can only partially convey the warmth of the welcome I received, the meetings I had there, and the quality of the discussions we shared.    It exceeded my expectations. And the place itself!
