Well, let’s just say that I’m glad I heard about it and had the chance to be there.    When I felt ready and rested, I chose to resume my way towards Gietrzwałd, via Święta Lipka in Poland this time. This route would allow me to go around the small part of Russia that lies between Poland and Lithuania, as I didn’t want to cross Russia (visas and administrative costs are troubles a pilgrim can do without). In doing so, it also took me through Kaunas.    Kaunas is the second-largest city in Lithuania, but let me specify that the concept of a big city is very subjective. Second-largest city in Lithuania—that must be considered at the scale of the country, of course. I say this for my Indian friends, for example, for whom the second-largest city in their country must be Mumbai, with a population six times greater than the entire Lithuanian population, not counting the Mumbai agglomeration...   Although I am not fond of walking through large cities, the need to renew some of my equipment, wardrobe, and shoes made the stop necessary. The presence of a military store that could provide more durable materials and equipment, combined with the old town and many beautiful buildings and churches, made the prospect more appealing. Additionally, I was informed about the presence of a pilgrim shelter there, which made the city all the more accessible, and ultimately, the choice as a stopover was made quite naturally.    And I’m really glad I did...    First and foremost, because the trip between Šiluva and Kaunas was one of the most picturesque country paths I’ve had the opportunity to walk. In the midst of verdant nature with autumnal colors, I walked along a small stream, then a bigger one, taking care to enjoy these magnificent and almost wild places as much as possible.    Besides, I would like to tell you about a meeting with this nature that happened there, but I want to do it nicely and fully, and I’m afraid it might be too long. Too much of a digression for here, so I will include it as a postscriptum.    Then, and I know it becomes redundant, but I am not tired of it—the welcome I received in this city was really, really nice. I was lucky to be hosted in the center of the old town, probably the most beautiful part of the city. And so, as hoped, I took advantage of the pretty town (churches, old streets, squares, and buildings), but also of the practical side (buying the necessary equipment and food, washing my sleeping bag that was smellily screaming for it!).  And the meetings—again, always, everywhere. I was not only welcomed, guided, and accompanied in my efforts but also taken to visit superb places that would otherwise have remained unknown to me (it’s very annoying not to be able to show you pictures!).  And there again, in those meetings—I am not tired of it—each time, the kindness, the availability, the generosity, and the accompaniment, if needed or desired.   Then I resumed my way towards the border. Easy and slow. Really slow because over the past few weeks, my back pains have given me small reminders. Nothing in comparison to before, but still, I’ve learned to be gentler with myself and to listen to my body’s complaints. I forced myself to walk only one day out of two, sometimes one day out of three. It was necessary and beneficial.    I am stretching better and better, more and more, which is a really good sign! The way—to be walked far and long—teaches you to be kind and fair to yourself. The need is to be happy. Happiness gives wings. But not only that; somehow, I believe it heals...   I am now in Poland, in the small town of Gołdap, from where I am writing to you. It is 3 km from the Russian border.   If you keep up with "current affairs," you are likely informed about the situation with the instrumentalization of migrants from the Middle East, flown by charters to Belarus and then guided to Poland and Lithuania with the obvious aim of political destabilization and financial gain. For me, this results in being checked by flying customs controls—up to three times a day.    Nothing unpleasant—the checks often end in nice discussions about what moves me...    And it’s not just the border police cars that stop; sometimes people do so as well, just to check on me—with kindness, to help, or out of curiosity. And that’s how I met Andrzej (Andre, but we are in Poland, so you have to add “z” or “w” all over the place. I’m sure it’s just to make certain words unpronounceable for tourists or pilgrims. Only certain words, though, because in this example, Andrzej is written unpronounceable but pronounced Andre. Crazy tongue movements in my mouth...).    But to make it short, the car stops, the window goes down, and Andrzej gets very enthusiastic when I finish the short briefing of Emmanuel Gump—the roadside version...   He is seriously ill. A former soldier in forced retirement due to an unknown or poorly understood illness (we discussed in English, and Andrzej’s English is certainly much better than my Polish, but still a little light for technical details). He tells me it’s very good that we meet, and asks if I could bring prayer intentions to Gietrzwałd for him.    Of course—certainly—it’s my pilgrim duty, and I ask him to write them down in the notebook I reserve for this purpose.    He then asks about my route and exclaims that I’ll be passing through his city, where I must stop. He doesn’t guarantee that his wife will agree to lodge me, but he says he’ll speak to the priest and assures me that I’ll be welcomed anyway. I have no doubt about that. Truly. No matter where, when, or how, I know it’s going to be alright.    We exchange phone numbers, and I resume my journey.  The next day, I receive an SMS from him with a photo of "his" church. He gives me an appointment there the following day at 5 p.m.    Funny thing—when I arrive in Gołdap the next day as planned, but much earlier (around 12:30 p.m.), I look at my map for the church. Seeing only one, I head for it. But when I see its steeple, I realize it doesn’t match the photo he sent. And I can’t see any other church nearby.    So I decide to ask passersby. First, a lady who doesn’t speak English (nor French, nor Tamil—well, okay, I didn’t ask about Tamil). Then a delivery boy who eventually speaks Russian. Finally, I consider approaching the only individual remaining in the area, a few hundred meters down the street. I think that if he doesn’t speak English either, that’s fine—I’ll just call Andrzej.   But before I can reach him, he speaks to me from a distance—in English—to ask if I need anything. Before I can respond, he’s already reached me.    Guess what: it’s Andrzej!  He was passing by on his way back home from a friend’s house. He couldn’t believe the coincidence. I don’t want to sound jaded, but I’m used to it now. For him, it’s a big coincidence; for me, it’s Friday. I mean, it’s been 13 months that everything has been going better than expected, and I’m finally really confident.    At the beginning, faced with this level of coincidence, I might have hesitated (not for long) to consider the possibility of surveillance of the pilgrim’s activities by the Polish secret services. But now I know it’s just like this. It’s become routine (but not boring!). Welcome to the pilgrim world...    We talk together while walking. There is indeed a room waiting for me. Yup! Hot shower (necessary...) and everything else that goes with a roof in general—you know the drill already...    He leaves me at the church, where I have to wait for someone to pick me up. The priests are busy; it may take a while. Andrzej is also very busy and has to leave immediately. So I stay in the church, which suits me well.    It’s small, cute, warm, old, and nice. I put my backpack in the entrance, sit on a bench, close my eyes, and before I realize it, an hour and a half have passed. It feels good to close your eyes sometimes. This was one of those times.    When I take my backpack back, because Father Mathieu comes to get me and invites me to follow him to my room, I notice a plastic bag placed on it, under my hat, which was on top. Inside: a chocolate bar, bananas, and dry sausages.    Someone, totally unknown to me—Andrzej, the priests, or someone else—went to the store next door after seeing my bag, or me, or both, bought these little treats, and left them under my hat. I didn’t see anything and have no idea who could have done it.    But I’ve been here less than two hours, and this has already happened. Isn’t it touching? Seriously. Sweetness. Kind attention.    I’ll give away the dry sausages—I’m a vegetarian, you know—but I’ll keep the intention well in my heart. This kind of attention feeds a man well. The chocolate, too, for sure! ??   I live this permanently... I do not know if you realize... for the past 13 months. Sometimes, remembering the "mainstream" discourse of the media, or the almost universally morose discourse, I feel like I’m not on the same planet. Be careful, I was warned when I left: nowadays, you never know!    I am careful—I pay attention with enthusiasm and interest, because yes, you never know. The good, the beautiful, the kindness could crash joyfully against my armor of projections, prejudices, certainties, and precautions. Without paying attention, without being careful, I might not realize it and miss all of this. That would be a pity—a shame—sad...    I am currently staying in one of the parish houses in the city. Father Mathieu and Father Albert are welcoming me with a touching quality as well. And again, I meet and discover. I stayed two full days here; there were a lot of repairs to be done on my backpack (I had to buy stronger sewing thread).    When I’m ready to resume my journey, it will be with a backpack filled with homemade cheeses I was offered, dishes prepared for my journey by Ewa, the housekeeper here, a jar of very good honey, a dozen eggs from Father Albert’s mother’s house, and a bottle of hooch that, if I understood Father Albert correctly, is very good for me.    He explained—in pretty good French, considering how long it’s been since he last practiced it—that this drink, made from black elderberries, has powerful "reheating" properties, which should help during the winter. At 82 degrees of alcohol, I can believe it. I haven’t tried it yet—I’m saving it for the big frosts in the tent. Along with the bottle of "homemade," he gave me a small hooch glass on a pendant with straps and a leather pouch. I’m well-equipped for the road.    Our Lady of Gietrzwałd, here I come...    Voilà. That’s all for today. Well, almost, because I went on a "little" bit in the postscript...    Anyway, I wish you all well and happy!    Emmanuel    PS (long one):    In the photos, there was one of my tent by a river. I took it on the woodland route, superb in color during this autumn season, when I was along this river between Šiluva and Kaunas... Bucolic... natural... green... Superb...    I surely wasn’t the only one who thought this place deserved a stop since a wooden bench had been placed there, in the middle of this great nothingness full of nature. A few meters from the bank of the river below, in the middle of a small grassy meadow, with a magnificent view despite the bumps and hollows, like small hills and valleys. There was a small patch of flat grass next to the bench, flat and large enough for me to pitch my tent.    There was no hesitation. It was obvious that I was going to sleep here. I had to sleep here.    It may seem strange to you or hard to believe, but for over a year that I’ve been sleeping here and there, many of the places where I decide to stay the night impose themselves on me rather than the other way around. And often, those are the places where I sleep well. It’s astonishing, but when I come across these places, it’s obvious, certain. I sleep there... and I sleep well.    Once the tent was set up, the bench that had been waiting there all along did its job. I sat and watched the water flow. It’s good to watch the water flow. Really good.    And it must have been a while since I started watching the water because the sun had gone down behind me by the time she arrived.    I say “she,” but actually, I have no idea if it was a she or a he. The other thing I didn’t know was what it was.    But it was super cute, that’s for sure—really super cute.   It is often in those moments when I find myself at a standstill—whether for rest or contemplation—when my noisy and olfactory intrusion has finished disturbing the place and those who live there, when calm and silence prevail again through my immobility, and with a little luck, a contrary wind, that the most beautiful encounters occur.    And this one was a magnificent one. Do you remember the wolf that appeared, which I observed a few months ago in Poland? But there have been many others—many, but all unique and memorable... A pair of foxes once followed each other and played together, wild boars and baby boars, roe deer, deer, hinds, birds... It’s always captivating to me.    This was the first time I saw her. Her and her kind. For now, we’ll agree—very arbitrarily—that it was a she. But a what? I’m not sure... To be honest, I really don’t know.    I do know her family well, however—the mustelids. The problem is, it’s a (very) large family: from polecats to martens, including badgers, weasels, wolverines, ferrets, minks, and more. Well, these are the ones I’ve heard of or even seen, but there are many more. I haven’t yet looked for a picture online, but I’ll try to find it...    Because, of course, at that moment, even though I really wanted to take her portrait—because she was as cute as can be, and I assure you, those little beasts are insanely cute—even though I really wanted to, I didn’t move an inch. Not even a hair.    I wanted to watch her. Take my time. Not move and spoil the moment, as I did with the wolf.   I observed, prolonging the moment as much as possible before she realized, with horror, that she was within just a few steps—3 meters at most—of the most harmful and dangerous species of mammal on earth (and perhaps even of the universe; we don’t yet have proof to the contrary): a human...    A little smaller and thinner than a ferret, with pretty light gray fur. Lighter than mouse gray—ash gray, I would say.    She had just climbed the embankment from the bank of the river to the small clearing where I was going to spend the night. She stood there, motionless, and I couldn’t tell if she was looking at me or frozen, on the lookout for the slightest movement or smell, perhaps blinded by the sun, which was now behind me but certainly in her eyes.    After a wonderfully long moment of stillness, she got on her hind legs and stood above the grass to get a better view (animals know that to see better, sometimes you need to gain height! Oh captain, my captain!).    If she was cute before, suddenly, I had no words for what she became now. I was speechless—and couldn’t have spoken anyway. I was barely breathing.    Then she continued on her way, resuming whatever she had been doing before, without haste—therefore probably without fear—completely unaware of the horror of her encounter. (What could be more horrifying for a wild animal than meeting a human! Meeting two humans?)    Leaving me in awe of her beauty, I went to bed happy like a kid who had just seen his first wild mustelid and loved it.    I ate a little, then "closed" the tent (which is a big word since the zippers of both the flysheet and the inner tent are long gone). I use safety pins to close the flysheet effectively (it works very well, phew!) and have given up, months ago, on the idea of closing the inner tent. Goodbye mosquito net and privacy. Everything that can pass under the flysheet has direct access to the half-wild and hopefully sound-asleep Emmanuel. Hello spiders, beetles, earwigs, and so on.    The slugs and snails, though, are the ones whose "cuddling" I appreciate the least. Who likes sloppy wet kisses, I ask you?    So I "closed" my tent and fell asleep in an instant as soon as it got dark. Basically at 5 p.m. Well, yes, the days were still long back then. Now it’s more like 3:30 p.m. for sunset and 4:00 p.m. for full night. It’s strange to me, I admit.    And I slept really well. Very well—until I woke up. And I woke up.    That, too, is something surprising. When we sleep "outside," there’s a sort of inner wakefulness, as if part of our brain (reptilian?) remains alert to give warning if necessary. Like a sudden attack of slobbery wet kisses, for example—brrr—or a creature wriggling at my feet.    Now fully awake but taking care to remain still and breathe calmly, listening, I tried to determine what had woken me. And without waiting too long, an animal, about the size of a cat, began to fidget—right at my feet, and even partly on them.    Do you remember that night when a cat came to visit me? After overcoming its apprehensions, it entered my tent and stayed for the night. Frenzied cuddles several times during the night, followed by purring and sleeping on my sleeping bag—it was a warm encounter, full of sweetness.    But I was pretty sure it wasn’t a cat this time. Most likely, it was my afternoon friend.   I say friend—I was fully her friend. From my side, at least. As for her feelings, I didn’t really know yet.    But I admit, I had hope...    She was walking between the flysheet and the inner tent. A few times, she put her front legs on the stretched canvas of the inner tent, giving me the feeling she was climbing on my feet...    How to tell you—I was full of hope that the brotherly meeting of two predators, one of which was super cute and both super hairy, could end in sweet hugs. She wasn’t afraid; just for that, I liked her. No particular inhibition, from what I could tell, because I started to move, and she stayed. Any other animal would have scampered away in fright and howls. But not her. She was like this, you see...    Soon, I started talking to her softly.    Okay, let me stop you right there—no, I wasn’t talking to her so much to tell her something, and even less to expect an answer. I’m not that crazy yet. But I used my voice to convey feelings of calm, harmlessness, and assurance.    Animals have an intuitive, nonverbal perception capacity. We do too, of course—it’s what allows us to perceive during a phone conversation that the person on the other end is smiling. But animals are even better at this. They can feel our attitude.    And it must have worked, at least a little, because she didn’t flee despite my words. She paused for a moment, then resumed her activity.    I was really starting to consider contact! Seriously! Being able to stroke the animal would be like Christmas come early!!! We weren’t there yet, but hey—you know boys!    I took my phone to use the flashlight function and discovered two very disappointing things.    The first is that the flashlight function is antagonistic to the camera. So I couldn’t show you the magnificent little creature. Well, I say little, but she was about the size of a good-sized cat. Shorter legs. And a small muzzle with lovely whiskers.    The second—and this crushed my romantic hopes of spontaneous contact between two critters—was that she was busy with the little bag containing my rubbish and food scraps. I always take care to gather these while waiting for the opportunity to dispose of them in the first trash can I come across.    She had grabbed the bag, carried it to my feet, and began extracting its contents.    That might mean nothing to you, but for me, it meant she wasn’t there for my beautiful eyes, but for the olfactory hope of a nighttime snack.    It was a hard blow—for me and my dreams of soft, furry caresses. (Bah, yes, it must be super soft in addition to being super cute! People make coat collars out of it, let me remind you! And let’s admit it, the fur really makes you want to touch it. Forget the fine teeth at one end of the thing and the fart-spray anal glands at the other!)    It puts things in perspective and me back in my place.    And yet, I still wanted to believe it. After waiting for her to move to the other side of the tent, I reached out to retrieve the plastic bag—not easy at all, but I thought it was better to do it now than later, when all its contents would be scattered everywhere!   And then, as she still didn’t leave and my romantic hopes revived, I decided to try indirect contact—through the thin canvas of the tent. I touched her, almost stroked her. Almost, because there was the thin tent canvas between us and, quite honestly, because she didn’t really let it happen.    She still didn’t run away but didn’t let herself be touched either. As soon as the sensation became more than her own friction against the canvas—my hand pressing gently against her through the fabric—she changed position. She didn’t leave, but she wouldn’t let herself be caressed.    Finally, she began to focus her activity on my left side, right at the height of my elbow. To be precise, exactly where I store my food in the tent. Food that was protected only by the thin canvas and a Tupperware box, though she couldn’t know about the latter.    So yes, she was only here for the promises of her nose. I, meanwhile, counted for nothing. The story—our story—was doomed to failure before it could even begin.    Realizing this, the whole situation suddenly seemed absurd, a bit drawn out, a waste of time. I figured it was better to let the night offer the possibility of good sleep.    That hope vanished abruptly when she began to emit little shrill cries that, without a shadow of a doubt, reflected frustration, annoyance, and finally, anger.    It was around this time that the cute little furry creature began to turn into a real little evil pest. Forgive the expression.   She started to attack the tent—or rather, not attack it outright, but in her frustration and in trying to reach what she was smelling, she began biting or trying to bite the canvas of the inner tent.    Biting a stretched canvas is not an easy task.   I was watching her, resting on my elbow, using the arm whose hand held my phone. The phone’s flashlight beam projected between the flysheet and the inner tent, while my right hand pulled on the tent canvas to widen the gap between the two, clearing my view of the otherwise cramped space where she was putting on her show.    We were 12 inches apart—snout to snout.    Now visibly frustrated, she managed to sink her teeth into the canvas. When her grip was firm, she gave a sharp little jerk, pulling with her whole body and stepping back in short, jerky movements...    There, I really stopped agreeing with the situation. As cute as she was (I mean, you should have seen her jerking back—it was adorable!).    "But would you stop, you little evil," I said, remembering that the tone was more important than the words themselves.    We had to find an arrangement quickly, or it was going to be a very long night. An idea—almost a plan—came to me and seemed relevant: if she was no longer hungry, she would leave me alone. To sum it up.    So I opened the magic box, took out my knife, and opted for a piece of Brie. A good piece of Brie stuck at the end of the knife.    She sniffed, then very quickly grabbed the piece, took a few steps back (it’s super cute when they go backwards!), landed on her hind legs, chest upright, holding the piece of cheese with her front paws. She began tearing off small pieces, chewing them carefully before swallowing.    You might say I’m repeating myself, but God, this little beast was cute when eating something other than my tent! I could have watched her like that for hours.    She devoured the first piece very quickly, the second too, and the third more slowly. I never got bored. In addition to the hope of having satiated her so she would leave me alone, watching her eat the Brie—me being from Normandy—I felt a kind of connection, a kind of sympathy. After all, we shared certain tastes. It wasn’t all totally hopeless between us...    And finally, she left.    I was a little disappointed, all the same. I am sure of the potential for fraternization. After all, these animals have been tamed for a long time, either as pets or as burrow-hunting animals...    But she was gone. And I could relax, go back to sleep.    But she came back.    And by the time she woke me up for the second time, she had already made a hole 7 cm long by 4 cm wide.    That’s when I went for contact—but more firmly this time. No caresses.    With my phone light in one hand, I watched her closely. Each time she was about to bite the canvas, I hit her on the muzzle from the other side.    At first, just gentle taps, accompanied by reprimands with no real conviction—I mean, I was still under her charm and couldn’t bring myself to hit or scold her in anger.    But I have to admit, my patience was slowly running out.    I was really impressed by her determination—and her insolence too! After all, wasn’t she aware that she was in the presence of the worst mammal in the galaxy? Seriously? The representative of the supreme masters of all other forms of life on Earth, because intelligent, industrious, and artistic (and egocentric too...)?    She took a dozen taps on the muzzle. The last one was no longer a joke—it was a slap. A good one. And the beast fled. Phew!    Sad that it had to come to this—for a piece of Norman cheese! But now, my tent had two big torn holes and several smaller bite marks...   I was exhausted and needed sleep, but I couldn’t fall back asleep right away. The night was dragging on. And just as I was finally dozing off again, guess what—of course, she came back a third time.    Around two in the morning, another wake-up, another hole.    At that point, I began to doubt my victory over the little monster. The separation had to happen—now. A divorce, before she took the whole tent apart. But how to do that without resorting to brutality? I couldn’t go beyond the slap; it had already made my heart ache.  I really wondered how to get out of this relational impasse without ending in a brutal heartbreak...   That’s when I remembered the little pepper spray given to me by a Ukrainian security guard in Germany. He had handed it to me, saying it was for wildlife and possibly humans (apparently, sprays specifically for wildlife are stronger but forbidden for use on humans). He had insisted on telling me that there were a lot of junkies around.    Well, personally, in the middle of the woods, I had very rarely encountered junkie attacks. (The junkie is, after all, an urban animal.) But we all have our fears, I suppose. Mine? Slobbering wet kisses attacks...    In short, I looked for the small spray and, despite the probable discomfort of using it in a closed—or almost closed—space, I threatened my assailant with it.    And at that moment, I also decided that for being so persistent, she had to be a he.    Yes, I know—big discriminatory clichés, totally against any concept of gender equality.    But hey, it was the feeling of the moment, at three in the morning, on a restless night.   The first pchitt was almost nonexistent and therefore totally ineffective. I was reluctant... But when he started working on his fourth hole, he got a proper pchitt on the muzzle. A little one. Half a second. Maybe even less.    I didn’t even see him leave—it was so fast.    But it had worked.    And now I was there, and he was gone. I was relieved but disappointed. Disappointed and a little sad...   Fortunately, I had the opportunity to take some air for a good hour, to clear my head and properly ventilate the tent!   I hope the critter hasn’t had any problems because of this. I don’t think so. I am a little disappointed, not really surprised—except by his cheek, his daring, his determination...    But honestly, I remain under his spell. I assure you, these little furballs are so cute. Really...    And now, I won’t advise you to go on the internet to check whether mustelids might be a key link in triggering an unprecedented historical event—a panzootic (animal-to-human pandemic). According to Wikipedia in 2020, “mink farms are the animal farms that have been most affected by the SARS-CoV-2 virus responsible for COVID-19. If this virus were to spread among wild mustelids, the latter could become a permanent reservoir of infection for other animal species, as was the case with rabies transmitted to raccoons and skunks, or with bovine tuberculosis transmitted to badgers, or with paratuberculosis, transmissible to many wild ruminants and sometimes to immunosuppressed humans.”    But hey, without going as far as "Haaa, my God, it’s awful, we’re all going to die," it’s true that mustelids become less cute when you read that.    I guess.   On my side, I loved the encounter. Even if I now have three big holes in my tent (though compared to the gaping hole at the entrance where the zipper is completely out of use, the three side holes feel conceptually negligible).    And he looked in great shape—fully healthy, the little devil!
blog/meeting-with-a-bear/index.html:
Meeting with a Bear


		11/7/2023
	
      It’s been a long time again, and I feel and sense some impatience. It’s nice to know that my news messages are awaited. It’s somehow a form of support for my journey.     I have now been in Romania for a few weeks, and I really appreciate what I am experiencing and seeing here.   But since Slovakia, I’ve been dragging my feet. I feel tired, physically exhausted, without this being justified by walking. This is because my walk is slow and interrupted by many breaks to enjoy the landscape, an encounter, a stone, a stump, or a bench perfectly placed for me to rest on. I walk, contemplate, and meditate—sometimes all at the same time. It’s a pleasant exercise, during which the inner chatter eventually dies out, and I find myself alone, silent, and content.   The breaks under the walnut tree, on the warm trunk of a tree in the local sun, stretch on without me worrying about it, without any movement occurring either inside or outside. A flat encephalogram (which some might say must be easy for me—see the end of the message...) certainly, but with vigilance, with purposeless concentration, if that makes sense to you. As a result, my average mileage drops quickly, but since the goal is not athletic, as you understood, I don’t care.    However, for some time now, not only has my walking slowed down, but the breaks have grown longer and far more frequent. This made me consider the possibility of a health problem, which prompted me to change my route and pass through a big city to consult a doctor for a check-up. After all, it’s been 4 or 5 years since I’ve had any follow-up care, and almost 3 years that I’ve been walking in living conditions that some would call precarious.    So, to reassure you right away: the examination and analyses revealed nothing abnormal. The doctor who examined me at the hospital simply told me that I needed to rest...    So, that’s what I’m doing.    Before continuing, I would like to point out that the Romanian health system is welcoming. Any individual is received and treated free of charge for 72 hours, regardless of their nationality. This will probably not impress the French, whose health system also has some good aspects, but when you experience this attention, it is touching. Really. The Hippocratic oath no longer feels hypocritical... and it feels good.     So here it is: for a month, I have been walking for one day, then resting for two or three. And I feel like it’s paying off, as I now feel better rested and often eager to start again—something I had been missing lately.    But I’m seeing the good side of things: I’m spending a lot of time in the countryside. When I stop, it’s often in the forest, which here finally covers the land that, to the east of where I came from, was sadly bare. I don’t know where you are, but here it’s hot or very hot, and as soon as it gets too much, we get a storm. A real summer storm with torrential downpours (think Indian or Nepalese monsoon), thunder that shakes the ground, and lightning that gets me out of my tent to check if the tree next to me was hit.     After that, the temperature becomes much more bearable, but it’s incredibly heavy because of the humidity. It might seem unpleasant, but you have to look at the whole picture: when it’s hot and very humid, it feels heavy and uncomfortable, but—and I allow myself to use capital letters here—BUT, all the conditions are suddenly perfect for the appearance of our fungal friends.    I picked summer ceps in mid-June. Yes! And they were a delight. At the end of June, I was invited to breakfast by a local mushroom enthusiast who prepared a fricassee of chanterelles. You can imagine that if I spend time in the woods, I eat mushrooms regularly. And to me, that’s divine.   On the other hand, the local forests have one major drawback: bears. And I admit, there are many. Even in a small wood, like a one-hectare thicket, there is likely a bear in it. I didn’t really believe it at first—just like in Slovakia. But here, I see traces every day. Fresh traces, even very fresh ones. I’ve even had morning visits. In wolf and dog form. Their schedule seems to be around 3:30–4:00 a.m.    I discovered that even when we sleep in the middle of the woods, a part of us continues to "listen." I was amazed to realize this, but I believe that our ears continue to hear, and our brain processes information intuitively. It’s strange to notice, like finally becoming aware of your unconscious.    The two times a bear approached my tent while I was sleeping, I woke up immediately, as if shaken by my subconscious warning me of danger. There was no gentle awakening phase where you take your time, where reality is still blurred by the paradoxical sleep phase, free cinema... No, I opened my eyes instantly, no transition—I was alert, attentive, concentrated, and immediately ready to act.    I already knew there was something on the other side of the thin fabric of my tent. My first thought, clear and certain, was: a bear. About ten meters from the tent, I then heard heavy but hesitant footsteps. Without hesitation, without even thinking, I began to sing—softly but loudly—while at the same time lighting up the tent with the headlamp given to me by a firefighter from Târgu Mureș. I knew that my tent would then become a softly glowing lamp, about 3 meters long and 1.2 meters high. A beautiful sight for the bear, I imagined, lying there, motionless.    Singing right away when you wake up because a bear is outside might seem like a crazy idea. But let me explain:    The only bear attacks in Europe are related to surprise—when a bear is startled by a human who was too discreet (the bear neither hears nor senses them), or to fear—when an aggressive human mistakenly thinks that making a lot of noise or acting threateningly will scare away a 350 kg beast. The bear, feeling threatened, might attack instead of fleeing. Another situation is when an inattentive human finds themselves between a bear and her cubs, triggering a protective maternal instinct—with claws and teeth.    Other attacks are linked to predatory behavior, triggered when a human runs (or cycles or skis) in front of a bear. This activates the bear’s predatory or attack reflex, much like what happens with an excited dog that is likely to bite if you run from it.     So, I tell myself that if the bear has approached me despite the unmistakable olfactory signals for its sense of smell—signals I deliberately place around and on my tent (a cloth soaked in diesel between the roof and the double roof of the tent, and my urine poured on the trunks of trees around my campsite)—it’s because the bear is curious (like many animals I’ve noticed) and opportunistic (hoping the human is gone and has left something to eat).    Of course, the bear probably doesn’t have a clear concept of UFOs, but the tent must seem like a very strange object to it—especially when it lights up.    When I wake up, I sing so the bear knows I’m there, in the tent. Singing, unlike shouting or howling, is far less aggressive. It also benefits me: singing has a soothing effect, both on the one who hears the song and on the one who sings it. You can’t sing while being completely paralyzed with fear. Singing keeps fear at bay.     In short, my theory is that, like many animals I’ve known since childhood, bears are not so much receptive to what I say but rather to the tone in which I say it. They are not as affected by my movements as they are by my attitude—my mental state, in a way.    I believe that singing is a way to show my presence while maintaining a relaxed and peaceful attitude. It reassures the animal while informing it of my presence and my nature.     Both times this happened, the bear ran away immediately. The second time, it was really close to me and let out a kind of nasal breath, an impressive Mmufffff. Either I wasn’t mistaken about its presence, or I sing really badly!    Also impressive is the sound of cattle running through the undergrowth. You might not know this, but when we sleep in the woods, sounds are amplified—not only by the acoustics of the place but also by the unconscious analysis our brain performs. It’s probably a remnant from the time when we lived outdoors and were a tasty treat for many predators.    At night, a simple beetle can seem like a huge rat snooping around. A toad becomes je ne sais quoi weighing at least 20 kilograms... A bird landing on the ground and scratching with its claw for food becomes a wild boar. I assure you, it’s destabilizing to realize how much our brain exaggerates these sounds.    Over time, with practice, the brain recalibrates, and you can relax completely despite the many noises of the forest. I now sleep in the woods as comfortably as I would in a bed in my room—even though, in reality, I haven’t had a room or a bed for more than 28 years.    So, I believe bears aren’t really the danger. They represent a risk, because, in the end, nothing prevents encountering a bad-tempered one—there are difficult characters in all mammals; it’s not exclusive to bipeds in an upright position. But I think that with certain precautions and behaviors, the risk is ultimately very small.     I accept this risk because, ultimately, I have no choice if I want to continue my journey.    When I spend several days in the same place, choosing the right location is essential. A sheltered spot—from the sun, so it’s possible to stay under the tent, and from view, to avoid worrying or being disturbed. Some places lend themselves perfectly: a small clearing of a few dozen square meters of flat and sparsely sown ground, where dense vegetation around and above filters the direct light... A small stream of clear water to cool off during the heat of the afternoon, and to wash, too.     This is where I was yesterday and the day before. Superb... Magnificent... Ideal.     Until the storm.    The rain began to fall in large drops, accompanied by a deafening clap of thunder that tore through the silence and my senses. It became so intense that I went out to check the stream, only a few meters away. The rain was so heavy that, already soaked, I decided to take out the soap and wash myself in the deluge.     When I returned to the tent, I knew there was a risk the water would rise and the stream might overflow. But there was space...     So I lay down and thought about something else. The rain stopped, and after looking outside, I assessed the risk of flooding as acceptable. The groundsheet of my new tent is waterproof and can withstand being in a layer of water up to 5 cm without compromising the interior.And inside, I have a small self-inflating mattress a few centimeters thick.     Even if water were to penetrate a little, most of my belongings would still be sheltered.     The happy optimist who sees the glass half full... I fell asleep like a child.     As I write this, I am washing all of my belongings and gear. I was awakened by the tent shaking and pushing me aside. Water was penetrating inside, and by the time I began organizing my things and planning my escape, I was in more than eight inches of water.     Of course, night was falling, and I had to move all my stuff to a place that wasn’t flooded, about 50 meters away. By the time I finished, the torrent covering the whole area was 40 cm deep. Suffice to say, the stream below was no longer visible at all.     The tent was almost lying in the water, and dismantling it became a major emergency before it broke. The battery in the headlamp chose this moment to signal that it needed energy. I realized that if I handled things poorly, I would lose a lot—some of my equipment had already been carried away. I removed all the pegs and fought to get the tent out of the water without it being swept away by the current.     I managed it, securing the tent in a safe place and getting back to it later. I spent the next day rinsing my belongings of the fine, sticky mud and the whole afternoon looking for what had been carried away: water bottles, clothes, bags.     I found almost everything, which feels almost miraculous.     But I confess, I’m not proud of myself. There were signs I ignored because I thought everything would be fine. I listened to optimism until it turned into foolishness!     Fortunately, in the village where I arrived, there’s a small guesthouse. I’m staying there to wash my clothes, clean the mud off absolutely everything, and dry everything in the sun.     Finally, everything is fine.   Tomorrow, I’m back on my way—a day of walking to a suitable place, then two days of rest. With a little luck, in a few weeks, I’ll be able to resume a normal rhythm.     In the meantime, I wish you all the best.     See you soon.
blog/levoca/index.html:
Levoca


		1/12/2022
	
     Levoca, Slovakia     1 December 2022     2 years, 2 months, 1 week, and 2 days on the way.     Approximately 6575 km walked.   Today, I’ll stay inside. For today and two more nights, I am in a monastery in the center of Levoca. I need to stay in town for a bit because I have to buy some materials to repair my backpack, tent, and some parts of my clothes.     I also need to figure out how to keep my bear spray accessible while walking, without it getting in the way. Yes, bear spray is essential in Slovakia, especially if you sleep in forests and mountains as I do. No joke—there are about 2,500 brown bears in the country. That’s a lot. After doing some research and watching homemade videos from people’s homes, I decided to take the matter seriously. So, I bought a few things to reduce the risk of being attacked. The spray is one of them, but I need to find a way to have it close at hand and easily accessible.    You might say it’s unnecessary because of the season—bears are supposed to hibernate. They were, but with climate warming, bears are now seen year-round.     So, I have many things to do.    But being inside makes it much easier. I don’t know about you, but here it’s winter. Minus 5°C all day long, dropping to minus 10°C or 12°C at night, especially in the mountains. Stitching is difficult. Actually, everything is difficult with frozen fingers.     Inside is nice. Warm. I hope not too warm, though, because I can’t sleep in a hot room anymore. Don’t get me wrong, I like the cold. I enjoy it. Minus ten doesn’t bother me—it’s beautiful, quiet, and feels pure. And I sleep very well in it. Really, it’s a pleasure. But stitching in the cold is hard!Another thing I’ll appreciate while I’m here is hot water. Washing in rivers or mountain springs is lovely—really. But I can’t use soap then, because the water is so pure I drink it. I’m not about to put shampoo or soap in it, right? So, nature baths are nice, but incomplete. And cold—really, really cold. Painfully cold. So, they’re very brief. Brother Thomas told me I could wash my clothes here if I wanted, and of course, I do! A washing machine is a blessing!     Once I’ve done all this, I’ll walk uphill to the Mariánska Hora basilica, probably set up my tent near the water source, and enjoy a few days of meditation.Then, I’ll be on my way again. I’ll let you know where next.     So, you see, everything is beautiful and nice. I enjoy my way as much as I hope my way enjoys me.     I wish you happiness and well-being.     Emmanuel    P.S.: Today, I received a parcel via post restante—a birthday gift from friends I met in Poland. Isn’t that lovely and kind? They sent me a high-quality power bank. It charges very fast, which is great because I’ll be able to recharge it whenever I stop at a restaurant or café. It also has a huge capacity, so once it’s fully charged, I can use it to charge my phone many times.     That’s really, really cool! And very useful to me. I’m deeply grateful for it.     So, as you can see, I’m still being taken care of on my journey, and that helps me keep going.     And so, I go...
blog/krincinas/index.html:
The Windmill and Hill of Crosses


		28/9/2021
	
    I walk and come across many places, people, magnificent trees—majestic ones even—and buildings... Walking gives you time to see, to approach slowly. It gives time for curiosity to form, for interest to be born.    For example, this windmill. From afar, it seemed strange, then obvious. I couldn’t resist and went to knock on the door of the house next to it to ask if I could go see it, photograph it for you, and maybe step inside. Whaaaa! I felt like I was stepping into a mechanical wooden watch. Five levels of pulleys, toothed wheels, giant gears, and belts. And of course, stone grindstones.    Although it was still operational about ten years ago, the mill no longer works. It was built in 1904 and is now too expensive to repair or even restore.    What a pity. What a marvel of engineering as well as carpentry. I’m attaching photos that, as often, only partially do it justice...     I walk even slower than before. I no longer have any concerns about distance—only direction, because I’m always heading somewhere—but I don’t care when I get there. I walk... Look... Rest... Walk again...    The weather is getting much cooler. In just a few days, we’ve gone from 20 to 28 degrees Celsius during the day to between 9 and 14. I imagine winter is coming soon...   The day before yesterday, I arrived in the small village of Krincinas. It was the birthday celebration of a local priest/poet, after whom the school is named. It was the director of this school—also the director of three others (budget cuts to the Lithuanian national education department!)—who welcomed me so kindly. He showed me around his school, asked the maintenance technician to turn on the hot water circuit so I could take a shower in the gym locker rooms, and then accompanied me on a short walk through the village park to show me a sulphurous water spring there.     We parted ways after spending a few hours together, including time with the students, who I could sense really liked their school. It’s nice to see...     After spending the night in a grove at the edge of a small unpaved road (very little noise from the occasional passing cars), I resumed my journey. Along the way, I passed by a place with about fifteen large crosses. I, of course, stopped to rest for a bit, sit on a bench, close my eyes, and meditate. I didn’t take any pictures, so you won’t see the place. Maybe I should have, because fifteen crucifixes aren’t planted for no reason.     What I’m going to share now is probably well-known to most Europeans, but I don’t believe it’s familiar to many of my Indian, Nepalese, and other friends...     This place was a commemoration site for an event as significant as something from the lives of Mahatma Gandhi or Nelson Mandela.    On August 23, 1989, at 7 p.m., two million people (fewer, according to the "prefecture," of course, and much more, according to participants—obviously!) joined hands to form a 700-kilometer-long human chain. It was non-violent, fraternal, and stretched across the three Baltic countries—the three sisters (Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia)—connecting their capitals (Vilnius, Riga, Tallinn).    The date was chosen to mark the anniversary of the secret Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, where the Soviets and Nazis had agreed on the partition of Europe, leading to the annexation of the three countries by the Soviet Union. This human chain was an act of resistance, a revolt, or at least activism, against the occupation.    These kinds of actions move me deeply. Truly. Tyranny undermined by benevolent brotherhood, without violence. The undeniable power of non-violent collective refusal...    You can find plenty of information on the internet about what’s called “The Baltic Way,” which is now classified by UNESCO in the Register of the Memory of the World.     I should have taken a photo...    And then I arrived in the small town of Pasvalys for the town's annual party. Am I not really lucky! Small city. A very warm little party. I arrived just in time to listen to a woman singing, and I’m attaching the audio file to this message. I found it very pretty. Sad but pretty. Obviously, I don’t understand a word of the song, but the whole performance seems to me like a lament or an observation of the difficulties of life. Of course, this is just my personal interpretation, based on the emotion and the timbre of a voice in a language unknown to me. I sat and watched her sing, accompanied by her friend on guitar.     And then I walked around the fair. Friendly. Truly. Simple and friendly...    A painter approached me to ask me what, why, when, and finally where I was sleeping. He told me to come and see him if the priest couldn’t accommodate me. When I came back from the very beautiful church, empty-handed, he was a little drunk—not clumsy drunk, but drunk enough to shout over the general hubbub, which you can imagine. He called out to someone, who shouted to another, who shouted to yet another person, until finally, the last man came and invited me to his hotel. Graciously. Any room is comfortable at this price! And then—a hot shower, phone charging...     I went to meditate a bit, and then to have dinner. When it came time to pay, the person behind me in the queue walked ahead and offered to pay for my meal! He heard that I was a pilgrim and wanted to participate in my adventure.     I am in the dreamlike sweetness of my journey. Wait—it’s not over!    The next morning, I went to church again. The priest, who now knew a little better who this backpack-wearing wanderer with a stick was, came toward me, shook my hand energetically, and gave me a big smile. He thanked me and left. In my hand was 100 euros. I was puzzled—he didn’t even give me time to respond.    I left the church and went to eat before continuing my way. At the restaurant in the square, I ordered and waited, looking at the topographic map on my phone, which I had plugged into an outlet nearby. The restaurant owner came to talk with me, holding a bottle of cognac and two small glasses. He was an interesting man—passionate, a hot air ballooning champion, and a former resistance fighter. I enjoyed our conversation—and the cognac!    When I picked up my bag to leave, the waitress told me I didn’t have to pay. The bill was covered by the house.    Do you understand why I doubt my reality? Why I am so moved by my experience with others? With strangers?    Finally, just before saying goodbye, I wanted to tell you that yesterday I passed through the Hill of Crosses. It is also a place of resistance—religious resistance, in a way. This hill is covered with more than 250,000 crucifixes. Crucifixes planted, heaped, hanging from others, clustered together... Destroyed by the Soviets, rebuilt, destroyed again, and rebuilt once more.    The place is intense. Seriously. I was worried it might feel spooky or creepy, but instead, I had one of my deepest meditations there. If you ever pass by on your journey, don’t hesitate to stop. Even if only out of curiosity.    Voilà. It’s time for me to go.    I am 50 km from Šiluva, my next and fourth destination...    Lots of good things for you.    Goodbye...
blog/happiness/index.html:
Happiness


		30/3/2023
	
     ​I thought I was going to send some solid news today, and that passing the 7000 km mark would be my pretext. But I have to be honest—this is fake news. I don’t really know where I am in terms of kilometers. I have this estimation due to my intimate relationship with topographic applications that I use every day to navigate, avoid busy roads, impassable rivers, and just not lose my way. Let’s say I suspect the distance, but I haven’t calculated it. It must be around 7000 km, give or take 10%. Although, in general, it’s probably less than more, because I believe that in my situation, we tend to evaluate rather higher than lower...     But hey... Let’s leave the kilometers aside.   I travel places, I meet people. And since my departure, everyone has been magnificent—welcoming, generous. This makes my path magnificent as well, and I walk it serenely, without its vagaries being a burden in any way.    For some time now, I’ve been crossing villages that consist of two parts: one “normal” village, and then further out, on the outskirts or in a small remote corner, a second part that’s much more dilapidated—almost like slums. It’s very visible, and you can recognize a population of “Roms,” as they are called. The former Gypsies, sedentarized by the Soviet governments, living in difficult conditions without really being able to escape them, even though it seems local and governmental aid is mobilized to help.     I come across these places. Poverty. Promiscuity, with everything that always accompanies it... precariousness.    And yet, I must say that I don’t think I’ve come across one of these places without someone inviting me at least once to eat, drink coffee, or sleep.     It’s a lesson in humility for me every time. I am forced to appreciate the welcome and the gift, contrasted against their living conditions. How touching.     Ah yes, speaking of touching...   For some time now, I’ve been scratching a lot. It’s not touching—it’s irritating, but let me explain. I was scratching a lot (like, really a lot and uncontrollably), and it didn’t take me long to realize I had scabies. Local generosity? A dirty towel in a restaurant bathroom? A questionable bed in a questionable motel? It’s hard to know how or by whom. Especially since it’s the first time in my life that I’ve caught it (I’ve never had lice or crabs either...). But that’s the thing—when it’s the first time, and the body doesn’t know the problem, in this case, Mr. Sarcoptes scabiei from the mite family, it can take time for symptoms to appear. Sometimes 15 days or more before the itching starts. So, it becomes difficult to determine the origin of the contamination.     But here, I tried to contact all the people with whom I spent time to warn them about the possibility of contagiousness. It’s really contagious, those small beasts...      But no panic, I often wash my hands with soap or hydroalcoholic gel, so a handshake doesn’t involve much risk. No, the risk was when I got invited to sleep inside.      The problem is that with the practice of pilgrimage as I do, it’s difficult to get rid of the beast without a very effective treatment: ivermectin. And this product is prohibited in Hungary, where I am, and that’s problematic because the remaining solutions are really cumbersome. While the ivermectin treatment consists of taking pills with a large glass of water twice at eight-day intervals, the alternative treatments require brushing your entire body with a lotion, letting it stand for 8 or 12 hours depending on the mixture, applying a second layer, waiting again, and then washing with hot water and soap. At the same time, washing clothes—all clothes—at 60 degrees. And the groundsheet. And the sleeping bag. A lot of work...     You can see how it becomes really complicated for the camper that I am.    While I was explaining this on the phone to the people who had invited me to spend three nights with them some time after my contamination a few weeks ago—they live in the last big city in Slovakia before the border with Hungary—Michaela and her neighbor Bruno (Branislav) decided, without me being able to dissuade them, not only to find ivermectin on the black market (it’s also forbidden in Slovakia, as a result of European policies concerning coronavirus treatments, if I understood correctly—some drugs have been blacklisted...), but also to drive four hours to bring it to me in the neighboring country. And with homemade cake—two, in fact, because both of them had made one for me.     You see...     It leaves me speechless. Silent. Calm, in every way.     When I resumed my journey, after a coffee offered for the three of us by the pilgrims' inn where I was staying, I was immersed in a deep silence. Deep and full. Not empty. I was calm, serene, grateful, confident. I walked calmly. I sat down whenever I felt the need, wherever the place was suitable, and I took time to contemplate this silence and sink into it.     There is nothing to say... nothing to be said.    Of course, there are times when loud shouts try to reach my ears or my eyes. This is always the case. Whether it’s the din of war that I circumvent geographically, or those more distant, like the rumblings from French streets at the moment, or more simply, a bistro conversation I come across while having a coffee (or a slivovica!)...    But once I’ve finished paying attention to it, the trace of the writing, the sight, or the sound fades almost instantly. There are no leftovers, no residual clutter. It becomes like distant knowledge that doesn’t truly reach me—at least not until I decide, with conscious effort, to pay attention to it again.     This distancing is pleasant. The noise of the world remains distant, even as I cross it. When it is present, this distance, born of healthy silence, feels like crossing or visiting myself with each step. I say "healthy silence" because it comes from the calm of the one experiencing it, not from the absence of noise around them.    So, I regularly spend weeks alone in the woods, then pass through towns or villages, meeting people and forming connections. When I leave again, there’s this same distancing—I rediscover the silence where I left it and sink into it, burying myself pleasantly in its embrace. I am privileged; I am aware of it.    The practice of pilgrimage, or perhaps simply long-term walking, gently forces me into this abandonment. It constrains with a certain tenderness. The need to adapt to the path, in order to walk it for a long time, is both mandatory and essential. To achieve this, it’s necessary to move toward what is pleasant, nourishing, and reassuring, while abandoning what is not.     I had to leave behind objects too heavy to carry in my bag to avoid the pain of carrying them. Finally, it’s clear: to feel good, you must stop hurting yourself. It seems obvious, and yet I notice so many counterexamples.     This principle has slowly extended from the backpack on my back to the inner one, in my head and chest.     It’s no longer the non-essential objects I leave behind now, but the petty fears and anxieties of everyday life.     Where am I going?     Will I have enough to eat?     To drink?     To sleep?     What if this path leads nowhere?     And then, the worries about the future—because I will have to work, earn money, and return someday...     We can’t go long without leaving these false hassles aside. This is the moment when we begin to learn freedom and happiness. And the more one realizes this, the more one likes it, the less difficult it is to realize it and participate in it. In fact, the more you walk on its path, the easier it becomes to walk there...    I learn freedom, I learn happiness. I’ve discovered that you can’t find them, you can’t receive them, or give them—the only way to live them is to learn to be. And it doesn’t need much; in a way, it just “stops preventing them” from being, naturally...     The most frequent question I receive concerns the number of kilometers I do per day. But this is a question that no longer makes sense to me. The preoccupation with the number of kilometers traveled no longer exists at all. You now understand what I wrote earlier concerning the 7000 km fake news. A glance at the map tells me that I’m almost there, but in the end, I don’t know. I haven’t made the effort to calculate, despite being asked very often.     I measure my days, if I must, by the quality of the time that has passed. I walk when I want or need to. I stop as soon as it’s pretty enough to look at, and the notion of average mileage is completely absent. I don’t feel bad or guilty for having walked a little—that’s something that took me a long time to give up: feeling bad for not having walked a lot today. The concept of obligation, if it still exists, has been transferred to the pleasure of being.     And in my long walk experience, finding a pretty spot is extremely pleasant. Finding a suitable place to pitch the tent is pleasant. A source of fresh water to fill my water bottles and refresh myself. A lake or river where I can bathe, wash myself... A hot shower. A coffee. A glass of slivovica (a little plum!). A smile.     I take pleasure in such trivial details, and I’m amazed at the power they possess, the strength they wield. To say that finding mushrooms on my way, lighting a fire to cook them, and eating while sitting on the ground in front of my tent nourished me is an understatement. It certainly nourished my body, but also a whole part of me which, until I let it enjoy and live, was curled up in a withering and sterile non-existence.     The silence I listen to is a fullness, not an emptiness...   Then the inner discourse slowly fades away... The incessant brouhaha, which we no longer realize deafens our inner ears to the point of not only deafening ourselves but others too—not only inside but also outside—eventually dries up and goes silent. There is then nothing to hinder the full enjoyment of the contentment of a deep breath of fresh air, the freshness of a sip of spring water, the sight of a wild animal, the song of a bird, the scent of a fir tree, the delicacy of a flower petal, or the taste of a hazelnut...     And here I am, with an almost ecstatic feeling, even though no event has occurred to provoke it. I find myself laughing without having thought of anything funny. A huge smile splits my face as I stand totally alone in the woods. And yet, I can’t stop this smile that I don’t offer to anyone.     I am well. I am here. And it’s good...    I made the mistake of writing this text in French and translating it afterward. It’s not the same when I do that... But I hope you still get the point.     I wish you all the best. Be well and happy.
blog/meeting-with-a-doe/index.html:
Meeting with a Doe


		20/7/2024
	
     Hello everyone,     Three months without news—I’m overdoing it a bit.     Here’s the update:     Since last time, many good things have happened, and no bad things. That’s a decent balance.    Still, I feel like complaining. Firstly, because it’s a basic human need, and secondly, because I’m French. As the cliché goes, the French love to complain, followed by a good protest.     My chosen subject of complaint: the temperature. For the past two and a half months, it’s been consistently 35⁰C, with spikes to 38⁰C and even 43⁰C on three occasions.   It’s unbearable. Walking in this sun and heat is no longer just challenging; it’s becoming dangerous. I’ve had to adjust my walking schedule to avoid the midday extremes.     I now wake up 30 minutes to an hour before sunrise to pack my things. When daylight breaks, I fold the tent and start walking early, continuing until around 11 a.m. or noon—longer if I haven’t found a suitable resting spot. Romania is an hour ahead of Central Europe, so the timing feels slightly off.  I stop in the shade of forests, caves, or villages—often meeting new people in cafés or restaurants. These breaks allow me to recharge my batteries—both electrical and social. Sometimes, I’m invited to stay, which I often accept, drawn by the promise of a shower and good company.     I set out again around 4:30 or 5 p.m., walking until I find a welcoming place to stop or until the sun sets, usually around 8 p.m.    I don’t always pitch the tent. In this summer weather, sleeping under the stars is comfortable, with the Milky Way serving as my sleeping bag. It also saves time tidying up in the morning.    Sleeping outdoors has taught me to tolerate the local fauna. Insects often crawl over me as I sleep, but I’ve learned not to react. An earwig running across my skin or a beetle tangled in my hair no longer bothers me as much. I used to think they got caught intentionally, but after observing, I realized their shell design is to blame. If I don’t carefully untangle them, they risk losing legs or antennae—or worse, pulling out my hair.    Some beetles pinch, likely to express their discomfort, creating mine. When that happens, I wake up, fully aware of the incident—unlike many other encounters that don’t disturb my sleep. It’s like how we notice a sore knee only when we bump it, even though we probably hit it just as often when it doesn’t hurt. A beetle in your hair is a similar, unforgettable experience.    Larger creatures, from shrews and hedgehogs to grass snakes, foxes, and weasels, tend to keep their distance. Without the tent obscuring their view or smell, they quickly recognize me as human—the ultimate nightmare—and flee without hesitation.     If they are sane, everyone flees. So when that doesn’t happen, it’s a notable and often touching event.     For example, one morning during this pilgrimage, I was lying on my mattress (it’s still necessary to isolate yourself from the dampness of the ground to sleep better), my head resting on my hand, against my bag, and leaning against a tree at the edge of a wood. Like a hunting dog curled up and asleep, I faced a small grassy clearing. I was awakened by a presence.    It didn’t feel alarming. I stayed calm, listening. I believe the brain, even while asleep, can hear and analyze sounds in the immediate environment, alerting us if necessary. I’ve experienced this four times now during nocturnal visits from bears. But this time, there was no urgency, no danger.    I opened my eyes. About fifteen meters away, an enormous doe was grazing nonchalantly. I say enormous because it was not a deer but an adult doe—and an adult doe is large. She grazed noisily on the grass. Well, noisy for someone like me, now awake and trying to be still. In the calm morning silence of nature, after a good night’s sleep, I lay motionless, amazed by the spectacle. Usually, such encounters are fleeting, as frightened animals quickly flee.    I savored the moment, staying as still as possible while observing her. Then, about ten meters away, I noticed a small fawn, likely old enough to have lost its spots. I wanted to lift my head slightly to see it better but didn’t dare move.     Eventually, I had to adjust—or perhaps my breathing changed—because the doe suddenly raised her angular head. Her whole body tensed, motionless, on alert.     That’s when we locked eyes. We stared at each other, directly into each other’s gaze—a moment suspended in time. It felt so real that it was almost unreal. Probably just a fraction of a second, but it felt eternal. Both of us were frozen in attentive silence.    And then, as nothing happened, she seemed to decide that I wasn’t a threat and resumed grazing.    That’s what moved me the most. The moment of eye contact was intense, but her choice to start grazing again, despite knowing the worst of predators—the most destructive of creatures—was nearby, truly touched me. It felt as though she had decided to trust me.     I felt accepted, as if I had become part of her world. You can’t imagine how proud this made me. It’s a moment etched in my memory, one that strengthens me when I recall it. Hindus have a term for such experiences: “Darshan.”    We stayed like that for a few minutes. She tore at the tender grass, taking a step between each bite, while I remained still, listening to my heart pound as if I were receiving a kiss for the first time.     These are the kinds of moments that can happen when you sleep under the stars.   I’m nearing the Serbian-Romanian border. My journey continues toward the sanctuary of Medjugorje in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which means crossing Serbia.     I hope the summer won’t be as hot as the spring, though I’m not optimistic.     I hope everything is going well for you and wish you health and happiness.     See you soon.     P.S.:     I have a good excuse for being late with updates. I’ve overexposed myself to phone screens while working on putting a blog online. I’ll share the address once it’s ready.    Writing and sending these updates, attaching photos, and sending them to all my contacts has become tedious. Platforms like Signal or WhatsApp only allow sending to five contacts at a time. Between each batch, I have to reselect text and photos, then sift through my contact list to choose the next five while remembering who hasn’t received it yet.     With several hundred contacts—and the list growing—the process isn’t getting any easier.    The blog should simplify things while improving practicality. It might even reach others who haven’t met me but could appreciate the content.     What content? Nearly all the updates I’ve sent since starting this pilgrimage in September 2020, plus a selection of the best photos, and complete answers to frequently asked questions.     Voila. A good excuse, right?
