Vilnius


		6/7/2021
	
     ​I know, I should have told you about Vilnius, my second destination. It's already been a week since I left the place...    I would have shared my arrival, and all the people I met on my way since my last update. So many nice people. Always. Only.     For example, I would have told you about this lovely elderly couple, Maceliai and Vingriu. I say "elderly," but honestly, they felt so young in spirit. He, for instance, had the energy and enthusiasm of a supercharged teenager, practically hopping as he spoke. Both of them had bright, keen eyes. It was such a nice meeting.    From the street, I asked them for water. He came straight to the gate, opened it, and invited me in—all smiles. And what a smile! You can see it in the photos—genuine happiness! They offered me tea, and soon fresh cheese appeared, pressed that very morning, along with honey (forest flowers), bread, and pickles.    We talked, though it wasn't easy since they didn’t speak a word of English, but were fluent in German and Russian. They were from that generation that doesn’t give a phone translator enough time to work—reading translations aloud as they appear, causing the phone to misunderstand and start translating again, erasing the previous text. After a few tries, we mostly gave up on the translation app, but we still managed to have a great conversation.     He showed me an ultralight plane he built himself—including the plans! Then he gave me a tour of his workshops: first the mechanical one, with a milling machine, lathe, and welding tools; then the woodshop, equipped with a router, planer, jointer, and bandsaw. Next came his greenhouse and his homemade sauna, heated with a wood stove. Everything at his home had his personal touch, including a visit to his beehives.     The man must be hyperactive, a genius, and incredibly skilled with his hands. Everything was simple yet impressive. He even offered me a shower in a small building in his garden, where the water tank was made from a repurposed Russian bomb shell that holds 3,000 liters, heated naturally by the sun. With the week’s temperatures at 35°C, you can imagine how welcome that shower was!     They were deeply connected to nature—everything organic and healing. He showed me a small wooden hut designed for naps. The "bed" was actually two beehives, with the roof made from two more. You’re surrounded by bees, enveloped in the soothing scents of wax, honey, pollen, propolis, and pinewood, while the buzzing sound of thousands of bees hums like a lullaby. You can even feel the subtle vibrations, as if the whole hut is purring. He even built a periscope so you can observe the activity inside the beehives while you drift off, counting bees instead of sheep! It's supposed to be healing.     I don’t know if it works, but I can say this: a nap there must be amazing, and I’d love to be as healthy as he is at 77 years old!     They also showed me a pagan ceremony they participate in—shamanic practices around a fire with songs and tambourines.      It was truly a beautiful encounter.     Or there’s Rasa—how I ended up in her garden is a story of its own. I had lost my track in the forest and, being too lazy to retrace my steps, I decided to just keep going, thinking, "There are no mistakes, after all—the path I take becomes my path." A bit of high philosophy that ultimately led to me crossing a river on a fallen tree trunk and battling my way up a steep riverbank through tall grass, nettles, and brambles. This adventure ended with me stumbling into the back of her property.     After asking for water, she offered me coffee, then lunch. Later, to make myself useful, I mowed her garden lawn with her mower, clearing it up nicely before we sat back down on her veranda to chat. I ended up staying the night, and since it poured rain the next day, she took me for a drive in her car to visit at least six beautiful spots I would have passed without noticing otherwise.     On the way back, we stopped at a wine shop where I managed to find some Côte du Rhône AOP, which paired perfectly with the “real cheese” you might remember from my previous update. That evening, we enjoyed the wine on her veranda while her neighbor joined us for a chat. It was a delightful French-Lithuanian evening.     Rasa and I stayed in touch, and we met again in Vilnius a week or so later. It turned out the countryside house where I met her was her holiday home. She normally lives in Vilnius, works in a bank, and is very connected—she even has one of those smartwatches that keeps her updated on everything happening on her phone. It’s impressive how efficient she is.     I’d also tell you about another couple who offered me dinner and a place to stay just a few days later, which turned out to be perfect timing because the weather forecast predicted a massive storm. And I mean massive—at one point, my phone, even in flight mode, emitted a warning buzz, displaying an alert directly from the government. That’s when you realize flight mode is just a software setting, not a physical switch!    Even though the alert was in Lithuanian, it was clear enough: bad weather was on the way. Camping in the forest during a storm isn’t exactly the safest idea—imagine what protection a tent offers against falling branches! So, staying in their beautiful garden was not only safer but also lovely. We spent the evening watching the lightning and talking, enjoying the storm from a safe and cozy vantage point.     So I finally arrived in Vilnius, and I could have told you about my first night camping near the Gate of Dawn, where a morning rainstorm turned into a river that flooded my tent, soaking everything—my belongings and me included. I could have told you how I spent four hours the next day drying everything out, especially my battery packs, which were literally dripping. I was lucky enough to find an air dryer and used it on low heat to avoid frying them. (The internet says it’s a terrible idea to let your battery packs get wet—it kills them, apparently, and should never happen. So, I guess I’m really lucky because all of mine survived! I would have been especially disappointed to lose the last one, a gift from someone on my way, with such excellent capacity and quality. This one might even be waterproof!)    I could have told you about Our Lady of the Gate, the Basilica, or the beautiful churches scattered throughout the town—or just about the town itself.    I could have also told you how I was invited to a convent near the Gate of Dawn, where I met some wonderful sisters and stayed for four days. They gave me the time and space I needed to take care of everything I had to do.     There are so many things I could have shared, and I guess I’ve mentioned a little of it now. But what I really want to tell you about is something I witnessed—something that left a strong impression on me.    One Saturday evening, I was coming back from a dinner I had prepared with Rasa at her place in Vilnius. It was a way to thank her for her warm hospitality and to enjoy a "French dinner" that we cooked together (though I really screwed it up). I also had the chance to meet her friends, which was another lovely experience.     So, it was quite late, around 11:30 p.m., and I was sitting on a tram in the suburbs of the capital, replaying in my head how the spinach tourte had gone so wrong, when I saw what I’m about to describe.    The tram had stopped, and more people were getting in than getting out. I was standing in the middle, with only a few seats still available—two of them right in front of me. A young guy, who had just boarded through the front door, spotted the seats and immediately picked up his pace, eager to claim them before anyone else. So far, it was a completely ordinary scene, the kind you see all the time. He was probably around 19 years old, chatting noisily but cheerfully with his friend, as young people often do on a Saturday night.    At first, I didn’t pay much attention and turned my gaze toward the rear of the tram, where the back door was letting in a few more passengers. And there, the same situation was unfolding. Two Afro-Lithuanian guys, dressed in the full rapper-style outfit—caps, T-shirts, gold chains, the whole look—had also spotted the same seats...    At that moment, it was obvious—I was about to witness a social tension event. You know, one of those moments you see coming. Both parties had that seat in mind, both sped up to claim it for themselves. They accelerated, and suddenly everything seemed to play out in slow motion. My head went from right to left, and back again, faster as they got closer, and then—bing! Of course, they reached the spot at the same time. Standing face to face, just a foot apart, one with his hand on the back of the seat, the other gripping the vertical bar in front of it.    This is the moment where you'd expect frustration to explode. You know the scenario: the closer someone gets to their goal, the higher the expectation; the higher the expectation, the worse the frustration when they’re deprived. Basic psychology! And obviously, one of them wasn’t going to sit. Someone was going to be frustrated!   It felt like such a pivotal moment to watch—something that could reveal so much about the social dynamics of the place... about human behavior. And, let’s be honest, maybe I’d learn a few colorful swear words in the process.    I projected my expectations, drawing parallels. Paris suburbs, Saturday night, young people on public transport... I braced myself for at least some incivility, if not outright violence. Verbal aggression seemed like the bare minimum I could expect.    But no.    They stood there, facing each other, realized the situation, and—together, at the same time—offered the seat to the other!    "You first!"    "No, you!"    "Please, it's okay, take it!"    "Are you sure?"    "Yes, yes, go ahead!"    And then, one of them sat down with his friend, while the other held out his fist for a friendly bump. You know the gesture: Hey, give me five! Yeah, bro!    They smiled. They were relaxed. They were human.   I was impressed. How can I describe it? I felt comfortable, confident, and at ease on public transport in the suburbs of the capital, late on a Saturday night, surrounded by a big group of young people, some of whom were lightly tipsy.     Now, you might not think this is a big deal. I mean, sure, you could argue that this should just be normal. But in my experience—at least mine—for far less than this, I’ve seen middle fingers raised and unsavory comments about people’s mothers thrown around.    It’s hard for me to tell if I’m just hypersensitive to this now. Spending ten months mostly alone, following a discipline where most of my time is spent in meditation, contemplation, prayer, or the recitation of mantras as part of my yoga practice—all of it aimed at what we often call spirituality—might have changed how I see the world.    I’m aware of this shift, but I can’t measure its extent. I know I’m not objective, but I don’t know how much I’ve changed. So many things I witness now seem surreal at first, but because they happen every day, they’ve become my new normal. Meanwhile, what’s conventionally considered "normal" often feels unbearably sad in comparison.    I’m not sure what’s more significant here: the scene itself or my perception of it. What’s certain is that my experience of pilgrimage—my Sadhana—has altered me.    One thing I know for sure: it makes me happy. It makes me feel good. It gives me a sense of reconciliation with humanity, a stark contrast to the pervasive fear mainstream media loves to sell. The message of the world is always “Be careful. Outside is dangerous.”    But my experience?    People are nice.    So be confident. Be trusting. Be grateful, be kind. And love… laugh… smile. Life is beautiful, in a beautiful world with beautiful people. Even if you sleep outside every day, cannot wash yourself every day, cannot wash your clothes every week, don’t have hot coffee in the morning, or cannot dry yourself when it’s raining… it’s still nice to live. (So imagine when you have a house, a car, a family around you, a hot shower, a coffee machine...).    Ok. I swear I didn’t drink. Or smoke. Or anything else…    Let me tell you another one!    Two days ago, as I was on my way to Aglona in Latvia (my next and third destination), I arrived in a small town and came across a cute church bordered by a small park with a little river running around it. A really beautiful place. I decided to stop for a while and splash myself in the river. So I went down the alley to get closer, and I saw a bank full of people sitting there.    No problem, I stopped about 20 meters away, dropped my backpack, and sat on it to take my shoes off. Before I could even do that, one of the three guys called out to me, waving a bottle of vodka and saying something that could have been “hey heu euuuu ah beee labbbeu heuuu”... though I can’t be entirely sure of the translation.   This is another good example of self-projection—where I, like many others, find myself assuming things. I thought, Ah, just a bunch of homeless, drunken guys squatting in the park. But I got over that quickly. I reminded myself that I, too, might look like someone who sleeps outside, doesn’t wash every day, and so on. You see what I mean…    So I said hello and accepted their offer to join them, figuring I could explain a bit about myself. They turned out to be really jovial, sympathetic, and friendly. I hadn’t even started introducing myself—my name or the fact that I was a pilgrim—when one of them handed me a shot of vodka.    Okay… I took it and began my explanation. Before I could finish—pretty quickly, I might add—I had to politely refuse the fourth shot.    It could have ended there: just some drunk people sharing drinks with a stranger who probably looked like one of them. But then, a woman passed by on the path, and they gave her the same warm welcome, offering her a drink as well.    I had serious doubts about this. I thought, This is a bad idea. There’s no way she’ll engage with them—she’ll just walk by with an air of disdain. But to my surprise, she stopped. She talked with them a bit and even found out that they were celebrating one of their birthdays. And then—they hugged.    No way. They must have known each other. Surely, I thought, they were longtime acquaintances.    But no. This same thing happened three more times while I stood there with them. Two more people joined and had a shot of vodka with them. Another woman even sat down with them for a while.    After splashing myself in the river (which they assured me was totally fine to do), one of the men offered to introduce me to the priest of the church. He knew where the priest lived, just a few hundred meters away, and thought maybe I could find accommodation there. He came with me, and that’s how I left this merry group of people—people I’m now ashamed to have initially judged as drunken homeless.    Okay, sure, they were drunk. And yes, they were drinking outside in a park. But the way they made me feel—like we were neighbors who had known each other for years—was humbling.    That’s it. Maybe it doesn’t seem like much to you. But for me, here, in my nearly ten months of walking now, I can assure you I’m taking these small, seemingly insignificant things as truly important—little everyday miracles. And even though I’m not particularly fond of vodka, I gladly drank with them from their glass. I was happy to answer whatever questions they asked, happy to share moments with total strangers I probably would have ignored in my “normal” life.    And when I left, I felt genuinely happy. A big smile on my face... (The vodka might have helped with that because, honestly, I’m really not used to it...).    Today, I was supposed to get moving since yesterday was already a day off! But it’s raining hard. Really hard. So I decided to stay in my tent again. I have enough water in my bottles, enough food, and enough battery to write a long message to give you an update!   And you know what? I just received a message from Rasa. She’s planning to take her car and meet me this weekend by a lake I’ll be passing on my way—just like that. Just to spend an afternoon on the shore with a guy she’s only met twice...    I hope you’re well and happy.    And I hope my update isn’t too long...    But I needed to say this, and I did...    See you...

Transylvania


		23/7/2023
	
     ​Yesterday, I told myself that I would take the road again after spending two days near this stream at the edge of the village, where the local children, Gypsies, had built a kind of small swimming pool out of odds and ends—sticks, plastics, and stones. The small water reservoir was really appealing. I relaxed in it, washed myself, and washed my clothes there. Every evening, when it was quiet, I returned to soak until I was fully satisfied or until the sun disappeared and night fell.     I had placed my tent in the hedge adjacent to the spot, where it was thick enough to shelter me from the sun, which burns strongly when it’s not raining. I was in the shade and protected from the view of passers-by on the road or the swimmers who came during the day. The spot was perfect—so hidden that even if someone walked less than five meters away, it was almost impossible to see my tent. Even I, knowing its location, had to make a real effort to spot it when heading to the river, about 50 meters downhill.    That morning, as had been the case for some time, I was torn between continuing my journey or staying another day, knowing the consequences. I had one banana and one madeleine left to eat, and three liters of water to drink. The water was enough to last until the next evening and the walk the day after to the next well or spring, whether natural or human-made.     As for food, it was tight. I decided to save the madeleine for the next evening and the banana for the departure the day after because walking on a completely empty stomach slows me down more than I already am from fatigue. So, I chose to stay and enjoy the luxury of a garden swimming pool, even if it meant fasting for a while. Fasting now and then is good...    When I finally left, my plan was to pass through the next village, 7 km away, to look for a grocery store (though none was indicated on my map) to buy food. Then, I’d walk another 2 km to find a place in the forest to pitch my tent and spend two days resting. You know the cycle I already described in my last message. I also needed to figure out how to recharge my power banks. I had no charge left in two of the three, and only 40% in the last one.    Normally, I expect to be invited to charge my batteries at the grocery stores or bars in the villages I pass through. After buying food and sipping coffee or a drink, I typically spend an hour or so charging everything.     But here’s the problem: I had no more money with me. The local currency is Lei, and I had only 15 Lei left. I had Euros and my bank card, but the small village grocery store didn’t accept either. You can see the complexity here—no way to buy food and no real excuse to ask to stay an hour to recharge my phone. This was a situation that could potentially become problematic, forcing me to walk 45 km to the next ATM.     But it’s been three years that everything has gone wonderfully well, and I am starting to get used to it—a certain confidence is becoming anchored.   When I speak of habit, I should clarify that it does not alter the quality of perception and wonder. At least, I hope not to get used to it in that way. Simply, the occurrence of these positive outcomes is such that I no longer listen to anxieties, doubts, or uncertainties. Despite what could easily become unpleasant or even difficult, I’ve reached an irrational yet very real serenity: it’s going to be fine.     So, here I am in this village. And there’s a grocery store! I find it easily. The lady running it does not accept cards or Euros, as expected and anticipated.     But she tells me to wait, grabs her phone, and calls her boss. He arrives 15 minutes later, agrees to exchange some Euros for me, and allows me to recharge my batteries in the shop.     I wait outside, sitting on the benches set up for the local regulars. Thirty minutes pass. An hour. The first battery gets recharged, but the other two, which typically take five hours, are not done yet. I tell myself that I can continue charging them partially until my phone, which is also charging, reaches 100%. Then I’ll leave. So I begin writing this message...     My bag is full of food and water. I’m ready...    And then the boss comes back with a friend and a bottle, offering me a beer and a polanta (a little plum! Or in this case, a pear). We talk.    He also has a guesthouse in the village, and after hearing my plan to pitch my tent in the next forest, he suggests I set it up in the garden of his guesthouse instead. I can shower and do laundry if I want—and of course, I will! I can also finish recharging my batteries there.     I met a couple of very nice hosts there, about to leave as they were taking the road early in the morning. I was invited by the owner of the place to share supper—a good hot vegetable soup. It was a nice change from bread, cheese, and tomatoes.    We spent the evening together discussing various things. They offered me a packet of dried fruit, a kilo of apricots, a bar of chocolate, a dozen hard-boiled eggs, and two cereal bars.    I said goodbye to them in the early morning and took the opportunity to remove my laundry from the line where it was trying to dry, because despite the lingering night, the sky was heavy with clouds. And, in fact, a few moments before I went back to sleep in the shelter of my tent, the rain began to fall.    Now, I’m seated at the patio table. Everyone has gone, and I’m alone. I’ll close the gate when I leave, as agreed. I’m finishing this message while charging my phone. In a moment, I’ll be back on the road, freshly washed, my clothes clean, my batteries and phone fully charged, my bags full of food and fruit, my water bottles full of water, and my pocket full of Lei (well, full enough 😜).    I don’t know why, but again I feel the need to explain these small, almost intangible things. Actually, it’s not so much about explaining as it is about sharing. But to share, I feel compelled to explain everything in detail: everything is fine... It went well. Kindness is a succulent spice.     It’s been like this for three years. In addition to being really pleasant to live with, it’s fortifying.     Voilà. That was a little hello from Transylvania.    P.S.: Sad news—my felt hat has given up the ghost. After almost three years of (almost) good service, after several repairs, seams, and other DIY rescue operations, it has finally reached a point of no return, with the material disintegrating. I gave it the last care and attention it deserved before letting it go. Even though the hat wasn’t much to look at just three months after I started my journey, its loss feels a little painful.     But hey! Good news: three hours after the lid of the trash can definitively sealed the fate of the first one, a gentleman offered me a new hat. He warned me that the gift was really fragile—not to say of poor quality—but, as he pointed out very pertinently, it would hold up until I could find a real one: a sturdy one, a solid one, a "real" hat.     So voilà, I walk protected temporarily, with the hope that finding a robust hat is not a utopia—that the very concept of a solid hat is not a myth.    Re-P.S.: Yes, I walk with garlic in my backpack. But no, that has nothing to do with the fact that I’m in Transylvania. It’s because I encounter far more mushrooms than vampires. With all the precipitation here, combined with the heat, mushrooms grow nicely and profusely. And it must be said, a little garlic suits them particularly well when I simmer them over a wood fire.    As for the vampires, the tale of the Count of Dracula and all that—I believe it’s a myth. A bit like solid hats, I guess...    And P.S. again, but the last one, I swear: I wanted to measure whether, and how much, my long messages are actually read. So, I thought that to check, you could write a secret code at the beginning of your reply message next time you write to me. This would allow me to gauge the relevance of persisting in writing and sending such long texts to people who might not have time to read them all. 😃    Now, as for the secret code—I have no real idea. That is to say, the idea of a secret code seemed very good to me when I thought of it, but I didn’t get any further than that. Well then, I’ll let you choose what seems most appropriate. Just make sure to specify that it’s indeed the code... ​😜😜😜

Meeting with a Bear


		11/7/2023
	
      It’s been a long time again, and I feel and sense some impatience. It’s nice to know that my news messages are awaited. It’s somehow a form of support for my journey.     I have now been in Romania for a few weeks, and I really appreciate what I am experiencing and seeing here.   But since Slovakia, I’ve been dragging my feet. I feel tired, physically exhausted, without this being justified by walking. This is because my walk is slow and interrupted by many breaks to enjoy the landscape, an encounter, a stone, a stump, or a bench perfectly placed for me to rest on. I walk, contemplate, and meditate—sometimes all at the same time. It’s a pleasant exercise, during which the inner chatter eventually dies out, and I find myself alone, silent, and content.   The breaks under the walnut tree, on the warm trunk of a tree in the local sun, stretch on without me worrying about it, without any movement occurring either inside or outside. A flat encephalogram (which some might say must be easy for me—see the end of the message...) certainly, but with vigilance, with purposeless concentration, if that makes sense to you. As a result, my average mileage drops quickly, but since the goal is not athletic, as you understood, I don’t care.    However, for some time now, not only has my walking slowed down, but the breaks have grown longer and far more frequent. This made me consider the possibility of a health problem, which prompted me to change my route and pass through a big city to consult a doctor for a check-up. After all, it’s been 4 or 5 years since I’ve had any follow-up care, and almost 3 years that I’ve been walking in living conditions that some would call precarious.    So, to reassure you right away: the examination and analyses revealed nothing abnormal. The doctor who examined me at the hospital simply told me that I needed to rest...    So, that’s what I’m doing.    Before continuing, I would like to point out that the Romanian health system is welcoming. Any individual is received and treated free of charge for 72 hours, regardless of their nationality. This will probably not impress the French, whose health system also has some good aspects, but when you experience this attention, it is touching. Really. The Hippocratic oath no longer feels hypocritical... and it feels good.     So here it is: for a month, I have been walking for one day, then resting for two or three. And I feel like it’s paying off, as I now feel better rested and often eager to start again—something I had been missing lately.    But I’m seeing the good side of things: I’m spending a lot of time in the countryside. When I stop, it’s often in the forest, which here finally covers the land that, to the east of where I came from, was sadly bare. I don’t know where you are, but here it’s hot or very hot, and as soon as it gets too much, we get a storm. A real summer storm with torrential downpours (think Indian or Nepalese monsoon), thunder that shakes the ground, and lightning that gets me out of my tent to check if the tree next to me was hit.     After that, the temperature becomes much more bearable, but it’s incredibly heavy because of the humidity. It might seem unpleasant, but you have to look at the whole picture: when it’s hot and very humid, it feels heavy and uncomfortable, but—and I allow myself to use capital letters here—BUT, all the conditions are suddenly perfect for the appearance of our fungal friends.    I picked summer ceps in mid-June. Yes! And they were a delight. At the end of June, I was invited to breakfast by a local mushroom enthusiast who prepared a fricassee of chanterelles. You can imagine that if I spend time in the woods, I eat mushrooms regularly. And to me, that’s divine.   On the other hand, the local forests have one major drawback: bears. And I admit, there are many. Even in a small wood, like a one-hectare thicket, there is likely a bear in it. I didn’t really believe it at first—just like in Slovakia. But here, I see traces every day. Fresh traces, even very fresh ones. I’ve even had morning visits. In wolf and dog form. Their schedule seems to be around 3:30–4:00 a.m.    I discovered that even when we sleep in the middle of the woods, a part of us continues to "listen." I was amazed to realize this, but I believe that our ears continue to hear, and our brain processes information intuitively. It’s strange to notice, like finally becoming aware of your unconscious.    The two times a bear approached my tent while I was sleeping, I woke up immediately, as if shaken by my subconscious warning me of danger. There was no gentle awakening phase where you take your time, where reality is still blurred by the paradoxical sleep phase, free cinema... No, I opened my eyes instantly, no transition—I was alert, attentive, concentrated, and immediately ready to act.    I already knew there was something on the other side of the thin fabric of my tent. My first thought, clear and certain, was: a bear. About ten meters from the tent, I then heard heavy but hesitant footsteps. Without hesitation, without even thinking, I began to sing—softly but loudly—while at the same time lighting up the tent with the headlamp given to me by a firefighter from Târgu Mureș. I knew that my tent would then become a softly glowing lamp, about 3 meters long and 1.2 meters high. A beautiful sight for the bear, I imagined, lying there, motionless.    Singing right away when you wake up because a bear is outside might seem like a crazy idea. But let me explain:    The only bear attacks in Europe are related to surprise—when a bear is startled by a human who was too discreet (the bear neither hears nor senses them), or to fear—when an aggressive human mistakenly thinks that making a lot of noise or acting threateningly will scare away a 350 kg beast. The bear, feeling threatened, might attack instead of fleeing. Another situation is when an inattentive human finds themselves between a bear and her cubs, triggering a protective maternal instinct—with claws and teeth.    Other attacks are linked to predatory behavior, triggered when a human runs (or cycles or skis) in front of a bear. This activates the bear’s predatory or attack reflex, much like what happens with an excited dog that is likely to bite if you run from it.     So, I tell myself that if the bear has approached me despite the unmistakable olfactory signals for its sense of smell—signals I deliberately place around and on my tent (a cloth soaked in diesel between the roof and the double roof of the tent, and my urine poured on the trunks of trees around my campsite)—it’s because the bear is curious (like many animals I’ve noticed) and opportunistic (hoping the human is gone and has left something to eat).    Of course, the bear probably doesn’t have a clear concept of UFOs, but the tent must seem like a very strange object to it—especially when it lights up.    When I wake up, I sing so the bear knows I’m there, in the tent. Singing, unlike shouting or howling, is far less aggressive. It also benefits me: singing has a soothing effect, both on the one who hears the song and on the one who sings it. You can’t sing while being completely paralyzed with fear. Singing keeps fear at bay.     In short, my theory is that, like many animals I’ve known since childhood, bears are not so much receptive to what I say but rather to the tone in which I say it. They are not as affected by my movements as they are by my attitude—my mental state, in a way.    I believe that singing is a way to show my presence while maintaining a relaxed and peaceful attitude. It reassures the animal while informing it of my presence and my nature.     Both times this happened, the bear ran away immediately. The second time, it was really close to me and let out a kind of nasal breath, an impressive Mmufffff. Either I wasn’t mistaken about its presence, or I sing really badly!    Also impressive is the sound of cattle running through the undergrowth. You might not know this, but when we sleep in the woods, sounds are amplified—not only by the acoustics of the place but also by the unconscious analysis our brain performs. It’s probably a remnant from the time when we lived outdoors and were a tasty treat for many predators.    At night, a simple beetle can seem like a huge rat snooping around. A toad becomes je ne sais quoi weighing at least 20 kilograms... A bird landing on the ground and scratching with its claw for food becomes a wild boar. I assure you, it’s destabilizing to realize how much our brain exaggerates these sounds.    Over time, with practice, the brain recalibrates, and you can relax completely despite the many noises of the forest. I now sleep in the woods as comfortably as I would in a bed in my room—even though, in reality, I haven’t had a room or a bed for more than 28 years.    So, I believe bears aren’t really the danger. They represent a risk, because, in the end, nothing prevents encountering a bad-tempered one—there are difficult characters in all mammals; it’s not exclusive to bipeds in an upright position. But I think that with certain precautions and behaviors, the risk is ultimately very small.     I accept this risk because, ultimately, I have no choice if I want to continue my journey.    When I spend several days in the same place, choosing the right location is essential. A sheltered spot—from the sun, so it’s possible to stay under the tent, and from view, to avoid worrying or being disturbed. Some places lend themselves perfectly: a small clearing of a few dozen square meters of flat and sparsely sown ground, where dense vegetation around and above filters the direct light... A small stream of clear water to cool off during the heat of the afternoon, and to wash, too.     This is where I was yesterday and the day before. Superb... Magnificent... Ideal.     Until the storm.    The rain began to fall in large drops, accompanied by a deafening clap of thunder that tore through the silence and my senses. It became so intense that I went out to check the stream, only a few meters away. The rain was so heavy that, already soaked, I decided to take out the soap and wash myself in the deluge.     When I returned to the tent, I knew there was a risk the water would rise and the stream might overflow. But there was space...     So I lay down and thought about something else. The rain stopped, and after looking outside, I assessed the risk of flooding as acceptable. The groundsheet of my new tent is waterproof and can withstand being in a layer of water up to 5 cm without compromising the interior.And inside, I have a small self-inflating mattress a few centimeters thick.     Even if water were to penetrate a little, most of my belongings would still be sheltered.     The happy optimist who sees the glass half full... I fell asleep like a child.     As I write this, I am washing all of my belongings and gear. I was awakened by the tent shaking and pushing me aside. Water was penetrating inside, and by the time I began organizing my things and planning my escape, I was in more than eight inches of water.     Of course, night was falling, and I had to move all my stuff to a place that wasn’t flooded, about 50 meters away. By the time I finished, the torrent covering the whole area was 40 cm deep. Suffice to say, the stream below was no longer visible at all.     The tent was almost lying in the water, and dismantling it became a major emergency before it broke. The battery in the headlamp chose this moment to signal that it needed energy. I realized that if I handled things poorly, I would lose a lot—some of my equipment had already been carried away. I removed all the pegs and fought to get the tent out of the water without it being swept away by the current.     I managed it, securing the tent in a safe place and getting back to it later. I spent the next day rinsing my belongings of the fine, sticky mud and the whole afternoon looking for what had been carried away: water bottles, clothes, bags.     I found almost everything, which feels almost miraculous.     But I confess, I’m not proud of myself. There were signs I ignored because I thought everything would be fine. I listened to optimism until it turned into foolishness!     Fortunately, in the village where I arrived, there’s a small guesthouse. I’m staying there to wash my clothes, clean the mud off absolutely everything, and dry everything in the sun.     Finally, everything is fine.   Tomorrow, I’m back on my way—a day of walking to a suitable place, then two days of rest. With a little luck, in a few weeks, I’ll be able to resume a normal rhythm.     In the meantime, I wish you all the best.     See you soon.

Meeting with a Doe


		20/7/2024
	
     Hello everyone,     Three months without news—I’m overdoing it a bit.     Here’s the update:     Since last time, many good things have happened, and no bad things. That’s a decent balance.    Still, I feel like complaining. Firstly, because it’s a basic human need, and secondly, because I’m French. As the cliché goes, the French love to complain, followed by a good protest.     My chosen subject of complaint: the temperature. For the past two and a half months, it’s been consistently 35⁰C, with spikes to 38⁰C and even 43⁰C on three occasions.   It’s unbearable. Walking in this sun and heat is no longer just challenging; it’s becoming dangerous. I’ve had to adjust my walking schedule to avoid the midday extremes.     I now wake up 30 minutes to an hour before sunrise to pack my things. When daylight breaks, I fold the tent and start walking early, continuing until around 11 a.m. or noon—longer if I haven’t found a suitable resting spot. Romania is an hour ahead of Central Europe, so the timing feels slightly off.  I stop in the shade of forests, caves, or villages—often meeting new people in cafés or restaurants. These breaks allow me to recharge my batteries—both electrical and social. Sometimes, I’m invited to stay, which I often accept, drawn by the promise of a shower and good company.     I set out again around 4:30 or 5 p.m., walking until I find a welcoming place to stop or until the sun sets, usually around 8 p.m.    I don’t always pitch the tent. In this summer weather, sleeping under the stars is comfortable, with the Milky Way serving as my sleeping bag. It also saves time tidying up in the morning.    Sleeping outdoors has taught me to tolerate the local fauna. Insects often crawl over me as I sleep, but I’ve learned not to react. An earwig running across my skin or a beetle tangled in my hair no longer bothers me as much. I used to think they got caught intentionally, but after observing, I realized their shell design is to blame. If I don’t carefully untangle them, they risk losing legs or antennae—or worse, pulling out my hair.    Some beetles pinch, likely to express their discomfort, creating mine. When that happens, I wake up, fully aware of the incident—unlike many other encounters that don’t disturb my sleep. It’s like how we notice a sore knee only when we bump it, even though we probably hit it just as often when it doesn’t hurt. A beetle in your hair is a similar, unforgettable experience.    Larger creatures, from shrews and hedgehogs to grass snakes, foxes, and weasels, tend to keep their distance. Without the tent obscuring their view or smell, they quickly recognize me as human—the ultimate nightmare—and flee without hesitation.     If they are sane, everyone flees. So when that doesn’t happen, it’s a notable and often touching event.     For example, one morning during this pilgrimage, I was lying on my mattress (it’s still necessary to isolate yourself from the dampness of the ground to sleep better), my head resting on my hand, against my bag, and leaning against a tree at the edge of a wood. Like a hunting dog curled up and asleep, I faced a small grassy clearing. I was awakened by a presence.    It didn’t feel alarming. I stayed calm, listening. I believe the brain, even while asleep, can hear and analyze sounds in the immediate environment, alerting us if necessary. I’ve experienced this four times now during nocturnal visits from bears. But this time, there was no urgency, no danger.    I opened my eyes. About fifteen meters away, an enormous doe was grazing nonchalantly. I say enormous because it was not a deer but an adult doe—and an adult doe is large. She grazed noisily on the grass. Well, noisy for someone like me, now awake and trying to be still. In the calm morning silence of nature, after a good night’s sleep, I lay motionless, amazed by the spectacle. Usually, such encounters are fleeting, as frightened animals quickly flee.    I savored the moment, staying as still as possible while observing her. Then, about ten meters away, I noticed a small fawn, likely old enough to have lost its spots. I wanted to lift my head slightly to see it better but didn’t dare move.     Eventually, I had to adjust—or perhaps my breathing changed—because the doe suddenly raised her angular head. Her whole body tensed, motionless, on alert.     That’s when we locked eyes. We stared at each other, directly into each other’s gaze—a moment suspended in time. It felt so real that it was almost unreal. Probably just a fraction of a second, but it felt eternal. Both of us were frozen in attentive silence.    And then, as nothing happened, she seemed to decide that I wasn’t a threat and resumed grazing.    That’s what moved me the most. The moment of eye contact was intense, but her choice to start grazing again, despite knowing the worst of predators—the most destructive of creatures—was nearby, truly touched me. It felt as though she had decided to trust me.     I felt accepted, as if I had become part of her world. You can’t imagine how proud this made me. It’s a moment etched in my memory, one that strengthens me when I recall it. Hindus have a term for such experiences: “Darshan.”    We stayed like that for a few minutes. She tore at the tender grass, taking a step between each bite, while I remained still, listening to my heart pound as if I were receiving a kiss for the first time.     These are the kinds of moments that can happen when you sleep under the stars.   I’m nearing the Serbian-Romanian border. My journey continues toward the sanctuary of Medjugorje in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which means crossing Serbia.     I hope the summer won’t be as hot as the spring, though I’m not optimistic.     I hope everything is going well for you and wish you health and happiness.     See you soon.     P.S.:     I have a good excuse for being late with updates. I’ve overexposed myself to phone screens while working on putting a blog online. I’ll share the address once it’s ready.    Writing and sending these updates, attaching photos, and sending them to all my contacts has become tedious. Platforms like Signal or WhatsApp only allow sending to five contacts at a time. Between each batch, I have to reselect text and photos, then sift through my contact list to choose the next five while remembering who hasn’t received it yet.     With several hundred contacts—and the list growing—the process isn’t getting any easier.    The blog should simplify things while improving practicality. It might even reach others who haven’t met me but could appreciate the content.     What content? Nearly all the updates I’ve sent since starting this pilgrimage in September 2020, plus a selection of the best photos, and complete answers to frequently asked questions.     Voila. A good excuse, right?

Ask Bilbo!


		23/8/2021
	
     ​I know, it hasn’t been that long since I gave you my latest news. But I have to share what seems so important to me in my journey. I know I am redundant, and yet each time again, I am touched and moved by this kindness that welcomes me.     I must begin by telling you that the last days since I left Aglona have been wonderful. I have been alone and in silence since resuming my walk. The intermittent rain refreshes pleasantly this end of summer. However, it is not too important to hinder my progress. When the rain is really too strong, I stop, put up the tent and take refuge there, but it’s not that often. A few days ago though, I got a downpour that was Hollywood chewing gum level event, if you remember the nineties advertisement. It was so huge, so tropical shower level that it becomes fun in itself. You no longer have to worry about getting wet, it’s so impossible not to that it’s no longer a problem.    So it’s true that the atmosphere is really humid, but the good in that is that it attracts mushrooms which end up throwing themselves at my feet begging me to pick them up (yes like this). That’s awesome! I eat raw Boletus Edulis, because they are so fresh that there is no need to cook them. Which is good because I have nothing to cook anymore from a long time now. Yesterday I found the flesh of a big champagne cork shape one really sweet. It surprised me. Crunchy and sweet. Happiness...    And then I also collect Chanterelles. I keep them in a bag and try to dry them a bit as much and as often as possible. I always end up being invited by someone to cook them...     And then I arrived in this village where a grocery store was at the entrance. It was good because I needed to fill my backpack with food again. I did my shopping there, paid for everything, and the lady in charge of the grocery store asked me where I was coming from and what I was doing. She then offered to charge my phone if I needed, and we chatted.     It’s crazy how what I do—walking like this, a long pilgrimage, a long-lasting spiritual discipline—can inspire or make sense to the people I meet. It is even disturbing. My approach, however very particular, very surprising, very unusual, very incongruous even, turns out to be full of meaning also for those I meet... Full of meaning and nourishing too. Strange, isn’t it? There is even a kind of envy that I feel, a craving. As if I were realizing in this journey what many would like to, what many are starving for... I guess that’s why having the rule to take the time to share with whoever is interested is important.     After a while, she kindly offered me a coffee, which I gratefully accepted, because coffee is good! Especially when it’s offered like this. Of course, the coffee was served with many biscuits, chocolate, and white cheese bars sweetened and coated with chocolate or caramel (it’s pasty, somewhere between hard cream and fresh cheese, and sweet. I like it...).   We chatted using Google Translate until a client, an English teacher at the village college, arrived. So we chatted in English. Nice exchange.     Of the few new customers who passed by during my break at the grocery store, a dozen I would say, I had a friendly exchange with ten. More than half spoke with me or with the grocer, who told them about what we had already discussed. Four of them offered me their phone numbers in case I needed anything or help on my way.     Before going to sleep near the village lake, the grocer gave me a bag of tomatoes and cucumbers (the Baltic countries seem to have an impressive addiction to cucumbers... Small cucumbers, like big pickles... Over the past month, there hasn’t been a single day I’ve spent without cucumbers...).     I spent four hours in her shop, chatting with her while she worked or with her customers. It was really relaxed, and I managed to recharge my phone and power banks. Great! I gave her the bag of Boletus edulis mushrooms and chanterelles that I had picked that morning. It felt completely natural to give them to her. Then we said goodbye.     The evening was good! A swim in the lake, washing myself and my clothes. A beautiful night without rain (which is nice because the sound of rain on the tent canvas can be really loud!). And this morning, I resumed my journey.     In the afternoon, I arrived at a small country road—unpaved, with no tarmac—where I noticed someone walking about 100 meters ahead of me. It was a lady. Elderly. Old, but still walking briskly (87 years old! Respect!). It took me nearly a kilometer to catch up and walk alongside her. I could immediately tell she was a character—a nice one.    When she heard someone approaching behind her (I had deliberately rubbed my foot on the ground to make a little noise, so as not to startle her), she turned around with a warm smile, not a trace of fear or surprise. That alone says a lot.     We introduced ourselves and decided to walk together to her house, half a kilometer away. We had not gone 50 meters before I inherited one of the bags of tomatoes from her garden, which she carried in each hand.    Arriving in front of her house, I was invited in for a coffee. I gladly accepted! A good cup of coffee never hurts! (French proverb—or if not, it should become one soon...).    Watch the little movie I made—sorry, it’s in French; I didn’t think about it at the time. But aside from showing the beautiful place where she and her husband live, you can see her smile, her enthusiasm, her kindness. Notice the touching gesture of the small tablecloth she placed on the table for me, to hold the cup of coffee, along with a few slices of cheese on a plate, homemade donuts, and the white cheese treats I mentioned before.     Then I met her husband, as kind as she was.    I was invited to stay the night.    I was invited to use the sauna and shower.   I was invited to visit the property—a superb estate that belonged to her grandparents. It included a house, a barn, a garage, a henhouse, a sauna, and toilets behind the barn. There was a magnificent vegetable garden with enormous raspberries and blackcurrants. By the way, the homemade blackcurrant jam I ate with evening porridge was delicious.    Even the grass was soft and comfortable to walk on barefoot—something I was invited to do almost immediately.    She told me that tomorrow morning, before I leave, we will eat the mushrooms she collected, with potatoes. How does she know it’s my favorite dish at the moment—fresh mushrooms and potatoes, seriously! Ask Bilbo!!!    And then, go look at the pictures—come on, watch that splendid breakfast! ??    Finally, her husband showed me his workshop and his neatly arranged wood; she showed me her sober and simple interior. He showed me the sauna; she showed me the henhouse...    I’m falling asleep as I write these words... The evening meal, the sauna, the comfortably firm sofa bed, the faint smell of wood fire coming from the burner...    Once again, these people touch me and move me with the warmth of their welcome, the smiles in their kind eyes, and the care they show me, even though I’m a total stranger, completely unknown to them.

Aglona


		17/8/2021
	
      Hello to everyone,      It’s time to move on.     The festival here in Aglona has ended.   It was huge, and even though far fewer people came this year, the entire event was still impressive. Security was tight, with police, the army, secret services, TV, radio, journalists, and everything else you'd expect from a festival important enough to draw the country’s president and many VIPs.     One of the most special parts was the choir singing every day for a week beforehand. Even if you’re not a fan of religious music, hearing those voices live, right in front of you, is deeply moving.    The last two days were crowded and busy, especially Sunday from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., but just two hours after it ended, the entire place was empty. All the cars and buses were gone, military tents dismantled, civil security tents packed away, cameras, sound systems, and lights all removed, food trucks vanished. Everything became quiet again.    I spent the next day organizing myself—saying goodbye to the priests who so kindly welcomed me, buying food for my journey, washing my clothes, and enjoying a hot shower in the monastery to be fresh and ready to leave in the morning.     Aglona, in Latvia, is a beautiful place. There’s a Basilica dedicated to Maria, set in the middle of a lovely park with a lake and a spring. The water from the spring is so good—really fresh, not cold, but refreshing and soft, with a great taste. I drink far more than I need every time I go to fill my bottle. It’s that nice. Of course, I’m not the only one. One of the priests, smiling, told me there are more people coming to fill their bottles at the spring than there are visiting the Maria icon! But since the spring is sacred and said to be miraculous, it’s all good.     The journey here was, as always, wonderful. I met kind people (including a truly sweet dog who welcomed me in such a heartwarming way. She barked, yapped, and moaned the way dogs do when they’re happy to see someone. It felt like I was her master returning after a long absence. She moved me deeply with her softness and gentleness, and we walked together for two hours before she returned home. Such a beautiful encounter).    I was also invited to stay for two days in a small town just after crossing the border. It was amazing to have warm, homemade meals prepared by my host, who said she wanted me to feel at home—and I did. She was such a lovely person, a former doctor in epidemiology for 16 years before working at customs. You can imagine how fascinating our conversations were!     This has been a truly wonderful time.     But you might get bored if I describe again how wonderful it is to walk through unknown places and feel so welcomed. So I think I’ll skip that part...    Instead, I’ll tell you about my plans for what’s next: I plan to wait until this evening to decide where I’ll go next.    Let me explain, because I get this question a lot. I always focus on my destination, and only my destination, until I finish my visit to that place I set out to reach. I stay dedicated to it, fully immersed in the experience. Then (and here’s a playful word twist—“end/and”), once the visit is over, I decide what’s next.    This approach gives me the freedom to wait until the last moment. Maybe someone will suggest a beautiful place nearby that I hadn’t considered. In that case, I can make it my next destination. If no one suggests anything, I have a few ideas in mind and choose one based on logic and my current location.    This creates a very satisfying sense of liberty. It feels like everything is open and possible, that I don’t even have to think about it until the last moment, and then it can be anything. It feels good. Simple. And once the choice is made, it becomes my goal. I don’t care how long it will take, or what the exact path will be. I just go. I put one foot in front of the other and repeat, repeat, repeat. Whatever I’m meant to see, I’ll see. Whoever I’m meant to meet, I’ll meet. Whatever challenges arise, I’ll face them. And here’s something I can assure you: I’m confident that everything will turn out fine.    Confidence is a delicious warmth, and my experiences over these past 11 months have given me that—a warm and fulfilling confidence that everything is and will be good.    Isn’t it beautiful to live this way, especially in these times? I wish I could share the feeling with you more fully, but words seem so weak compared to what I feel.    I wish you happiness and well-being.    Happiness is a duty—our first duty!    Sincerely,    Emmanuel    Post scriptum:    You know what? Last week, I found around 700 grams of chanterelles (Cantharellus cibarius or girolles in French). They were so tasty! We ate them together—four people who had invited me to share their meal by the lakeside. It was perfect because I had no way to cook them, and they had everything needed. They seemed to love mushrooms as much as I do, and they knew that the first chanterelles of the year are especially delicious.     But that’s not even the best news. Okay, let’s agree that’s great news. But the better news is this: just before I arrived in Aglona, I found a Boletus edulis. A small one, shaped like a champagne cork. I left it there because it was all alone, hoping it will grow into a big family. But do you see my point? It’s mid-August, and there are already Boletus edulis popping up—not even in the woods, but right in the middle of the path! If that’s not a sign of good things in life, I don’t know what is.    Post scriptum 2:   I’m now headed toward Šiluvos atlaidai in Lithuania, west-southwest from where I am. On the way—about 50 km from my destination—I plan to visit the Hill of Crosses, which has caught my interest.   I left Aglona after lunch today, walking until a heavy rain came down, forcing me to stop. I pitched my tent and tried to “dry” whatever I had on me. I’ll start again tomorrow!

Accident


		28/8/2023
	
     The story I’m about to tell you made me cry—really cry—hot and heavy tears for over an hour. Yet, I’m pretty sure you’ll laugh...    Life in the tent is punctuated by rituals. Unpacking and repacking your backpack every day, without forgetting anything and ensuring that everything is properly placed, requires it. Every item comes out of the bag, goes into the tent, and then back into the bag again.     I sleep on the right side. Nothing to do with the “right side of the bed” couples talk about—it’s simply that the zipper of the tent entrance, which is a mosquito net, makes it more convenient to be on this side rather than 30 cm further.     My half-full backpack, stuffed with winter clothes, is to my left, level with my thigh. It fits well in that spot, as long as it’s positioned slightly at an angle and, importantly, with the straps facing me. This way, the rounded part of the bag aligns with the tent floor without pressing against the tent wall. The goal is to avoid contact between the tent fabric and the double roof. If the two fabrics touch and it rains, capillary action will cause water to seep through. We don’t want that.    This bag position also allows easy access to the two belt pockets on the backpack and the anti-bear spray, which is fixed midway up in a pocket I designed myself on the shoulder strap. It’s pointless to keep a spray at the bottom of the bag. If needed, you can ask a bear to wait a minute—but I assure you, it’s completely useless.     Near my left arm are two waterproof (well, nearly waterproof) boxes I use to store food. These prevent any leaks from finding their way onto my sleeping bag. I’m sure you get the idea.     At the level of my head, in the corner, are my water bottles and canteens. Finally, at my feet, I store items that I won’t need in the evening: the compression sack for the sleeping bag, my hat...     In the tent’s awning, my shoes are placed at the top right. The left side has an elastic band used to roll up and secure the door when it’s open. However, when it rains, the seam of this elastic slowly lets water in. It drips—not much, but enough that if a shoe is left there overnight, it might be filled with water by morning. We definitely don’t want that.   To the left of the awning is where I place rubbish—paper, plastic, and similar items—until morning, when I collect it all to throw into the first trash bin I find.    Then there’s a large bottle with a wide neck that I’ve had for a while now. It’s placed on the opposite side of the shoes. I could explain what it’s for, but it’s not essential to the story, and some of you might not be ready for that. Let’s just say that when sleeping in a tent, such a bottle is incredibly handy for men in their fifties who don’t want to waste the hard-earned warmth in their sleeping bags by getting up multiple times during the night...     Why am I telling you all this?     Well, imagine that tonight, as I was turning to adjust my pillow (my jacket and pants rolled up in a very specific way, offering real comfort all night long), I got on all fours on my self-inflating mattress. This mattress, about 3 or 4 cm thick, inflates on its own when unrolled and only requires a few breaths to make it comfortable before closing the valve. It allows you to sleep on damp and cold ground—even on snow or ice, as often happens to me in winter.     And then disaster struck.   From that moment, everything happened quickly—a rapid succession of actions, reactions, questions, decisions, and regrets, all compressed into a few dozen seconds, probably less than a minute.     As I got into position, on all fours, ready to reshape my pillow, I heard a loud Pchiiiittttt and felt a breath of air against my thigh. My first thought was that I had just punctured my mattress with my knee pressing on a sharp stone or thorn. I assumed it was likely a cutting stone because the Pschiiit was powerful, and I felt the air escaping against my skin, indicating a large opening.   Of course, I instinctively shifted and turned around to see what was happening—my first mistake, albeit an understandable one. Anyone would have done the same.    It’s worth noting that this happened in a tent with a roof height of maybe one meter and a ground width of 1.20 meters. As I turned and prepared to inspect the situation, my vision blurred—a kind of cloud was there, as if mist had entered the tent.     And then everything escalated.     I inhaled, and the mist scratched my throat and lungs. Something was very wrong. That’s when I realized what had happened: I had accidentally triggered the bear spray.    Normally, the spray has a safety pin to prevent this from happening. But today, I had walked under many low-hanging branches, and it’s entirely possible that one of them dislodged the pin without me noticing.     I don’t check my gear in the evening anymore. I know it would be more logical to do so—I used to at the beginning of my pilgrimage—but for some time now, after a long day of walking, I’m too exhausted to do anything but lie down and rest. I only check my equipment in the morning. That’s when I inspect for holes in my clothes, loose straps, places that need reinforcing, and, of course, the bear spray—specifically, whether its safety pin is in place. I devote about two evenings a week to equipment maintenance. It’s not as though “we” build solid things these days...     So there I was, turning around, my face in the cloud, breathing in. I told myself, "It itches, but it’s fine... It’s not that strong. I’ll finish this breath, hold it, and go out." I even thought, This spray isn’t very effective. It’s not strong enough to repel a bear determined to steal my cheese.   That was a mistake—an important one. Looking back, I now believe that if you ever find yourself in the same situation, it doesn’t matter whether you’re inhaling or exhaling—just block your breath immediately, wherever it is... for about 40 minutes, at least. If you pass out, even better—it will spare you what’s coming next.    And remember to close your eyes. I almost forgot that part. Closed eyes are better, even if, like me, you think it’s too late. Just close them.     With my breath held, lungs full, and in a high position, I turned around as quickly as I could and felt for the zipper tab. Thankfully, I knew where it was because of practice and the way I position myself in the tent—it’s always in the same spot. That was fortunate, because by this time, my eyes were blurred with tears beginning to form. But my eyes weren’t the main issue—it was my throat.     My throat itched severely, burning like hell (if you’ll allow the comparison). It was awful. Then I started coughing, which didn’t help me open the mosquito net, let alone hold my breath. Every cough required me to inhale, which was both inevitable and excruciating.     I managed to reach the main opening in the double roof. It has two zippers that leave the upper central part of the fabric open for ventilation when desired, which I’d left open that night. I plunged my head out into the “fresh” air. I say “fresh” because, with the burning sensation in my throat, it didn’t feel refreshing at all.     Now on my knees in the awning, I found the two zippers and pulled them down simultaneously to close the opening.     The coughing became violent. It felt like I was about to cough my lungs out. I wished my throat would simply cease to exist. My face, hands, and thigh burned like I’d received four overlapping sunburns all at once.    I was terrified of vomiting. I had to concentrate hard to prevent it—not just because of the cleanup that would follow, but also because the combination of coughing, extreme difficulty in breathing, and vomiting could be dangerous, even suffocating.    I manage to extract myself from the tent, crawling on all fours. I move about ten meters away and collapse there, feeling like I might die—or almost. Suffocation... Violent coughing, my eyes streaming, my nose running, my mouth burning, and saliva dripping onto the ground. I can only breathe in short, jerky gasps, focusing intensely on calming myself enough to get some oxygen. Oxygen is important, after all...    And then the burning starts. It was already burning, but now it intensifies. It rises and rises, building even more. Touching the affected areas is a serious mistake—don’t do it. Don’t touch. Must not touch. I’m pretty sure it’s swelling too. I have to wait... 10 minutes... 20 minutes... 30 minutes...     Finally, it starts to subside. And that’s when I have the worst good idea of the year.    I’m camped next to a water source. It’s great to have running water when you’re sleeping in a tent. Spring water means freshness. Really fresh, even cold. With the burning sensation, you can imagine the allure, the temptation. It’s like a jug of lemonade with ice cubes clinking in front of someone lost in the Sahara! Or like a Coulommiers cheese on a table in front of a homesick Norman expat! Or a basket of chanterelles in front of... well, you get the point.     I stand up and walk past the tent to grab the tea towel/handkerchief/cleaning rag drying on top of it. I’m already imagining the bliss of a cloth soaked in clear, fresh water, gently placed on my burning skin. I even wonder if it will make a sizzling sound, like water hitting a hot pan, when I put it over my face.    Bitter mistake. The cold relief never comes. At first, it seems fine—good, even. But no. It’s a mirage. Placebo effect. The burning sensation returns, worse than before. But not immediately! No, it gives you just enough time to wet all the affected areas you thought would be soothed. And then, it hits. Too late, though—you’ve already committed. And now you’re crying again...     Anyway, I’ve just endured two truly painful hours, and now I’m waiting for the right moment to go back into the tent and try to sleep. Meanwhile, I’m wondering what I’ll do if I don’t find the spray’s safety pin. The chances of finding it are slim, but I have hope because one of the spots where the branches rubbed against my gear is just above the spring near where I set up camp. Maybe, with a little luck...     Et voilà.    This, along with the time my tent flooded a few months ago, will definitely remain one of the most ridiculous experiences I’ve had on this pilgrimage. Definitely. But this one is already funny, in hindsight. So everything is fine... no real harm done.      See you soon.      I wish you all well and happy...     P.S. 1: Do not try to reproduce this experience at home. I want to clarify that this was done by an experienced moron—I mean, an experienced and over-trained pilgrim. A professional.      P.S. 2: I may send a review to the tent manufacturer:      VENTILATION: Tested bear spray indoors and nearly died. 0/10.     By the way, if there’s a lawyer among you, I wonder if there’s a way to sue. At no point in the instructions does it say the spray shouldn’t be used alone in the evening in your tent!     P.S. 3: I’m kidding, of course. No need to send me legal advice! I mention this more for those who are worried about the NSA and Chinese spies.     P.S. 4: Ah yes! On another note, I need to digress: the secret code/password thing seems to have confused a lot of you, and I’m sorry for that. It was just a way for me to measure how much of my messages were being read. By asking the reader to reply with a password in their next message, I could be fairly certain they had read the text to the end.     So don’t worry if you didn’t know what to put—your confusion was as much proof of reading as the best of codes. (Some of my favorites were: “GTOULU” (French phonetic for "IReadAll"), “Draculement,” and “AZERTY734”...) The NSA has nothing to do with it. No need for tinfoil hats; the Chinese hear perfectly fine anyway.   P.S. 5: Speaking of paranoia—I think I heard the bears laughing at me in the distance. They probably smelled what had happened (they can detect an animal carcass 35 km away and go straight to it) and likely heard me coughing my lungs out. I imagine that in the local dens, the story will now be told by mother bears to their cubs to help them fall asleep for hibernation.     I can even picture two bears meeting, one standing on its hind legs with one paw on a tree and the other clutching its stomach, recounting the tale of the pilgrim gassed in his tent to another bear lying on the ground, hitting the dirt with its paw in laughter.     That thought makes me smile... but I think I was already asleep by then.     P.S. 6: I’ve totally broken my postscript record!

Feast with Gabriel


		8/8/2023
	
     I would like to drive the point home, because some nails deserve to be nailed, and the subject of the last message is one of them. I hope this expression makes sense in English, as it does in French.    So, coming back to my last message: I wrote it as I was leaving a pretty little village to head toward the mountains (or rather hills—no offense, but I spent several years in the high Himalayan altitudes, so...) of the Carpathians. To be precise, sub-Carpathian Transylvania! Yeah, I know, it sounds professional. It was a history/geography teacher friend of mine who tipped me off to the full designation.    In short, coming back (and by coming back so much, I’m sure I’ll finally get there) to these nails that deserve to be driven in: after spending three days in these hills—yes, yes, these magnificent mountains, which are truly beautiful—I descended on the other side to a small village. I had the same hope as always: to find a grocery store, preferably one that accepts credit cards, to recharge my batteries, and to wash myself. The pilgrim classics.    Upon entering the village, a welcoming concrete wall seemed to have been built just for my backpack and me to rest against. It’s 36 degrees Celsius in the shade... and I’m not in the shade. So, I’m soaked in sweat and happy to breathe while sitting, almost comfortably, with my bag supporting my back.     A car stops. The gentleman, speaking through the open window, says something to me. After a few gestures on my part to explain “French/Pilgrim/Not understanding,” he points to a spot further up one of the streets at the intersection where we are. In English that’s as good as my Hungarian, he says: “Vateur. Oundrund méteur.” Which translates as: “If you want, there’s a source of drinking water a hundred meters higher up this street.”    Yes, I know, it’s just a few words, but I include the non-verbal gestures and the tone in my translation—it adds something.    This is great news, I think to myself as the man drives away, because all my water bottles are empty, and I’m thirsty. It’s funny how the moment you realize you’re out of water, thirst immediately kicks in, as if by magic. The mind is strange, isn’t it? In short, thirst is real.     The information is tempting, even though it’s uphill and not on my route. Spring water is often very fresh—if not outright cold—and frequently very tasty, which fits my situation perfectly. It’s the kind of water you drink even when you’re not thirsty, until your stomach feels tight because you’ve overdone it. Yes, I assure you... I speak from experience. Anyway, subjectively, I estimate I’ll drink at least three liters.     So, I get up and walk.    The place does not disappoint. It’s a small spring, like many I’ve come across: two rectangular, interconnected basins, with a pipe coming out of the rock, pouring clear liquid. And the water is really good... and really fresh.    And I drink. Not three liters, but at least one, then half of another shortly after. I splash water on my head and wet my hat (which prolongs the cooling effect while it dries—about five minutes).    As I lounge, wash my hands, re-wet my face, re-re-wet my head, and soak my arms, a gentleman comes to do much the same as me.     We greet each other, and the conversation begins. After a few moments, comes the comment to which I am now accustomed—common to my situation—delivered with a handshake: Respect! Yes, many people use this word after I play them the brief message recorded in my translator, which succinctly summarizes my situation over the past three years, listing, among other things, the countries I’ve crossed. Respect.   So, Tibor and I talk, and I go into a little more detail... The landscapes, the silence, the encounters, the freedom, the joy of living, the happiness, the kindness received, the welcomes... All of it, you see.   Then, two women pass by on foot. They greet Tibor and exchange a few words, without stopping completely. That is, until he seems to speak of me, because I recognize the words “French” and “kilometers”. I translate this in my mind, with some detailed extrapolation, as: “This is a French pilgrim who has walked 7,500 km to get here. Do you know where he could sleep tonight?”    The women stop for a moment, then leave. Tibor tells me via the translator that I should follow them because they might ask their boss about getting me a room for the night. They work in a sort of hotel or motel, he explains—they are in the kitchen.    I finish filling my water bottles, say goodbye to Tibor, take my backpack, and leave at a rapid pace (fortunately, it’s downhill) to catch up with the women and follow them to the establishment. It’s just opposite where I had been sitting previously... Small world. Though, admittedly, the village is small too—but that’s not the point.   They invite me inside, and while they try to reach the boss, they offer me a meal: a good vegetable soup, some sautéed potatoes, and pan-fried cheese. In the end, they can’t get me a room at the hotel because everything is booked—apparently, there’s a wedding.    But they tell me a friend of theirs is inviting me to her house. I finish eating, and she comes to pick me up to take me there.    She’s a petite lady, around 75 years old (72, in fact). Very kind, she walks with me up the street where the spring is located but further along, to her house. She shows me a sofa bed in the living room, which she immediately begins to prepare while I still have my backpack on my back.     Once I un-shoulder my backpack and take off my shoes, she shows me the bathroom. A shower! My God! Have I already said how good a shower feels? Because, my God, a shower feels amazing...     So, here I am, lying down now. It’s 7:45 p.m., and I’ll sleep soon. My batteries are recharging. Earlier, I went shopping at the store, knowing it would be closed tomorrow, Sunday. Margret—that’s her name—cooked the hard-boiled eggs I bought for the road, just to add some variety. We shared a little aperitif under the pergola in her garden, a ‘little pear.’    She invited me to dinner, but as I had a late and rather heavy lunch (cheese in the pan...), I preferred to lie down. And write to you, to tell you... A little tap on the nail’s head, because I think it deserves it.    And since you have to strike the nail while it’s hot (I’m sure this is a saying—maybe not as common as the one about iron, but still), I might as well continue.     This morning, on my way down to the church, I filled all my bottles and canteen at the spring I visited the day before. I filled up completely because my plan was to set up my tent in the forest 4 km past the village and rest there for two days and three nights. You know the drill.    But one of the first lessons of the road is learning to easily let go of your plans to be guided by others—plans that often turn out to be much better... Certainly in my case...     Margret tells me to wait for her after mass so we can say goodbye. And, as planned, at the end of the mass, just outside the church, I see her as well as the gentleman from the day before, Tibor.    He is a teacher here and would like to introduce me to a friend who speaks French: Gabriel. Contrary to his habit, Tibor sat especially next to Gabriel during the service this morning to inform him of my presence and the opportunity to practice a language that is otherwise hard to use in the area.     Gabriel does indeed speak very good French, occasionally using English for words that escape him due to lack of practice. Thanks to him, my "goodbyes" to Margret and Mr. Teacher are smooth and direct.     When it’s time for me to get back on my way, Gabriel asks if I’m in a hurry or if I have time for a coffee at his place, just five minutes away on foot. After "checking my schedule", I assure him that I have all the time necessary to meet and answer any questions. This is one of the rules I’ve set for myself: to remain available to share what I receive. It also helps me avoid drying out, which is always a risk for a hermit.     So, I spend the morning chatting in French with him and his wife. Then, because he has errands to run, he invites me to accompany him. Together, we feed the farm animals a few kilometers from the village, visit a miraculous spring whose water has been renowned since the Middle Ages, and stop at a recently rebuilt chapel next to the ruins of the one built by King "Machin" after the spring water below cured his army of the infection that was decimating his ranks. We also visit a small wildlife reserve hidden deep in the countryside, where a pond fed by another spring—delicious and fresh water again—houses many rainbow trout that Gabriel regularly feeds.     Along the way, he shows me numerous signs of plantigrade activity. Apparently, there are a few bears in the immediate vicinity, five if I understood correctly. (I know this is a long parenthesis, but I’ll close it now.)     During all this, Gabriel invites me to stay and rest at a small chalet on the farm where we fed the sheep, pigs, chickens, and dogs. In addition to having the renowned spring nearby, the place is special, he says. Certainly bucolic, but more than that. It seems conducive to healing.    And I have to admit, without fully understanding why, it’s one of those places where you feel good—immediately and simply. Gabriel suggests I stay more than two days. In fact, he says, I could stay as long as I want to enjoy the place.     He also offers that, if I want, I could see the family doctor, a general practitioner with extensive experience, who could prescribe more thorough examinations than those done at the hospital last time.
