Germany


		27/11/2020
	
     Hello!     It’s been such a long time since I last gave any news. Please forgive me. It’s not that the life of a pilgrim is so busy—though, actually, it kind of is—but more that during these coronavirus days, it’s a bit harder to recharge my phone. I need it frequently for accessing maps, so I’ve had to prioritize that over writing messages, which use up a lot of battery.     But anyway, I have to check in sometimes, and today the circumstances are just right.     So, what to say? Well, I’ve crossed France, a tiny bit of Belgium, all of Luxembourg from west to east, and now I’m in Germany—a little past Frankfurt, heading south. I think I’ll be in Germany for about three more weeks, but it’s hard to say for sure.    The weather has been changing over the past two weeks. It went from heavy rain (great for making mushrooms sprout everywhere—like, really everywhere) to cold, which sadly ended the mushroom madness. No more evening mushroom soup, and that is really sad. If you hadn’t guessed already, I’m a big mushroom fan... 😉 But to be precise, I’m a fan of whatever nature provides. It’s the generosity of nature that moves me the most, whether it’s mushrooms, nuts, apples, or berries.     The cold also stopped the rain! Youpi! It’s so nice not to be wet anymore. And soon, it will start snowing. But let’s keep that for the future...     I’m good. Happy.   I’ve reached a stage of consciousness where I can easily slip into a contemplative, automated walking state. That’s what I’m interested in, what I’m seeking—to make that state last as long as possible, maybe even permanent, rather than just fleeting moments throughout the day. But I’m happy. Everything is fine.     One thing I really enjoy is meeting so many people. It’s not that there’s a huge number, but I do meet a lot of people, and almost without exception, I encounter kindness, goodwill, and generosity. It’s such a warm and beautiful experience.      I mean, the general narrative these days is that we should be cautious when going out, that we should be suspicious or even afraid of people because “you never know.” We’re told to be careful, to “watch our six,” and so on. But my daily experience is the complete opposite.     Every day, the people I meet are incredibly kind and eager to help. They’re curious about what I’m doing and love to talk. They invite me to share meals or give me food because there might not be a shop on my route. They offer me the chance to take a hot shower in their homes (and yes, I definitely want that!).     They’re human, and it’s so nice and comforting to experience that.     Voilà.     That’s it for today.     I hope you’re well and happy.     Wishing you all the best.   Next, I’m sharing lots of pictures I’ve taken along the way. Hope you enjoy them! I won’t comment on them since there are so many.
blog/archives/11-2021/index.html:
Goldap and Andrzej


		22/11/2021
	
    The fact that I am receiving more and more messages asking me for news tells me that I may have once again stretched the time limit for updating my progress. And now, as I reread myself, I realize that this message is going to be really long. Maybe to compensate for the delay. Well, if it’s too much, don’t hesitate to complain.     And something else: regarding the photos, I am experiencing an as-yet unsolved problem. They are missing, or at least a large part of the period I am writing about now. I do not know why or if I will be able to find them in the depths of my phone’s memory, or if they are definitely gone. So I apologize to those of you who enjoy the photos—especially those who don’t care much for the reading and just like to look at the pictures!     The last time I wrote to you, I stopped at the Hill of Crosses, of which I have fond memories, though they already feel a little distant. There has been a lot of water under the bridge since then—and lots of things floating with it.    There was Šiluva, the fourth destination on my journey. A place I’ll let you discover on the internet if you wish, as it is described there far better and in more detail than I could manage. I stayed there for four days, hosted by the pilgrims’ center. The team in charge of the center and welcoming pilgrims was very dynamic and enthusiastic. Once again, I can only partially convey the warmth of the welcome I received, the meetings I had there, and the quality of the discussions we shared.    It exceeded my expectations. And the place itself! Well, let’s just say that I’m glad I heard about it and had the chance to be there.    When I felt ready and rested, I chose to resume my way towards Gietrzwałd, via Święta Lipka in Poland this time. This route would allow me to go around the small part of Russia that lies between Poland and Lithuania, as I didn’t want to cross Russia (visas and administrative costs are troubles a pilgrim can do without). In doing so, it also took me through Kaunas.    Kaunas is the second-largest city in Lithuania, but let me specify that the concept of a big city is very subjective. Second-largest city in Lithuania—that must be considered at the scale of the country, of course. I say this for my Indian friends, for example, for whom the second-largest city in their country must be Mumbai, with a population six times greater than the entire Lithuanian population, not counting the Mumbai agglomeration...   Although I am not fond of walking through large cities, the need to renew some of my equipment, wardrobe, and shoes made the stop necessary. The presence of a military store that could provide more durable materials and equipment, combined with the old town and many beautiful buildings and churches, made the prospect more appealing. Additionally, I was informed about the presence of a pilgrim shelter there, which made the city all the more accessible, and ultimately, the choice as a stopover was made quite naturally.    And I’m really glad I did...    First and foremost, because the trip between Šiluva and Kaunas was one of the most picturesque country paths I’ve had the opportunity to walk. In the midst of verdant nature with autumnal colors, I walked along a small stream, then a bigger one, taking care to enjoy these magnificent and almost wild places as much as possible.    Besides, I would like to tell you about a meeting with this nature that happened there, but I want to do it nicely and fully, and I’m afraid it might be too long. Too much of a digression for here, so I will include it as a postscriptum.    Then, and I know it becomes redundant, but I am not tired of it—the welcome I received in this city was really, really nice. I was lucky to be hosted in the center of the old town, probably the most beautiful part of the city. And so, as hoped, I took advantage of the pretty town (churches, old streets, squares, and buildings), but also of the practical side (buying the necessary equipment and food, washing my sleeping bag that was smellily screaming for it!).  And the meetings—again, always, everywhere. I was not only welcomed, guided, and accompanied in my efforts but also taken to visit superb places that would otherwise have remained unknown to me (it’s very annoying not to be able to show you pictures!).  And there again, in those meetings—I am not tired of it—each time, the kindness, the availability, the generosity, and the accompaniment, if needed or desired.   Then I resumed my way towards the border. Easy and slow. Really slow because over the past few weeks, my back pains have given me small reminders. Nothing in comparison to before, but still, I’ve learned to be gentler with myself and to listen to my body’s complaints. I forced myself to walk only one day out of two, sometimes one day out of three. It was necessary and beneficial.    I am stretching better and better, more and more, which is a really good sign! The way—to be walked far and long—teaches you to be kind and fair to yourself. The need is to be happy. Happiness gives wings. But not only that; somehow, I believe it heals...   I am now in Poland, in the small town of Gołdap, from where I am writing to you. It is 3 km from the Russian border.   If you keep up with "current affairs," you are likely informed about the situation with the instrumentalization of migrants from the Middle East, flown by charters to Belarus and then guided to Poland and Lithuania with the obvious aim of political destabilization and financial gain. For me, this results in being checked by flying customs controls—up to three times a day.    Nothing unpleasant—the checks often end in nice discussions about what moves me...    And it’s not just the border police cars that stop; sometimes people do so as well, just to check on me—with kindness, to help, or out of curiosity. And that’s how I met Andrzej (Andre, but we are in Poland, so you have to add “z” or “w” all over the place. I’m sure it’s just to make certain words unpronounceable for tourists or pilgrims. Only certain words, though, because in this example, Andrzej is written unpronounceable but pronounced Andre. Crazy tongue movements in my mouth...).    But to make it short, the car stops, the window goes down, and Andrzej gets very enthusiastic when I finish the short briefing of Emmanuel Gump—the roadside version...   He is seriously ill. A former soldier in forced retirement due to an unknown or poorly understood illness (we discussed in English, and Andrzej’s English is certainly much better than my Polish, but still a little light for technical details). He tells me it’s very good that we meet, and asks if I could bring prayer intentions to Gietrzwałd for him.    Of course—certainly—it’s my pilgrim duty, and I ask him to write them down in the notebook I reserve for this purpose.    He then asks about my route and exclaims that I’ll be passing through his city, where I must stop. He doesn’t guarantee that his wife will agree to lodge me, but he says he’ll speak to the priest and assures me that I’ll be welcomed anyway. I have no doubt about that. Truly. No matter where, when, or how, I know it’s going to be alright.    We exchange phone numbers, and I resume my journey.  The next day, I receive an SMS from him with a photo of "his" church. He gives me an appointment there the following day at 5 p.m.    Funny thing—when I arrive in Gołdap the next day as planned, but much earlier (around 12:30 p.m.), I look at my map for the church. Seeing only one, I head for it. But when I see its steeple, I realize it doesn’t match the photo he sent. And I can’t see any other church nearby.    So I decide to ask passersby. First, a lady who doesn’t speak English (nor French, nor Tamil—well, okay, I didn’t ask about Tamil). Then a delivery boy who eventually speaks Russian. Finally, I consider approaching the only individual remaining in the area, a few hundred meters down the street. I think that if he doesn’t speak English either, that’s fine—I’ll just call Andrzej.   But before I can reach him, he speaks to me from a distance—in English—to ask if I need anything. Before I can respond, he’s already reached me.    Guess what: it’s Andrzej!  He was passing by on his way back home from a friend’s house. He couldn’t believe the coincidence. I don’t want to sound jaded, but I’m used to it now. For him, it’s a big coincidence; for me, it’s Friday. I mean, it’s been 13 months that everything has been going better than expected, and I’m finally really confident.    At the beginning, faced with this level of coincidence, I might have hesitated (not for long) to consider the possibility of surveillance of the pilgrim’s activities by the Polish secret services. But now I know it’s just like this. It’s become routine (but not boring!). Welcome to the pilgrim world...    We talk together while walking. There is indeed a room waiting for me. Yup! Hot shower (necessary...) and everything else that goes with a roof in general—you know the drill already...    He leaves me at the church, where I have to wait for someone to pick me up. The priests are busy; it may take a while. Andrzej is also very busy and has to leave immediately. So I stay in the church, which suits me well.    It’s small, cute, warm, old, and nice. I put my backpack in the entrance, sit on a bench, close my eyes, and before I realize it, an hour and a half have passed. It feels good to close your eyes sometimes. This was one of those times.    When I take my backpack back, because Father Mathieu comes to get me and invites me to follow him to my room, I notice a plastic bag placed on it, under my hat, which was on top. Inside: a chocolate bar, bananas, and dry sausages.    Someone, totally unknown to me—Andrzej, the priests, or someone else—went to the store next door after seeing my bag, or me, or both, bought these little treats, and left them under my hat. I didn’t see anything and have no idea who could have done it.    But I’ve been here less than two hours, and this has already happened. Isn’t it touching? Seriously. Sweetness. Kind attention.    I’ll give away the dry sausages—I’m a vegetarian, you know—but I’ll keep the intention well in my heart. This kind of attention feeds a man well. The chocolate, too, for sure! ??   I live this permanently... I do not know if you realize... for the past 13 months. Sometimes, remembering the "mainstream" discourse of the media, or the almost universally morose discourse, I feel like I’m not on the same planet. Be careful, I was warned when I left: nowadays, you never know!    I am careful—I pay attention with enthusiasm and interest, because yes, you never know. The good, the beautiful, the kindness could crash joyfully against my armor of projections, prejudices, certainties, and precautions. Without paying attention, without being careful, I might not realize it and miss all of this. That would be a pity—a shame—sad...    I am currently staying in one of the parish houses in the city. Father Mathieu and Father Albert are welcoming me with a touching quality as well. And again, I meet and discover. I stayed two full days here; there were a lot of repairs to be done on my backpack (I had to buy stronger sewing thread).    When I’m ready to resume my journey, it will be with a backpack filled with homemade cheeses I was offered, dishes prepared for my journey by Ewa, the housekeeper here, a jar of very good honey, a dozen eggs from Father Albert’s mother’s house, and a bottle of hooch that, if I understood Father Albert correctly, is very good for me.    He explained—in pretty good French, considering how long it’s been since he last practiced it—that this drink, made from black elderberries, has powerful "reheating" properties, which should help during the winter. At 82 degrees of alcohol, I can believe it. I haven’t tried it yet—I’m saving it for the big frosts in the tent. Along with the bottle of "homemade," he gave me a small hooch glass on a pendant with straps and a leather pouch. I’m well-equipped for the road.    Our Lady of Gietrzwałd, here I come...    Voilà. That’s all for today. Well, almost, because I went on a "little" bit in the postscript...    Anyway, I wish you all well and happy!    Emmanuel    PS (long one):    In the photos, there was one of my tent by a river. I took it on the woodland route, superb in color during this autumn season, when I was along this river between Šiluva and Kaunas... Bucolic... natural... green... Superb...    I surely wasn’t the only one who thought this place deserved a stop since a wooden bench had been placed there, in the middle of this great nothingness full of nature. A few meters from the bank of the river below, in the middle of a small grassy meadow, with a magnificent view despite the bumps and hollows, like small hills and valleys. There was a small patch of flat grass next to the bench, flat and large enough for me to pitch my tent.    There was no hesitation. It was obvious that I was going to sleep here. I had to sleep here.    It may seem strange to you or hard to believe, but for over a year that I’ve been sleeping here and there, many of the places where I decide to stay the night impose themselves on me rather than the other way around. And often, those are the places where I sleep well. It’s astonishing, but when I come across these places, it’s obvious, certain. I sleep there... and I sleep well.    Once the tent was set up, the bench that had been waiting there all along did its job. I sat and watched the water flow. It’s good to watch the water flow. Really good.    And it must have been a while since I started watching the water because the sun had gone down behind me by the time she arrived.    I say “she,” but actually, I have no idea if it was a she or a he. The other thing I didn’t know was what it was.    But it was super cute, that’s for sure—really super cute.   It is often in those moments when I find myself at a standstill—whether for rest or contemplation—when my noisy and olfactory intrusion has finished disturbing the place and those who live there, when calm and silence prevail again through my immobility, and with a little luck, a contrary wind, that the most beautiful encounters occur.    And this one was a magnificent one. Do you remember the wolf that appeared, which I observed a few months ago in Poland? But there have been many others—many, but all unique and memorable... A pair of foxes once followed each other and played together, wild boars and baby boars, roe deer, deer, hinds, birds... It’s always captivating to me.    This was the first time I saw her. Her and her kind. For now, we’ll agree—very arbitrarily—that it was a she. But a what? I’m not sure... To be honest, I really don’t know.    I do know her family well, however—the mustelids. The problem is, it’s a (very) large family: from polecats to martens, including badgers, weasels, wolverines, ferrets, minks, and more. Well, these are the ones I’ve heard of or even seen, but there are many more. I haven’t yet looked for a picture online, but I’ll try to find it...    Because, of course, at that moment, even though I really wanted to take her portrait—because she was as cute as can be, and I assure you, those little beasts are insanely cute—even though I really wanted to, I didn’t move an inch. Not even a hair.    I wanted to watch her. Take my time. Not move and spoil the moment, as I did with the wolf.   I observed, prolonging the moment as much as possible before she realized, with horror, that she was within just a few steps—3 meters at most—of the most harmful and dangerous species of mammal on earth (and perhaps even of the universe; we don’t yet have proof to the contrary): a human...    A little smaller and thinner than a ferret, with pretty light gray fur. Lighter than mouse gray—ash gray, I would say.    She had just climbed the embankment from the bank of the river to the small clearing where I was going to spend the night. She stood there, motionless, and I couldn’t tell if she was looking at me or frozen, on the lookout for the slightest movement or smell, perhaps blinded by the sun, which was now behind me but certainly in her eyes.    After a wonderfully long moment of stillness, she got on her hind legs and stood above the grass to get a better view (animals know that to see better, sometimes you need to gain height! Oh captain, my captain!).    If she was cute before, suddenly, I had no words for what she became now. I was speechless—and couldn’t have spoken anyway. I was barely breathing.    Then she continued on her way, resuming whatever she had been doing before, without haste—therefore probably without fear—completely unaware of the horror of her encounter. (What could be more horrifying for a wild animal than meeting a human! Meeting two humans?)    Leaving me in awe of her beauty, I went to bed happy like a kid who had just seen his first wild mustelid and loved it.    I ate a little, then "closed" the tent (which is a big word since the zippers of both the flysheet and the inner tent are long gone). I use safety pins to close the flysheet effectively (it works very well, phew!) and have given up, months ago, on the idea of closing the inner tent. Goodbye mosquito net and privacy. Everything that can pass under the flysheet has direct access to the half-wild and hopefully sound-asleep Emmanuel. Hello spiders, beetles, earwigs, and so on.    The slugs and snails, though, are the ones whose "cuddling" I appreciate the least. Who likes sloppy wet kisses, I ask you?    So I "closed" my tent and fell asleep in an instant as soon as it got dark. Basically at 5 p.m. Well, yes, the days were still long back then. Now it’s more like 3:30 p.m. for sunset and 4:00 p.m. for full night. It’s strange to me, I admit.    And I slept really well. Very well—until I woke up. And I woke up.    That, too, is something surprising. When we sleep "outside," there’s a sort of inner wakefulness, as if part of our brain (reptilian?) remains alert to give warning if necessary. Like a sudden attack of slobbery wet kisses, for example—brrr—or a creature wriggling at my feet.    Now fully awake but taking care to remain still and breathe calmly, listening, I tried to determine what had woken me. And without waiting too long, an animal, about the size of a cat, began to fidget—right at my feet, and even partly on them.    Do you remember that night when a cat came to visit me? After overcoming its apprehensions, it entered my tent and stayed for the night. Frenzied cuddles several times during the night, followed by purring and sleeping on my sleeping bag—it was a warm encounter, full of sweetness.    But I was pretty sure it wasn’t a cat this time. Most likely, it was my afternoon friend.   I say friend—I was fully her friend. From my side, at least. As for her feelings, I didn’t really know yet.    But I admit, I had hope...    She was walking between the flysheet and the inner tent. A few times, she put her front legs on the stretched canvas of the inner tent, giving me the feeling she was climbing on my feet...    How to tell you—I was full of hope that the brotherly meeting of two predators, one of which was super cute and both super hairy, could end in sweet hugs. She wasn’t afraid; just for that, I liked her. No particular inhibition, from what I could tell, because I started to move, and she stayed. Any other animal would have scampered away in fright and howls. But not her. She was like this, you see...    Soon, I started talking to her softly.    Okay, let me stop you right there—no, I wasn’t talking to her so much to tell her something, and even less to expect an answer. I’m not that crazy yet. But I used my voice to convey feelings of calm, harmlessness, and assurance.    Animals have an intuitive, nonverbal perception capacity. We do too, of course—it’s what allows us to perceive during a phone conversation that the person on the other end is smiling. But animals are even better at this. They can feel our attitude.    And it must have worked, at least a little, because she didn’t flee despite my words. She paused for a moment, then resumed her activity.    I was really starting to consider contact! Seriously! Being able to stroke the animal would be like Christmas come early!!! We weren’t there yet, but hey—you know boys!    I took my phone to use the flashlight function and discovered two very disappointing things.    The first is that the flashlight function is antagonistic to the camera. So I couldn’t show you the magnificent little creature. Well, I say little, but she was about the size of a good-sized cat. Shorter legs. And a small muzzle with lovely whiskers.    The second—and this crushed my romantic hopes of spontaneous contact between two critters—was that she was busy with the little bag containing my rubbish and food scraps. I always take care to gather these while waiting for the opportunity to dispose of them in the first trash can I come across.    She had grabbed the bag, carried it to my feet, and began extracting its contents.    That might mean nothing to you, but for me, it meant she wasn’t there for my beautiful eyes, but for the olfactory hope of a nighttime snack.    It was a hard blow—for me and my dreams of soft, furry caresses. (Bah, yes, it must be super soft in addition to being super cute! People make coat collars out of it, let me remind you! And let’s admit it, the fur really makes you want to touch it. Forget the fine teeth at one end of the thing and the fart-spray anal glands at the other!)    It puts things in perspective and me back in my place.    And yet, I still wanted to believe it. After waiting for her to move to the other side of the tent, I reached out to retrieve the plastic bag—not easy at all, but I thought it was better to do it now than later, when all its contents would be scattered everywhere!   And then, as she still didn’t leave and my romantic hopes revived, I decided to try indirect contact—through the thin canvas of the tent. I touched her, almost stroked her. Almost, because there was the thin tent canvas between us and, quite honestly, because she didn’t really let it happen.    She still didn’t run away but didn’t let herself be touched either. As soon as the sensation became more than her own friction against the canvas—my hand pressing gently against her through the fabric—she changed position. She didn’t leave, but she wouldn’t let herself be caressed.    Finally, she began to focus her activity on my left side, right at the height of my elbow. To be precise, exactly where I store my food in the tent. Food that was protected only by the thin canvas and a Tupperware box, though she couldn’t know about the latter.    So yes, she was only here for the promises of her nose. I, meanwhile, counted for nothing. The story—our story—was doomed to failure before it could even begin.    Realizing this, the whole situation suddenly seemed absurd, a bit drawn out, a waste of time. I figured it was better to let the night offer the possibility of good sleep.    That hope vanished abruptly when she began to emit little shrill cries that, without a shadow of a doubt, reflected frustration, annoyance, and finally, anger.    It was around this time that the cute little furry creature began to turn into a real little evil pest. Forgive the expression.   She started to attack the tent—or rather, not attack it outright, but in her frustration and in trying to reach what she was smelling, she began biting or trying to bite the canvas of the inner tent.    Biting a stretched canvas is not an easy task.   I was watching her, resting on my elbow, using the arm whose hand held my phone. The phone’s flashlight beam projected between the flysheet and the inner tent, while my right hand pulled on the tent canvas to widen the gap between the two, clearing my view of the otherwise cramped space where she was putting on her show.    We were 12 inches apart—snout to snout.    Now visibly frustrated, she managed to sink her teeth into the canvas. When her grip was firm, she gave a sharp little jerk, pulling with her whole body and stepping back in short, jerky movements...    There, I really stopped agreeing with the situation. As cute as she was (I mean, you should have seen her jerking back—it was adorable!).    "But would you stop, you little evil," I said, remembering that the tone was more important than the words themselves.    We had to find an arrangement quickly, or it was going to be a very long night. An idea—almost a plan—came to me and seemed relevant: if she was no longer hungry, she would leave me alone. To sum it up.    So I opened the magic box, took out my knife, and opted for a piece of Brie. A good piece of Brie stuck at the end of the knife.    She sniffed, then very quickly grabbed the piece, took a few steps back (it’s super cute when they go backwards!), landed on her hind legs, chest upright, holding the piece of cheese with her front paws. She began tearing off small pieces, chewing them carefully before swallowing.    You might say I’m repeating myself, but God, this little beast was cute when eating something other than my tent! I could have watched her like that for hours.    She devoured the first piece very quickly, the second too, and the third more slowly. I never got bored. In addition to the hope of having satiated her so she would leave me alone, watching her eat the Brie—me being from Normandy—I felt a kind of connection, a kind of sympathy. After all, we shared certain tastes. It wasn’t all totally hopeless between us...    And finally, she left.    I was a little disappointed, all the same. I am sure of the potential for fraternization. After all, these animals have been tamed for a long time, either as pets or as burrow-hunting animals...    But she was gone. And I could relax, go back to sleep.    But she came back.    And by the time she woke me up for the second time, she had already made a hole 7 cm long by 4 cm wide.    That’s when I went for contact—but more firmly this time. No caresses.    With my phone light in one hand, I watched her closely. Each time she was about to bite the canvas, I hit her on the muzzle from the other side.    At first, just gentle taps, accompanied by reprimands with no real conviction—I mean, I was still under her charm and couldn’t bring myself to hit or scold her in anger.    But I have to admit, my patience was slowly running out.    I was really impressed by her determination—and her insolence too! After all, wasn’t she aware that she was in the presence of the worst mammal in the galaxy? Seriously? The representative of the supreme masters of all other forms of life on Earth, because intelligent, industrious, and artistic (and egocentric too...)?    She took a dozen taps on the muzzle. The last one was no longer a joke—it was a slap. A good one. And the beast fled. Phew!    Sad that it had to come to this—for a piece of Norman cheese! But now, my tent had two big torn holes and several smaller bite marks...   I was exhausted and needed sleep, but I couldn’t fall back asleep right away. The night was dragging on. And just as I was finally dozing off again, guess what—of course, she came back a third time.    Around two in the morning, another wake-up, another hole.    At that point, I began to doubt my victory over the little monster. The separation had to happen—now. A divorce, before she took the whole tent apart. But how to do that without resorting to brutality? I couldn’t go beyond the slap; it had already made my heart ache.  I really wondered how to get out of this relational impasse without ending in a brutal heartbreak...   That’s when I remembered the little pepper spray given to me by a Ukrainian security guard in Germany. He had handed it to me, saying it was for wildlife and possibly humans (apparently, sprays specifically for wildlife are stronger but forbidden for use on humans). He had insisted on telling me that there were a lot of junkies around.    Well, personally, in the middle of the woods, I had very rarely encountered junkie attacks. (The junkie is, after all, an urban animal.) But we all have our fears, I suppose. Mine? Slobbering wet kisses attacks...    In short, I looked for the small spray and, despite the probable discomfort of using it in a closed—or almost closed—space, I threatened my assailant with it.    And at that moment, I also decided that for being so persistent, she had to be a he.    Yes, I know—big discriminatory clichés, totally against any concept of gender equality.    But hey, it was the feeling of the moment, at three in the morning, on a restless night.   The first pchitt was almost nonexistent and therefore totally ineffective. I was reluctant... But when he started working on his fourth hole, he got a proper pchitt on the muzzle. A little one. Half a second. Maybe even less.    I didn’t even see him leave—it was so fast.    But it had worked.    And now I was there, and he was gone. I was relieved but disappointed. Disappointed and a little sad...   Fortunately, I had the opportunity to take some air for a good hour, to clear my head and properly ventilate the tent!   I hope the critter hasn’t had any problems because of this. I don’t think so. I am a little disappointed, not really surprised—except by his cheek, his daring, his determination...    But honestly, I remain under his spell. I assure you, these little furballs are so cute. Really...    And now, I won’t advise you to go on the internet to check whether mustelids might be a key link in triggering an unprecedented historical event—a panzootic (animal-to-human pandemic). According to Wikipedia in 2020, “mink farms are the animal farms that have been most affected by the SARS-CoV-2 virus responsible for COVID-19. If this virus were to spread among wild mustelids, the latter could become a permanent reservoir of infection for other animal species, as was the case with rabies transmitted to raccoons and skunks, or with bovine tuberculosis transmitted to badgers, or with paratuberculosis, transmissible to many wild ruminants and sometimes to immunosuppressed humans.”    But hey, without going as far as "Haaa, my God, it’s awful, we’re all going to die," it’s true that mustelids become less cute when you read that.    I guess.   On my side, I loved the encounter. Even if I now have three big holes in my tent (though compared to the gaping hole at the entrance where the zipper is completely out of use, the three side holes feel conceptually negligible).    And he looked in great shape—fully healthy, the little devil!
blog/archives/12-2020/index.html:
East Germany


		23/12/2020
	
​     Good evening from the former East Germany.     It's hard to say how much I enjoy the country, to be honest, because most of the time I’m alone in nature, and it feels very similar to home. When I pass through a village or town, perhaps due to the virus, the weather, and the end-of-year period, it often feels like a ghost town everywhere. I appreciate the architecture, but I can’t really get a sense of the area’s atmosphere—it’s the people who create that, and here, they are absent.    I do notice a strong difference between West and East Germany in terms of the wealth of housing, cars, and infrastructure. The west is impeccable, while the east is much less so.     So, let’s just say I like what I see most of the time, as well as my walking experience...     I have a few more weeks in East Germany, and then it will be Poland.     Yesterday, as a sort of duty to humanity, I made a detour to the former Nazi concentration camp of Buchenwald, which was later transformed by the Soviets into a special internment camp (causing more deaths than under the Nazi regime). Suffice it to say, the place has a "tense" atmosphere, and it feels incredibly heavy. It was closed due to Corona, so guided tours and access to the exhibition buildings weren’t possible. However, the entire camp itself was open, and a few explanatory panels outside provided the essentials. That was enough—I can imagine the rest.     Today, I came across ostriches. It was strange to see them at a bend in the path, in a meadow...     I also came across a dead penguin!     The last photo shows its corpse lying on the ground! 🤭😂    The large buildings visible just above, which look like towering communist administration or propaganda headquarters, are, in fact, a biscuit factory!     I have a fascination with twisted trees. An abnormal tree can be very beautiful... like these faces!    I also met a gentleman after Leipzig who has a collection (apparently in the world’s top 20!) of metal bottle caps, classified by country, type, and era! Like all enthusiasts, it was great to listen to him talk about his passion—especially how it all started. His three-year-old son had found a very colorful bottle cap while walking with his parents (which, from what I’ve observed, Germans do a lot. A LOT! Really... It’s such a healthy habit). Anyway, the child refused to let go of the bottle cap for several days, so the dad started bringing him a new one every day, placing it on his bedside table. And this is how, 28 years later, he ended up with a collection of over 100,000 metal bottle caps...     He also has several tens of thousands of duplicates and triplicates, all intended for exchanges...

The Alpha Point


		15/12/2020
	
​     The Alpha Point!     I’ve just entered the former East Germany. Suddenly, there are relics and memorials everywhere. Here, a piece of the wall; there, the different barbed wire barriers and more. Antipersonnel mines were placed between each barrier all along the border—1,800,000 mines in total. Warlike dogs, intentionally starved to make them aggressive and dangerous, patrolled between the barbed wire fences. Finally, between the last fences, the ground was plowed and harrowed regularly to detect traces of any attempted crossings. All of this just to prevent its own population from leaving! 😨    Seeing this leaves a really unpleasant impression because, ultimately, it’s not that far removed from us—in any sense. There are some truly scary and sad memories here...

Fulda


		6/12/2020
	
     A beautiful day. I first discovered the beautiful city of Fulda, which is historically very attractive.    Then, a very nice family with whom I’ve been chatting all afternoon until now—it all started with an invitation to lunch when I asked for water to refill my bottles. I had noticed a scallop shell hanging from a nail on the facade of their house, and I thought to myself that they must be people who had made the famous pilgrimage to Saint Jacques de Compostela... or at least sympathizers of the pilgrim that I am.     And then I was offered a hot shower, a wash for my clothes, a charge for my phone’s battery, and a very friendly fight with the dog Bruno (because he’s brown).   I’m sleeping in the camper van parked in the yard tonight. It’s very practical, the bed is comfortable, and I’m indoors. This saves me from setting up and taking down my tent, which I would have otherwise placed in the garden.     We just had a traditional hot spiced wine—red wine, lots of spices, a little sugar, and that’s it. It’s a drink for this season, and yes, it keeps you warm.      Everything is okay... I’ll sleep well, even if I didn’t make much progress today. I walked maybe 10 or 12 km, but it was a beautiful day... Gray skies, but beautiful nonetheless...
blog/archives/11-2023/index.html:
Decision


		18/11/2023
	
     ​Again, it’s been a while since I shared my journey with you. I had nothing new or special to say. No change in the pilgrim’s experience of the path.   But ultimately, I’m not required to be original or new all the time, especially when there is nothing new to share. So, I might as well pick up the nail where I left it last time—if you remember the metaphor.     So, here it is.    I came down from the forest through a small grassy meadow to reach a small road downhill. I had just spent three nights in this lovely forest, in a quiet and protected area. When I first arrived there, I was in a bit of a hurry. It was my birthday.    I had stopped at a restaurant to enjoy a hot meal and a power outlet. When I left, I quickly felt the urgent need to find a bathroom—in real hurry. It happens. For the restaurant’s defense, I don’t think the food quality was to blame, but rather the possible presence of non-vegetarian elements in the preparation. Something like pork fat for cooking, perhaps. For many people who are unfamiliar with vegetarianism, inattentive, or simply mischievous, cooking vegetables with lard still counts as a vegetarian dish...   For someone like me, who has abstained from meat products for more than 32 years, my digestive system reacts immediately—and violently.     Of course, this isn’t ideal on a busy road where each side is occupied by buildings and fenced-off properties. The few kilometers that followed were epic: tiring, distressing, and punctuated by numerous “open toilet breaks.”     Happy birthday, Emmanuel!     So I didn’t really choose where to stop. As soon as I saw a perpendicular path leading to a forest, I followed it until I found a welcoming place. I came down from that spot well-rested after three nights there. As I arrived at this small road, intending to follow it to a larger one, a gentleman in his garden spotted me and called out from afar.     He was far enough away that he had no idea who I was or what I was doing there, just that I had the look of a backpacker. Far enough, too, that I couldn’t really hear him, but I could see he was calling out. So I changed my direction and walked toward him. When I got within earshot, I said my usual line: "French/pilgrim/not understand." He replied, “Ah, okay! Coffee?”    The proposition was clear and tempting. A hot coffee early in the morning is always welcome, especially with the chill of the season. So, getting one just as I was starting my day was unexpected but very pleasant.     We sipped it together, joined by his wife on the terrace of their house, where he was finishing work on an outbuilding. It was a very nice encounter—simple and full of kindness. After an hour with them, I got back on the road. The main road wasn’t pleasant to walk along, as important roads often aren’t. The number of vehicles, and especially their speeds, made walking uncomfortable, stressful, and dangerous.   But I had no alternative, so I carefully monitored the traffic coming toward me. I wore headphones to block out the noise—whether with music, an audiobook, or even just silence.     At the intersection where I needed to take the left branch, a pedestrian crossed the road to meet me and asked what I was doing there. I showed him the short text recorded in my translator, summarizing the main ideas in one paragraph. After several handshakes and a few "very goud, very goud," I continued my walk toward the small grocery store located right at the intersection.     With my backpack emptied of all food, and having not eaten the day before or that morning, I thought a stop for provisions would be welcome. I placed my bag on one of the benches on the small terrace near the entrance—village grocery stores often have a café/bar attached with a terrace—and went inside.     Two cans of vegetable pâté, a block of cheese, five nicely red tomatoes, two bananas, and a loaf of sliced bread later, I stepped outside to grab the coins I had forgotten in the jacket on my bag, intending to add them to the 50 lei note I had already given. I wanted to simplify payment by offering a rounded amount. When I returned to the counter, the lady indicated that I owed nothing. “It’s for me,” she said. “Drum bun. Have a nice journey.”     Isn’t that surprising? Isn’t it pleasant? Isn’t it touching?     Apparently, the gentleman I had met earlier had entered after me, and while I was choosing my cans of pâté, he briefly introduced me to the lady. That’s how she ended up giving me back my money and saying, “It’s for me.”     After carefully putting the entire donation into the appropriate boxes in my bag, I resumed my journey, only to discover a roadside restaurant just a little further along the way. A sort of container-turned-chip shop/French fry/kebab stand. The idea of a hot and different meal tempted me. After all, I could save what I had bought for later. Hot food isn’t an everyday luxury. So I stopped.     Leaning on the counter, the gentleman ahead of me saw me, and we exchanged greetings. After my customary "French/pilgrim/not understanding" introduction, he began speaking in surprisingly good French—leftovers from high school, he said. It was not only practical but also pleasant to have a conversation and a translator for my order, just to ensure the hamburger I was ordering was truly vegetarian!     When his order was ready, he shook my hand and went on his way. A very nice meeting with a local teacher—Romanian, of course. While waiting for my burger, wallet in hand and ready to pay, I noticed the lady preparing it was on her phone, while another finished assembling a bag of fries and another burger.     I assumed it was a phone order—until she handed me her phone. On the screen was a message she had just written and translated for me: “The two burgers and fries are for you. It’s free. We wish you well. Have a nice journey.” I don’t want to sound melodramatic, but I nearly cried.   It’s not just the gesture itself—it’s the repetition, the frequency. The consistency. It touches something deep inside. You see? So the nail sinks in...    It was still only midday, and I had about ten kilometers left before reaching my destination: the Basilica of Cacica. I’m here now. Well, not precisely in the basilica as I write these words, but I’m right next door—maybe 200 meters away. I’m staying in a family home. It was one of the priests from the basilica who approached me as I was leaving. Night had already fallen; it was almost 5 p.m.     “Do you know where to sleep?” he asked me.     “No, not yet,” I replied.     “Come with me,” he said.     He led me to a neighbor’s house, and the neighbor then took me to another house, just behind his, on the other side of the garden.    He showed me the kitchen as he plugged in the refrigerator. Then he led me upstairs to the bathroom, saying there would soon be hot water (he knew the exact words a pilgrim would appreciate—or perhaps my smell made it clear how necessary it was!). And then he showed me the bedroom. “You stay as long as you want,” he said.     I’ve been experiencing this for three years. Three years!    Maybe you don’t realize—I don’t know. You can only read what I can write, and many things cannot be put into words. But imagine living this...     So.     Today, I decided something important.    Three years was the length of time I initially hoped to experience when I decided to go beyond southern Poland and the Czestochowa Monastery. It seemed enough—not to learn everything I wanted, but to establish something permanent.     Certainly, the impression is profound. Certainly, the imprint is there, the trace is marked. But I feel its fragility. I intuitively sense that there is much more. The nails can go further, deeper, to ensure they don’t come out.     I’m probably not a good student. I’m a very slow learner.     But I want to continue. It’s not that I don’t want to stop—I want to continue.     The nuance is very important.     So.    I’m heading back tomorrow morning. This may seem obvious to you, but it wasn’t. In recent months, I’ve experienced certain conditions that made me doubt—doubt the relevance of continuing this path, at least in this way. And the desire to continue is not a sufficient condition for a serious practitioner. Alone, it can lead to confusion, which is the opposite of what I’m seeking.    So I stopped to reflect on the path—the one I’ve traveled and the one ahead. But neither is as eloquent as the silence and well-being I feel this morning, walking under the snow that has been falling heavily since yesterday.     It’s beautiful. It’s good. I feel good. I feel free. I am happy.     I think I’ll wait until I truly can’t continue before stopping.   Put yourself in my place—wouldn’t you look further for what the nail fixes? What work it participates in and contributes to? Would you have better things to do?     I wish you the best.     See you soon.
blog/archives/12-2022/index.html:
Levoca


		1/12/2022
	
     Levoca, Slovakia     1 December 2022     2 years, 2 months, 1 week, and 2 days on the way.     Approximately 6575 km walked.   Today, I’ll stay inside. For today and two more nights, I am in a monastery in the center of Levoca. I need to stay in town for a bit because I have to buy some materials to repair my backpack, tent, and some parts of my clothes.     I also need to figure out how to keep my bear spray accessible while walking, without it getting in the way. Yes, bear spray is essential in Slovakia, especially if you sleep in forests and mountains as I do. No joke—there are about 2,500 brown bears in the country. That’s a lot. After doing some research and watching homemade videos from people’s homes, I decided to take the matter seriously. So, I bought a few things to reduce the risk of being attacked. The spray is one of them, but I need to find a way to have it close at hand and easily accessible.    You might say it’s unnecessary because of the season—bears are supposed to hibernate. They were, but with climate warming, bears are now seen year-round.     So, I have many things to do.    But being inside makes it much easier. I don’t know about you, but here it’s winter. Minus 5°C all day long, dropping to minus 10°C or 12°C at night, especially in the mountains. Stitching is difficult. Actually, everything is difficult with frozen fingers.     Inside is nice. Warm. I hope not too warm, though, because I can’t sleep in a hot room anymore. Don’t get me wrong, I like the cold. I enjoy it. Minus ten doesn’t bother me—it’s beautiful, quiet, and feels pure. And I sleep very well in it. Really, it’s a pleasure. But stitching in the cold is hard!Another thing I’ll appreciate while I’m here is hot water. Washing in rivers or mountain springs is lovely—really. But I can’t use soap then, because the water is so pure I drink it. I’m not about to put shampoo or soap in it, right? So, nature baths are nice, but incomplete. And cold—really, really cold. Painfully cold. So, they’re very brief. Brother Thomas told me I could wash my clothes here if I wanted, and of course, I do! A washing machine is a blessing!     Once I’ve done all this, I’ll walk uphill to the Mariánska Hora basilica, probably set up my tent near the water source, and enjoy a few days of meditation.Then, I’ll be on my way again. I’ll let you know where next.     So, you see, everything is beautiful and nice. I enjoy my way as much as I hope my way enjoys me.     I wish you happiness and well-being.     Emmanuel    P.S.: Today, I received a parcel via post restante—a birthday gift from friends I met in Poland. Isn’t that lovely and kind? They sent me a high-quality power bank. It charges very fast, which is great because I’ll be able to recharge it whenever I stop at a restaurant or café. It also has a huge capacity, so once it’s fully charged, I can use it to charge my phone many times.     That’s really, really cool! And very useful to me. I’m deeply grateful for it.     So, as you can see, I’m still being taken care of on my journey, and that helps me keep going.     And so, I go...
blog/archives/12-2021/index.html:
Spine


		2/12/2021
	
     Here, freshness is here. Some would say cold. But I prefer to save that word for when it will be minus 20... 😜    It's beautiful. I enjoy it a lot—except for the slippery side. It's really slippery. The temperature dropped very suddenly, and the weather was very wet just before. So there’s ice under the snow, which is a great recipe for finding ourselves on all fours on the floor...    Luckily, I have my faithful and strong stick. Its name is "Spine." Yes, I gave a name to my stick. But it saves me from falling at least ten times a day. I still find myself on all fours sometimes, but I get there much slower and safer with it.    But who cares—see the beauty instead. The pictures help.​    Try to find my tent in one of them... 😋
blog/previous/2/index.html:
Meeting with a Bear


		11/7/2023
	
      It’s been a long time again, and I feel and sense some impatience. It’s nice to know that my news messages are awaited. It’s somehow a form of support for my journey.     I have now been in Romania for a few weeks, and I really appreciate what I am experiencing and seeing here.   But since Slovakia, I’ve been dragging my feet. I feel tired, physically exhausted, without this being justified by walking. This is because my walk is slow and interrupted by many breaks to enjoy the landscape, an encounter, a stone, a stump, or a bench perfectly placed for me to rest on. I walk, contemplate, and meditate—sometimes all at the same time. It’s a pleasant exercise, during which the inner chatter eventually dies out, and I find myself alone, silent, and content.   The breaks under the walnut tree, on the warm trunk of a tree in the local sun, stretch on without me worrying about it, without any movement occurring either inside or outside. A flat encephalogram (which some might say must be easy for me—see the end of the message...) certainly, but with vigilance, with purposeless concentration, if that makes sense to you. As a result, my average mileage drops quickly, but since the goal is not athletic, as you understood, I don’t care.    However, for some time now, not only has my walking slowed down, but the breaks have grown longer and far more frequent. This made me consider the possibility of a health problem, which prompted me to change my route and pass through a big city to consult a doctor for a check-up. After all, it’s been 4 or 5 years since I’ve had any follow-up care, and almost 3 years that I’ve been walking in living conditions that some would call precarious.    So, to reassure you right away: the examination and analyses revealed nothing abnormal. The doctor who examined me at the hospital simply told me that I needed to rest...    So, that’s what I’m doing.    Before continuing, I would like to point out that the Romanian health system is welcoming. Any individual is received and treated free of charge for 72 hours, regardless of their nationality. This will probably not impress the French, whose health system also has some good aspects, but when you experience this attention, it is touching. Really. The Hippocratic oath no longer feels hypocritical... and it feels good.     So here it is: for a month, I have been walking for one day, then resting for two or three. And I feel like it’s paying off, as I now feel better rested and often eager to start again—something I had been missing lately.    But I’m seeing the good side of things: I’m spending a lot of time in the countryside. When I stop, it’s often in the forest, which here finally covers the land that, to the east of where I came from, was sadly bare. I don’t know where you are, but here it’s hot or very hot, and as soon as it gets too much, we get a storm. A real summer storm with torrential downpours (think Indian or Nepalese monsoon), thunder that shakes the ground, and lightning that gets me out of my tent to check if the tree next to me was hit.     After that, the temperature becomes much more bearable, but it’s incredibly heavy because of the humidity. It might seem unpleasant, but you have to look at the whole picture: when it’s hot and very humid, it feels heavy and uncomfortable, but—and I allow myself to use capital letters here—BUT, all the conditions are suddenly perfect for the appearance of our fungal friends.    I picked summer ceps in mid-June. Yes! And they were a delight. At the end of June, I was invited to breakfast by a local mushroom enthusiast who prepared a fricassee of chanterelles. You can imagine that if I spend time in the woods, I eat mushrooms regularly. And to me, that’s divine.   On the other hand, the local forests have one major drawback: bears. And I admit, there are many. Even in a small wood, like a one-hectare thicket, there is likely a bear in it. I didn’t really believe it at first—just like in Slovakia. But here, I see traces every day. Fresh traces, even very fresh ones. I’ve even had morning visits. In wolf and dog form. Their schedule seems to be around 3:30–4:00 a.m.    I discovered that even when we sleep in the middle of the woods, a part of us continues to "listen." I was amazed to realize this, but I believe that our ears continue to hear, and our brain processes information intuitively. It’s strange to notice, like finally becoming aware of your unconscious.    The two times a bear approached my tent while I was sleeping, I woke up immediately, as if shaken by my subconscious warning me of danger. There was no gentle awakening phase where you take your time, where reality is still blurred by the paradoxical sleep phase, free cinema... No, I opened my eyes instantly, no transition—I was alert, attentive, concentrated, and immediately ready to act.    I already knew there was something on the other side of the thin fabric of my tent. My first thought, clear and certain, was: a bear. About ten meters from the tent, I then heard heavy but hesitant footsteps. Without hesitation, without even thinking, I began to sing—softly but loudly—while at the same time lighting up the tent with the headlamp given to me by a firefighter from Târgu Mureș. I knew that my tent would then become a softly glowing lamp, about 3 meters long and 1.2 meters high. A beautiful sight for the bear, I imagined, lying there, motionless.    Singing right away when you wake up because a bear is outside might seem like a crazy idea. But let me explain:    The only bear attacks in Europe are related to surprise—when a bear is startled by a human who was too discreet (the bear neither hears nor senses them), or to fear—when an aggressive human mistakenly thinks that making a lot of noise or acting threateningly will scare away a 350 kg beast. The bear, feeling threatened, might attack instead of fleeing. Another situation is when an inattentive human finds themselves between a bear and her cubs, triggering a protective maternal instinct—with claws and teeth.    Other attacks are linked to predatory behavior, triggered when a human runs (or cycles or skis) in front of a bear. This activates the bear’s predatory or attack reflex, much like what happens with an excited dog that is likely to bite if you run from it.     So, I tell myself that if the bear has approached me despite the unmistakable olfactory signals for its sense of smell—signals I deliberately place around and on my tent (a cloth soaked in diesel between the roof and the double roof of the tent, and my urine poured on the trunks of trees around my campsite)—it’s because the bear is curious (like many animals I’ve noticed) and opportunistic (hoping the human is gone and has left something to eat).    Of course, the bear probably doesn’t have a clear concept of UFOs, but the tent must seem like a very strange object to it—especially when it lights up.    When I wake up, I sing so the bear knows I’m there, in the tent. Singing, unlike shouting or howling, is far less aggressive. It also benefits me: singing has a soothing effect, both on the one who hears the song and on the one who sings it. You can’t sing while being completely paralyzed with fear. Singing keeps fear at bay.     In short, my theory is that, like many animals I’ve known since childhood, bears are not so much receptive to what I say but rather to the tone in which I say it. They are not as affected by my movements as they are by my attitude—my mental state, in a way.    I believe that singing is a way to show my presence while maintaining a relaxed and peaceful attitude. It reassures the animal while informing it of my presence and my nature.     Both times this happened, the bear ran away immediately. The second time, it was really close to me and let out a kind of nasal breath, an impressive Mmufffff. Either I wasn’t mistaken about its presence, or I sing really badly!    Also impressive is the sound of cattle running through the undergrowth. You might not know this, but when we sleep in the woods, sounds are amplified—not only by the acoustics of the place but also by the unconscious analysis our brain performs. It’s probably a remnant from the time when we lived outdoors and were a tasty treat for many predators.    At night, a simple beetle can seem like a huge rat snooping around. A toad becomes je ne sais quoi weighing at least 20 kilograms... A bird landing on the ground and scratching with its claw for food becomes a wild boar. I assure you, it’s destabilizing to realize how much our brain exaggerates these sounds.    Over time, with practice, the brain recalibrates, and you can relax completely despite the many noises of the forest. I now sleep in the woods as comfortably as I would in a bed in my room—even though, in reality, I haven’t had a room or a bed for more than 28 years.    So, I believe bears aren’t really the danger. They represent a risk, because, in the end, nothing prevents encountering a bad-tempered one—there are difficult characters in all mammals; it’s not exclusive to bipeds in an upright position. But I think that with certain precautions and behaviors, the risk is ultimately very small.     I accept this risk because, ultimately, I have no choice if I want to continue my journey.    When I spend several days in the same place, choosing the right location is essential. A sheltered spot—from the sun, so it’s possible to stay under the tent, and from view, to avoid worrying or being disturbed. Some places lend themselves perfectly: a small clearing of a few dozen square meters of flat and sparsely sown ground, where dense vegetation around and above filters the direct light... A small stream of clear water to cool off during the heat of the afternoon, and to wash, too.     This is where I was yesterday and the day before. Superb... Magnificent... Ideal.     Until the storm.    The rain began to fall in large drops, accompanied by a deafening clap of thunder that tore through the silence and my senses. It became so intense that I went out to check the stream, only a few meters away. The rain was so heavy that, already soaked, I decided to take out the soap and wash myself in the deluge.     When I returned to the tent, I knew there was a risk the water would rise and the stream might overflow. But there was space...     So I lay down and thought about something else. The rain stopped, and after looking outside, I assessed the risk of flooding as acceptable. The groundsheet of my new tent is waterproof and can withstand being in a layer of water up to 5 cm without compromising the interior.And inside, I have a small self-inflating mattress a few centimeters thick.     Even if water were to penetrate a little, most of my belongings would still be sheltered.     The happy optimist who sees the glass half full... I fell asleep like a child.     As I write this, I am washing all of my belongings and gear. I was awakened by the tent shaking and pushing me aside. Water was penetrating inside, and by the time I began organizing my things and planning my escape, I was in more than eight inches of water.     Of course, night was falling, and I had to move all my stuff to a place that wasn’t flooded, about 50 meters away. By the time I finished, the torrent covering the whole area was 40 cm deep. Suffice to say, the stream below was no longer visible at all.     The tent was almost lying in the water, and dismantling it became a major emergency before it broke. The battery in the headlamp chose this moment to signal that it needed energy. I realized that if I handled things poorly, I would lose a lot—some of my equipment had already been carried away. I removed all the pegs and fought to get the tent out of the water without it being swept away by the current.     I managed it, securing the tent in a safe place and getting back to it later. I spent the next day rinsing my belongings of the fine, sticky mud and the whole afternoon looking for what had been carried away: water bottles, clothes, bags.     I found almost everything, which feels almost miraculous.     But I confess, I’m not proud of myself. There were signs I ignored because I thought everything would be fine. I listened to optimism until it turned into foolishness!     Fortunately, in the village where I arrived, there’s a small guesthouse. I’m staying there to wash my clothes, clean the mud off absolutely everything, and dry everything in the sun.     Finally, everything is fine.   Tomorrow, I’m back on my way—a day of walking to a suitable place, then two days of rest. With a little luck, in a few weeks, I’ll be able to resume a normal rhythm.     In the meantime, I wish you all the best.     See you soon.

Happiness


		30/3/2023
	
     ​I thought I was going to send some solid news today, and that passing the 7000 km mark would be my pretext. But I have to be honest—this is fake news. I don’t really know where I am in terms of kilometers. I have this estimation due to my intimate relationship with topographic applications that I use every day to navigate, avoid busy roads, impassable rivers, and just not lose my way. Let’s say I suspect the distance, but I haven’t calculated it. It must be around 7000 km, give or take 10%. Although, in general, it’s probably less than more, because I believe that in my situation, we tend to evaluate rather higher than lower...     But hey... Let’s leave the kilometers aside.   I travel places, I meet people. And since my departure, everyone has been magnificent—welcoming, generous. This makes my path magnificent as well, and I walk it serenely, without its vagaries being a burden in any way.    For some time now, I’ve been crossing villages that consist of two parts: one “normal” village, and then further out, on the outskirts or in a small remote corner, a second part that’s much more dilapidated—almost like slums. It’s very visible, and you can recognize a population of “Roms,” as they are called. The former Gypsies, sedentarized by the Soviet governments, living in difficult conditions without really being able to escape them, even though it seems local and governmental aid is mobilized to help.     I come across these places. Poverty. Promiscuity, with everything that always accompanies it... precariousness.    And yet, I must say that I don’t think I’ve come across one of these places without someone inviting me at least once to eat, drink coffee, or sleep.     It’s a lesson in humility for me every time. I am forced to appreciate the welcome and the gift, contrasted against their living conditions. How touching.     Ah yes, speaking of touching...   For some time now, I’ve been scratching a lot. It’s not touching—it’s irritating, but let me explain. I was scratching a lot (like, really a lot and uncontrollably), and it didn’t take me long to realize I had scabies. Local generosity? A dirty towel in a restaurant bathroom? A questionable bed in a questionable motel? It’s hard to know how or by whom. Especially since it’s the first time in my life that I’ve caught it (I’ve never had lice or crabs either...). But that’s the thing—when it’s the first time, and the body doesn’t know the problem, in this case, Mr. Sarcoptes scabiei from the mite family, it can take time for symptoms to appear. Sometimes 15 days or more before the itching starts. So, it becomes difficult to determine the origin of the contamination.     But here, I tried to contact all the people with whom I spent time to warn them about the possibility of contagiousness. It’s really contagious, those small beasts...      But no panic, I often wash my hands with soap or hydroalcoholic gel, so a handshake doesn’t involve much risk. No, the risk was when I got invited to sleep inside.      The problem is that with the practice of pilgrimage as I do, it’s difficult to get rid of the beast without a very effective treatment: ivermectin. And this product is prohibited in Hungary, where I am, and that’s problematic because the remaining solutions are really cumbersome. While the ivermectin treatment consists of taking pills with a large glass of water twice at eight-day intervals, the alternative treatments require brushing your entire body with a lotion, letting it stand for 8 or 12 hours depending on the mixture, applying a second layer, waiting again, and then washing with hot water and soap. At the same time, washing clothes—all clothes—at 60 degrees. And the groundsheet. And the sleeping bag. A lot of work...     You can see how it becomes really complicated for the camper that I am.    While I was explaining this on the phone to the people who had invited me to spend three nights with them some time after my contamination a few weeks ago—they live in the last big city in Slovakia before the border with Hungary—Michaela and her neighbor Bruno (Branislav) decided, without me being able to dissuade them, not only to find ivermectin on the black market (it’s also forbidden in Slovakia, as a result of European policies concerning coronavirus treatments, if I understood correctly—some drugs have been blacklisted...), but also to drive four hours to bring it to me in the neighboring country. And with homemade cake—two, in fact, because both of them had made one for me.     You see...     It leaves me speechless. Silent. Calm, in every way.     When I resumed my journey, after a coffee offered for the three of us by the pilgrims' inn where I was staying, I was immersed in a deep silence. Deep and full. Not empty. I was calm, serene, grateful, confident. I walked calmly. I sat down whenever I felt the need, wherever the place was suitable, and I took time to contemplate this silence and sink into it.     There is nothing to say... nothing to be said.    Of course, there are times when loud shouts try to reach my ears or my eyes. This is always the case. Whether it’s the din of war that I circumvent geographically, or those more distant, like the rumblings from French streets at the moment, or more simply, a bistro conversation I come across while having a coffee (or a slivovica!)...    But once I’ve finished paying attention to it, the trace of the writing, the sight, or the sound fades almost instantly. There are no leftovers, no residual clutter. It becomes like distant knowledge that doesn’t truly reach me—at least not until I decide, with conscious effort, to pay attention to it again.     This distancing is pleasant. The noise of the world remains distant, even as I cross it. When it is present, this distance, born of healthy silence, feels like crossing or visiting myself with each step. I say "healthy silence" because it comes from the calm of the one experiencing it, not from the absence of noise around them.    So, I regularly spend weeks alone in the woods, then pass through towns or villages, meeting people and forming connections. When I leave again, there’s this same distancing—I rediscover the silence where I left it and sink into it, burying myself pleasantly in its embrace. I am privileged; I am aware of it.    The practice of pilgrimage, or perhaps simply long-term walking, gently forces me into this abandonment. It constrains with a certain tenderness. The need to adapt to the path, in order to walk it for a long time, is both mandatory and essential. To achieve this, it’s necessary to move toward what is pleasant, nourishing, and reassuring, while abandoning what is not.     I had to leave behind objects too heavy to carry in my bag to avoid the pain of carrying them. Finally, it’s clear: to feel good, you must stop hurting yourself. It seems obvious, and yet I notice so many counterexamples.     This principle has slowly extended from the backpack on my back to the inner one, in my head and chest.     It’s no longer the non-essential objects I leave behind now, but the petty fears and anxieties of everyday life.     Where am I going?     Will I have enough to eat?     To drink?     To sleep?     What if this path leads nowhere?     And then, the worries about the future—because I will have to work, earn money, and return someday...     We can’t go long without leaving these false hassles aside. This is the moment when we begin to learn freedom and happiness. And the more one realizes this, the more one likes it, the less difficult it is to realize it and participate in it. In fact, the more you walk on its path, the easier it becomes to walk there...    I learn freedom, I learn happiness. I’ve discovered that you can’t find them, you can’t receive them, or give them—the only way to live them is to learn to be. And it doesn’t need much; in a way, it just “stops preventing them” from being, naturally...     The most frequent question I receive concerns the number of kilometers I do per day. But this is a question that no longer makes sense to me. The preoccupation with the number of kilometers traveled no longer exists at all. You now understand what I wrote earlier concerning the 7000 km fake news. A glance at the map tells me that I’m almost there, but in the end, I don’t know. I haven’t made the effort to calculate, despite being asked very often.     I measure my days, if I must, by the quality of the time that has passed. I walk when I want or need to. I stop as soon as it’s pretty enough to look at, and the notion of average mileage is completely absent. I don’t feel bad or guilty for having walked a little—that’s something that took me a long time to give up: feeling bad for not having walked a lot today. The concept of obligation, if it still exists, has been transferred to the pleasure of being.     And in my long walk experience, finding a pretty spot is extremely pleasant. Finding a suitable place to pitch the tent is pleasant. A source of fresh water to fill my water bottles and refresh myself. A lake or river where I can bathe, wash myself... A hot shower. A coffee. A glass of slivovica (a little plum!). A smile.     I take pleasure in such trivial details, and I’m amazed at the power they possess, the strength they wield. To say that finding mushrooms on my way, lighting a fire to cook them, and eating while sitting on the ground in front of my tent nourished me is an understatement. It certainly nourished my body, but also a whole part of me which, until I let it enjoy and live, was curled up in a withering and sterile non-existence.     The silence I listen to is a fullness, not an emptiness...   Then the inner discourse slowly fades away... The incessant brouhaha, which we no longer realize deafens our inner ears to the point of not only deafening ourselves but others too—not only inside but also outside—eventually dries up and goes silent. There is then nothing to hinder the full enjoyment of the contentment of a deep breath of fresh air, the freshness of a sip of spring water, the sight of a wild animal, the song of a bird, the scent of a fir tree, the delicacy of a flower petal, or the taste of a hazelnut...     And here I am, with an almost ecstatic feeling, even though no event has occurred to provoke it. I find myself laughing without having thought of anything funny. A huge smile splits my face as I stand totally alone in the woods. And yet, I can’t stop this smile that I don’t offer to anyone.     I am well. I am here. And it’s good...    I made the mistake of writing this text in French and translating it afterward. It’s not the same when I do that... But I hope you still get the point.     I wish you all the best. Be well and happy.
