As soon as I appeared, he jumped at the opportunity to ask if I could answer a few questions for the local newspaper.     So I cancelled my morning plans—I had intended to go to the church and then to a big shop to buy food. But as I’ve told you, there’s no such thing as making plans when you’re on a pilgrimage. I accepted his offer to chat over breakfast. A three-hour breakfast.     But I was glad to answer his questions and did my best to do it well and sincerely. He was so enthusiastic and excited, and he seemed to really enjoy hearing about my experiences and adventures.     I suppose my story will now reach many people in the area. Perhaps some of them saw me passing through the town and will soon learn that I am a pilgrim—not a tourist, trekker, or vagabond. I wouldn’t say that was the reason for what happened, but now that it’s happened, I have no issue with how it turned out. Even if it wasn’t the way I would have preferred at first.     The director said he would send me a copy of the article. I’ll let you know.     Later, I received an impersonal alert message warning of great risks of blizzards and violent winds. I found a beautiful, quiet place near the river just outside the city. It’s a small natural bowl, hollow with a flat, very slightly sloped bottom, surrounded by many small fir trees. It’s perfect for pitching the tent—protected from the wind as well as from view. I’m going to spend two days here because, indeed, the wind and blizzard have arrived, but the place is very comfortable.     It happens more often these days that I take a day off. Maybe it’s the winter. Maybe I’m getting worn out, as well as my gear! But that’s fine. I take it easy. I think if I push myself too hard, I won’t be able to go far for long. So, I go slow. I hurry slowly and gently.     During the night, I woke up. I thought a pine cone had fallen on my tent—it makes a big noise inside when that happens. I went back to sleep, finding it strange that a pine cone had fallen when there were no pines around where I was...     In the morning, I realized it wasn’t a pine cone but one of the aluminum frames that support the tent. It had broken under the combined effect of the cold and the tension of the tent fabric, which stretches as it dries. Without any additional force, the small aluminum pipe snapped and, of course, cut the flysheet of the tent by 3 cm as it broke.     Really, sometimes I feel like just looking too hard at those tubes when they’re frozen might be enough to break them...     I’ll have to find a solution for this. I still have a few spares, but I go through them quickly. I’ll need to find a gear shop soon.     Today, I arrived in a village 6 or 8 km before a town. I planned to stop at the edge of the town, sleep there, and cross it tomorrow. I didn’t want to cross the town today because it’s Sunday, and most shops would be closed. So today would be a short one. That meant I had time, so I could enjoy a coffee at the village grocery store. See how the mind is tricky?     But it was minus 12 degrees Celsius, and somehow hot liquid feels good in those conditions... So I went to the grocery store and ordered a coffee. The woman refused to let me pay for it—it was free for me, she said. Thank you, madame. A coffee given freely always warms better...    I went outside, under the shade of the store, which was made for that. A guy was there drinking, too. And so, we started talking. His boots were of very good quality, I could see—paramilitary or police, or something like that. Turned out he was a fireman, on a day off, working for the fire department in the town.    I thought he was the right person to understand my equipment needs and maybe tell me if there was a shop in town that could fulfill them. And you know what? The guy was friends with the owner of the only shop in town that might have some of the things I needed. He directly proposed to call her to check. Nice coincidence, right?     The lady from the shop proposed to come and pick both of us up where we were, take us to visit the warehouse where all her stock is stored (both for the shop and online sales), as well as the shop itself, to see if I could find what I needed. Then, she would drive us back to our starting point so I could continue my journey while still being able to say I had covered it all on foot.     How cool is that?! On a Sunday afternoon, no less.     She even called her son in England to act as a translator for the whole thing, as neither she nor my fireman friend spoke enough English.     Just stop for a minute and consider the whole situation. Consider my perspective as well. I mean, I’m on foot and can’t easily wander around looking for shops. And yet, I meet these people exactly when I need them. I broke my tent this morning! And here are such kind people who, without even knowing me at all, decide to help me so kindly. Seriously?     And all of this happened because I went to get a hot coffee at the grocery store. This kind of thing has happened with everything I’ve needed since the start of my journey. Anytime I’ve been in need, these crazy, nice encounters have occurred. Or sometimes, I’ve just found what I needed lying on the ground along the path, as if someone had dropped it there for me.     For 16 months now, this has built a strong confidence in me—the belief that I should drop all worries. All is fine, and all will be fine. After dropping the unnecessary items from your backpack, a pilgrim begins to drop the unnecessary burdens they carry within themselves, like worries...     And it feels good!     It feels so good!     We feel light. We feel confident. We feel free. We feel loved.     When she drove me back to the grocery store where it all started, it was the beginning of the afternoon. I had plenty of time to walk to the small forest I had seen at the town’s entrance, near the river. I could take it easy there, and even stop at the pizzeria I had spotted a hundred meters ahead. Everything was going well. Really well, because the pizzeria was open now—it hadn’t been this morning. There was an electrical outlet next to where I sat, so I started writing what you are reading now. And I told myself that the world is well made...    I had to cross the town again today, on foot this time, and it was nice. Not all towns are comfortable to walk through, but this one was. The center had old buildings, and the churches I visited were massive and beautiful. At the end of the town, I came across a big supermarket. I stopped to refill my bag with food and then continued. Just a few hundred meters later, I saw a restaurant. It was open, even though it was only 11:30. They told me, in perfect English, that I could wait inside for 20 minutes.     The thought of a hot lunch won me over. I sat there, charging my phone while writing what you are reading. A nice vegetarian meal followed, during which a friend of the owner—fluent in English—came over to talk. He offered to take me by car, after my coffee, to a few places I would probably miss otherwise.     I left my backpack at the restaurant, and we went by car to three places: the ruins of a very old monastery that was a pilgrimage site to Mary before it was destroyed, the ruins of a Teutonic castle, and a viewpoint over the valley where I would likely follow my path. After that, he brought me back to the restaurant. I took my bag and continued on my way.     Isn’t it amazing that someone would take three hours of their time to show me these places?I walked for a few kilometers before darkness fell, then set up my tent and prepared for the night.     I started walking this morning on the path that runs along this small river. It was very cute. And quiet. After a few kilometers, the path took me behind the garden of someone who was in it. He crossed the garden, taking off his gloves to come and greet me. We chatted a bit. He asked if I needed anything, and I said I wasn’t really in need of anything but then corrected myself directly, as I actually needed to refill my water bottles. I had emptied all five liters while staying in the same place for two days. So he invited me inside and offered me coffee. While we talked, my phone was charging. Great!     Then he proposed calling a friend of his, who lived about 7 km further along my way, to see if she could welcome me for the night. She would be happy to receive a pilgrim. Of course, I was interested—you know, all the things: a new meeting, a hot shower, full battery charging...     And so, like that, it happened. I got invited to come to her place, and she said she would cook a soup while I walked there. Voilà.    The walk was nice, following an old railway. I tried to visit some trees I’d been told were beautiful, a little off the path inside the forest. It wasn’t far, and I had time. But I couldn’t find the place, so I returned to the railway and continued on. I arrived at her place quite early. Finally, a small walking day! But that was fine, as everything was going so smoothly.     I received such a warm welcome when I arrived—like we had known each other for a long time. She really put me at ease right away. She had a beautiful, large smile and a kind, vibrant energy. We went directly for the soup, and God knows it was a good soup. I was lucky to meet her—she’s vegetarian like me, so she had made a soup I could enjoy. But you know, with that special touch vegetarians have: a little spice, some turmeric, a bit of ginger... Whaaaa...     A soup that was perfect! And not just because soup is perfect in cold weather, not just because it was vegetarian, not just because it was a change in my culinary routine—the soup was really, really good. Thank you, Maria! (That’s her name.)     Then she went to work, in the next room. Nowadays, people work from home, you know... I took advantage of that to have a nice, hot shower, and afterward, I wrote these few words on my phone. A little later, she went shopping for a few things, including what was needed to make an apple tart! When she got back, we cooked together and ate while talking. A very nice day that ended late.     I left in the morning after a nice breakfast. It was quite late, I remember, because it was 11:11.That made me think of a French humorist, Desproges, in one of his sketches, playing a maniac who loved how this time of day looked perfectly organized on his electronic watch. For me, it was a kind of sign—to recall my concentration...     Nice snow carpet. About a dozen centimeters. Small, tiny flakes. Less wind, but it’s really cold. Walking in this is a real pleasure. The way is beautiful today—forest and lakes. I enjoy my walk but also my rests.     As I’m resting on the trunk of a tree, cut down by beavers on the side of a lake, enjoying the scenic view, the fresh air, and the quietness, I am joined by a group of three young adults who also enjoy walking. We only met for a few minutes, but we had a very nice interaction. After our small chat, they went on their way. I stayed there for more than an hour, watching the water, watching myself, my thoughts, my breathing. It was really nice. And then I went on.     The forest was large, and I stayed inside it until the end of the afternoon. I was getting tired and thought I’d probably find a place to pitch my tent somewhere around—just a bit off the main path. Somehow, those paths seemed well-used by many walkers, dog walkers, and cyclists.     I was actually considering a little group of trees that looked like a good place to hide myself for the night. But I thought I’d wait until the path cleared of people before heading into the woods. You know, so no one would see me going in—it can look strange to people. So I sat on a big rock to wait for the path to clear.     A man jogging passed by, and before I could go, I saw two ladies coming. So I waited for them to pass as well. When they reached me, they started talking. They were mother and daughter—the first spoke French much better than I speak Polish, and the second was fluent in English. They invited me to their home, which was in the center of the next town, about 7 or 8 kilometers further.    I wasn’t sure at first because I was kind of afraid they were inviting me out of fear for me sleeping outside. In that case, I would prefer to reassure them that it’s totally okay and safe for me to sleep outside, even in the cold. But they insisted. They were happy to invite me, having been pilgrims themselves on the Jacobs Way a few times. Well, they went on their way, wanting to finish their walk before heading back home in their car. As for me, I followed the path to their house, having checked their address on the map.     Wonderful evening. The family of four—though one son isn’t here—tends to have an Italian-style communicative hubbub. Noisy talk, very enthusiastic, with lots of teasing and joking. A really nice evening full of laughter but also full of questions, answered very thoroughly by the dad, who is a history teacher and, like all history teachers, passionate. I don’t know about you, but for me, all the history teachers I’ve met are always the most passionate ones...     I’m writing this in the bed of the room they told me I could occupy for several nights if I want to rest. I don’t know yet if I will, but it’s tempting, as the family is really cool and their invitation feels genuine. It’s 10:30 p.m., and since I usually sleep around 6 p.m. when I’m in my tent—and considering I had a nice long walk today—it won’t take long for me to fall asleep. And I’ll sleep well.     Finally, I decided to stay today. I’d like to go see the church I passed yesterday—a magnificent building of the Teutonic Order. And then, a little rest can’t hurt, especially after a good hot shower!     It’s Sunday morning. My hosts are obviously more of the evening than the morning type. These days, I’m more of a morning person—as you know, if I sleep at 6 p.m., it’s natural... Although I went to bed late last night. But it’s good—I’m writing. So I wait until I hear movement. I’m in a room next to the kitchen and dining room, so I’ll know as soon as someone comes.    It’ll be Małgorzata (Margareth) who moves first. After a small breakfast, she’ll take me to the church, and after that, we’ll visit the center of town a bit. We’ll go back home for lunch, which will be as lively as yesterday’s dinner—full of talking, laughter, and kind teasing of each other. Then, Darius will propose giving me a historical tour of the town. That would be great indeed. And his wife will tell me about another plan: going to a very special place, a pilgrimage site dedicated to Mary, to see the Tsigane Virgin Mary, about 50 km from here. Super great!     And so the entire afternoon was about running around with Dareck (almost literally running). He was so enthusiastic and eager to show and explain everything that the tour turned into a race, with me trotting behind him each time, straining my ears to catch the translations of his explanations via Google Translate.     But this was obviously Dareck’s first time using the translator, and it’s hard to be enthusiastic, thorough, and rushed all while managing the app. Add to that the noise of the streets and the fact that we were constantly darting right and left, and the visit quickly became an exhausting exercise. Super interesting, but I came home on my knees, as we say in France, having listened to—and eventually only heard—far more information than my brain could process in such a short time.   I, who have become accustomed through my pilgrimage to calm, serenity, and silence, all approached gently and slowly, experienced the visit as an overwhelming task. One should restrain themselves to smaller visits; more can be counterproductive.     After the afternoon snack, the three of us—since the children (grown-up but you understand) weren’t joining—went to visit the place of the Tsigane Virgin. That was so cool because I had really been thinking of going there when I first heard about it in the morning. So all was well.     When we got back home, Margaret’s French teacher was there, as well as a family friend’s son, who is a journalist. We spent two hours talking, and then we had dinner. The conversation continued late into the night. Having a history teacher available to answer questions was very valuable to me because I must say Polish history is very complex and complicated—and until recently, it was completely unknown to me. And since Dareck was so eager to inform me, using a lot of charts and explanations, I took the opportunity to ask all my questions.     I must admit, though, that of all our discussions, the one we had on Monday morning was the most beneficial to me.     I got up at the same time as Margaret to say goodbye to her before she left for work. My night was short (as I had talked with Dareck until late), but I wanted to see her off. She was the first person I met from this family, and it was she who invited me. I also wanted to thank her for the warm welcome. And so, in the morning, after she left, Dareck came back—he was on holiday—and we talked again. This time it was quieter, just the two of us. As he was getting much more comfortable with the translator, the conversation went much better.     Finally, I left around 11 a.m.! To be honest, I walked only a little that day, found a nice spot for my tent, and stayed there the next day to recover! And also to write. But I admit, I slept most of the day.     You see now how beautiful my experience of the pilgrimage is. This is just the past 15 days. And it has been like this from the very beginning. I mean, you might think that Polish people are very kind, generous, and lovely—and they are—but it was the same in France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, Lithuania, and Latvia. And I’m only talking about external experiences here.    You will excuse me if I keep my intimate experiences to myself for now, so I can fully benefit from their depth without diluting their essence. Maybe I will share them later, when I’ve assimilated them.   But in the meantime, just the external experiences—adventures, encounters—that alone is already magnificent, surprising, surreal, almost marvelous and extraordinary. Really.     Do you see it?      I hope so.    If not, here’s one last example before you go: This morning, as I was leaving the magnificent medieval town of Toruń, I stopped for a small rest on an urban works signaling element at the end of the bridge over the river. A team of construction workers was there, working on the bridge. After a few moments, we started talking. Eventually, a cyclist stopped, and that was fortunate because he spoke English and could translate for everyone. Then one of the construction workers, Maciek, asked me if I needed anything. But I didn’t, as I was just coming out of the city, my backpack full of food and water. Since Toruń is a big city, I had also stocked up on new equipment (a sleeping mat and other camping gear). So, all was fine. I told him this three times because he kept asking. And then he offered me money for my way. I refused. I refused because I have enough for now, and it’s very hard for me to accept money.     Many times, people I meet help me with a night inside, a hot shower, a meal, or some food from their garden or elsewhere. That I accept easily and gladly. But accepting money feels different to me—it’s harder to take.     Yet he insisted, and his gesture was kind, sincere, and simple. He really wanted to participate and help me. I refused three times. But then, I saw him folding a 100 Zlotys note, and as I tried to stop him, he pushed my hand away, placed the money in the pocket of my vest, and locked it there by zipping it shut. I thought it wouldn’t be right to refuse his generosity. I was touched by his kindness, by his gesture toward me and my pilgrimage. I was just sitting there. And this happened.     I finally went on my way, with the cyclist riding alongside me for a while to show me the right direction. After a nice walk, I found a beautiful spot next to the river. I took pictures and recorded a small video there to show you.     In the evening, I reached into my pocket and took out the money. It wasn’t a single 100 Zlotys note. It was 18 notes of one hundred.     It nearly made me cry...     I thought, “This is crazy. Maybe I should go back and return it—it must be a mistake.”     But no, it wasn’t.      We exchanged messages by phone, and it was a kind gift for my way.    This evening, I spent a long time sitting at the foot of a big tree under which my tent was pitched, watching the river flow by, thinking that somehow, I am cared for so well and so warmly that I can’t be wrong in my way. Hopefully.     Voilà. That’s it for today.     It takes a lot of time and a lot of battery to write this on the phone.     I hope you enjoyed it.

Gietrzwald and Olsztyn


		2/1/2022
	
     I am walking, walking, walking, and somehow, now we are in winter. Of course, I had a few hints and clues—everything is white. Everything is frozen. Literally, outside or inside (which, to be honest, are very blurry concepts anyway). My food has turned into ice-cream: fruit ice-cream, tomato ice-cream, cheese ice-cream, hummus ice-cream—you get the idea. I can’t even cut a piece of butter; it’s too hard. So I eat frozen bread with frozen camembert (when I can find some)...     Ah yes, I’m back to sleeping with my bottle of water inside the sleeping bag. It’s the only way to have something drinkable by morning. Not much room in there, but that’s okay—she’s not a bad bed companion, except when the cork leaks. (And it’s absolutely necessary to avoid rolling onto it during the night... Otherwise, it’s fine.)    But you know what? It’s beautiful. Really beautiful. It’s so cold that the snow stays perfectly white, even after cars drive over it. Sounds are muffled, and the contrasts are sharper, making it much easier to spot wildlife. I see animals from far away or very close when they’re trying to hide. They stay completely still, totally immobile but highly alert, thinking they’re invisible, just waiting for me to pass. But on the white snow, I can see them clearly. I enjoy that a lot.     Oh, and my backpack feels lighter because I’m wearing almost all my clothes. I know it’s just a trick—after all, I’m still carrying the same weight—but I guess it’s a psychological thing. My backpack doesn’t feel so heavy!    Temperatures have dropped to minus 16°C at night, and now it’s even that cold during the day. I guess we’ll soon hit minus 20°C at night.     I’ll send photos this time, as I’ve managed to take and keep some. Unfortunately, the ones from my last message seem to be lost—or maybe they’re just hiding too well in my phone...     Today is the New Year, I’ve been told. That explains all the fireworks last night that woke me up in my tent in the small woods where I was camping. Well, to be honest, I knew it was coming—first, because it happens roughly every year at the same time! And secondly, someone reminded me of it a few days ago.    I chose to spend the night in the woods because I didn’t feel like being in the town that was the next stop on my journey. I wasn’t inclined toward big noises, excitement, or anything else that comes with New Year’s celebrations in town. I guess I’ve become more interested in quietness and silence. That’s the effect of spending all day in peace and sleeping in forests!    It’s strange, though. Even when I’m invited to stay indoors nowadays (which happens often), I find myself missing the cold. My hosts, out of kindness and worry—or maybe trying to compensate for the nights I’ve spent outside at minus 15°C—always propose to turn up the heating in the room I’m sleeping in, to make it cozy and warm. But I can’t. These days, I sleep best in the cold. Just being inside is enough—no heating required!    Now that you have a sense of the atmosphere of these days, I have to tell you about my journey. Since the last time I wrote, I’ve crossed the border and arrived in Poland. Thanks to the help of a Polish friend—whom I’ve officially declared my topographic planner-in-chief—I’ve joined one of the Jacobs Ways. (For my Indian or Nepalese friends who might not know, Jacobs Ways are part of a network of pilgrimage routes across Europe that lead to Santiago de Compostela in Spain.)    Following these routes is great for many reasons. First, they are usually very well signposted, making navigation easier. Second, they are designed to avoid big roads as much as possible. And third, they are planned by locals to guide you through beautiful places—old villages, historical sites, or cultural gems you might otherwise miss if you don’t know the area or can’t speak the language. (Speaking of which, did I mention that Polish is a nightmare to pronounce? I think I’ve sprained my tongue!)    And here’s the best part: the Camino I’m currently following passes through three places I really wanted to visit.    Święta Lipka, a very famous Baroque-style basilica dedicated to Mary, is located in a rather small village. It has a huge organ, and I tried to record it with my phone. Unfortunately, the phone isn’t the best tool for live recordings, and I’m afraid the result doesn’t do justice to the incredible concert I was lucky enough to stumble upon the day I arrived. Still, you can listen and let me know what you think.    Then there was Gietrzwałd. I have to say, it’s an incredibly beautiful place. I enjoyed my time there immensely.     Initially, I had planned to arrive in Gietrzwałd on Christmas Eve, but that morning, as I woke up in the forest just outside the town, I felt so comfortable, so at peace with the place where I had spent the night, that the idea of entering the town during the hustle and excitement of Christmas Eve made me a little anxious. So, I decided to stay in the woods for another day and night and only arrived in Gietrzwałd on the 25th. It was a wonderful decision. Honestly, if you ever take a walk and don’t know where to go, head there—it’s such a special place to be!     Now, I’m on my way to Licheń, about 350 km ahead. Licheń isn’t on the Jacobs Way, but I just have to leave the path at one point, and it’s only 40 km south.     One of the best parts of this journey has been crossing through beautiful old villages and towns. On the way, I’ve also encountered castles.   One castle I passed was open for visits, and it even had a restaurant inside—double jackpot! When I arrived at the restaurant, I met some very kind people visiting Poland with their Canadian friends. It was a lovely encounter, but by now, I guess you know that all the encounters I’ve had have been wonderful—always, everywhere. It’s crazy how true that is.    They invited me to share their table for lunch and were very curious about my walk. After lunch, we explored the castle together. At first, I was thrilled—walking inside a castle is like living a childhood dream, and I loved it. But then, I was disturbed by what I saw on display. I had expected swords, crossbows, armor, and chain mail—things that stir the imagination of an adventurer. Instead, 90% of the exhibition consisted of torture instruments and machines from the Middle Ages, used by the Inquisition and other authorities of the time.    It was overwhelming, even sickening, to see such an extensive collection. The sheer variety, complexity, and elaborateness of these devices left me feeling deeply unsettled. The contrast between the cruelty on display and the peaceful, meaningful journey I’ve been on for the past 15 months created a dissonance I found hard to bear.    Thankfully, shortly after that, I was warmly welcomed by a community of religious sisters. Their kindness and hospitality quickly helped erase the heavy feeling, restoring my sense of peace.    And then, sometime later, I arrived in the town with the castle where Copernicus lived for many years! That was a much nicer visit!   Yes, I am a pilgrim, not a tourist. I don’t go out of my way to visit many places, but when something is directly on my path, of course, I let the child in me enjoy it. What could be better than a drawbridge, a dungeon, a crenellated guardrail, a trebuchet, a mangonel, a ballista, or a catapult?    Voila. This whole journey feels like a dream I am living. Truly, it seems like my feet barely touch the ground these days. Maybe that’s why my backpack feels so heavy! Did I tell you I gave it a name? "Expiation"—I find it very fitting while making a Christian pilgrimage.    Even when something bad happens, I am so lucky that it often turns into something good. Let me give you another example because I’m not sure it’s easy to imagine how much, how often, and in what ways things just seem to work out.    One day, I was invited by a religious sister I met as I was leaving the church next to her congregation house. She welcomed me to stay the night, which meant I had a bed, but most importantly—a bathtub. A hot bath. I hadn’t taken a full hot bath in over three years! (I see you raising an eyebrow: yes, three years without a bath, but I take showers... sometimes.) But a bath! You know what I mean—being fully submerged in steaming hot water, getting clean, sure, but more than that, truly relaxing... until, of course, the phone rings or someone knocks on the door, because that’s a universal truth of bathtubs!    At the time, I was expecting a parcel from my friends in France for my birthday. I asked the sister to call my next destination to see if they could receive the parcel and hold it for me until I arrived. Unfortunately, it wasn’t possible. I wasn’t too worried because, these days, solutions always seem to appear.    And, sure enough, the next morning, Sister Alina (yes, I think it’s fine to share her name) came to me with a solution. Someone who overheard her story about the failed parcel plan, without knowing me at all, without ever having met me, offered to have the parcel sent to his home. Not only that, but he and his wife promised to bring it to me by car, wherever I might be!    I explained to him that I didn’t know exactly where I would be when the parcel arrived and that I was afraid I might be far away by then. But he simply said, “No problem, I’ll drive to you.” And that’s exactly what happened! Ten days later, he received the parcel, contacted me for my location, and after finishing his workday, he and his wife drove two hours to meet me. They handed over the package, chatted with me for a while, and then drove back home. Just like that.    And here’s the kicker: that very night, after I received the parcel—which included replacement parts for my tent—the temperature dropped so much that the aluminum structure of my tent froze and snapped. Like... well, like frozen aluminum. (A very apt analogy, wouldn’t you agree?) But because I had just received the new parts, I was able to repair the tent immediately.    This morning, another aluminum pole snapped... But it’s just that I walked exactly where I shouldn’t have. There are mornings like this. But hey, you know what? I arrived in a village just after that and got invited to stay for the night, even though it was still morning. So after spending a few hours talking, washing myself, and doing my laundry, I managed to repair my tent, so tomorrow will be fine! Great, no?    I used the extra time to write you this message. The phone’s flashlight beam projected between the flysheet and the inner tent, while my right hand pulled on the tent canvas to widen the gap between the two, clearing my view of the otherwise cramped space where she was putting on her show.    We were 12 inches apart—snout to snout.    Now visibly frustrated, she managed to sink her teeth into the canvas. When her grip was firm, she gave a sharp little jerk, pulling with her whole body and stepping back in short, jerky movements...    There, I really stopped agreeing with the situation. As cute as she was (I mean, you should have seen her jerking back—it was adorable!).    "But would you stop, you little evil," I said, remembering that the tone was more important than the words themselves.    We had to find an arrangement quickly, or it was going to be a very long night. An idea—almost a plan—came to me and seemed relevant: if she was no longer hungry, she would leave me alone. To sum it up.    So I opened the magic box, took out my knife, and opted for a piece of Brie. A good piece of Brie stuck at the end of the knife.    She sniffed, then very quickly grabbed the piece, took a few steps back (it’s super cute when they go backwards!), landed on her hind legs, chest upright, holding the piece of cheese with her front paws. She began tearing off small pieces, chewing them carefully before swallowing.    You might say I’m repeating myself, but God, this little beast was cute when eating something other than my tent! I could have watched her like that for hours.    She devoured the first piece very quickly, the second too, and the third more slowly. I never got bored. In addition to the hope of having satiated her so she would leave me alone, watching her eat the Brie—me being from Normandy—I felt a kind of connection, a kind of sympathy. After all, we shared certain tastes. It wasn’t all totally hopeless between us...    And finally, she left.    I was a little disappointed, all the same. I am sure of the potential for fraternization. After all, these animals have been tamed for a long time, either as pets or as burrow-hunting animals...    But she was gone. And I could relax, go back to sleep.    But she came back.    And by the time she woke me up for the second time, she had already made a hole 7 cm long by 4 cm wide.    That’s when I went for contact—but more firmly this time. No caresses.    With my phone light in one hand, I watched her closely. Each time she was about to bite the canvas, I hit her on the muzzle from the other side.    At first, just gentle taps, accompanied by reprimands with no real conviction—I mean, I was still under her charm and couldn’t bring myself to hit or scold her in anger.    But I have to admit, my patience was slowly running out.    I was really impressed by her determination—and her insolence too! After all, wasn’t she aware that she was in the presence of the worst mammal in the galaxy? Seriously? The representative of the supreme masters of all other forms of life on Earth, because intelligent, industrious, and artistic (and egocentric too...)?    She took a dozen taps on the muzzle. The last one was no longer a joke—it was a slap. A good one. And the beast fled. Phew!    Sad that it had to come to this—for a piece of Norman cheese! But now, my tent had two big torn holes and several smaller bite marks...   I was exhausted and needed sleep, but I couldn’t fall back asleep right away. The night was dragging on. And just as I was finally dozing off again, guess what—of course, she came back a third time.    Around two in the morning, another wake-up, another hole.    At that point, I began to doubt my victory over the little monster. The separation had to happen—now. A divorce, before she took the whole tent apart. But how to do that without resorting to brutality? I couldn’t go beyond the slap; it had already made my heart ache.  I really wondered how to get out of this relational impasse without ending in a brutal heartbreak...   That’s when I remembered the little pepper spray given to me by a Ukrainian security guard in Germany. He had handed it to me, saying it was for wildlife and possibly humans (apparently, sprays specifically for wildlife are stronger but forbidden for use on humans). He had insisted on telling me that there were a lot of junkies around.    Well, personally, in the middle of the woods, I had very rarely encountered junkie attacks. (The junkie is, after all, an urban animal.) But we all have our fears, I suppose. Mine? Slobbering wet kisses attacks...    In short, I looked for the small spray and, despite the probable discomfort of using it in a closed—or almost closed—space, I threatened my assailant with it.    And at that moment, I also decided that for being so persistent, she had to be a he.    Yes, I know—big discriminatory clichés, totally against any concept of gender equality.    But hey, it was the feeling of the moment, at three in the morning, on a restless night.   The first pchitt was almost nonexistent and therefore totally ineffective. I was reluctant... But when he started working on his fourth hole, he got a proper pchitt on the muzzle. A little one. Half a second. Maybe even less.    I didn’t even see him leave—it was so fast.    But it had worked.    And now I was there, and he was gone. I was relieved but disappointed. Disappointed and a little sad...   Fortunately, I had the opportunity to take some air for a good hour, to clear my head and properly ventilate the tent!   I hope the critter hasn’t had any problems because of this. I don’t think so. I am a little disappointed, not really surprised—except by his cheek, his daring, his determination...    But honestly, I remain under his spell. I assure you, these little furballs are so cute. Really...    And now, I won’t advise you to go on the internet to check whether mustelids might be a key link in triggering an unprecedented historical event—a panzootic (animal-to-human pandemic). According to Wikipedia in 2020, “mink farms are the animal farms that have been most affected by the SARS-CoV-2 virus responsible for COVID-19. If this virus were to spread among wild mustelids, the latter could become a permanent reservoir of infection for other animal species, as was the case with rabies transmitted to raccoons and skunks, or with bovine tuberculosis transmitted to badgers, or with paratuberculosis, transmissible to many wild ruminants and sometimes to immunosuppressed humans.”    But hey, without going as far as "Haaa, my God, it’s awful, we’re all going to die," it’s true that mustelids become less cute when you read that.    I guess.   On my side, I loved the encounter. Even if I now have three big holes in my tent (though compared to the gaping hole at the entrance where the zipper is completely out of use, the three side holes feel conceptually negligible).    And he looked in great shape—fully healthy, the little devil!

The Windmill and Hill of Crosses


		28/9/2021
	
    I walk and come across many places, people, magnificent trees—majestic ones even—and buildings... Walking gives you time to see, to approach slowly. It gives time for curiosity to form, for interest to be born.    For example, this windmill. From afar, it seemed strange, then obvious. I couldn’t resist and went to knock on the door of the house next to it to ask if I could go see it, photograph it for you, and maybe step inside. Whaaaa! I felt like I was stepping into a mechanical wooden watch. Five levels of pulleys, toothed wheels, giant gears, and belts. And of course, stone grindstones.    Although it was still operational about ten years ago, the mill no longer works. It was built in 1904 and is now too expensive to repair or even restore.    What a pity. What a marvel of engineering as well as carpentry. I’m attaching photos that, as often, only partially do it justice...     I walk even slower than before. I no longer have any concerns about distance—only direction, because I’m always heading somewhere—but I don’t care when I get there. I walk... Look... Rest... Walk again...    The weather is getting much cooler. In just a few days, we’ve gone from 20 to 28 degrees Celsius during the day to between 9 and 14. I imagine winter is coming soon...   The day before yesterday, I arrived in the small village of Krincinas. It was the birthday celebration of a local priest/poet, after whom the school is named. It was the director of this school—also the director of three others (budget cuts to the Lithuanian national education department!)—who welcomed me so kindly. He showed me around his school, asked the maintenance technician to turn on the hot water circuit so I could take a shower in the gym locker rooms, and then accompanied me on a short walk through the village park to show me a sulphurous water spring there.     We parted ways after spending a few hours together, including time with the students, who I could sense really liked their school. It’s nice to see...     After spending the night in a grove at the edge of a small unpaved road (very little noise from the occasional passing cars), I resumed my journey. Along the way, I passed by a place with about fifteen large crosses. I, of course, stopped to rest for a bit, sit on a bench, close my eyes, and meditate. I didn’t take any pictures, so you won’t see the place. Maybe I should have, because fifteen crucifixes aren’t planted for no reason.     What I’m going to share now is probably well-known to most Europeans, but I don’t believe it’s familiar to many of my Indian, Nepalese, and other friends...     This place was a commemoration site for an event as significant as something from the lives of Mahatma Gandhi or Nelson Mandela.    On August 23, 1989, at 7 p.m., two million people (fewer, according to the "prefecture," of course, and much more, according to participants—obviously!) joined hands to form a 700-kilometer-long human chain. It was non-violent, fraternal, and stretched across the three Baltic countries—the three sisters (Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia)—connecting their capitals (Vilnius, Riga, Tallinn).    The date was chosen to mark the anniversary of the secret Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, where the Soviets and Nazis had agreed on the partition of Europe, leading to the annexation of the three countries by the Soviet Union. This human chain was an act of resistance, a revolt, or at least activism, against the occupation.    These kinds of actions move me deeply. Truly. Tyranny undermined by benevolent brotherhood, without violence. The undeniable power of non-violent collective refusal...    You can find plenty of information on the internet about what’s called “The Baltic Way,” which is now classified by UNESCO in the Register of the Memory of the World.     I should have taken a photo...    And then I arrived in the small town of Pasvalys for the town's annual party. Am I not really lucky! Small city. A very warm little party. I arrived just in time to listen to a woman singing, and I’m attaching the audio file to this message. I found it very pretty. Sad but pretty. Obviously, I don’t understand a word of the song, but the whole performance seems to me like a lament or an observation of the difficulties of life. Of course, this is just my personal interpretation, based on the emotion and the timbre of a voice in a language unknown to me. I sat and watched her sing, accompanied by her friend on guitar.     And then I walked around the fair. Friendly. Truly. Simple and friendly...    A painter approached me to ask me what, why, when, and finally where I was sleeping. He told me to come and see him if the priest couldn’t accommodate me. When I came back from the very beautiful church, empty-handed, he was a little drunk—not clumsy drunk, but drunk enough to shout over the general hubbub, which you can imagine. He called out to someone, who shouted to another, who shouted to yet another person, until finally, the last man came and invited me to his hotel. Graciously. Any room is comfortable at this price! And then—a hot shower, phone charging...     I went to meditate a bit, and then to have dinner. When it came time to pay, the person behind me in the queue walked ahead and offered to pay for my meal! He heard that I was a pilgrim and wanted to participate in my adventure.     I am in the dreamlike sweetness of my journey. Wait—it’s not over!    The next morning, I went to church again. The priest, who now knew a little better who this backpack-wearing wanderer with a stick was, came toward me, shook my hand energetically, and gave me a big smile. He thanked me and left. In my hand was 100 euros. I was puzzled—he didn’t even give me time to respond.    I left the church and went to eat before continuing my way. At the restaurant in the square, I ordered and waited, looking at the topographic map on my phone, which I had plugged into an outlet nearby. The restaurant owner came to talk with me, holding a bottle of cognac and two small glasses. He was an interesting man—passionate, a hot air ballooning champion, and a former resistance fighter. I enjoyed our conversation—and the cognac!    When I picked up my bag to leave, the waitress told me I didn’t have to pay. The bill was covered by the house.    Do you understand why I doubt my reality? Why I am so moved by my experience with others? With strangers?    Finally, just before saying goodbye, I wanted to tell you that yesterday I passed through the Hill of Crosses. It is also a place of resistance—religious resistance, in a way. This hill is covered with more than 250,000 crucifixes. Crucifixes planted, heaped, hanging from others, clustered together... Destroyed by the Soviets, rebuilt, destroyed again, and rebuilt once more.    The place is intense. Seriously. I was worried it might feel spooky or creepy, but instead, I had one of my deepest meditations there. If you ever pass by on your journey, don’t hesitate to stop. Even if only out of curiosity.    Voilà. It’s time for me to go.    I am 50 km from Šiluva, my next and fourth destination...    Lots of good things for you.    Goodbye...

Ask Bilbo!


		23/8/2021
	
     ​I know, it hasn’t been that long since I gave you my latest news. But I have to share what seems so important to me in my journey. I know I am redundant, and yet each time again, I am touched and moved by this kindness that welcomes me.     I must begin by telling you that the last days since I left Aglona have been wonderful. I have been alone and in silence since resuming my walk. The intermittent rain refreshes pleasantly this end of summer. However, it is not too important to hinder my progress. When the rain is really too strong, I stop, put up the tent and take refuge there, but it’s not that often. A few days ago though, I got a downpour that was Hollywood chewing gum level event, if you remember the nineties advertisement. It was so huge, so tropical shower level that it becomes fun in itself. You no longer have to worry about getting wet, it’s so impossible not to that it’s no longer a problem.    So it’s true that the atmosphere is really humid, but the good in that is that it attracts mushrooms which end up throwing themselves at my feet begging me to pick them up (yes like this). That’s awesome! I eat raw Boletus Edulis, because they are so fresh that there is no need to cook them. Which is good because I have nothing to cook anymore from a long time now. Yesterday I found the flesh of a big champagne cork shape one really sweet. It surprised me. Crunchy and sweet. Happiness...    And then I also collect Chanterelles. I keep them in a bag and try to dry them a bit as much and as often as possible. I always end up being invited by someone to cook them...     And then I arrived in this village where a grocery store was at the entrance. It was good because I needed to fill my backpack with food again. I did my shopping there, paid for everything, and the lady in charge of the grocery store asked me where I was coming from and what I was doing. She then offered to charge my phone if I needed, and we chatted.     It’s crazy how what I do—walking like this, a long pilgrimage, a long-lasting spiritual discipline—can inspire or make sense to the people I meet. It is even disturbing. My approach, however very particular, very surprising, very unusual, very incongruous even, turns out to be full of meaning also for those I meet... Full of meaning and nourishing too. Strange, isn’t it? There is even a kind of envy that I feel, a craving. As if I were realizing in this journey what many would like to, what many are starving for... I guess that’s why having the rule to take the time to share with whoever is interested is important.     After a while, she kindly offered me a coffee, which I gratefully accepted, because coffee is good! Especially when it’s offered like this. Of course, the coffee was served with many biscuits, chocolate, and white cheese bars sweetened and coated with chocolate or caramel (it’s pasty, somewhere between hard cream and fresh cheese, and sweet. I like it...).   We chatted using Google Translate until a client, an English teacher at the village college, arrived. So we chatted in English. Nice exchange.     Of the few new customers who passed by during my break at the grocery store, a dozen I would say, I had a friendly exchange with ten. More than half spoke with me or with the grocer, who told them about what we had already discussed. Four of them offered me their phone numbers in case I needed anything or help on my way.     Before going to sleep near the village lake, the grocer gave me a bag of tomatoes and cucumbers (the Baltic countries seem to have an impressive addiction to cucumbers... Small cucumbers, like big pickles... Over the past month, there hasn’t been a single day I’ve spent without cucumbers...).     I spent four hours in her shop, chatting with her while she worked or with her customers. It was really relaxed, and I managed to recharge my phone and power banks. Great! I gave her the bag of Boletus edulis mushrooms and chanterelles that I had picked that morning. It felt completely natural to give them to her. Then we said goodbye.     The evening was good! A swim in the lake, washing myself and my clothes. A beautiful night without rain (which is nice because the sound of rain on the tent canvas can be really loud!). And this morning, I resumed my journey.     In the afternoon, I arrived at a small country road—unpaved, with no tarmac—where I noticed someone walking about 100 meters ahead of me. It was a lady. Elderly. Old, but still walking briskly (87 years old! Respect!). It took me nearly a kilometer to catch up and walk alongside her. I could immediately tell she was a character—a nice one.    When she heard someone approaching behind her (I had deliberately rubbed my foot on the ground to make a little noise, so as not to startle her), she turned around with a warm smile, not a trace of fear or surprise. That alone says a lot.     We introduced ourselves and decided to walk together to her house, half a kilometer away. We had not gone 50 meters before I inherited one of the bags of tomatoes from her garden, which she carried in each hand.    Arriving in front of her house, I was invited in for a coffee. I gladly accepted! A good cup of coffee never hurts! (French proverb—or if not, it should become one soon...).    Watch the little movie I made—sorry, it’s in French; I didn’t think about it at the time. But aside from showing the beautiful place where she and her husband live, you can see her smile, her enthusiasm, her kindness. Notice the touching gesture of the small tablecloth she placed on the table for me, to hold the cup of coffee, along with a few slices of cheese on a plate, homemade donuts, and the white cheese treats I mentioned before.     Then I met her husband, as kind as she was.    I was invited to stay the night.    I was invited to use the sauna and shower.   I was invited to visit the property—a superb estate that belonged to her grandparents. It included a house, a barn, a garage, a henhouse, a sauna, and toilets behind the barn. There was a magnificent vegetable garden with enormous raspberries and blackcurrants. By the way, the homemade blackcurrant jam I ate with evening porridge was delicious.    Even the grass was soft and comfortable to walk on barefoot—something I was invited to do almost immediately.    She told me that tomorrow morning, before I leave, we will eat the mushrooms she collected, with potatoes. How does she know it’s my favorite dish at the moment—fresh mushrooms and potatoes, seriously! Ask Bilbo!!!    And then, go look at the pictures—come on, watch that splendid breakfast! ??    Finally, her husband showed me his workshop and his neatly arranged wood; she showed me her sober and simple interior. He showed me the sauna; she showed me the henhouse...    I’m falling asleep as I write these words... The evening meal, the sauna, the comfortably firm sofa bed, the faint smell of wood fire coming from the burner...    Once again, these people touch me and move me with the warmth of their welcome, the smiles in their kind eyes, and the care they show me, even though I’m a total stranger, completely unknown to them.

Aglona


		17/8/2021
	
      Hello to everyone,      It’s time to move on.     The festival here in Aglona has ended.   It was huge, and even though far fewer people came this year, the entire event was still impressive. Security was tight, with police, the army, secret services, TV, radio, journalists, and everything else you'd expect from a festival important enough to draw the country’s president and many VIPs.     One of the most special parts was the choir singing every day for a week beforehand. Even if you’re not a fan of religious music, hearing those voices live, right in front of you, is deeply moving.    The last two days were crowded and busy, especially Sunday from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., but just two hours after it ended, the entire place was empty. All the cars and buses were gone, military tents dismantled, civil security tents packed away, cameras, sound systems, and lights all removed, food trucks vanished. Everything became quiet again.    I spent the next day organizing myself—saying goodbye to the priests who so kindly welcomed me, buying food for my journey, washing my clothes, and enjoying a hot shower in the monastery to be fresh and ready to leave in the morning.     Aglona, in Latvia, is a beautiful place. There’s a Basilica dedicated to Maria, set in the middle of a lovely park with a lake and a spring. The water from the spring is so good—really fresh, not cold, but refreshing and soft, with a great taste. I drink far more than I need every time I go to fill my bottle. It’s that nice. Of course, I’m not the only one. One of the priests, smiling, told me there are more people coming to fill their bottles at the spring than there are visiting the Maria icon! But since the spring is sacred and said to be miraculous, it’s all good.     The journey here was, as always, wonderful. I met kind people (including a truly sweet dog who welcomed me in such a heartwarming way. She barked, yapped, and moaned the way dogs do when they’re happy to see someone. It felt like I was her master returning after a long absence. She moved me deeply with her softness and gentleness, and we walked together for two hours before she returned home. Such a beautiful encounter).    I was also invited to stay for two days in a small town just after crossing the border. It was amazing to have warm, homemade meals prepared by my host, who said she wanted me to feel at home—and I did. She was such a lovely person, a former doctor in epidemiology for 16 years before working at customs. You can imagine how fascinating our conversations were!     This has been a truly wonderful time.     But you might get bored if I describe again how wonderful it is to walk through unknown places and feel so welcomed. So I think I’ll skip that part...    Instead, I’ll tell you about my plans for what’s next: I plan to wait until this evening to decide where I’ll go next.    Let me explain, because I get this question a lot. I always focus on my destination, and only my destination, until I finish my visit to that place I set out to reach. I stay dedicated to it, fully immersed in the experience. Then (and here’s a playful word twist—“end/and”), once the visit is over, I decide what’s next.    This approach gives me the freedom to wait until the last moment. Maybe someone will suggest a beautiful place nearby that I hadn’t considered. In that case, I can make it my next destination. If no one suggests anything, I have a few ideas in mind and choose one based on logic and my current location.    This creates a very satisfying sense of liberty. It feels like everything is open and possible, that I don’t even have to think about it until the last moment, and then it can be anything. It feels good. Simple. And once the choice is made, it becomes my goal. I don’t care how long it will take, or what the exact path will be. I just go. I put one foot in front of the other and repeat, repeat, repeat. Whatever I’m meant to see, I’ll see. Whoever I’m meant to meet, I’ll meet. Whatever challenges arise, I’ll face them. And here’s something I can assure you: I’m confident that everything will turn out fine.    Confidence is a delicious warmth, and my experiences over these past 11 months have given me that—a warm and fulfilling confidence that everything is and will be good.    Isn’t it beautiful to live this way, especially in these times? I wish I could share the feeling with you more fully, but words seem so weak compared to what I feel.    I wish you happiness and well-being.    Happiness is a duty—our first duty!    Sincerely,    Emmanuel    Post scriptum:    You know what? Last week, I found around 700 grams of chanterelles (Cantharellus cibarius or girolles in French). They were so tasty! We ate them together—four people who had invited me to share their meal by the lakeside. It was perfect because I had no way to cook them, and they had everything needed. They seemed to love mushrooms as much as I do, and they knew that the first chanterelles of the year are especially delicious.     But that’s not even the best news. Okay, let’s agree that’s great news. But the better news is this: just before I arrived in Aglona, I found a Boletus edulis. A small one, shaped like a champagne cork. I left it there because it was all alone, hoping it will grow into a big family. But do you see my point? It’s mid-August, and there are already Boletus edulis popping up—not even in the woods, but right in the middle of the path! If that’s not a sign of good things in life, I don’t know what is.    Post scriptum 2:   I’m now headed toward Šiluvos atlaidai in Lithuania, west-southwest from where I am. On the way—about 50 km from my destination—I plan to visit the Hill of Crosses, which has caught my interest.   I left Aglona after lunch today, walking until a heavy rain came down, forcing me to stop. I pitched my tent and tried to “dry” whatever I had on me. I’ll start again tomorrow!

Vilnius


		6/7/2021
	
     ​I know, I should have told you about Vilnius, my second destination. It's already been a week since I left the place...    I would have shared my arrival, and all the people I met on my way since my last update. So many nice people. Always. Only.     For example, I would have told you about this lovely elderly couple, Maceliai and Vingriu. I say "elderly," but honestly, they felt so young in spirit. He, for instance, had the energy and enthusiasm of a supercharged teenager, practically hopping as he spoke. Both of them had bright, keen eyes. It was such a nice meeting.    From the street, I asked them for water. He came straight to the gate, opened it, and invited me in—all smiles. And what a smile! You can see it in the photos—genuine happiness! They offered me tea, and soon fresh cheese appeared, pressed that very morning, along with honey (forest flowers), bread, and pickles.    We talked, though it wasn't easy since they didn’t speak a word of English, but were fluent in German and Russian. They were from that generation that doesn’t give a phone translator enough time to work—reading translations aloud as they appear, causing the phone to misunderstand and start translating again, erasing the previous text. After a few tries, we mostly gave up on the translation app, but we still managed to have a great conversation.     He showed me an ultralight plane he built himself—including the plans! Then he gave me a tour of his workshops: first the mechanical one, with a milling machine, lathe, and welding tools; then the woodshop, equipped with a router, planer, jointer, and bandsaw. Next came his greenhouse and his homemade sauna, heated with a wood stove. Everything at his home had his personal touch, including a visit to his beehives.     The man must be hyperactive, a genius, and incredibly skilled with his hands. Everything was simple yet impressive. He even offered me a shower in a small building in his garden, where the water tank was made from a repurposed Russian bomb shell that holds 3,000 liters, heated naturally by the sun. With the week’s temperatures at 35°C, you can imagine how welcome that shower was!     They were deeply connected to nature—everything organic and healing. He showed me a small wooden hut designed for naps. The "bed" was actually two beehives, with the roof made from two more. You’re surrounded by bees, enveloped in the soothing scents of wax, honey, pollen, propolis, and pinewood, while the buzzing sound of thousands of bees hums like a lullaby. You can even feel the subtle vibrations, as if the whole hut is purring. He even built a periscope so you can observe the activity inside the beehives while you drift off, counting bees instead of sheep! It's supposed to be healing.     I don’t know if it works, but I can say this: a nap there must be amazing, and I’d love to be as healthy as he is at 77 years old!     They also showed me a pagan ceremony they participate in—shamanic practices around a fire with songs and tambourines.      It was truly a beautiful encounter.     Or there’s Rasa—how I ended up in her garden is a story of its own. I had lost my track in the forest and, being too lazy to retrace my steps, I decided to just keep going, thinking, "There are no mistakes, after all—the path I take becomes my path." A bit of high philosophy that ultimately led to me crossing a river on a fallen tree trunk and battling my way up a steep riverbank through tall grass, nettles, and brambles. This adventure ended with me stumbling into the back of her property.     After asking for water, she offered me coffee, then lunch. Later, to make myself useful, I mowed her garden lawn with her mower, clearing it up nicely before we sat back down on her veranda to chat. I ended up staying the night, and since it poured rain the next day, she took me for a drive in her car to visit at least six beautiful spots I would have passed without noticing otherwise.     On the way back, we stopped at a wine shop where I managed to find some Côte du Rhône AOP, which paired perfectly with the “real cheese” you might remember from my previous update. That evening, we enjoyed the wine on her veranda while her neighbor joined us for a chat. It was a delightful French-Lithuanian evening.     Rasa and I stayed in touch, and we met again in Vilnius a week or so later. It turned out the countryside house where I met her was her holiday home. She normally lives in Vilnius, works in a bank, and is very connected—she even has one of those smartwatches that keeps her updated on everything happening on her phone. It’s impressive how efficient she is.     I’d also tell you about another couple who offered me dinner and a place to stay just a few days later, which turned out to be perfect timing because the weather forecast predicted a massive storm. And I mean massive—at one point, my phone, even in flight mode, emitted a warning buzz, displaying an alert directly from the government. That’s when you realize flight mode is just a software setting, not a physical switch!    Even though the alert was in Lithuanian, it was clear enough: bad weather was on the way. Camping in the forest during a storm isn’t exactly the safest idea—imagine what protection a tent offers against falling branches! So, staying in their beautiful garden was not only safer but also lovely. We spent the evening watching the lightning and talking, enjoying the storm from a safe and cozy vantage point.     So I finally arrived in Vilnius, and I could have told you about my first night camping near the Gate of Dawn, where a morning rainstorm turned into a river that flooded my tent, soaking everything—my belongings and me included. I could have told you how I spent four hours the next day drying everything out, especially my battery packs, which were literally dripping. I was lucky enough to find an air dryer and used it on low heat to avoid frying them. (The internet says it’s a terrible idea to let your battery packs get wet—it kills them, apparently, and should never happen. So, I guess I’m really lucky because all of mine survived! I would have been especially disappointed to lose the last one, a gift from someone on my way, with such excellent capacity and quality. This one might even be waterproof!)    I could have told you about Our Lady of the Gate, the Basilica, or the beautiful churches scattered throughout the town—or just about the town itself.    I could have also told you how I was invited to a convent near the Gate of Dawn, where I met some wonderful sisters and stayed for four days. They gave me the time and space I needed to take care of everything I had to do.     There are so many things I could have shared, and I guess I’ve mentioned a little of it now. But what I really want to tell you about is something I witnessed—something that left a strong impression on me.    One Saturday evening, I was coming back from a dinner I had prepared with Rasa at her place in Vilnius. It was a way to thank her for her warm hospitality and to enjoy a "French dinner" that we cooked together (though I really screwed it up). I also had the chance to meet her friends, which was another lovely experience.     So, it was quite late, around 11:30 p.m., and I was sitting on a tram in the suburbs of the capital, replaying in my head how the spinach tourte had gone so wrong, when I saw what I’m about to describe.    The tram had stopped, and more people were getting in than getting out. I was standing in the middle, with only a few seats still available—two of them right in front of me. A young guy, who had just boarded through the front door, spotted the seats and immediately picked up his pace, eager to claim them before anyone else. So far, it was a completely ordinary scene, the kind you see all the time. He was probably around 19 years old, chatting noisily but cheerfully with his friend, as young people often do on a Saturday night.    At first, I didn’t pay much attention and turned my gaze toward the rear of the tram, where the back door was letting in a few more passengers. And there, the same situation was unfolding. Two Afro-Lithuanian guys, dressed in the full rapper-style outfit—caps, T-shirts, gold chains, the whole look—had also spotted the same seats...    At that moment, it was obvious—I was about to witness a social tension event. You know, one of those moments you see coming. Both parties had that seat in mind, both sped up to claim it for themselves. They accelerated, and suddenly everything seemed to play out in slow motion. My head went from right to left, and back again, faster as they got closer, and then—bing! Of course, they reached the spot at the same time. Standing face to face, just a foot apart, one with his hand on the back of the seat, the other gripping the vertical bar in front of it.    This is the moment where you'd expect frustration to explode. You know the scenario: the closer someone gets to their goal, the higher the expectation; the higher the expectation, the worse the frustration when they’re deprived. Basic psychology! And obviously, one of them wasn’t going to sit. Someone was going to be frustrated!   It felt like such a pivotal moment to watch—something that could reveal so much about the social dynamics of the place... about human behavior. And, let’s be honest, maybe I’d learn a few colorful swear words in the process.    I projected my expectations, drawing parallels. Paris suburbs, Saturday night, young people on public transport... I braced myself for at least some incivility, if not outright violence. Verbal aggression seemed like the bare minimum I could expect.    But no.    They stood there, facing each other, realized the situation, and—together, at the same time—offered the seat to the other!    "You first!"    "No, you!"    "Please, it's okay, take it!"    "Are you sure?"    "Yes, yes, go ahead!"    And then, one of them sat down with his friend, while the other held out his fist for a friendly bump. You know the gesture: Hey, give me five! Yeah, bro!    They smiled. They were relaxed. They were human.   I was impressed. How can I describe it? I felt comfortable, confident, and at ease on public transport in the suburbs of the capital, late on a Saturday night, surrounded by a big group of young people, some of whom were lightly tipsy.     Now, you might not think this is a big deal. I mean, sure, you could argue that this should just be normal. But in my experience—at least mine—for far less than this, I’ve seen middle fingers raised and unsavory comments about people’s mothers thrown around.    It’s hard for me to tell if I’m just hypersensitive to this now. Spending ten months mostly alone, following a discipline where most of my time is spent in meditation, contemplation, prayer, or the recitation of mantras as part of my yoga practice—all of it aimed at what we often call spirituality—might have changed how I see the world.    I’m aware of this shift, but I can’t measure its extent. I know I’m not objective, but I don’t know how much I’ve changed. So many things I witness now seem surreal at first, but because they happen every day, they’ve become my new normal. Meanwhile, what’s conventionally considered "normal" often feels unbearably sad in comparison.    I’m not sure what’s more significant here: the scene itself or my perception of it. What’s certain is that my experience of pilgrimage—my Sadhana—has altered me.    One thing I know for sure: it makes me happy. It makes me feel good. It gives me a sense of reconciliation with humanity, a stark contrast to the pervasive fear mainstream media loves to sell. The message of the world is always “Be careful. Outside is dangerous.”    But my experience?    People are nice.    So be confident. Be trusting. Be grateful, be kind. And love… laugh… smile. Life is beautiful, in a beautiful world with beautiful people. Even if you sleep outside every day, cannot wash yourself every day, cannot wash your clothes every week, don’t have hot coffee in the morning, or cannot dry yourself when it’s raining… it’s still nice to live. (So imagine when you have a house, a car, a family around you, a hot shower, a coffee machine...).    Ok. I swear I didn’t drink. Or smoke. Or anything else…    Let me tell you another one!    Two days ago, as I was on my way to Aglona in Latvia (my next and third destination), I arrived in a small town and came across a cute church bordered by a small park with a little river running around it. A really beautiful place. I decided to stop for a while and splash myself in the river. So I went down the alley to get closer, and I saw a bank full of people sitting there.    No problem, I stopped about 20 meters away, dropped my backpack, and sat on it to take my shoes off. Before I could even do that, one of the three guys called out to me, waving a bottle of vodka and saying something that could have been “hey heu euuuu ah beee labbbeu heuuu”... though I can’t be entirely sure of the translation.   This is another good example of self-projection—where I, like many others, find myself assuming things. I thought, Ah, just a bunch of homeless, drunken guys squatting in the park. But I got over that quickly. I reminded myself that I, too, might look like someone who sleeps outside, doesn’t wash every day, and so on. You see what I mean…    So I said hello and accepted their offer to join them, figuring I could explain a bit about myself. They turned out to be really jovial, sympathetic, and friendly. I hadn’t even started introducing myself—my name or the fact that I was a pilgrim—when one of them handed me a shot of vodka.    Okay… I took it and began my explanation. Before I could finish—pretty quickly, I might add—I had to politely refuse the fourth shot.    It could have ended there: just some drunk people sharing drinks with a stranger who probably looked like one of them. But then, a woman passed by on the path, and they gave her the same warm welcome, offering her a drink as well.    I had serious doubts about this. I thought, This is a bad idea. There’s no way she’ll engage with them—she’ll just walk by with an air of disdain. But to my surprise, she stopped. She talked with them a bit and even found out that they were celebrating one of their birthdays. And then—they hugged.    No way. They must have known each other. Surely, I thought, they were longtime acquaintances.    But no. This same thing happened three more times while I stood there with them. Two more people joined and had a shot of vodka with them. Another woman even sat down with them for a while.    After splashing myself in the river (which they assured me was totally fine to do), one of the men offered to introduce me to the priest of the church. He knew where the priest lived, just a few hundred meters away, and thought maybe I could find accommodation there. He came with me, and that’s how I left this merry group of people—people I’m now ashamed to have initially judged as drunken homeless.    Okay, sure, they were drunk. And yes, they were drinking outside in a park. But the way they made me feel—like we were neighbors who had known each other for years—was humbling.    That’s it. Maybe it doesn’t seem like much to you. But for me, here, in my nearly ten months of walking now, I can assure you I’m taking these small, seemingly insignificant things as truly important—little everyday miracles. And even though I’m not particularly fond of vodka, I gladly drank with them from their glass. I was happy to answer whatever questions they asked, happy to share moments with total strangers I probably would have ignored in my “normal” life.    And when I left, I felt genuinely happy. A big smile on my face... (The vodka might have helped with that because, honestly, I’m really not used to it...).    Today, I was supposed to get moving since yesterday was already a day off! But it’s raining hard. Really hard. So I decided to stay in my tent again. I have enough water in my bottles, enough food, and enough battery to write a long message to give you an update!   And you know what? I just received a message from Rasa. She’s planning to take her car and meet me this weekend by a lake I’ll be passing on my way—just like that. Just to spend an afternoon on the shore with a guy she’s only met twice...    I hope you’re well and happy.    And I hope my update isn’t too long...    But I needed to say this, and I did...    See you...

Arrival in Lithuania


		10/6/2021
	
     ​So, how to say this... I’m a bit shy to share my arrival in Lithuania. I’m afraid you might think I’m exaggerating or embellishing things, or maybe that I ate the wrong mushroom, or even that I’m having some kind of psychological breakdown—I don’t know. But honestly, even I have difficulty believing I’m not dreaming all of this.      It’s been a week now since I arrived in Lithuania, and I have to say, the place I came through is stunning. The northern part of Poland was already breathtaking, with its national parks, wetlands, and all. But once I crossed the border, I’ve been in a kind of ecstasy.     The landscape is overwhelmingly beautiful: vast forests, crystal-clear lakes, and charming little rivers. Seriously, wait until you see the pictures—you’ll understand!     As the weather is clearly turning to summer, the walking can get sweaty.
