So far, I’ve been able to wash, swim, or splash myself every single day in places so idyllic you’d think they were taken from a summer vacation brochure or a postcard—no, better than postcards! The water is crystal clear and wonderfully refreshing, cool enough to take all the heat out of your body but not so cold as to leave you shivering.     The ground here is mainly sandy, whether on the roads or forest trails. Taking a swim, washing, or rinsing clothes (without soap, of course, to protect the environment—but with fine, soft sand that scrubs gently) has been such a pure pleasure that it fills me with joy. At least, it does for me. These stunning spots are everywhere, as lakes range from several kilometers wide to just a few hundred meters, and I come across one every 5 km at most.     You see?     Now, to complete the picture, imagine the air filled with the scent of pine resin, mixed with the intoxicating fragrances of the season. Every day, I pass dozens of blooming lilacs, carpets of lily of the valley with a scent so strong it’s almost overwhelming, and countless flowering trees, bushes, and meadows. Every open field between forests is covered in flowers!     You might think I’m being overly enthusiastic. But I grew up in the countryside; I know what flowered meadows are. And yet, I’m amazed by what I’m seeing here. Just wait until you see the pictures—really, the whole picture! No wonder the place where I entered Lithuania is a national park and a popular tourist destination for Russians, Belarusians, and Ukrainians.     And the wildlife! The mosquitoes are so in love with French cuisine—utterly enthusiastic about French gastronomy!     And the birds! My God, the birds! There are still swallows here, you know. And robins. And cuckoos. And... well, I’ll stop now. You get the idea.     Now, about the people!    You might think that no country can have it all—the beauty, the landscapes—and also have kind, welcoming people. That would be too much, wouldn’t it? Unfair! Unrealistic! But you’d be completely wrong. Totally wrong.     At first, even I didn’t believe it. After a few encounters, I thought, “This is too much—it can’t be real.” I half expected a hidden camera to pop out or something. But let me give you some examples...     The first village I crossed was a small one, just a few kilometers past the border. I was walking along the road/path out of the forest, taking in the charm of a new country, with a touristy air about me, my nose in the air, admiring the scenery. Most of the houses are made of wood. Many don’t even have fences, and if they do, they’re often beautifully crafted from wood.  The roads are mostly dirt, which means sand—brown sand, yellow sand, black sand... Comfortable for walking, let’s say, but dusty. Only a few are paved, and honestly, that’s nice because cars drive slower (though dustier, too—I just step aside and position myself with the wind to avoid being coated in it).     At a crossroads, a couple about my parents' age called out to me with enthusiastic gestures and started walking through their garden toward me. At that point, I honestly thought I was about to be told I was on a private path or trespassing. But when they reached me, I realized—almost strangely—that they just wanted to say hello, ask who I was, and what I was doing.     I had barely finished saying "Emmanuel" when the woman immediately invited me to come to the veranda for a coffee! Seriously? The whole thing felt surreal—pleasant, but a bit beyond reality in how fast and simply it all happened, completely out of the blue.   I ended up staying with them for maybe two hours, first over coffee, which turned into breakfast, and eventually lunch. But wait—the best part? For the first hour, we couldn’t even communicate properly! They didn’t speak any English or French, and my phone was painfully slow downloading the Lithuanian language set for Google Translate. So you can imagine how tenuous our conversations were. A cool arrival and a perfect first contact with the place. I left feeling happy, well-fed, caffeinated—and with a fully charged phone!     Before continuing, please check out the pictures of their place. I mean, come on—what a gorgeous spot! A wooden house flanked by two buildings: one a cute barn and the other a series of stables, chicken coops, and workshops you’d expect to find on a farm. In front of it all was a tiny, picturesque house, and behind, down their backyard, lay a lake. The view was just breathtaking. God... It was a beautiful arrival.     And then I went on my way again, with freshly repaired shoes and a big smile on my face. I walked around the lake for maybe two hours, though I was a little too far to actually see it—remember, the forest?     Suddenly, I heard someone running behind me and calling out. It was a man who had seen me on the road from his house and had run out after me just to chat! We tried to communicate as best as we could, at least enough to establish the basics: that I was a Frenchman who had arrived here on foot, and for him to tell me that it was great! They had come by bike, on foot, or by car from nearby villages or even farther away. A quick splash in the water, a short swim, a bit of friendly chatting—and then, before I knew it, evening came, and they were all gone.     When I arrived, I asked if it was a public spot, free to access, free of charge, and whether it was okay to camp and swim. Really, it felt so nice.     I set up my tent, swam for maybe an hour, washed all my clothes for another hour, hung my clean laundry on a string someone else had stretched between two trees, and then went into my tent and fell asleep like a baby in his loving mother’s arms.     What is wonderful about those places where you sleep is that they are still there in the morning when you wake up!     And the early mornings in those places are spectacular. The loud concert of birds, the soft and warm sunlight filtering through the trees and reflecting on the water, the gentle lapping of the water—it all rocks you and invites you to linger a bit longer in your half-awake dream.     I got up a little later than usual, feeling fully rested and completely relaxed, thinking that place and the last few days had been just perfect. I wished for more, craved more. And I wasn’t disappointed. In fact, it was so perfect that I even began to doubt my experience. I arrived at the church just before ten o’clock and went inside, only to discover it was packed and crowded. Mass was about to start in 20 minutes, so I decided to stay.     It was my first Lithuanian celebration, and I have to say, the priest was really special to me. He smiled a lot, joked with people, and moved from one person to another, seeming genuinely happy to say hello and exchange a few words with each and every one. Kornelija—that’s her name—was with her older sister and her mother. She was elegantly dressed in a beautiful summer dress, which she had chosen especially for church that day to please her mother.     I immediately thought of an old French song that goes: "Salade de fruits, jolie, jolie, tu plais a mere, tu plais a mon pere..." But that reference might not mean much to you if you’re not French...    She struck me as a dynamic, beautiful, slender, tall young woman of 28, who could easily be mistaken for 20 when she smiled or for 35 when she thought seriously. She had particularly beautiful, delicate, and slender hands. Her blue eyes sparkled with intelligence, playfulness, and a gentle, soft rebellion. Even though I sensed she could be stern or severe, her warm openness and enthusiasm made it nearly impossible to say anything but "yes" to whatever she asked.     We planned to meet 12 kilometers away, which she estimated would take me about four hours, at her grandmother’s old farm where I could stay, rest, and meet her family, including her brothers. And with that, she said, "See you later," and she was gone...     I went shopping and started my way, which, as she said, would be on the same path leading to her place. I thought of that meeting as another beautiful one.     About half an hour later, as I was leaving the village, a car stopped beside me. She popped out, hugged me, and asked if I wanted them to take my luggage in their car. I politely declined, explaining that I preferred to carry it myself—it’s part of my journey, my karma. She introduced me to her mother, who was driving, got back in the car, and left, waving enthusiastically as they drove off.     I stayed two nights in a beautiful place. The entire family is just incredibly lovely. They are all beautiful—not just physically, but their souls seem to shine a little through them. They have a brilliance about them. And I’m not just talking about Kornelija studying pure mathematics, or her youngest brother studying political science, or the fact that they are all fully fluent in English, Norwegian, and Russian. No, I’m talking about their shiny, smiling eyes that radiate kindness and intelligence.     You know me well enough to understand that I have very little experience with close family dynamics, so I might be easily surprised and impressed—and yes, I absolutely was! But it felt completely legitimate:     They talk to each other! It’s like they genuinely care about what the other says! They hold hands and close their eyes to pray before meals. They smile at each other and hug to say hello or goodbye. They ask their mother for blessings, which she gives by tracing a small cross on their foreheads with her thumb. They care for each other—it’s obvious.     This isn’t my world. I come from somewhere else entirely. But it’s a wonderful world, and they invited me into it so completely, so trustingly, so gently. It felt surreal. It couldn’t be real. And yet it was—for two magical days.     I met everyone I could. We ate flowers and raw food, bathed in the river, and talked for hours. Then we cooked over a wood fire before enjoying a sauna until midnight. A traditional sauna—jumping into the river behind the garden to cool off when it got too hot and sweaty. Later that night, Kornelija joined us on her bike after finishing whatever had kept her in town for so long.     We spent the evening and part of the night sitting around a fire, sharing stories and laughter after a lovely dinner.     In the morning, we bathed together in a nearby lake, went to see a farmer to get some "real cheese" for the French guy (me), and said our goodbyes.     Ignas stayed with me the whole day again so we could walk together to the next town and talk along the way.     Now, if I tell you that the town we’re in is one of the most beautiful and peaceful towns I’ve ever seen, would you believe me? Afterward, we met his cousin and went to a restaurant together, then took a long walk through the town park, talking the entire way. Finally, we returned to the flat, where I am now in bed, ready to sleep and writing this message.     Ignas went out for the evening. I wanted to go to bed early to start my journey early tomorrow. He had some plans to figure out for his next move and the coming weeks. So we said our goodbyes in case I leave tomorrow morning without seeing him again.     Before I leave, I need to switch off the flat’s utilities: turn off the main water tap, take out the trash, close the windows, lock the door, and put the key in the mailbox. Then I’ll go.     I’m alone in the flat of people I only met this past Sunday. And you know what? I already miss them...     Am I just that lucky? Or blessed? Or maybe both? But seriously, think about it: how many people do you know who would give their home for the night to a total stranger who doesn’t even speak their language?     I feel like I’m living in a dream. A beautiful dream. The only way it could get better would be if the mosquitoes became vegetarian!     And honestly, I’m starting to believe it could happen. Why not?

Hippie Family


		25/5/2021
	
​     Good morning!     I’m doing really well, still immersed in this beautiful experience. I’m living a rare and precious freedom, experiencing kindness, goodness, and benevolence in almost all the exchanges I have with others, which is deeply satisfying. I revel in the noisy silence of nature and the quiet stillness of solitude. I’m living a childhood dream of escape, reliving Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn.     The only possible downside is that, according to the universal law of impermanence, this will have to end at some point…      In the meantime, I’m enjoying it to the fullest!     Today I’m staying indoors, which is nice.     I’m with a “hippie family” in northern Poland. They’re incredibly welcoming—pure peace and love. The father is no longer here. There are four children, aged 21 to 2. The mother is a tour guide in the national park! As a result, she knows the flora and fauna exceptionally well.     She makes decoctions from dandelion petals, ointments from some roots I can’t name (a local plant along with Whichstings in Ball, Whichstinks in Flower, Whichstains of the Spring, and Noideawhat in Branches), healing balms, laxative jams, regenerative juices... She walks barefoot, doesn’t drink alcohol (we’re in Poland! Some told me there were locals who don’t, but most people insisted that was a modern myth. And yet, here they are—crazy, isn’t it?).     And she doesn’t smoke either. Hippies without drugs!     (Note: not all mushrooms are recognizable ???).     She also runs workshops on plant knowledge, glass painting, talisman and jewelry making…     Her house is an incredible mess—something between a provincial antique store, a grandfather's attic, and what you’d imagine a healer’s cabin deep in the woods might look like. There are plucked dreamcatchers and necklaces, small whitened vertebrae, horned or toothed skulls, rusty tools, and a big old nail... Antlers from deer, roe deer, and elk. Lanterns—lots of kerosene lanterns. Pots, bottles, and flasks—some not entirely empty, plump or thin, tinted and translucent, but rarely transparent due to deposits inside or outside. Carpets and cushions. Tables completely covered with no space for seats. A fish trap. Homemade candles scented with relaxing plant oils sit next to hypoallergenic, superfatted handmade soaps.     Jars of more or less dusty preserved things: a demijohn with raspberries discolored by alcohol, jars filled with who-knows-what floating in more or less liquid substances, mushrooms, shelled nuts, bouquets of dried nettles, and countless flowers—of what exactly, I couldn’t say.    The numerous shelves overflow as much as the tables and every other horizontal surface. The walls and beams are covered with all sorts of hanging items—likely suspended from nails she must have scavenged from the garden. There’s even a dangling teddy bear... or something resembling one.     When she first saw me—dragged along by an inebriated individual, Andreï, who insisted at the village grocery store that I absolutely had to come and see this place—she hugged me. I barely had time to feel self-conscious about not having used a bottle of water to wash myself beforehand. Without even asking who I was, she welcomed me in, immediately showing me where to leave my backpack and where I could sleep in one of the free dormitories. No concern for a key—it seems the place doesn’t have one.    "It's a blue house leaning against the hill. We don't knock; those who live here threw away the key long ago!" she said. (I couldn’t help but think of Maxime Le Forestier’s song San Francisco from 1974—exactly this vibe. But I guess you’d have to be an old French person to remember that big hit from the '70s.)     She pointed out a small high table, with a tray fixed to the wall next to a socket from which a kettle protruded, offering tea or coffee. She told me not to worry and that I could stay as long as I wanted, just like the all-smiling gentleman next to me, now chatting with Andreï. He had apparently arrived months ago during a bike ride and never left.     She then asked if I wanted to come with her to visit the neighbors. She was already super late (though this seemed rather normal based on her casual demeanor and what I later observed). I completely understood—my own sense of time is so blurred from walking for months that days and months feel surreal. She reassured me she’d make breakfast when we returned (yes, Andreï, it’s still morning!).     Note: At least he was only drinking beer—it could have been vodka!    There was no time to feel unsure of myself, no opportunity to feel embarrassed. Just pure, unfiltered welcome, as though I’d already been part of this place for three years. And so, I smiled.     In short, a few hundred years ago, she would have been burned in the village square by the Inquisition, or even stoned by some virtuous person in power—no doubt about it!     But now, between journalists showing up with booms and cameras at the fair where she was selling her creations and products while simultaneously teaching people how to make lucky dolls from scraps of fabric (you just sit on the pile and get started...), and the television crew set to arrive the next day for a reportage and interview, she has become well-known and appreciated—not just as a curiosity.     I saw people bringing her game animals taken during herd management, killed by hunters for the forest department. Others brought her coffee because they had just returned from Africa and thought of her. It’s truly heartwarming to see. Her daughter even told me, “She’s famous.”     At the festival/street market where we were, the stand next to hers was thrilled to be placed beside her. The vendor told me her presence would bring him more visibility and customers.     What were the chances of meeting her, of encountering this world, this reality? Seriously?     Anyway…    Phone charging. A burning hot shower (because wood-fired heating is not thermoregulated). Clean clothes (finally—my socks were starting to sting my eyes without me even bending down!). Black coffee. A hot meal—not just bread, butter, cheese, tomato, or banana this time. (She’s a great cook, I must admit.)     And conversations.     Silence.     More conversations.     Another way of living. Another way of seeing. Other ways, in general...     It’s nice.     Voilà!     Wishing you lots of good things,     Peace and love.     P.S. You can check her out online—just type Biebrzańska Wiedźma into Google.

Meeting with a Wolf


		14/5/2021
	
     Today I saw a wolf!     That’s the second time. The first was in East Germany, and I initially thought it was a big jackal or something, but after checking online, I realized it was a European wolf.     Today, I was comfortably sitting on a small mossy bank by the side of a beautiful path I’ve been following for the past two days in this huge forest. I was enjoying a gentle breeze on my face as the afternoon wore on, hot and sunny. Just sitting there, eyes closed, soaking in the noisy chirping of the place—maybe I’d been there for 15 minutes or more. That gives you an idea of the rhythm of my walk!     When I opened my eyes, he was there. Hardly 25 meters away, right in the middle of the path, watching something on the opposite bank. Maybe a rodent, or whatever had caught his full attention. He didn’t match the typical European image of a wolf—more like a medium-sized, skinny dog. Honestly, he looked almost pitiful, especially with his irregular fur, patches sticking out like tufts of longer hair. Then I realized it was the remnants of his winter coat, still clinging in places.     He was completely absorbed in whatever had his focus, with an air of mischievous curiosity.     And then, like a pure, thoughtless tourist, I decided to take a picture to share with you. Slowly, I moved my hand toward the pocket where my phone usually is, thinking I could pull it off. But I’d barely moved 20 cm when he turned his head in my direction, saw me—and ran. He ran like the wind. In three seconds, he was 60 meters away, and my phone had barely managed to focus...    What did I capture? A fantastic blur! Yes, a great blurry photo! But still, I can share it. Now, look closely—in the center of the picture, zoom in. That blurry shape? That’s a wolf’s ass! Yes! Impressive, right?

Winter in Poland (Czestochowa, Warsaw)


		19/2/2021
	
​     Hello!    Where to start? I’m well into Poland now, but my progress has been quite slow. The weather conditions are some of the coldest and harshest in years, as many people have told me. For some, it hasn’t been this cold in 20 years; for others, since their childhood. Like everywhere in Europe, winters in the past were very different from now.    I mean, I remember being stuck at home for two extra weeks of Christmas holidays because snow had blocked the roads! I remember playing sword fights with icicles in at least 40 cm of snow for a few weeks every year. But I guess that’s just a detail... Let’s say we’re having a proper, beautiful winter here.    It’s full of cold (between -10°C and -16°C during the day), full of snow (every day—sometimes very thick, sometimes soft, with heavy snowflakes at times, but more often tiny ones). The snow is so powdery that I can’t even make snowballs! I press it between my hands, and when I release the pressure, it crumbles through my fingers like dry sand.     And then there’s the wind (it feels really cold and turns those tiny snowflakes into little needles that sting any exposed skin). I guess you could call it a blizzard. I feel so lucky to walk and sleep in this beauty!    Of course, I’m wearing seven layers of clothing! Of course, I gave up on my five-finger shoes—I still need my toes! So I bought proper shoes and socks. Naturally, most of my food is now frozen: frozen oranges, frozen cheese, rock-hard butter, frozen carrots, and radishes... everything just freezes! Even the wet wipes and my shoes freeze at night.     So nice... sorry, I mean: so ice!    But that’s not why I’m so slow in my progress. It just doesn’t help. No, what’s really keeping me here for weeks when it should be days is that the Polish people I meet are dangerously welcoming! I mean, you can’t really get away! It almost always starts with a simple “Come inside for a coffee,” but then it turns into “You’ll stay for lunch!” and somehow ends up as “It’s too late to leave now; you’ll sleep here tonight and go tomorrow!”     And then it happens again the next day. Seriously! Even when we can’t communicate properly, as many people here speak fluent German or Russian but not much English, and rarely French...     I’ve set a few rules for myself during this journey, and one of them is that I shouldn’t stay in the same place for more than three nights. It’s meant to keep me moving! But I find myself using this rule almost every three days. Do the math, and you’ll understand just how much I’m not walking! That should give you an idea of how welcoming people here are.   I finally managed to arrive in a beautiful city, Wrocław (see the photos I’ve attached to this message). It’s stunning because of its architecture and history—now imagine it under 30 cm of snow! It’s been four days since I got here. I know you’re thinking, What about the three-night rule? But the rule has an exception for sickness. I’m not that rigid. Don’t worry, though—it’s nothing serious, just an ear infection. With the current weather conditions, I decided to accept the kind offer of Martin, a guy who invited me to stay in the room he rents, right next to a 93-year-old woman (an absolute master at checkers, by the way). She has no mercy for me—the crushed loser—and plays without a hint of compassion. A true checkers killer.    I met Martin while he was putting salt on the icy floor of the church where he works. I had stopped to ask if the priests offered a pilgrim shelter, and when they didn’t, Martin invited me to his place. He called a friend, bought a bottle of spiced hot wine, and voilà! Three days later, here I am—lazy and feverish (just a mild one), my right ear ringing and hurting as if I’d been slapped repeatedly.    It’s getting better now, and I’m already thinking about my departure. I’m also wondering how many days it will take me to escape the kindness and generosity here without offending anyone—except maybe the lady next door, whom I’d really like to beat at checkers before I leave!    That’s all for now.    I hope you’re well and happy.    I wish you the best.    I’ll keep in touch.    Emmanuel.

First Week in Poland


		28/1/2021
	
     Dear friends, hello.     It’s been a while since I shared any news. Please note that this is probably the last update you’ll receive from me on WhatsApp. Following the latest (and, let’s face it, imposed) update to the app and my strong disagreement with its privacy policy concerning the use of personal data—especially since WhatsApp was acquired by Facebook—and knowing that there’s an equivalent to WhatsApp that seems more trustworthy (among other things, it’s non-profit), I’ve decided to migrate to Signal.​     I am therefore leaving WhatsApp and strongly encourage you to do the same. You can download Signal here: https://signal.org/install.     So, that’s that.     Now for the news.     I’ve been in Poland for a week and I’m still moving forward, but perhaps even more slowly. The weather over the past 15 days has been a bit harsh, and even though I enjoy the cold, walking under snow and wind significantly slows my progress. Folding up a frozen tent in the morning takes much longer, too.    I must admit that everything feels more tiring. I imagine I’m burning more calories due to the conditions, but I also think that having walked for nearly 4 months non-stop, apart from the occasional day off spent resting in the tent (about one day of rest per week or every 10 days), is finally taking its toll. I’m starting to feel the combined weight of walking and carrying the backpack. So, I’m not forcing myself—I’m taking it easy to ensure I can keep going further.     Add to that my painful feet (I’m essentially walking barefoot in my five-finger shoes), cold and wet from slush (up to 25 cm deep), and it’s easy to see why I’m only managing about a dozen kilometers per day. I’ll definitely need a vacation when I arrive!    My arrival in Poland was under good omens. Under normal circumstances, I wouldn’t have been able to cross the border due to movement restrictions from the virus. However, a phone call the day before from my German host to the police at the border in Görlitz reassured me. The officer on duty explained that crossing the border to buy cigarettes or alcohol (as prices differ significantly between Germany and Poland) was out of the question. But for a guy walking all the way from France on a pilgrimage to Częstochowa? That was a totally different story. Of course, I was allowed to cross the border, and so I did.    My first interaction with the locals—well, “native indigenous people”, if you’ll pardon the redundancy—was equally reassuring. I stopped to ask for water to refill my bottles, and the man invited me into his home. He told me to put my bag down, take off a few layers, and have coffee. He refilled my bottles with hot tea, filled my thermos with hot coffee, gave me a little something to eat while chatting with his son on the phone, and even offered for me to stay the night since the snow had started falling even harder.     It was very difficult to refuse such a kind offer, but I wanted to make a bit more progress that day. Still, I spent three hours with an incredibly nice couple—super welcoming, caring, and enthusiastic—even though they didn’t speak a word of English or French!     This will be a challenge to manage in Poland so far: people here don’t seem to speak English at all—not even basic phrases like “thank you” or “bye-bye”. However, I am in the countryside, where English might be less prevalent and is perhaps only taught to the younger generation.     So, I’m back to improvised sign language, mime, and Google Translate—when there’s network coverage! But goodwill makes everything surmountable.     There’s also something very heartening: when I mention that I’m on a pilgrimage to Jasna Góra, people immediately know what I’m talking about. It resonates with them, and they understand. That feels good.     Voilà.     I’m attaching some photos in “vrak”!     See you soon on Signal!

East Germany


		23/12/2020
	
​     Good evening from the former East Germany.     It's hard to say how much I enjoy the country, to be honest, because most of the time I’m alone in nature, and it feels very similar to home. When I pass through a village or town, perhaps due to the virus, the weather, and the end-of-year period, it often feels like a ghost town everywhere. I appreciate the architecture, but I can’t really get a sense of the area’s atmosphere—it’s the people who create that, and here, they are absent.    I do notice a strong difference between West and East Germany in terms of the wealth of housing, cars, and infrastructure. The west is impeccable, while the east is much less so.     So, let’s just say I like what I see most of the time, as well as my walking experience...     I have a few more weeks in East Germany, and then it will be Poland.     Yesterday, as a sort of duty to humanity, I made a detour to the former Nazi concentration camp of Buchenwald, which was later transformed by the Soviets into a special internment camp (causing more deaths than under the Nazi regime). Suffice it to say, the place has a "tense" atmosphere, and it feels incredibly heavy. It was closed due to Corona, so guided tours and access to the exhibition buildings weren’t possible. However, the entire camp itself was open, and a few explanatory panels outside provided the essentials. That was enough—I can imagine the rest.     Today, I came across ostriches. It was strange to see them at a bend in the path, in a meadow...     I also came across a dead penguin!     The last photo shows its corpse lying on the ground! 🤭😂    The large buildings visible just above, which look like towering communist administration or propaganda headquarters, are, in fact, a biscuit factory!     I have a fascination with twisted trees. An abnormal tree can be very beautiful... like these faces!    I also met a gentleman after Leipzig who has a collection (apparently in the world’s top 20!) of metal bottle caps, classified by country, type, and era! Like all enthusiasts, it was great to listen to him talk about his passion—especially how it all started. His three-year-old son had found a very colorful bottle cap while walking with his parents (which, from what I’ve observed, Germans do a lot. A LOT! Really... It’s such a healthy habit). Anyway, the child refused to let go of the bottle cap for several days, so the dad started bringing him a new one every day, placing it on his bedside table. And this is how, 28 years later, he ended up with a collection of over 100,000 metal bottle caps...     He also has several tens of thousands of duplicates and triplicates, all intended for exchanges...

The Alpha Point


		15/12/2020
	
​     The Alpha Point!     I’ve just entered the former East Germany. Suddenly, there are relics and memorials everywhere. Here, a piece of the wall; there, the different barbed wire barriers and more. Antipersonnel mines were placed between each barrier all along the border—1,800,000 mines in total. Warlike dogs, intentionally starved to make them aggressive and dangerous, patrolled between the barbed wire fences. Finally, between the last fences, the ground was plowed and harrowed regularly to detect traces of any attempted crossings. All of this just to prevent its own population from leaving! 😨    Seeing this leaves a really unpleasant impression because, ultimately, it’s not that far removed from us—in any sense. There are some truly scary and sad memories here...

Fulda


		6/12/2020
	
     A beautiful day. I first discovered the beautiful city of Fulda, which is historically very attractive.    Then, a very nice family with whom I’ve been chatting all afternoon until now—it all started with an invitation to lunch when I asked for water to refill my bottles. I had noticed a scallop shell hanging from a nail on the facade of their house, and I thought to myself that they must be people who had made the famous pilgrimage to Saint Jacques de Compostela... or at least sympathizers of the pilgrim that I am.     And then I was offered a hot shower, a wash for my clothes, a charge for my phone’s battery, and a very friendly fight with the dog Bruno (because he’s brown).   I’m sleeping in the camper van parked in the yard tonight. It’s very practical, the bed is comfortable, and I’m indoors. This saves me from setting up and taking down my tent, which I would have otherwise placed in the garden.     We just had a traditional hot spiced wine—red wine, lots of spices, a little sugar, and that’s it. It’s a drink for this season, and yes, it keeps you warm.      Everything is okay... I’ll sleep well, even if I didn’t make much progress today. I walked maybe 10 or 12 km, but it was a beautiful day... Gray skies, but beautiful nonetheless...

Germany


		27/11/2020
	
     Hello!     It’s been such a long time since I last gave any news. Please forgive me. It’s not that the life of a pilgrim is so busy—though, actually, it kind of is—but more that during these coronavirus days, it’s a bit harder to recharge my phone. I need it frequently for accessing maps, so I’ve had to prioritize that over writing messages, which use up a lot of battery.     But anyway, I have to check in sometimes, and today the circumstances are just right.     So, what to say? Well, I’ve crossed France, a tiny bit of Belgium, all of Luxembourg from west to east, and now I’m in Germany—a little past Frankfurt, heading south. I think I’ll be in Germany for about three more weeks, but it’s hard to say for sure.    The weather has been changing over the past two weeks. It went from heavy rain (great for making mushrooms sprout everywhere—like, really everywhere) to cold, which sadly ended the mushroom madness. No more evening mushroom soup, and that is really sad. If you hadn’t guessed already, I’m a big mushroom fan... 😉 But to be precise, I’m a fan of whatever nature provides. It’s the generosity of nature that moves me the most, whether it’s mushrooms, nuts, apples, or berries.     The cold also stopped the rain! Youpi! It’s so nice not to be wet anymore. And soon, it will start snowing. But let’s keep that for the future...     I’m good. Happy.   I’ve reached a stage of consciousness where I can easily slip into a contemplative, automated walking state. That’s what I’m interested in, what I’m seeking—to make that state last as long as possible, maybe even permanent, rather than just fleeting moments throughout the day. But I’m happy. Everything is fine.     One thing I really enjoy is meeting so many people. It’s not that there’s a huge number, but I do meet a lot of people, and almost without exception, I encounter kindness, goodwill, and generosity. It’s such a warm and beautiful experience.      I mean, the general narrative these days is that we should be cautious when going out, that we should be suspicious or even afraid of people because “you never know.” We’re told to be careful, to “watch our six,” and so on. But my daily experience is the complete opposite.     Every day, the people I meet are incredibly kind and eager to help. They’re curious about what I’m doing and love to talk. They invite me to share meals or give me food because there might not be a shop on my route. They offer me the chance to take a hot shower in their homes (and yes, I definitely want that!).     They’re human, and it’s so nice and comforting to experience that.     Voilà.     That’s it for today.     I hope you’re well and happy.     Wishing you all the best.   Next, I’m sharing lots of pictures I’ve taken along the way. Hope you enjoy them! I won’t comment on them since there are so many.

Mushrooms and Orval Abbey


		26/10/2020
	
     Porcini mushrooms (Boletus edulis) everywhere! My God, I can't pick them all. It’s no use—my stove is broken, so I only take those I can eat raw. And of course, I limit myself to one kilo, because carrying more gets heavy, and I know I'll find more tomorrow...     Anyway, it feels strange to leave behind nice, big Corks (in France, we call them "Corks" because they resemble the shape of champagne corks). I already have 4 or 5 in my portable pantry...     Some very young porcini mushrooms (the ones in the photos were a bit too mature to eat raw without seasoning, but they were majestic. One of them must have weighed nearly a kilo—very firm), some Pinkys (our nickname in France for Agaricus campestris because of the lovely pink color under the cap), and some Airy Coprins (Coprinus comatus). It’s been a long time since I last ate those. They’re really, really good... in fricassee or soup (considering how much water they release when cooking, a bit of butter and garlic turns them into a lovely evening soup).     But since my stove is damaged, I eat them raw too. They’re tender and melt in your mouth, but of course, they don’t last long—they quickly turn into a thick black paste, almost like ink...     Also, I’ve never eaten so many nuts! All the walnut trees I come across are laden with fruit, and the ground beneath them is scattered with fallen nuts. People in the region leave them on the ground, so I take full advantage.     And the apples! I collect some every day. Apparently, no one picks them, even though they’re absolutely delicious. Far better than the dull, floury ones you find in supermarkets...     Luckily, I come across all this bounty along the way—it really eases the food stress when passing through these deserted villages. Sometimes there’s not a single grocery store for four days. As a result, my pantry empties out, only to refill with nuts, apples, and occasionally pears, as well as mushrooms.    Often, when I’m about to admit—almost ashamed—that “there’s nothing left in our villages these days,” a local will kindly offer me something to eat. How touching. Sometimes it’s a sandwich, a slice of cake, or some fruit...     I’m happy to see and experience exactly the opposite of what the media say. The usual, “My God, you have to be careful these days! Anything can happen! You can be attacked at any crossroads, robbed, raped, or even beheaded!” Instead, all I encounter is kindness, goodness, and benevolence wherever I go and whoever I meet.     Imagine this: on several occasions, total strangers have invited me to their homes to take a shower! I’m invited to come in, eat, drink coffee, wash… It really doesn’t make me want to like television or newspapers, spreading these ideas...    But it’s funny sometimes to see how even those same people—kind and welcoming—have reflexes conditioned by that mainstream, vague, and formless fear hovering over everyone:     “But aren’t you afraid?”     “Afraid of what?”     “Well… everything, bad encounters, all that...”     “Well, no. Look, I’m meeting you, and it’s going well.”     “Yes, but it’s not the same. We can see you’re a nice guy...”     Honestly, I don’t think there are that many bad people out there. But hey, let’s stay careful—you never know... 😜    Oh, the other day, a gentleman who was vaguely part of my conversation with a mechanic couple left for ten minutes to go home. When he came back, he handed me a bag with two bananas, four clementines, two yogurts, and a packet of biscuits. I didn’t ask him for anything—I never ask—but he told me, “There’s no grocery store in the next villages you’ll pass through.”     It’s moments like these that reconcile you with society, with humanity… well, if you were ever dis-conciled. 😁     That’s all I wanted to say.     I’m doing fine. Slowly but surely, I walk the trails as much as possible. Sometimes it doesn’t rain, and even when it does, it rarely rains all day—it’s only happened three times so far.     Today, I’m staying in Orval Abbey. It’s in Belgium, right on the border. It’s nice—shower and hot meal on the agenda. Feels so good. Their beer is great.     See you soon.     P.S. Let’s break our televisions!

France


		16/10/2020
	
     Here I am, staying in a communal pilgrims' house in Château-Porcien.     Happiness!    First, a hot shower... Because biodegradable pre-impregnated wipes and a large bottle of water for washing are fine for 3 or 4 days, but after that, they're not enough... In short, a shower is definitely better and feels really good...​     And then, washing clothes! Well, yes, that's necessary too... Thanks to 'genius without rubbing' (a French brand of hand washing liquid soap), where you still have to rub the clothes just the same. But hey, it is a good catchy name, isn't it? So yes, washing clothes is essential. Walking socks in humid or even wet weather, with no other drying than the natural 37-degree Celsius radiator, can create quite an odor. I don’t need to draw you a picture; olfactorily, it stings a bit and can make the eyes water...     And then washing and drying the tent! The first time it will be dry since I left...   Finally, a patch on the inflatable ground mattress, which was punctured by a bramble stem ignominiously hidden in a comfortable tuft of grass when I dropped my backpack in the wilderness... So the last few nights were less comfortable than the first ones. The ground is damp, cold, and angular without the mattress, so 3 cm of compressed air is good, but it can burst...    In short, it's a very nice little pilgrims' house. I even cooked a hot meal tonight! And I'll have hot black coffee tomorrow morning!    And I got to recharge my phone and the additional battery.    Happiness is easy, I tell you!

The Bizarre Scene


		26/9/2020
	
     ​Hello!     I just stopped at a camping site... So, I got a hot shower! Yay!     The 'Bois Joli' camping (the pretty grove), which is 400 m from the GR 11 (GR in France stands for 'Grande randonnée', meaning long-distance hiking trail) is located in the French Vexin (and not the Norman Vexin, which people have been insisting on, something I didn't know...), not very far from Méru... 😁     Four days of walking, just 20 km today. This is the warm-up period, and my body is adapting. So, sore feet, sore calves, sore thighs, sore shoulders... In a few days, this will pass. And the hot shower really helps. It feels really good, even if the token used doesn't really give me the time to enjoy it for long...     I am ready to head due east from now on, almost to the German border (still far away). I am therefore avoiding Paris to the north.      Did I already say that a hot shower feels good?     Today, I came across a bizarre sight where a car had gone halfway into the wall of someone's house. The homeowner had built a temporary wall around it, and the municipality reconstructed the signpost and the sidewalk, leaving the car still in place! This gives a surreal picture where the car "protrudes" from a wall onto the sidewalk without there being any sign that it was in fact an accident. Surreal, I tell you.​     Then I found some nuts, mainly walnuts. I found lots and lots of nuts along the way, which often made up my meals, but here, I must admit, I had never seen such big ones... Really impressive. And good in addition to being very full. A real treat.     Then I came across a beautiful, really beautiful church...     See the photos.     Well, that's all for today...     I wish you well and happiness.     See you soon.

Beginning of the Pilgrimage


		24/9/2020
	
     Hello.     I started my pilgrimage trip 2 days ago. I'm on my way to travel about 1500 km through France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, and finally Poland. This is the first step, to get warmed. The second might be much longer, I hope...​     I am going slowly and stopping at every church to pray and meditate. Today I visited 4, one in each village I passed through. Beautiful places to stop, rest, and recenter a bit...     I writing to you from my small tent in a forest where I have stopped for the night. I finished my dinner, a vegetable soup cooked on my tiny stove. That really nice and comforting to eat something hot some time.     Rain is pouring. That is good because it means the mushrooms will come! 😁What a gift it is to eat from nature, I mean to walk and find food around. Already many hazelnuts, walnuts, soon chestnuts...     That's nice.​     I wish you well and happiness, and keep you in touch.
